en: (1.1.1) Oṃ! Speak greatness for me; speak splendor for me; speak glory for me; speak praise for me; speak enjoyment for me; speak everything for me. May that protect me; may that enter me; through that may I enjoy. (1.1.2) Let the god go to the god; let Soma go to Soma by the path of Truth. (1.1.3) Having left behind all evil-doing.
(1.1.4) A wide path, a course for Soma; may I go to Soma.
(1.1.5) O Fathers, be present! O Fathers, be present! O Fathers, be present! (1.1.6) O you of manly mind, may I behold you who bear the upward offering, as one who bears the upward offering.
(1.1.7) Softened with clay, you are the ford of the gods, the altar; do not harm me.
(1.1.8) You are the head of Viṣṇu, the bestower of glory; bestow glory upon me.
(1.1.9) For food, for strength, for life, and for splendor.

(PB 1.2.1) I yoke for you the earth together with Agni; I yoke speech together with Sūrya; Vāta is yoked for you together with the intermediate space; the three purifiers of Sūrya are yoked. (PB 1.2.2) I sit upon the seat of Ṛta.
(PB 1.2.3) You are the vessel of Ṛta.

(1.2.4) You belong to the trees; you belong to Bṛhaspati; you belong to Prajāpati; you are the head of Prajāpati; you are the vessel for exceeding life; here I project myself forward for the sake of splendor and Vedic luster.
(1.2.5) O Maruts, sons of the Waters, free from disease, peaks of the mountains, falcons, swift ones—bear Indra with your voice, and by your roar drive away sickness! You are yoked; bear him along!
(1.2.6) Here I place this sacrificer among the cattle, and I place myself among the cattle and in Vedic luster.

(PB 1.2.7) May the Vasus cleanse you with the Gāyatrī metre; may the Rudras cleanse you with the Triṣṭubh metre; may the Ādityas cleanse you with the Jagatī metre. (PB 1.2.8) Your filter is spread out, O Brahmaṇaspati; as a lord, you go around its limbs on every side. One whose body has not been heated does not partake of that; only those who are cooked, bringing it together, have attained it.
(PB 1.2.9) May the divine inspiration flow forth from us like a well-fashioned chariot, like a prize-winning steed; cook me for long life, for splendor.

Flow for me, knowing [the way] from the earth and from the birthplace of heaven; let the waters flowing below hear this. Sing forth the *udgītha* for me for the sake of long life, for my spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), for the prosperity of the sacrificer, and for the sovereignty of so-and-so.

(PB 1.3.1) Your name is Vekurā; you are beloved by the gods. Homage to Speech! Homage to the Lord of Speech! O Goddess Speech, place me in that which is the honeyed sweetness of your speech. To Sarasvatī, *svāhā*!
(1.3.2) May Sūrya protect me from the destructive powers of heaven; may Vāyu protect me from those of the intermediate space; may Agni protect me from those of the earth. Svāhā!

(1.3.3) Whatever murderous weapon of the malevolent ones rises up today, whether it be the arrow of Viṣūkuha or the bow, may Varuṇa blow them away. (1.3.4) Whatever is my self, whatever is my progeny, and whatever are my cattle—with these I settle my mind and my speech.

(1.3.5) By the brilliance of Agni, by the power of Indra, by the splendor of Sūrya—may Bṛhaspati yoke you for the gods, for the sake of vital breath; may Agni yoke you with fervor so that Soma may carry the sacrifice; may Indra bestow sensory power; may the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled. (1.3.6) "I shall make food, I shall enter into food, I shall produce food."
(PB 1.3.7) Food have I made; food has come into being; food have I brought forth.

(PB 1.3.8) You are a hawk, having the *gāyatrī* as your meter; I take hold of you. May you carry me safely across. May the hymn reach the hymn of praise. Accompanied by Indra, may we win; may we enjoy progeny and nourishment.
(PB 1.3.9) We have united with luster, with milk, with austerities, with a gracious mind, and with discernment.

And by means of truthful words, so that I may speak most beautifully to you, may I be Indra for you to see, Sūrya for your sight, Vāta for your breath, Soma for your scent, and Brahman for your sovereign power.
Homage to the Gandharva who speaks in all directions! You are the bestower of splendor; bestow splendor upon me.
(1.4.1) O Lord of the paths, may there be well-being for me today on this path traveled by the gods.
(1.4.2) You are the sovereign, you are Kṛśānu. (1.4.3) You are Tutha, the sustainer of people; you are Nabhas; you are Pratakva; you are the unsullied one, the purifier of the oblation.
(1.4.4) You are Vibhu, the carrier. (1.4.5) You are Vahni, the bearer of oblations. (1.4.6) You are Śvātra, the wise one.
(1.4.7) Thou art Tutha, the all-knowing; thou art Uśij, the sage; thou art Aṅghāri, thou art Bambhāri; thou art Avasyu, the worshipper. (1.4.8) Thou art Śundhyu, the purifier; thou art Mārjālīya.
(1.4.9) Thou art Ṛtadhāman, whose light is heaven.
(10) You are the ocean, all-encompassing.
(11) You are the serpent of the deep.
(12) You are the one-footed goat.
(Sagarā asi budhnyaḥ) You are the ocean, the abyssal one.
(Kavyo 'si kavyavāhanaḥ) You are the sage, the bearer of the sage’s offerings.
(Pāta māgnayo raudreṇānīkena piṣṭata mā namo vo 'stu mā mā hiṃsiṣṭa) Protect me, O Agnis, with your fierce aspect; crush me not; homage be to you; do not harm me.

(PB 1.5.1) You are the two doors of *ṛta*; do not burn me! (PB 1.5.2) Homage to my friends who dwell before; homage to those who dwell beyond! (PB 1.5.3) A hawk, beholding men—O Agni, I gaze upon you with your eye.
O Indu, of thee who art drunk by Indra, possessed of power, having the *gāyatrī* metre, and accompanied by the whole host—I, being invited along with the whole host, partake of thee who art invited.

(PB 1.5.5) Standing upright, do thou attend upon the seven seers; drunk by Indra, O Lord of Speech, rise up toward the seven officiating priests; enjoy the world; do not go downward before us. (PB 1.5.6) O Soma, take delight in our heart; thou art our father, thou art mine; therefore, do not harm me.
O Soma, we who know speech increase you with our songs; enter us as one who is most gracious.
Swell up; let virile strength come to you from every side, O Soma; be present in the gathering of booty.

(1.5.9) Of that which has been consumed by the lower ones, by those above, by the seers, and by the fathers—of the honeyed *nārāśaṃsa* cup, for the sake of the whole assembly; being invited by the whole assembly, I partake of you who have been invited.

(1.5.10) With the color of consecration (*dīkṣā*), with the form of austerity (*tapas*), with the greatness of mind, and with the abundance of speech—may Prajāpati unite you for offspring, for out-breathing (*apāna*).
(1.5.11) May Vāyu unite the hymn (*stoma*) with the mind so that it may carry the sacrifice; may Indra bestow sensory power (*indriya*); may the desires of the sacrificer be true.

(PB 1.5.12) You are Vṛṣaka; you have the Triṣṭubh as your metre. I take hold of you. May you carry me safely across. May the hymn of the hymn reach [its goal]. Accompanied by Indra, may we win; may we enjoy offspring and nourishment.

(PB 1.5.13–14) O Indu, of you who are drunk by Indra, who possess power, whose metre is the Triṣṭubh, who are accompanied by all the hosts—with all the hosts invited, I partake of you who are invited.
May Sūrya yoke [the chariot] with speech so that the hymn may carry the sacrifice. May Indra bestow power upon us. May the desires of the sacrificer come true.

(1.5.15) You are the tone; you are the *gāyatrī*; you are the *jagatī* metre. I take hold of you. May you carry me safely across. May the hymn of the hymn reach me. Accompanied by Indra, may we win; may we enjoy progeny. (1.5.16) O Indu, of you who are drunk by Indra, who possess power, who have the *triṣṭubh* as your metre, and who are accompanied by all the hosts—being invited along with those invited—I partake of you.

(1.5.17) You are my life-span, my breath, and my mind. O Breath, [reside] in me, the consort of life-span, within the verse. That mind of mine which has gone to Yama, or that which has departed from me, let us recover that through King Soma once again within ourselves.

(PB 1.5.18) My mind that went to Yama, the son of Vivasvat, which has wandered far away—bring it back to me again for life, not for death, and for safety. (PB 1.5.19) With that [mind] by which he conquered the battle, having looked out; with which [he saw] the falcon, the bird, the fair-winged one; that which they call the infinite eye in Aditi—that sight, O Soma, the observer of men, may he bestow upon me.

(PB 1.6.1) Indra’s power has been released. Of that [Soma] of yours, O Indu, drunk by Indra, possessing power, having the *anuṣṭubh* meter, accompanied by the bay horses, and possessed of all its hosts—I, being invited along with all my hosts, partake of you who have been invited.

O Indu, of thee who art drunk by Indra, who possessest power, whose metre is the *anuṣṭubh*, and who art accompanied by all the *gaṇas*—I, being invited by the one who is invited and accompanied by all the *gaṇas*, partake of thee.
(PB 1.6.3) Of that which has been praised, thou art the praise; full of vigor, full of milk. May the praise of my praise reach me. Accompanied by Indra, may we win; may we enjoy offspring and food.

(PB 1.6.4) O divine Soma, of thee whose *yajus* has been offered, whose *stoma* has been praised, whose *uktha* has been recited, and who hast passed the night—the portion that brings horses and cattle, of that, being invited by the one who is invited, I partake.

(PB 1.6.5) "In the station of Viṣṇu, upon the place of the hymns of the gods, I release you for the sake of Truth (*ṛta*). You have come down to the hymns of the gods; may we attain a firm foundation. (PB 1.6.6) "O Soma, come hither with me! O Soma, come from the assembly together with power (*indriya*).

(PB 1.6.7) "You are well-being, the most excellent ray of the gods, the assembly of the gods. With that body by which you quicken the sacred word (*brahman*), quicken me; with that, procreate me; make me manifest."
(1.6.8) You are the flower of the waters, the essence of the plants, the most beloved oblation of Indra; *svāhā*!

(1.6.9) O divine Soma, of you who are yoked by bay horses, for whom the *yajus* has been offered, the *stoma* praised, and the *uktha* recited—of that portion which wins horses and wins cattle, being invited, I partake of what has been invited.
(1.6.10) You are the expiation for sin committed against the gods; you are the expiation for sin committed against the ancestors; you are the expiation for sin committed against men.

Thou art the expiation
O divine Soma, of you who are washed in the waters and pressed by men,
I make a honeyed portion;
[I take it] from the waters and the plants.
(Brahmaṇaspati 1.6.14) Bring to me whatever I desire.
(1.6.15) You are strength; bestow strength upon me. (1.6.16) O Soma-drinker, be watchful for my vital breath.
I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan, the victorious, the spirited steed. May he make our mouths fragrant; may he prolong our lives.
You are a horse; you are a racer; you are a source of joy; you are a courser; you are a prize-winner; you are a swift steed; you are a stallion.
Follow the path of the Ādityas; homage be unto you; do not harm me.
I receive you with the brilliance of Vāyu; I receive you with the form of the Nakṣatras; I receive you with the splendor of Sūrya. You are the Rathantara; you are the Vāmadevya; you are the Bṛhat.
The two chariot-poles on both sides of the chariot, which move toward the darkness at the forefront of the wind—the far-reaching weapon, powerful and winged—may those Agnis carry us across to safety.

Vaiśvānara has mounted the firmament as of old, rejoicing on the back of heaven with auspicious thoughts; like one of former times, he goes around the common path, watchful, bestowing wealth upon living beings.
This is your chariot, O Aśvins; this is your unharmed chariot, possessing all healing remedies.
O Kṛśānu, draw in the left [arrows];
O Dāsas, seize the right ones!
On the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins and the hands of Pūṣan, I receive you.

(1.8.2) "May Varuṇa lead you, O divine sacrificial fee; to Varuṇa I give the horse. Through this may I attain immortality. May there be vigor for the giver and joy for me, the receiver. (1.8.3) "May Varuṇa lead you, O divine sacrificial fee; to Rudra I give the cow. Through this may I attain immortality. May there be vigor for the giver and joy for me, the receiver.
(1.8.4) "May Varuṇa lead you, O divine sacrificial fee; to Agni I give the goat."

For Agni, gold. For Agni and Soma, goats. "May I attain immortality; may there be long life for the giver and well-being for me, the receiver. "The Lord of Food has given of food that is free from disease and full of vigor. Homage to the sustainer of all people! Do not harm me as you consume [this]."

(1.8.8) "May Varuṇa lead you, O goddess; for Tvaṣṭṛ on the right, may I attain immortality through this ewe; may there be long life for the giver and joy for me, the receiver. (1.8.9) "The Gnas cut you out, the Apas spun you out, the weavers wove you.
(1.8.10) "May Varuṇa lead you, O goddess; for Bṛhaspati as the garment, may I attain immortality through it; may there be long life for the giver and joy for me, the receiver."

(11) "May Varuṇa lead you, O divine Dakṣiṇā, for the sake of Utāna Āṅgirasa, while he was breathless. Through him may I attain immortality; may there be vigor for the giver and joy for me, the receiver.
(12) "May Varuṇa lead you, O divine Dakṣiṇā, for Pūṣan, as a camel.
(13) "For Vāyu, a deer. Through him may I attain immortality; may there be vigor for the giver and joy for me, the receiver."
To Prajāpati, an elephant; to Prajāpati, a boar; to Prajāpati, rice and barley—by means of these may I attain immortality. May there be long life for the giver and joy for me, the recipient.
O Goddess Dakṣiṇā, may Varuṇa lead you to Kṣetrapati. Sesame and beans—for these may I attain immortality. May there be long life for the giver and joy for me, the recipient.
(1.8.16) May Varuṇa lead you, O goddess Dakṣiṇā, to Savitṛ—whether it be a mule or a she-mule. Through her may I attain immortality; may there be long life for the giver and joy for me, the receiver.

(1.8.17) Who has given this to whom? Desire has given it to desire. Desire is the giver, desire is the receiver. Desire has entered the ocean. With desire I receive you; O Desire, this is yours. (1.9.1) You are a rein;
for habitation I take you, quicken the habitation. Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati.

(1.9.2) You are the advance; for the sake of the sacred law (*dharman*), quicken the sacred law; impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati! (1.9.3) You are the following; for the sake of heaven, quicken heaven; impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati! (1.9.4) You are the junction; for the sake of the intermediate space, quicken the intermediate space; impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati!
(1.9.5) You are a support; for the earth, you; quicken the earth. Impelled by Savitṛ, sing praise to Bṛhaspati.

(1.9.6) You are a buttress; for rain, you; quicken the rain. Impelled by Savitṛ, sing praise to Bṛhaspati. (1.9.7) You are the forward-moving; for the day, you; quicken the day. Impelled by Savitṛ, sing praise to Bṛhaspati.

(1.9.8) You are the follower of Night; quicken the Night. Impelled by Savitṛ, you are praised for Bṛhaspati. (1.9.9) You are the eager one; for the Vasus, I consecrate you. Quicken the Vasus. Impelled by Savitṛ, you are praised for Bṛhaspati. (1.9.10) You are the precursor; for the Rudras, I consecrate you. Quicken the Rudras. Impelled by Savitṛ, you are praised for Bṛhaspati.

(1.9.11) Thou art good splendor; for the Ādityas thee! Quicken the Ādityas! Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati! (1.9.12) Thou art vigor; for the Pitṛs thee! Quicken the Pitṛs! Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati! (1.10.1) Thou art the thread; for offspring thee! Quicken offspring! Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati!
(PB 1.10.2) You belong to the two worlds; for the plants, you—enliven the plants! Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati!

(PB 1.10.3) You are the conqueror of armies; for the cattle, you—enliven the cattle! Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati! (PB 1.10.4) You are the victorious; for the yoked thunderbolt, you—for Indra, you—enliven Indra! Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati!

(1.10.5) You are the overlord; for out-breathing, you; quicken the out-breathings. Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati. (1.10.6) You are the support; for in-breathing, you; quicken the in-breathings. Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati.
(1.10.7) You are the gliding one; for sight, you; quicken the sight. Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati.
(PB 1.10.8) You are the bestower of vitality; for the field, quicken the field! Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati!

(PB 1.10.9) You are the threefold; for the threefold, you! You are the well-grown; for the well-grown, you! You are the forward-grown; for the forward-grown, you! You are the following-grown; for the following-grown, you! Impelled by Savitṛ, praise Bṛhaspati! (PB 1.10.10) You are the downward-growing; for the downward-growing, you! You are the upward-growing; for the upward-growing, you! You are the forward-growing; for the forward-growing, you! You are the following-growing; for the following-growing, you! Impelled by Savitṛ, [praise] Bṛhaspati!

(1.10.11) You are the possessor of wealth; you are the desire for wealth; you are the glory of wealth. Impelled by Savitṛ, chant for Bṛhaspati! (1.10.12) You are the stepping; for stepping, I take you. You are the traversing; for traversing, I take you. You are the ascending; for ascending, I take you. You are the rising; for rising, I take you. Impelled by Savitṛ, [chant] for Bṛhaspati! (2.1.1) He makes the sound *hiṅ* three times; he makes the sound *hiṅ* with the first [verse]; he makes the sound *hiṅ* three times; he makes the sound *hiṅ* with the middle [verse]; he makes the sound *hiṅ* three times; he makes the sound *hiṅ* with the last [verse]. This is the *viṣṭuti* (mode of chanting) of the *trivṛt* (nine-versed hymn) when it is being raised.
(2.1.2) "The eldest, the son of the eldest, should praise.

(2.1.3) "He rises from the foremost to the foremost; the *viṣṭuti* is advancing. By means of the advancing [chant], one indeed prospers through the advancement of the sacrifice. Therefore, one should praise with this [chant] for the sake of prosperity itself. (2.1.4) It is a separation from evil and misfortune; he who praises with this remains free from evil. One who has not been overpowered is not held back, and one who has been held back does not fall into ruin."

The wicked man does not mount upon the superior; one generation does not overcome another; no one takes away another’s offspring; they prosper according to their respective fields. Yet Parjanya becomes rainless; for these worlds are the *ṛc*-verses, and he traverses them with the *hiṅkāra*.
This is indeed the established *viṣṭuti* of the *trivṛt*; he who praises with this finds firm support.
He utters *hiṅ* for three [verses], he utters *hiṅ* for three [verses] in forward order, he utters *hiṅ* for three [verses] in forward order; this is the revolving *triviṣṭuti*.

He who praises with this attains the revolution of the year. This *viṣṭuti* is continuous: out-breath (*prāṇa*), in-breath (*apāna*), and diffused breath (*vyāna*)—these are the verses; he unites them with the *hiṅ*-utterance. He who praises with this attains a full lifespan and does not die before his time. Parjanya becomes rainy. For these worlds are the triplets; he unites them with the *hiṅ*-utterance.
(2.2.3) But indeed, the Lord is like one who gently cleanses his cattle; and this [vocalization] is directed forward, so that he becomes better, and not merely as he was, nor worse.

(2.2.4) The Bhāllavayas worship this very [vocalization]; therefore, while responding with the *pratigara*, they do not deviate from the turns. (2.3.1) He utters *hiṅ* for three [verses]; he utters *hiṅ* for three [verses] in the forward direction; that which is the middle [verse] is the first.

That which is the last is the middle; that which is the first is the last—for he utters *hiṅ* three times. That which is the last is the first; that which is the first is the middle; that which is the middle is the last. This is the *kulāyinī* *trivṛt* *viṣṭuti*.
One who desires offspring or one who desires cattle should chant with this. Indeed, cattle are the nest (*kulāya*) of clans; thus, he becomes the very nest of clans.
One should perform this very [rite] for one who is slow to attain prosperity; by going to the head of these very people as they proceed, he goes to the head of his offspring.

One should perform this very [rite] for many sacrificers; in that all [the verses] are foremost, all are in the middle, and all are at the end, he makes them all equal sharers, so that none strikes down another; all [attain it].
Their faculties become equalized;
Parjanya becomes rain-giving, for these worlds are [composed of] triplets, and he unites them by means of the *hiṅkāra*.
However, there is a falling away into evil.

(2.3.7) When one has fallen from the higher to the lower, he goes as if obstructed; being obstructed, the inferior person mounts upon the superior. One group of people approaches another group, and they hand over each other’s offspring;
they do not prosper according to their own domain. (2.4.1) He utters *hiṅ* five times: three times with [the verse], once with [the verse], and once with [the verse]. He utters *hiṅ* five times.
He utters *hiṅ* with one [verse], then with three, then with one; he utters *hiṅ* with one, then with one, then with three.

This is the *pañcapañcinī* (five-by-five) *viṣṭuti* of the fifteen-versed hymn. Man is fivefold, and cattle are fivefold; by this [stotra] he obtains both man and cattle. Indeed, it is the thunderbolt.

When he arranges five by five, he arranges the thunderbolt itself for the sake of peace. This is indeed the established *viṣṭuti* of the fifteen-versed hymn; he who praises with it becomes firmly established.
He utters "hiṃ" for five [verses]: three times, once; for three [verses] he utters "hiṃ": [once] with the subsequent [verses]; for seven [verses] he utters "hiṃ": once, three times, three times.
(PB 2.5.2) One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should chant the praises using three hymns arranged in succession:
(PB 2.5.3) with five [verses] the fifteen-fold hymn (*pañcadaśa*), with three the nine-fold hymn (*trivṛt*), and with seven the seventeen-fold hymn (*saptadaśa*).

(PB 2.5.4) The hymns are indeed vigor; thus he gathers that vigor together in one place for the attainment of spiritual luster. He becomes radiant and possessed of spiritual luster who chants with this [sāman].

(2.6.1) He utters *hiṅ* for three [verses]; he does so with consecutive [verses]. For five [verses] he utters *hiṅ*: once, then three times, then once. For seven [verses] he utters *hiṅ*: once, then three times, then three times. This is the *viṣṭuti* of the fifteen-versed hymn when it is ascending.

(2.6.2) By means of this, indeed, the gods went to the heavenly world. One who desires the heavenly world should praise with this; it serves for the attainment of the heavenly world, and having praised, he does not fall from the heavenly worlds.
The *viṣṭuti* is advancing; for by means of that which advances, one prospers through the advance of the sacrifice. Therefore, one should praise with this [verse] for the sake of prosperity itself.

(PB 2.7.1) He utters *hiṃ* five times: once with three [verses], once with one, and once with one. He utters *hiṃ* five times: once with one, once with three, and once with one. He utters *hiṃ* seven times: once with one, once with three, and once with three.
The *viṣṭuti* of the seventeen-fold [stoma] consists of ten and seven [repetitions].
By this indeed the gods overcame the Asuras; he who praises with this overcomes evil and the rival.
This *viṣṭuti* is advancing; by means of that which is advancing, one prospers through the advancement of the sacrifice. Therefore, one should praise with this for the sake of prosperity alone.

The *viṣṭuti* is pregnant; he who praises with this [chant] is born forth with offspring and cattle. (PB 2.7.4–5) The seventeenfold [stoma] is indeed the people (*viś*); the king is its embryo. Thus, he makes the king the embryo of the people.
(PB 2.7.6) One who has not been overpowered does not fall into captivity, and one who has been overpowered does not descend [to the state of being overpowered].

The seventeenfold [stoma] is indeed food. Since there are seven in the middle and five on each side, food is thus placed in the center; consequently, the sacrificer becomes free from hunger, and his cattle become free from hunger.
Man is indeed related to the Vairāja [sāman]. There are seven domestic animals; since there are ten preceding [verses] and seven final ones, he thereby establishes the sacrificer among the cattle.
This is the established *viṣṭuti* of the seventeenfold [stoma]. He who praises with this becomes firmly established.
(PB 2.8.1) This very same arrangement consists of seven [verses] with one in the middle.

(PB 2.8.2) The first [verse] is the abode of the *brahman*, the middle one of the *kṣatra*, and the last one of the *viś*. Since the first is the most numerous, it causes [the other two] to share; thus it bestows power and vigor upon the *brahman* itself, and thereby makes the *kṣatra* subservient to the *brahman*.
"And he makes the people subject to this Kṣatriya; it becomes manifest for him who praises with this [sāman].
(PB 2.8.3) "The Tri-kharvas worship this very [sāman]; therefore, though they are competing, they do not perish.
(PB 2.9.1) "He utters *hiṅ* seven times: three times, three times, and once; he utters *hiṅ* after the three [verses] in forward order; he utters *hiṅ* seven times: once, three times, and..."
"One should praise with the three [verses] ending in *saptasthita* against a rival; just as one levels [the ground] with a seven-holed mattock, even so does he shatter his wicked rival.
One should perform this for many sacrificers; that which is the first *hiṅkāra*, it belongs to the first [verse].
In that he utters the *hiṅ* for her seven times, she thereby partakes of seven; in that exactly seven are placed in the middle, she thereby partakes of seven;
and that which is the final *hiṅ* is [for] the final [verse]. In that he utters the *hiṅ* for her seven times, she thereby partakes of seven;
thus he makes all of them equal sharers, so that they do not strike one another down.
"They possess equal faculties" (PB 2.9.4).
The Abhipratāriṇas worship this very [sāman]; therefore they are the most powerful among their own people (PB 2.10.1).
This is the same arrangement: both have seven [verses] with one in the middle, and no middle [verse].

One who is of low birth should chant this; for he who is of low birth has no world. Since there are seven verses first and seven last, with three in the middle—man consists of three syllables—he thereby creates a world for him in the very center, and he finds firm support in that world.

One desiring offspring should perform this very rite; for he who does not obtain offspring is as if rooted out from the middle. He thereby creates a world for him in the very center, and through offspring, he establishes himself in that world.

"And he is propagated along with cattle" (PB 2.10.4). One should perform this very [rite] for a *rājanya* who has been excluded. The seventeenfold [stoma] is indeed the people (*viś*); the king is its embryo. Thus, one strikes the king out from the very midst of the people; having fallen away, he is excluded, and being excluded, he goes down.

(2.10.5) One should perform this very [rite] for one who is being subjected to malevolent magic. Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold; verily they enter Prajāpati from the middle for the sake of non-destruction.
(2.11.1) He utters *hiṃ* for five [verses]: three times, once, and once. He utters *hiṃ* for three [verses]. He utters *hiṃ* for nine [verses]: three times, three times, and three times.

(2.11.2) One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should chant the praises using the four *stomas* as follows: with five [verses] the fifteen-fold (*pañcadaśa*), with three the nine-fold (*trivṛt*), and with nine the twenty-seven-fold (*triṇava*); the seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*) is naturally complete. The *stomas* are indeed vigor; thus he unites vigor in a single place for the attainment of spiritual luster. He who chants with this becomes radiant and possessed of spiritual luster.
He utters *hiṅ* for three [verses] with them in direct order; he utters *hiṅ* for five: once, then three times, then once; he utters *hiṅ* for nine: three times, three times, and three times.
This is the *viṣṭuti* of the seventeen-versed hymn.
By means of this, indeed, the gods went to the heavenly world; one who desires the heavenly world should praise with it.

For the sake of unification, he who praises with this [Viṣṭuti] does not fall from the heavenly world. The Viṣṭuti is "stepping forward"; it is for the sake of stepping forward, for by stepping forward one prospers through the sacrifice. Therefore, one should praise with this for the sake of prosperity itself. He utters *hiṃ* seven times: three times, three times, and once; he utters *hiṃ* five times.

He utters *hiṅ* with one [verse], with three, and with one; he utters *hiṅ* with five [verses]: with one, with one, and with three. This is the "bellows with the opening turned downwards" (*bhastrāvācīnabila*). One should perform it for him whom he hates, just as one would blow away [insects] with a bellows whose opening is turned downwards; in this way, he blows away the cattle of the sacrificer. The *viṣṭuti* (recitation method) departs [from its place]; by means of it, the cattle of the sacrificer depart.
"He becomes more wicked who praises with this [chant]:

he makes the sound *hiṅ* seven times—three times, three times, and once; he makes the sound *hiṅ* seven times—once, three times, and three times; he makes the sound *hiṅ* seven times—three times, once, and three times. (PB 2.14.1)
The *viṣṭuti* of the twenty-one-fold [stoma] is the "seven-sevens" (*saptasaptinī*).

There are seven domestic animals; he wins them by means of this [chant]. There are seven vital breaths in the head; the vital breaths are the senses. It is the senses that he obtains by means of this [chant].
This indeed is the established *viṣṭuti* of the twenty-one-fold [stoma]; he who praises with it becomes firmly established.
(From the *Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa* 2.15.1) He makes the sound *hiṅ* for five verses: three times, once, and once; he makes the sound *hiṅ* for seven verses:
once, three times, and three times; he makes the sound *hiṅ* for nine verses: three times, three times, and three times.
This is the *viṣṭuti* of the twenty-one-versed hymn when it is being raised upward.

By means of this [stotra], indeed, the gods went to the heavenly world. One who desires heaven should praise with it for the attainment of the heavenly world; having praised, he does not fall from the heavenly worlds. The *viṣṭuti* is "stepping forward"; it is for the sake of stepping forward, for by stepping forward one prospers in the sacrifice. Therefore, one should praise with this for the sake of prosperity itself.
This very [Sāman] has a threefold beginning and a threefold conclusion, in that the *bahiṣpavamāna* is threefold;
these nine [verses] become the last of the twenty-one-fold [stoma]. The threefold is indeed the vital breaths; thus he places the vital breaths on both sides.
Therefore, this [person] speaks with half-uttered words.
"The vital breath (*prāṇa*) reaches the full span of life for those subsequent vital breaths; he who praises with this [hymn] does not die before his time.
Those who hate strife worship this very [hymn]; therefore they reach the full span of life.
He makes the sound *hiṅ* for nine [verses]: three times with three [each], and five times with one."

He performs [the *hiṅ*] with one [verse], with three; he performs it with seven: with one, with three, and with three. This is the *pratiṣṭuti*. With nine [verses] he performs the *pratiṣṭuti* for the *trivṛt*; with five each for the *pañcadaśa*; with seven for the *saptadaśa*; the *ekaviṃśa* is accomplished by itself.

(ŚB 2.16.3) These very *stomas* carry the sacrifice; he satisfies them at the final chant (*uttama-stotra*). Just as one would satisfy oxen, horses, or mules after they have drawn [the load], even so does he satisfy the *stomas* at the final chant.
He who praises with this [chant] becomes satisfied with offspring and cattle.
(2.16.4) One desiring the office of the domestic priest (*purodhā*) should perform this very [stoma]. The *trivṛt* is indeed the Brahman, and the *ekaviṃśa* is the Kṣatra.

In that he proceeds from the *trivṛt* to the *ekaviṃśa*, he places the Brahman before the Kṣatra; he attains the office of the domestic priest and does not fall from that office, who praises with this [stoma].
The Prāvāhaṇyas venerate this very [Sāman]; therefore they do not fall away from their office.
He utters *hiṅ* for nine [verses]: three times with three [each]. He utters *hiṅ* for three [verses]; he utters *hiṅ* for nine [verses] in forward order:
three times with three [each]. It is like a metal rod blazing at both ends.

One who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should praise [with this]. The *trivṛt* is indeed splendor; man consists of three syllables. Since there are two *trivṛt*s on both sides and three in the middle, just as one would heat gold, so do these two *trivṛt*s heat him for the sake of splendor and spiritual luster.
"But indeed, it is not favorable to cattle; it is liable to burn up the cattle because of its lack of substance, for it burns away both [the good and the bad].
(PB 2.17.3) "One should perform this very [rite] for one who is being accused. Verily, impurity reaches him whom foul speech reaches.
Whatever foul speech that person speaks against him, that [impurity] he burns away with the *trivṛt* [stoma]; he becomes radiant who praises with this. (PB 2.17.4)
He utters *hiṅ* for nine [verses]: three times, five times, and once; he utters *hiṇ* for nine: once, three times, and five times; he utters *hiṅ* for nine:
five times, once, and three times. The *triṇava* is indeed a thunderbolt; he thus arrays the thunderbolt for the sake of pacification.
(PB 3.1.3) One [stoma] is established by five; cattle are fivefold, and the sacrificer is the one who serves. In that he establishes it with five, it becomes a single service;
thus he establishes the sacrificer among the cattle. This is indeed the established *viṣṭuti* of the twenty-seven-fold [stoma]. He who praises with this becomes firmly established.
(Prakṛti Brāhmaṇa 3.2.1) He utters *hiṃ* for seven [verses]: three times, once; he utters *hiṃ* for nine:
once, three times, five times; he utters *hiṃ* for eleven: five times, three times, three times.
This is the *viṣṭuti* of the twenty-seven-versed hymn (*triṇava*).

(3.2.2) By means of this [stotra], indeed, the gods went to the heavenly world. One who desires the heavenly world should praise with it for the attainment of the heavenly world; by praising, he does not fall from the heavenly world. The *viṣṭuti* is "stepping forward" (*abhikrāmantī*), for it is through stepping forward that one prospers by means of the sacrifice when it has been stepped upon. Therefore, one should praise with this for the sake of prosperity itself.
(3.3.1) He utters *hiṅ* eleven times: three times, seven times, and once; he utters *hiṅ* eleven times: once, three times, and seven times; he utters *hiṅ* eleven times:
seven times, once, and three times. (3.3.2) The thirty-threefold [stoma] is indeed the end; the thirty-threefold is the highest of the stomas. One [verse] is established by means of the seven.

The seven domestic animals are the attendants; the sacrificer is the attendant. In that he provides with seven, one becomes the attendant; thus, at the end, he establishes the sacrificer among the cattle. This is indeed the established *viṣṭuti* of the thirty-three-fold [stoma]; he who praises with this becomes firmly established.
(3.4.1) He utters *hiṅ* for eleven [verses]: three times with three verses each, once with five verses; he utters *hiṅ* for eleven [verses]:

three times with three verses each, once with five verses; he utters *hiṅ* for eleven [verses]: once with five verses, three times with three verses each; this is the "near-transition" (*nedīyaḥ-saṃkrama*).

The thirty-threefold [stoma] is indeed the end. Just as one who has climbed to the top of a great tree moves from one nearer foothold to another, so does he move from one nearer foothold to another by means of these nearer footholds.

(PB 3.4.3) Five [verses] are prescribed; there are three attendants (*paricarā*); cattle are fivefold. Man is of such a measure: namely, himself, offspring, and wife. In that he ordains with five, there are three attendants; thus he establishes the sacrificer among the cattle.
"He establishes [himself]; he becomes possessed of cattle, who praises with this [sāman].

He utters *hiṃ* nine times: three times, five times, and once. He utters *hiṃ* eleven times: once, three times, and seven times. He utters *hiṃ* thirteen times: seven times, three times, and [three times].

The *udyatī* is the *viṣṭuti* of the Trayastriṃśa [Stoma]. By means of this, indeed, the gods went to the heavenly world. One who desires heaven should praise with it for the attainment of the heavenly world;
having praised, he does not fall from the heavenly worlds. He ascends from height to height; the *viṣṭuti* is one that advances.
By advancing indeed does one advance; for by advancing one prospers in the sacrifice. Therefore, one should chant with this [verse] for the sake of prosperity alone.

(PB 3.6.1) He utters *hiṃ* for thirteen [verses]: three times, five times, and five times. He utters *hiṃ* for eleven [verses]: five times, three times, and three times. He utters *hiṃ* for nine [verses]: three times... he [utters it] three times.
The *viṣṭuti* of the thirty-three-fold [stoma] consists of three [sets] of three [verses each] for the descending.

(PB 3.6.2) Just as one might descend by grasping branch after branch after having climbed to the top of a great tree, even so does he descend to this world by means of this [chant], for the sake of stability. (PB 3.6.3) He goes forth with the nine-fold [stoma], and he ascends with the nine-fold; the nine-fold is indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Verily, he goes forth by means of the vital breath, and he ascends toward the vital breath. He attains a full lifespan; he who praises with this [chant] does not die before his time.

(3.6.4) Those who hate work worship this very [vow]; therefore they reach a full lifespan. (3.7.1) He utters *hiṅ* for fifteen [verses]: three times with three, five times with five, eleven times with *hiṅ*; three times with five, three times with three, three times with three; seven times with *hiṅ*:
three times with three, once with one, three times with three.
(PB 3.7.2) He who knows the thirty-threefold [stoma] as established upon the twenty-onefold establishes himself; for the twenty-onefold is indeed the foundation of the stomas.
In that these seven [verses] become the last of the thirty-threefold, it is the sevenfold *viṣṭuti* of the twenty-onefold;
thus he establishes the thirty-threefold upon the twenty-onefold. He who praises with this [chant] establishes himself.
(3.8.1) He utters *hiṃ* eight times: three times, four times, and once; he utters *hiṃ* eight times: once, three times, and four times; he utters *hiṃ* eight times:

four times, once, and three times. (3.8.2) The meters are indeed cattle. In that he utters *hiṃ* eight times [in each group], and since cattle have eight hoofs, he thereby obtains cattle hoof by hoof.
(3.8.3) One [stotra] is established by four [verses], while the other is a service [of four verses]. Cattle are four-footed, and the sacrificer is the one who serves.
In that he establishes [the first] with four and makes the other a service, he thereby establishes the sacrificer among the cattle.
This indeed is the established *viṣṭuti* of the twenty-four-fold [Stoma]; he who praises with this becomes firmly established.
(From PB 3.9.1) He utters *hiṃ* for fifteen [verses]: three times with three, once with eleven, and once with one; he utters *hiṃ* for fourteen:
once with one, three times with three, and once with ten; he utters *hiṃ* for fifteen: once with eleven, once with one, and three times with three.

The first [stoma] is the abode of the *brahman*, the middle one of the *kṣatra*, and the last one of the *viś*. When there are two fifteen-fold [stomas] as the first ones and a fourteen-fold as the last, he thereby bestows vigor and strength upon both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*; he makes the *viś* subject to both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*, and for him who praises with this [sāman], the manifestation becomes that of the *kṣatra*.

(3.9.3) These Chāndogas indeed lack the *stomas*, for the *stomas* are uneven while the *chandases* are even. Since this *viṣṭuti* of the forty-four-fold hymn is even, they are therefore not lacking the *stomas*.
(3.9.4) This is indeed the established *viṣṭuti* of the forty-four-fold hymn; he who praises with it becomes firmly established.
(3.10.1) He utters the *hiṅ* sound for fourteen verses: three times, ten times, and once. For fifteen [verses]...

He utters *hiṅ* with one [verse], with three, and with eleven; he utters *hiṅ* for fifteen [verses]—with eleven, with one, and with three. It is without a middle part (*nirmadhyā*). Indeed, this world exists, that world exists, and this intermediate space is as if hollow. In that this [hymn] is without a middle part, it is born after these very worlds; [the sacrificer] is propagated with offspring and with cattle.
"He who praises with this [sāman] is born" (PB 3.11.1).
He utters *hiṃ* for fifteen [verses]: he [utters it] with three, he with eleven, he with one; he utters *hiṃ* for fifteen:
he with one, he with three, he with eleven; he utters *hiṃ* for fourteen: he with ten.
"One with three" (PB 3.11.2)—the first belongs to the *ājya* chants, the second to the *pṛṣṭha* chants, and the third to the *uktha* chants (PB 3.11.3).
That which is among the *yājyā*s belongs to the Hotṛ; that which is among the *pṛṣṭha*s belongs to the Maitrāvaruṇa; and that which is among the *uktha*s belongs to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.

That which belongs to the Hotṛ is the same for the Acchāvāka; that which belongs to the Pṛṣṭhas is the *yājyā* of the Hotṛ, that of the Ukthas is the *yājyā* of the Maitrāvaruṇa, and that of the Yājyās is the *yājyā* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. That which belongs to the Hotṛ is the same for the Acchāvāka; that which belongs to the Ukthas is the *yājyā* of the Hotṛ, that of the Pṛṣṭhas is the *yājyā* of the Maitrāvaruṇa, and that of the Yājyās is the *yājyā* of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. That which belongs to the Hotṛ is the same for the Acchāvāka. All [verses] are in the Ājya-stotras, all in the Pṛṣṭha-stotras, and all in the Uktha-stotras.

(3.11.4) Cattle indeed are *samīṣantī*. In that this [chant] proceeds through all the pressings (*savana*), he thereby endows it with cattle at each pressing; he who praises with this becomes possessed of cattle. (3.12.1) He makes the sound *hiṅ* sixteen times: three times, twelve times, and once; he makes the sound *hiṅ* sixteen times:
once, three times, and twelve times; he makes the sound *hiṅ* sixteen times: twelve times... [and so on].
"He [sings] with one, with three" (PB 3.12.2).

The forty-eight-fold [stoma] is indeed the end; cattle are the Chandomas. In that he utters *hiṃ* after every sixteen [verses], and since cattle consist of sixteen parts, he thereby obtains cattle part by part (PB 3.12.3).
One *paricarā* is established with twelve [verses]; the year consists of twelve months, and the sacrificer is the *paricarā*.

That which he performs with twelve [verses]—one *paricarā* consisting of one [verse]—he thereby finally establishes the sacrificer himself in cattle at the end of the year. This indeed is the established *viṣṭuti* of the forty-eight-fold [stoma]. He who praises with this becomes firmly established. From sixteen [verses] he utters the *hiṅ* sound: three times with three [verses], ten times with ten [verses], and three times with three [verses]; from sixteen...

He utters *hiṅ* with three [verses], he [utters it] with three, he [utters it] with ten; he utters *hiṅ* for sixteen [verses]: he [utters it] with ten, he with three, he with three. These are the "near-ascents" (*nedīyaḥsaṃkrama*). The forty-eight [stomas] are indeed the end. Just as one, having climbed to the top of a great tree, ascends from a near-ascend, so does he ascend from a near-ascend by means of these near-ascents.

(3.13.3) Three attendants are appointed with ten [men]; the *virāj* consists of ten syllables; so great is man—namely, himself, his offspring, and his wife. In that they appoint them with ten and there are three attendants, he thereby finally establishes the sacrificer in the *virāj*, in the eating of food; he becomes an eater of food who praises with this [chant].

(4.1.1) The cows indeed performed this sacrificial session (*sattra*). After ten months, horns grew upon them. They said, "We have become horned; let us arise, for we have attained our goal. So they arose. (4.1.2) But some of them said, "Let us remain seated for these two further months; let us complete the year. After twelve months, horns sprouted upon them. They obtained all kinds of food. These are those very ones that are hornless (*tūpara*).

"Therefore, they impel all twelve months; for they obtained all food. He who knows thus obtains all food" (PB 4.1.3–4). "In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this universe. He desired, 'May I become many, may I procreate. He saw this Atirātra sacrifice; he performed it, and by means of it, he brought forth day and night."

(4.1.5) In that this is an Atirātra, they procreate in the very day and night; they find firm support in day and night. Day and night indeed constitute the year; thus, by means of day and night, they attain the year.

(4.1.6) In that it is a Jyotiṣṭoma, they prosper at the mouth of the sacrifice. In that it is an Uktha, it is for the non-interruption of the sacrificial rite. In that there is a night, it is for the attainment of everything.
He saw these *stomas*: Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyu. These worlds indeed are these *stomas*: this [earth] is Jyotis, this middle [atmosphere] is Gauḥ, and that [heaven] is Āyu.
Inasmuch as these *stomas* exist, they procreate these very worlds; they find firm support in these worlds.
He again fashioned this three-day period (*tryaha*); by means of that six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), he procreated the six seasons.
(4.1.10) In that this six-day period exists, they indeed procreate the seasons; they find firm standing in the seasons.
(4.1.11) He employed this six-day period again; by means of those two six-day periods, he procreated the twelve months.
(4.1.12) In that these two six-day periods exist, they indeed procreate the months; they find firm standing in the months.
He employed these two six-day periods again; by means of those four six-day periods, he generated twenty-four half-months.
In that there are these four six-day periods, they generate the half-months and they find firm support in the half-months.
Having generated this world, he placed vigor within himself by means of the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period.
(4.1.16) Since this is the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, they find firm support in vigor at the end.
(4.1.17) By means of that [six-day period], he generated the months and the year; since this month exists, they generate the year itself and find firm support in the year.
(4.2.1) This day is the introductory day (*prāyaṇīya*).

(4.2.2) By means of the Prāyaṇīya day, the gods went to the heavenly world; because they went forth (*prāyan*), that is the reason for the Prāyaṇīya’s being called *prāyaṇīya*. (4.2.3) Therefore, one must be the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) of the Prāyaṇīya day, for he who is the priest of this [day] is nearest to the heavenly world; he who is not the priest of this [day] is excluded from the heavenly world. (4.2.4) It consists of twenty-four [verses].
The *gāyatrī* consists of twenty-four syllables; the *gāyatrī* is brilliance and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Having undertaken brilliance and spiritual luster, they proceed.
There is a twenty-four-fold [stoma]; the year is indeed twenty-four-fold. Thus, they directly undertake the year.
As many as are the *stotrīyā* verses of the twenty-four-fold *uktha*, so many are the nights of the year. By means of the *stotrīyā* verses, they thereby attain the year.
(4.2.8) There are fifteen stotras; there are fifteen nights in a half-month; thus, by means of the half-months, they attain the year.

(4.2.9) There are fifteen stotras and fifteen śastras; [there are] twelve months in a year; thus, by means of the months, they attain the year. (4.2.10) Regarding this, they say: "This office of the Acchāvāka is, as it were, incomplete; for he completes his duty only after the Acchāvāka."

If [the sacrificer] says, "May I not become a lord," then the *aikakubha* and the *udvaṃśīya* should be established at the end; for these two are indeed power, and thus they find support in power at the conclusion.
Now, moreover, they say that the *agniṣṭoma* alone should be performed; for this *agniṣṭoma* is the sacrifice leading to heaven, since it concludes following the Hotṛ priest in an upward direction.
The Agniṣṭoma has twelve stotras; there are twelve months in a year; thus it is commensurate with the year.
There are twelve stotras and twelve śastras; that makes twenty-four; there are twenty-four half-months in a year;
thus it is commensurate with the year.
(4.2.13) Now, moreover, they say that the *uktha* alone should be performed for the sake of the success of the day. (4.2.14) All forms are performed, for everything is obtained by this day.
(4.2.15) "The Soma juices flow for the winning of booty, they with thousandfold power"—thus the opening verse (*pratipad*) should be one containing the word "thousand."
(4.2.16) This is the form of the year; with this [verse], he purifies all of them and addresses all of them.

(4.2.17) Now, moreover, they say: "Flow on, O foremost of speech"—this indeed must be performed. For that which is the beginning of speech is the mouth of the year; thus they take hold of the year from its very mouth. (4.2.18) This utterance is like a pair: "Flow on" is the form of the male, and "of speech" is the form of the female; "Soma" is the form of the male, and "with brilliant [songs]" is the form of the female. Thus, at the beginning of the sacrifice, they create a pair for these [deities].

"He bestows [it] for procreation" (PB 4.2.19). "O Agni, yoke those which are yours"—with this [verse], the *jarābodhīya* should be made the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*. By means of the year thus yoked, they set forth; it consists of twenty-four syllables, [which is] that of the *caturviṃśa-stoma*.
Now, moreover, they say that the *yajñāyajñīya* itself should be performed.
The *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed the path; thus they do not depart from the path. The *abhīvarta* becomes the *brahmasāman*.
By means of the *abhīvarta*, the gods turned toward the heavenly world; in that the *abhīvarta* becomes the *brahmasāman*, it is for the purpose of turning toward the heavenly world.

(4.3.3) It has a single syllable as its foundation; for speech indeed consists of a single syllable. By means of speech itself, they thus set out for the heavenly world. (4.3.4) They go from here by means of the *sāman*, and they return by means of the *ṛc*. (4.3.5) The *sāman* is indeed that world [the sky], and the *ṛc* is this world [the earth]. In that they go from here by means of the *sāman*, they set out having grasped the heavenly world; in that they return by means of the *ṛc*, they become firmly established in this world.

(PB 4.3.6) If they were to release the *sāman*, they would fall away from the heavenly world; if they were to release the *ṛc*, they would perish from this world. (PB 4.3.7) The *sāman* remains the same, while the *pragātha* is different; for one goes along a variegated path, [changing] from one to another.
(PB 4.3.8) This *abhīvarta* is indeed a bull, a depositor of seed; placing seed within the *pragāthas*, he goes forth from here.

The *sāman* is the same, while the *pragātha*s are different; thus they place seed. That which follows is a *pragātha* that is the same, while the *sāman*s are different; thus they cause the seed already placed to be procreated.
By means of the *sāman* he milks the *pragātha*s from here, and by means of the *pragātha* he milks the *sāman*s from beyond, for the sake of conformity (*salomatva*).
(4.3.10) Those who cause the path to turn back again do not travel it; those who do not cause it to turn back travel it.
(4.3.11) For those who perform what has already been praised, it is as if one were to sit down beside milk that has already been milked.
(4.3.12) But those who do not perform what has already been praised attain whatever desire they may wish for.

The exponents of Brahman say: "Are the years exhausted in their power, or are they not exhausted? They should reply: "They are not exhausted. For other hymns (*stotra*) are repeated; indeed, [the cycle] proceeds upward. During five months, the *bārhata* *pragāthas* are completed.
Once these have been completed, the two meters (*chandasī*) must be joined together.

(There should be) three *uṣṇih*s and one *gāyatrī*; these [four] become three *bṛhatī*s. Regarding this they say: "This is indeed a 'leakage' (*saṃśara*) among the meters when two meters are joined together. One should proceed by means of the meters increasing by four syllables [only].
The meters increasing by four syllables are indeed cattle; by means of cattle, they thus cause them to ascend to the heavenly world.
They should undertake one Gāyatrī for one day, one Uṣṇih for one day, one Anuṣṭubh for one day;
with the Bṛhatī they should proceed for five months; they should undertake the Paṅkti for one day; with the Triṣṭubh they should proceed for the sixth month; tomorrow will be the Viṣuvat.
"They shall come to be," [thus they] approached the earth.
Regarding this, they say: "These meters are indeed not properly arranged at the midday pressing; one should pile with both the *bṛhatī* and the *triṣṭubh*.
These two meters are powerful; these are the manifest form of the midday pressing."

(PB 4.4.10) On the day of the *rathantara*, a *bṛhatī* verse should be employed; for the *bṛhatī* is indeed the proper abode of the *rathantara*. Thus, the *rathantara* becomes firmly established in its own abode. On the day of the *bṛhat*, a *triṣṭubh* verse should be employed;
for the *triṣṭubh* is indeed the proper abode of the *bṛhat*. Thus, both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* become firmly established in their own respective abodes from this point onward.
(ŚB 4.4.11) One should proceed with thirty-three *pragāthas*; [thus] they go finding firm support in the deities, for there are thirty-three deities.

One should proceed with twenty-four; the year consists of twenty-four half-months; [thus] they go finding firm support in the year itself. One should proceed with twelve; the year consists of twelve months; [thus] they go finding firm support in the year itself.

They proceed while establishing themselves by means of six; they proceed while establishing themselves in the six seasons, for it is by six that one must go. They proceed while establishing themselves in cattle, for cattle have four feet, and it is by four that one must go. They proceed while establishing themselves in these worlds, for there are three worlds, and it is by three that one must go. They proceed while establishing themselves in the sacrificer’s own world, for the sacrificer has two feet, and it is by two that one must go.
"By stepping with one foot after another, a man moves along, treading upon the world.
(PB 4.5.1) "These [days] are the Svarasāmans.
(PB 4.5.2) "Svarbhānu, the Asura, pierced the sun with darkness; the gods rescued him by means of the *svaras*. That the Svarasāmans are performed is for the sake of rescuing the sun."

(4.5.3) By means of the *parās*, the gods indeed caused the Ādityas to cross over to the heavenly world; because they caused them to cross over (*apārayan*), that is the "crossing-nature" (*paratva*) of the *parās*.
(4.5.4) The *parās* cause him to cross over who knows thus.
(4.5.5) There are seventeen [verses].
Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold; they thus approach Prajāpati himself.
They consist of the *anuṣṭubh* metre; for Prajāpati is of the nature of the *anuṣṭubh*; they thus directly take hold of Prajāpati.
There are three [verses] before and three after.
The gods were afraid that the sun would fall from the heavenly world. They made it firm with these seventeen-fold *stomas*; in that these *stomas* exist, it is for the support of the sun.
There are thirty-four-fold [verses]; the thirty-four-fold is indeed the summit; verily by means of the summit they measure him out.

They were afraid that he would overstep [the boundary] in the backward direction. They surrounded him with all the *stomas*, with the *viśvajit* and the *abhijit*. These two *stomas* are indeed vigor; verily by means of vigor they [support] the sun.
"They remain for the sake of steadfastness, so that there may be no falling away and no overstepping.

Regarding this they say: "This [chant] is indeed like a leap over what ought to be done, in that they proceed from the thirty-three-fold stoma to the seventeen-fold; therefore, the *pṛṣṭhya* should be made in between."
(4.5.14) That which is the seventeenth day of it should be made the last, for the sake of conformity.

(4.5.15) Regarding this they say: "The seventeen-fold stoma is indeed the belly among the stomas; if they were to remove the seventeen-fold [stoma] from the middle, the offspring would become hungry, and the performers of the sacrificial session (*sattra*) would become hungry.

(4.5.16) One should approach the seventeen-fold [stoma] from the thirty-three-fold itself. The thirty-three-fold is the summit, and the seventeen-fold is the summit; thus, from the summit they ascend to the summit.
(4.5.17) "They say, 'The Ukthas should be performed separately,' provided that there are Ukthas.
(4.5.18) "The Ukthas are indeed cattle; cattle are peace. Thus, they approach the Viṣuvat day with peace itself.
(4.5.19) Regarding this, they say: "This is like a break in continuity, for the Viṣuvat is an Agniṣṭoma, while the Viśvajit and Abhijit are Agniṣṭomas, and the others would be Ukthas."
(PB 4.5.20) All [the days] should indeed be performed as Agniṣṭomas.

(PB 4.5.21) The Agniṣṭoma is indeed vigor; they establish themselves in the midst of vigor itself. There are nine recitations; there are nine breaths; they establish themselves in the breaths themselves.
(PB 4.6.1) This is the Viṣuvat day.
The Viṣuvat day is indeed the world of the gods; they thus ascend to the world of the gods.
It consists of the twenty-first [stoma]; for the sun is the twenty-first of this world; they thus ascend to the world of the sun.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first.
(4.6.5) They find firm support in the very center of the sacrifice.
(4.6.6) "O Vāyu, the bright [Soma] is offered to you"—this opening verse contains the word *śukra* (bright), which is the form of Āditya.
(4.6.7) Vāyu indeed has attained this among the deities; it belongs to the *anuṣṭubh* meter. If there were any other opening verse than this, it would consume [the sacrificer].

(4.6.8) "Those who proceed with the introductory verses (*pratipad*) of the *gāyatrī* go away from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)," they say. Since these [verses] belong to Vāyu, they do not go away from the vital breaths; for Vāyu is indeed the vital breath.
(4.6.9) Moreover, they pacify him by means of this [verse], for Vāyu is peace (*śānti*).
(4.6.10) "Come hither for the drinking of Soma"—this is a verse addressed to Soma, belonging to the *pavamāna* [laud].
(4.6.11) It contains the word *niyut*; for *niyuts* are cattle, and cattle are peace. Thus, by means of peace itself, they approach the Āditya.
(4.6.12) The *divākīrtya* is the *sāman*.
(4.6.13) Svarbhānu, the Asura, pierced the Āditya with darkness; the gods [dispelled] that darkness with the *divākīrtyas*.
"In that the *divākīrtyas* are performed, they strike away the darkness from him. For these *divākīrtyas* are indeed the rays of the sun; by means of the rays, they thus directly seize the sun.
The *bhrāja* and *abhrāja* [stotras] occur at the beginning of the *pavamāna*; by means of these two, they strike away his darkness from the very front."

The Mahādivākīrtya and the Vikarṇa occur in the middle; by these two, they strike away his darkness from the middle. The Bhāsa occurs at the end; by it, they strike away his darkness from the feet. There is the Daśastobha; the Virāj consists of ten syllables; thus they find firm support in the Virāj.

(4.6.17) As for what they say: "They travel the path for six months from here, and they return again after six months; where then is the heavenly world for the sake of which they perform the sacrificial session?
(4.6.18) With the words, "The head of heaven," they take hold of the heavenly world. (4.6.19) With the words, "The center of the earth," they establish themselves in this world.

"Vaiśvānara, Agni born from the *ṛta*," with these words, the form of the Viṣuvat itself is thereby produced. "The sage, the sovereign, who surpasses all people," with these words, they indeed obtain food. "From their mouths the gods generated the vessel," with these words, they are indeed born.

(4.6.23) That [stotra] occurs in *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* verses; for the Āditya is indeed of the nature of both *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī*. If it were to be in other [metres], they would fall away from the heavenly world.
(4.6.24) It occurs in verses containing the word *samrāj*; for the heavenly world is indeed sovereignty (*sāmrājya*). They thus find firm support in the heavenly world itself.
(4.7.1) This *viṣuvat* day is indeed the self of the year; these two [halves] on either side are its wings, by which...
They proceed with the *ceto-abhīvarta*; both that which is after [the *ceto-abhīvarta*] and the *pragātha* from another [source] should be performed at the *viṣuvat*.
Thus they place the two wings back upon the body of the sacrifice for the attainment of the heavenly world.
"O Indra, bring us mental power"—this is the *pragātha*.

Vasiṣṭha, when his son had been slain, saw this [hymn]; he multiplied with offspring and cattle because this *pragātha* occurs for the sake of procreation. "May we, living, attain light"—those who indeed pass through the year in safety, they attain light while living. "May not unknown, malicious, or inauspicious powers step upon us"—those who are thieves and enemies are the "malicious ones"; it is them that he thus overcomes.

(4.7.6) "With you as our guide, O Hero, may we cross over the ever-flowing waters of the downward slopes. The "ever-flowing waters of the downward slopes" are indeed the successive years; it is them that they thus cross over.

(4.7.7) "Today, today, tomorrow, tomorrow—O men, we [invoke] him today, yesteryday," such are the *pragāthas* of continuous sequence (*saṃtanaya*). Of these, one should perform only one, for the sake of conformity (*salomatva*). Thus, they extend the sequence toward the future. (4.7.8) Furthermore, they say: "One should perform only 'O Indra, bring us wisdom' (*indra kratuṃ na ābhara*) for the sake of success."

The months are those that descend again. Just as they climb up a tree from here, so do they descend again toward this [world]. Having ascended to the heavenly world, they find firm support in this world.
The *gauḥ* and *āyus* become the two *stomas*.
The sacrificer has two feet for the sake of stability.
There are [verses] deficient and redundant; after the deficient and the redundant, offspring are born; this is for the sake of procreation.
They consist of Vairāja verses; the Virāj is food; thus they find firm standing in the eating of food.
There are ten days of the twelve-day rite.
This [period] of ten days is indeed the Virāj, perfected; they find firm support in the Virāj, which is perfected.
There are the *pṛṣṭha* chants; the *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed vigor; they find firm support in vigor. Then follow the *chandomas*.

The Chandomas are indeed cattle; they find firm support in cattle. Now, this tenth day has its Stomas attained, its metres attained, its case-endings attained, and it is undefined and dedicated to Prajāpati.
When they recite [the verses] over it, they cause it to overflow; therefore, it should not be recited separately.
(4.8.9) They approach the *anuṣṭubh* metre in a hidden manner; for the *anuṣṭubh* is Prajāpati. If they were to approach it directly, they would encounter Prajāpati.

(4.8.10) He who knows the essence (*sat*) of the sacrificial session (*sattram*) becomes essential. Of the Sāmans, the Vāmadevya is the essence; of the deities, Agni; of the metres, the Virāj; of the Stomas, the Trayastrimśa.
Having gathered these together as one, they rise from the session.

The exponents of Brahman say: "From what [cause] did they rise? From what state did they stand? Those who rise after praising with the *rathantara* chant, from what they rise, one should say of them: "They will be without a firm foundation.
Those who rise after praising with the *bṛhat* chant, they rise from a state of stability; of them one should say: "This [stability] shall endure for them."
"There will be prosperity; they will become more prosperous" (PB 4.8.13).
Those who rise after praising with the Vāmadevya chant rise from being to being, from fullness to fullness, from abode to abode; for offspring have the intermediate space as their abode (PB 4.8.14).
It occurs in verses consisting of thirty-three syllables; thus, they rise having established themselves among the thirty-three deities.
The Vāmadevya [Sāman] belongs to Prajāpati; they rise having established themselves in Prajāpati himself. The Vāmadevya is indeed cattle; they rise having established themselves in cattle.
Having performed the *saṃyājya* offerings for the wives, they go out toward the east and worship the Āhavanīya fire with the *aticchandas* verse, "This [sacrificer], the thousandfold man.
The *aticchandas* verses are these very worlds; they thus find firm support in these worlds.
(4.9.3) "Gauḥ" is the *nidhana*; this is indeed the form of the *virāj*. Verily, they find firm support in the *virāj*.
(4.9.4) Having entered [the sacrifice] facing westward, they chant with the verses of the Sārparājñī.
(4.9.5) Arbuda the serpent cast off his dead skin by means of these [verses]; verily, by means of these [verses], they cast off their own dead skin.
(4.9.6) This [verse] is indeed the Sārparājñī; they find firm support in her alone.
(4.9.7) They praise with three [verses]; these worlds are three; they find firm support in these very worlds.
(4.9.8) He brings it back by means of the mind.

(4.9.9) For with the mind he utters *hiṃ*, with the mind he performs the *prastāva*, with the mind he sings the *udgītha*, with the mind he performs the *pratihāra*, and with the mind they reach the *nidhana*; this is for the completion of that which was incomplete. (4.9.10) Indeed, what they do not complete with speech, they complete with the mind.
(4.9.11) They chant in an enclosed space, for the sake of encompassing the *brahman*.
(4.9.12) They utter a theological discourse (*brahmodya*); thus they become established in spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
(4.9.13) The *hotṛ* recites the *caturhotṛ* formula; he thereby recites in accordance with what has been chanted, for that which is not followed by a recitation is not truly chanted.
(4.9.14) They revile Prajāpati; having indeed attained him, they recite [the formula], thinking, "Let us attain him to this extent."
The householder holds the staff of *udumbara* wood; for the householder is indeed the restrainer of strength (*ūrj*), and thus he bestows strength upon these [sacrificers].
They restrain their speech. At that time, the meters are as if milked out, exhausted, and contained within; they thereby cause them to swell again with sap.
(4.9.18) Moreover, they extend it toward the morrow.
(4.9.19) This sacrificial session (*sattra*) is indeed one where the self is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
(4.9.20) For when a man cuts off [a portion] from himself, whatever desire he desires, that he attains.
(4.9.21) With two [verses] he cuts off the hair; with two, the skin; with two, the flesh; with two, the bone; with two, the marrow; with two, the fat and the blood.
(4.9.22) They shave their topknots following the [hair]; thereby they strike away evil. "May we go to the heavenly world, becoming lighter," [they think].
(4.9.23) Moreover, they thus become conformable to cattle, for the attainment of all kinds of food.

Prajāpati created offspring; he was emptied, he fell away. The gods gathered around him and said, "Let us prepare for him a great vow that may satisfy him. For him, they collected whatever food ripens during the year and presented it to him. That [vow] brought him success; that satisfied him.
"Great indeed is the vow that he has satisfied this [world]"—this is the reason for the Mahāvrata's name, "the Great Vow.
Prajāpati is truly the Great One; his vow is food itself.
Regarding this, they say: "One should approach it in the middle of the year, for food, when eaten in the middle, satisfies."

Regarding this they say: "In that they perform [the rites] in the middle, they obtain half of the food and create discord for the other half. One should rather perform them at the end of the year; for it is in the year that all food ripens. There is a twenty-fourfold [stoma]; the year is indeed twenty-fourfold, and food is twenty-fivefold.
(4.10.6) Or rather, that which is the twenty-four-fold Prāyaṇīya is this very Udayanīya.
(4.10.7) That food which they collect throughout the year—this very Pañcaviṃśa [Stoma] arises from it.
(5.1.1) The Vāmadevya [Sāman] should be performed as the Mahāvrata.
The head is threefold, for the head indeed consists of the threefold: hair, skin, and bone.
The other body is fivefold: hair, skin, flesh, bone, and marrow.
(5.1.5) For they chant with their heads turned away, accompanied by a single utterance of *hiṃ*.

(5.1.6) Therefore, the limbs of the head become fat, yet do not become excessively fat; they become thin, yet do not become excessively thin. (5.1.7) They chant again with the other part of the body; therefore, that other part of the body both becomes fat and becomes thin.
The head consists of *gāyatrī* verses containing the word "arkavatī.
Food indeed is the *arka*, and the *gāyatrī* is spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Thus, he places both food and spiritual luster in their mouths at the beginning.
The two wings consist of the fifteenfold and seventeenfold stomas; for by means of the wings, the sacrificer, having become a bird, goes to the heavenly world.
Regarding this they say: "The two [stomas] should be made equal, either both fifteenfold or both seventeenfold, for the sake of providing a yoke-strap.

Regarding that they also say: "If they are equal, then they possess a single power; therefore, they should indeed be made fifteenfold and seventeenfold. For a bird flies most effectively by making its two wings even. The Bṛhat-sāman should be performed on the south; for the right side of the body is more powerful.

(5.1.14) Now, moreover, they say: the *bṛhat* [sāman] should be performed on the northern half of the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin*’s portion; for the *bṛhat* is of the *triṣṭubh* metre, the *brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* is of the *triṣṭubh* nature, and the fifteen-fold (*pañcadaśa*) *stoma* is of the *triṣṭubh* nature.

(5.1.15–16) On the southern side, the *rathantara* [sāman] should be performed on the half-verse of the *maitrāvaruṇa*; for the *rathantara* is of the *gāyatrī* metre, the *maitrāvaruṇa* is of the *gāyatrī* nature, and the seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*) *stoma* is of the *gāyatrī* nature. The tail consists of the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*) [stoma].
The twenty-onefold is indeed the foundation of the *stomas*; therefore, a bird, having established itself on its tail, flies up, and having established itself on its tail, it sits down.
The *yajñāyajñīya* should be made the tail, for the *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed the tail of the Mahāvrata.
Now, moreover, they say: "The *yajñāyajñīya* is the excellence of two-footed beings; it should be made auspicious for the sake of prosperity."

The Vāmadevya [Sāman] is to be made the Mahāvrata; its head is the Gāyatra, its two wings are the Bṛhat and Rathantara, and its tail is the Yajñāyajñīya. He who knows the thousandfold [sacrifice] woven into the Mahāvrata obtains a thousand cattle.
Its eastern direction is the head; that [head] is a thousand by means of the meters. That other wing consists of the Nakṣatras.

This one side consists of a thousand; it is a thousand through the herbs and the trees. The intermediate space is the self; it is a thousand through the birds. The western direction is the tail; it is a thousand through the fires and the rays.
He who knows this obtains cattle by the thousands.
Regarding this, they say: "The Vāmadevya lacks a *pṛṣṭha* chant, for it has no *nidhana*. That *sāman* which has no *nidhana* is indeed without a foundation;
therefore, the Rājana should be performed as the Mahāvrata.
This royal [sāman], which is fivefold, is indeed food manifest; for food is fivefold.
It possesses the *hiṅkāra*, and by that it has the form of the Vāmadevya.
It possesses the *nidhana*, and by that it has the form of the Pṛṣṭha.

(PB 5.2.10) In the *aticchandas* [verses], the *Vāmadevya* with five *nidhanas* should be performed as the *brahmasāman*. (PB 5.2.11) For this *aticchandas* exceeds the other meters; and this day, the *mahāvrata*, exceeds the other days. (PB 5.2.12) By means of the *brahmasāman* alone, he thus causes it to surpass the other days.
It has five *nidhanas*, for food is fivefold.
The *ilānda* should be made the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.
This *ilānda* is indeed manifest food; *irā* is food. Thus, they finally find firm support in *irā* itself, in the eating of food.
This metre is indeed the ocean, the watery, the hairy; he who performs it becomes like the ocean, like water, like hair.
Therefore, one should perform these [verses] for the sake of success. "Vrata" is the *nidhana*; thus the form of the Mahāvrata itself is produced. "Svar" [is the other *nidhana*].
"It becomes a *śakuna* for the attainment of the heavenly world; indeed, the sacrificer is like a *śakuna*, for having become a bird, he goes to the heavenly world.
The *yajñāyajñīya* should be performed as the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*.

(5.3.7) Or else, whatever other speech one might not speak beyond [it], that should be made the *agniṣṭomasāman*. For speech does not indeed speak beyond speech; the *yajñāyajñīya* is speech, and thus they finally find firm support in speech itself.
(5.3.8) The *vāravantīya* should be made the *agniṣṭomasāman*.

(5.3.9) Agni Vaiśvānara was burning this world, and the gods were afraid of him. They warded him off with a branch of the *varaṇa* tree; because they warded him off (*avārayanta*), it is therefore called the *vāravantīya*.

(5.3.10) Therefore the *varaṇa* is healing, for by it the gods protected themselves here. (5.3.11) Therefore a Brāhmaṇa should not drink from a *varaṇa* vessel, lest he should bring Vaiśvānara to ruin.
(5.3.12) The *vāravantīya* is indeed cattle; cattle are peace. Thus they rise up from that peaceful year.

(5.4.1) With the out-breath (*prāṇa*), they worship the Āhavanīya fire from the front; thereby they conquer the out-breath itself. (5.4.2) With the in-breath (*apāna*), they worship the tail from behind; thereby they conquer the in-breath itself.
(5.4.3) With the two wings of the vow (*vratapakṣa*), they worship the two wings; thereby they conquer the quarters themselves.
(5.4.4) They worship the Apikakṣa with the Heart of Prajāpati; thereby they win preeminence.
(5.4.5) They worship the Cātvāla with the Nihava of Vasiṣṭha; having reached the heavenly world, they proclaim their glory.
(5.4.6) There is a verse addressed to the Viśvedevas; for the form of cattle is manifold in form; thereby they win cattle.
(5.4.7) They worship the Āgnīdhra shed for the prosperity of the sacrificial session; verily, they find firm support in prosperity.
(5.4.8) The *nidhana* consists of four syllables; cattle have four feet; verily, they find firm support in cattle.
(5.4.9) They reach the *nidhana* at the very end; verily, they attain a full lifespan.

(5.4.10) With the Śloka and Anuśloka [Sāmans], they worship the two Havirdhāna sheds; thereby they conquer renown. (5.4.11) With the Yāma [Sāman], they worship the Mārjālīya shed; thereby they conquer the world of the ancestors.
(5.4.12) With the Āyu and Navastobha [Sāmans], they worship the Sadas; thereby they conquer both the Brahman and the Kṣatra.
(PB 5.4.13) They worship the Gārhapatya fire with the Sāman of the Ṛśya.

(PB 5.4.14) All beings praised Indra, but he perceived that one limb of his was not yet praised; he praised him with this [Sāman], and through it he attained his beloved abode. With this [Sāman] they attain his very beloved [abode].
(PB 5.4.15) If they were to employ a *nidhana* that is indirect (*parokṣa*), they would put on a shamed face; they employ it directly (*pratyakṣa*) and thus avoid putting on a shamed face.
Having ascended the throne, he sings the *udgītha*; thus he wins the victory of the assembly in the presence of the gods.
It is made of *udumbara* wood; the *udumbara* is vigor, so he secures vigor for himself.
It is one span high, to prevent this world from being overturned.
(5.5.4) One ascends by means of the meters; thus one ascends to that very world, the heavenly realm. (5.5.5) One descends by means of the meters; thus one becomes firmly established in this world.
(5.5.6) Having lifted [the chant] with one's entire self, it should be sung, thinking: "May I not be obstructed in these worlds."
When one *stotrīyā* verse remains unstudied, he brings forward his feet;

together with the *nidhana*, they attain a firm foundation, and they become established in these very worlds. Having ascended the swing, the *hotṛ* recites; thus the form of greatness itself is produced.
When indeed a great prosperity enters the people, then they mount the swings. Having mounted the plank, the Adhvaryu responds with the *pratigara*.
The others sit upon the grass-bunches; thus they go forth, truly ascending upwards.

There are two, the reviler and the one who is reviled; one censures them and another praises them. He who censures them strikes away their evil, while he who praises them utters aloud that which among them is well-sung and well-recited.
A Śūdra and an Ārya struggle over a hide; they cause the Āryan color to triumph over the two of them.

The gods and the Asuras contended for the sun; the gods conquered it, and from that the gods prospered while the Asuras were defeated.
