He who knows this prospers through his own self, and his rival is defeated. When they cause the noble class (*ārya-varṇa*) to exult, they thereby cause their very self to exult.
The hide is circular; thus the form of the sun itself is created.
Drums resound on all sides; they thereby conquer that speech which is in the trees. There is a ground-drum; they thereby conquer that speech which is upon the earth.
(5.5.20) They utter all speech; they conquer that very speech which exists in those worlds.
(5.5.21) Clad in armor and equipped with mail, they go around; thus the form of the sense-organ (*indriya*) is produced, and moreover, they magnify the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*).
(5.6.1) All the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) together should praise with the Great Vow.
The Adhvaryu, chanting the *udgītha*, constitutes the head; the Maitrāvaruṇa, the right wing; the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, the left wing; the Gṛhapati, the tail; and the Udgātṛ himself, the body.
Now, if they should perform it in this manner, they should approach the Udgātṛ with each unchanted *stotrīyā* verse.
Having chanted the *udgītha* for the Udgātṛ’s own self with three verses, he should then add that *stotrīyā* which belongs to the head, along with the subsequent ones.
He should chant the *udgītha* with three verses; then he should add that which is the *stotrīyā* of the southern wing with another three verses;
then he should chant the *udgītha* with [those] three verses; then he should add that which is the *stotrīyā* of the northern wing—whether it has been chanted with three verses or with one;
then he should add that which is the *stotrīyā* of the tail.
(5.6.5) They restore the limbs to the self itself for the attainment of the heavenly world.
(5.6.6) Now they say: "How should the Adhvaryu, who is a Bahvṛca, chant the Sāman? The Udgātṛ alone should chant it with everything; that is successful, and they find firm support in success itself.
(5.6.7) Having praised with their heads at the two Havirdhāna sheds, they should go westward, holding on to one another, along the south of the Dhiṣṇya hearths.
Having gone around to the west and sat down behind the Maitrāvaruṇa’s hearth, they should chant with the Rathantara Sāman on the Pañcadaśa Stoma;

they should then creep northward, passing behind the Hotṛ’s hearth and sitting down behind the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s hearth, where they should chant with the Bṛhat Sāman on the Saptadaśa Stoma; they should then withdraw by the same way they crept forward and exit to the north of the Āgnīdhra.
Having gone around behind and sat down by the *gārhapatya* fire, they should chant the praise with the twenty-one-fold [stoma] using the tail.
Having crept back out by the same way they went forth, and having sat down in their respective places, the *udgātṛ* mounts the throne-seat and chants the *udgītha* for himself.
The wives accompany this chanting with *apaghāṭilā* songs; thus the wives perform the priestly office (*ārtvijya*), thinking, "May we go together to the heavenly world."

(5.6.9) Food is prepared in every household; if they should ask, "What is this that they are doing?", they should say, "These sacrificers are about to eat food. (5.6.10) Whoever proclaims the evil of those who have been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) takes away for himself a third part of that evil: the eater of food [takes] a third, the ants [take] a third. (5.6.11) They proceed with the *parimād* verses; for these *parimād* verses are indeed the skin and the hair of the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*). Having thus obtained the skin and the hair of the Great Vow, they secure them for themselves.

(5.6.12) They stretch out the lute; the lute is indeed the end, and the Great Vow is the end. By means of the end, they thus pay homage to the end. (5.6.13) It has a hundred strings; man indeed has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundredfold vigor.

(5.6.14) One should scrape it [the skin], saying: "For out-breath thee! For in-breath thee! For diffused breath thee! Thus, having obtained out-breath, in-breath, and diffused breath, they secure them.
The *kumbhinī* women go around the *mārjālīya* fire-shed crying out, "This honey! This honey! Having thus become birds, they go together to the heavenly world with a great clamor.

The gods indeed divided speech among themselves; that essence of it which remained over became the *Gaurīvita*. It revolves following the *anuṣṭubh*; the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and the *Gaurīvita* is the essence of speech.
When they chant the praise daily with the *Gaurīvita*, they place the essence into speech by means of speech itself.
(5.7.3) "He speaks with speech that possesses flavor, he who knows thus," so it is said.

(5.7.4) There are two exclamations; these two are indeed the terminal points of the heavenly world. With the former [exclamation] they conclude the first day, and with the latter they speak beyond the second day. (5.7.5) This Gaurīvita is indeed the provision for the morrow of the sacrifice. If they were to omit the Gaurīvita, they would be without provisions for the morrow and childless.
(5.7.6) "One sacrifice indeed stands still," they say, "but Speech itself does not stand still. In that the Gaurīvita occurs on each successive day, they thereby employ Speech once again.
(5.7.7) The Svarṇidhana occurs on each successive day.
(5.7.8) Those who undertake the Svarṇidhana enter the domain of the gods; and these, indeed, are the performers of the sacrificial session.

"One should initiate him into the sacrificial session," they say, "he who would ascend to the domain of the gods. Indeed, one sitting in the domain of the gods does not meet with calamity. Since the *svarṇidhana* occurs every day, they do not meet with any calamity whatsoever.
"Those who undertake the *svarṇidhana* fall away from this world," they say; [but] because [it is performed] with a *ṛc*...

They go to their own nature; they find firm support in this world through the *ekāra*, in the intermediate space through the *sāman*, and in all worlds through the *svarnidhana*—for those who praise with it, there is perfect knowledge.

The gods, indeed, when going to the heavenly world, were afraid of the unknown; they saw this *saṃjñāna* (means of recognition), and by it they attained knowledge (*jñātra*). In that there is a *sujñāna* (easy-to-know) [hymn] on each day, they attain knowledge indeed. Those who eat speech as food become eaters of food; those who parch it become rough.

The Gaurīvita, the Śyāvāśva, and the Nihava—these indeed are the Sāmans that are the food of Speech; Speech is the food of these. In that these do not deviate, they consume Speech itself as their food; thereby, all become eaters of food.
They are [performed] with approach and withdrawal; for the nature of Speech is indeed characterized by approach and withdrawal.
(5.8.4) There is a raft for each day.
(5.8.5) Those who undertake the year-long rite are as if swimming across the ocean. He who crosses the ocean without a raft does not emerge from it; that there is a raft is for the sake of heaven.
(5.8.6) "May we cross beyond all difficulties"—by this [verse], they cross over whatever in their performance has been ill-chanted or ill-recited.

The *okanidhana* occurs at the beginning of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*). Those who go to the end of the six-day period go indeed to the furthest distance; in that the *okanidhana* occurs at the beginning of the six-day period, it is for the sake of clear understanding. When a man returns to his own home, then he understands everything; for him, everything becomes manifest by day.
(5.9.1) They should undergo initiation on the Ekāṣṭakā day.
(5.9.2) This Ekāṣṭakā is indeed the wife of the year; on this very night, having passed, they dwell. Thus, they undergo initiation by directly grasping hold of the year.
(5.9.3) Its failure is that when they descend into the waters without taking delight in them.
(5.9.4) Those who undergo initiation on the Ekāṣṭakā day indeed undergo initiation at the interruption of the year; the two seasons then become those called "the ends.
(5.9.5) Those who undergo initiation during the two seasons called "the ends" indeed undergo initiation at the affliction of the year.
(5.9.6) Therefore, one should not undergo initiation on the Ekāṣṭakā day.
(5.9.7) They should undergo initiation in the month of Phālguna.

(5.9.8) For Phālguna is indeed the mouth of the year; thus they undertake initiation by beginning the year from its very mouth. (5.9.9) Its completion occurs when the Viṣuvat day falls during the rainy season.

(5.9.10) They should undergo initiation on the full moon day of Citrā. (5.9.11) This full moon day of Citrā is indeed the eye of the year; the eye is at the front. Thus, having begun the year from the very front, they undergo initiation. For that [year], there is no going astray. (5.9.12) They should undergo initiation four days before the full moon.
For them, the purchase [of the Soma] falls on the Akāṣṭakā day; therefore, they do not perform the Ekāṣṭakā sacrifice.
For them, the pressing falls in the bright fortnight; the months proceed being completed in the bright fortnight, and they rise up in the bright fortnight.
As they rise up, the cattle and the plants rise up after them; for them, it is auspicious.
"Speech has spoken; these performers of the sacrificial session have succeeded," [it is said]. They indeed prosper. (PB 5.10.1) "Verily, they cause the year to swell who omit [the Soma].
(PB 5.10.2) Just as a leather bag when inflated, so is the year when it is not omitted. If they were not to omit it, they would be liable to die from urinary obstruction."

The year is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and the months are the up-breaths (*udāna*). When they release [the breaths], they place the up-breaths within the out-breath. If one who is consecrated dies, whatever impurity (*śuk*) there is of the unreleased year, that reaches him.
Regarding this, they say: "Should one release [the breaths] or should one not release them?"
(5) If they should omit the *ukthas*, they should omit them; that [omission] is indeed both omitted and not omitted.
(6) Now, moreover, they say: "The *ekatrika* should be performed; that is the direct omission they pour out. (7) "For those who omit the *stoma*, their year is indeed defective," so they say.
(5.10.8) They immolate the animal; thereby they immolate the *stoma* itself, for the *stoma* is indeed the animal.
(5.10.9) On the next day, saying "We have been released," they drive away the calves. In the morning they immolate the animal;
they proceed with its omentum, then with the *savaniya* cake on eight potsherds, then with the cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni, and then with the curd offering dedicated to Indra.
Then, with the *caru* for the Viśvedevas, they conclude that morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).

Then, with the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) on eleven potsherds; then with the *savanīya* cake on eleven potsherds; then with the cake for the Maruts on eleven potsherds; then with the *caru* for Indra—thereby they conclude that midday pressing (*mādhyandinaṃ savanam*).

(5.10.11) They proceed with the animal sacrifice; then with the *savanīya* cake on twelve potsherds; then with the *vaiśvadeva* cake on twelve potsherds; then with the *caru* for Agni and the Maruts. That is the third pressing.
(5.10.12) Having performed the rite with the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), they cause the wives to perform the *saṃyājana* offerings.
(6.1.1) Prajāpati desired, "May I become many, may I propagate. He beheld this Agniṣṭoma; he took it up; with it, he created these creatures.

By means of the eleventh *stotra* of the Agniṣṭoma, he created [the creatures] and by means of the eleventh month of the year; with the twelfth *stotra* of the Agniṣṭoma he enclosed them and with the twelfth month of the year. Therefore, after carrying the embryo for ten months, creatures are born in the eleventh; therefore, [they complete] the twelfth.
They do not transfer [the embryo], for they are encompassed by the twelfth; he who knows thus encompasses his offspring when born and causes those already born to be propagated.

Of those [offspring] that had been encompassed, a she-mule stepped aside; pursuing her, he took the seed and cast it into a mare. Because the mare has double seed, therefore the she-mule is barren, for her seed has been taken away.

Therefore, indeed, it is not worthy of a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇīya*), for it has surpassed the sacrifice. The sacrificial gift should belong to that which is redundant, for the sake of conformity (*salomatva*) with the *ṣoḍaśin* chant. One should give [the gift] at the *ṣoḍaśin* chant; for the *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed redundant, and thus the redundant [gift] belongs to the redundant [chant]. He desired: "May I create the sacrifice. He created the *trivṛt* from his very mouth. The *gāyatrī* meter was created for it, Agni as the deity, the Brāhmaṇa as the human, and the spring as the season. Therefore, the *trivṛt* is the first among the *stomas*.

The Gāyatrī is the foremost among meters, Agni among deities, the Brāhmaṇa among men, and spring among seasons. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa performs his heroic work with his mouth, for he was created from the mouth.
He who knows this performs his heroic work with his mouth.

From his chest, by means of his two arms, he created the Pañcadaśa-stoma; the Triṣṭubh metre was created after it, Indra the deity, the Rājanya the human being, and the Grīṣma season. Therefore, for the Rājanya, the Pañcadaśa-stoma is the chant, the Triṣṭubh the metre, Indra the deity, and the Grīṣma the season; and therefore he possesses strength in his arms, for he was created from the arms.
"He who knows thus performs heroic power with his two arms" (PB 6.1.10). From the very center of procreation, he created the Saptadaśa [Stoma]; after it, the Jagatī metre was created;
the Viśvedevas were the deity; the Vaiśya the human being; the rainy season the season. Therefore, the Vaiśya, even while being consumed, is not exhausted, because of procreation.

He was created from thought; therefore, he possesses many cattle, for he belongs to the Viśvedevas and his meter is the Jagatī, and the rainy season is his season. Therefore, he is to be eaten by both the Brāhmaṇa and the Rājanya, for he was created later.
Having established himself on the foot, he created the twenty-one-fold [stoma]; after him, the Anuṣṭubh meter was created.

No deity whatsoever was created after the Śūdra; he is a human being, therefore he is a Śūdra. Furthermore, although he possesses many cattle, he is unfit for sacrifice and is without deities, for no deity whatsoever was created after him. Therefore, he is not to be worshipped on foot, nor does he prosper; for he was created as one who moves on foot. Therefore, among the Stomas, the twenty-one-fold is the foundation, for he was created from the foundation. Therefore, they do not transpose the Anuṣṭubh among the meters.
(6.1.12) For the warding off of misfortune. (6.1.13) There is warding off of misfortune for one who knows thus.
(6.2.1) He who knows the *stomas* as possessing instruction becomes possessed of instruction.

The breath is indeed the threefold; the half-month is the fifteenfold; the year is the seventeenfold; the sun is the twenty-onefold. These, indeed, are the *stomas* that possess instruction. He who knows thus becomes possessed of instruction.
These worlds are indeed the twenty-sevenfold; by means of the Brāhmaṇa of the twenty-sevenfold, these worlds become ninefold again in three ways.
He who knows thus finds firm support in these worlds.
The thirty-three deities indeed are the thirty-three: eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Ādityas, and Prajāpati and the *vaṣaṭ*-call as the thirty-third.
He who knows thus sacrifices with the divine sacrifice.
(6.2.7) He who knows the overlord becomes an overlord. The thirty-three-fold hymn-form (*stoma*) is indeed the overlord of the *stomas*; it is the man, possessed of cattle.
(6.2.8) Therefore other animals eat with their faces turned downward, while the man eats looking upward, for he is the overlord.
(6.2.9) He who knows thus becomes the overlord of his equals.
(6.3.1) This, indeed, is the sacrifice that is the Agniṣṭoma.
(6.3.2) One sacrifice is performed for a single desire, but the Agniṣṭoma is performed for all desires.
(6.3.3) There are twelve stotras in the Agniṣṭoma; twelve months are a year, and cattle are produced in accordance with the year; therefore, it is conducive to cattle and prosperous.

There are twelve *stotras* and twelve *śastras*; that makes twenty-four. There are twenty-four half-months in a year. Cattle are born in accordance with the year; therefore, it is beneficial for cattle and prosperous.
In Agni the *stotra* finds its firm foundation, and in Agni the *śastra*; therefore, it leads to spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).

(6.3.6) "What is the Jyotiṣṭoma-ness of the Jyotiṣṭoma? they ask. "When it is completed, it becomes the Virāj; for the Virāj is the light among the meters. (6.3.7) "He who knows thus becomes the light among his equals. (6.3.8) "The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the sacrifice of the eldest."
Prajāpati created offspring; they did not submit to his supremacy. He saw this Agniṣṭoma; he performed it. Then the offspring submitted to his supremacy.
Those who know thus, their equals submit to their supremacy.
Now, as for what they say: "The morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī, the midday pressing to the Triṣṭubh, and the third pressing to the Jagatī; where then is the fourth metre, the Anuṣṭubh?"
(PB 6.3.12) By the loss of the meters, the sacrificer is lost.

(PB 6.3.13) The Gāyatrī has eight syllables, the *hiṅkāra* is the ninth; the Triṣṭubh has eleven syllables, and the Jagatī has twelve. Through the meters themselves, he obtains the Anuṣṭubh for the sake of the sacrificer’s non-loss.

(PB 6.3.14) He who knows the Anuṣṭubh as pervading everywhere and following after the pressings (*savana*)—he becomes a pervader everywhere. This Anuṣṭubh indeed pervades everywhere and follows after the pressings. That...
"He who knows thus becomes a protector everywhere" (PB 6.3.15).

When kings cause their horses to gallop along the road, they yoke those that are the most vigorous among the horses—the Trivṛt, the Pañcadaśa, and the Ekaviṃśa; for these are indeed the most vigorous of the Stomas. He yokes them for the attainment of the heavenly world.
(6.3.16) There is a Catuṣṭoma; the Catuṣṭoma is indeed a firm foundation; it serves for the sake of a firm foundation.
(6.4.1) Prajāpati distributed strength (*ūrj*) among the gods; from that the Udumbara tree arose.
The Udumbara belongs to Prajāpati, and the Udgātṛ priest belongs to Prajāpati; when the Udgātṛ takes hold of the Udumbara post with the first ritual act, he [does so] by means of his own [nature].
He chooses himself for the office of the officiating priest by means of that deity (PB 6.4.2).
He raises it up with the formula: "May Dyutāna Māruta raise thee up; support the sky, fill the mid-region, make firm the earth" (PB 6.4.3).
He touches it from behind with the formula: "I set thee in the seat of life, in the shadow of the well, in the heart of the ocean."
Sacrifice is indeed life; this [space] is made as its seat. Sacrifice is indeed protection; this [space] is made as its shade.
The heart is indeed in the middle of one's self; therefore, the Audumbarī post is erected in the middle of the *sadas*.
"Homage to the ocean, homage to the eye of the ocean," he says. Speech indeed is the ocean, and the mind is the eye of the ocean; by means of these two, he thus offers homage.
"The *sāman* was the youth-bearer," he says. The *sāman* indeed is the youth-bearer; he thus offers homage to the *sāman* when about to perform the office of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).
He who, having thus offered homage to the *sāman*, performs the office of the officiating priest with the *sāman*, does not fall away from the *sāman*, nor does the *sāman* desert him.
(PB 6.4.10) He who speaks ill of this [post] meets with misfortune.
(PB 6.4.11) "Thou art strength, giver of strength; grant me strength, bestow strength upon me; grant me food, bestow food upon me.
This *sadas* is indeed the belly of Prajāpati; the udumbara is strength. Therefore, the post made of udumbara wood is erected in the middle of the *sadas*.
"In the very middle, he bestows food and strength upon the subjects" (PB 6.4.12).
"Therefore, wherever this [chant] is performed when it has lost its vigor, there the subjects become hungry" (PB 6.4.13).
The *sāman* is the food of the gods; in the *sāman* itself, he bestows food and strength upon the gods. Having resorted to that very strength, he distributes strength among the subjects.

Sitting facing north, he sings the *udgītha*; thus he causes that [quarter] to partake of nourishment. Sitting facing west, he performs the *prastāva*; thus he causes that [quarter] to partake of nourishment. Sitting facing south, he performs the *pratihāra*; thus he causes that [quarter] to partake of nourishment.
The other priests perform their priestly duties facing east; therefore, this is the most powerful of the quarters, for it is this one that the greatest number gratify.

(Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.4.15) The exponents of Brahman say: "On what basis do the other priests perform their priestly duties facing east, while the Udgātṛs perform theirs by turning around? One should reply: "For the winning of the quarters, for the propitiation of the quarters. Therefore, food is found in all directions, for they have all been won and propitiated.

Prajāpati desired, "May I be many; may I procreate. He grieved. As he was grieving, the sun was emitted from his head. It struck his head and fell away; it became the *droṇakalaśa* vessel. In it, the gods drew the *śukra* cup. By means of that [cup], he indeed overcame the affliction of his life-span.
(6.5.2) He who knows thus lives beyond the reach of misfortune regarding his life-span.

(6.5.3) One should push it forward [with the formula]: "Thou art made of wood; thou art Bārhaspatya; thou art Prājāpatya; thou art the head of Prajāpati; thou art the vessel for exceeding life; here I push myself forward, facing eastward, for the sake of splendor.
(6.5.4) In that he says, "Thou art made of wood," he pushes it forward by means of truth itself.
When he says, "Belonging to Bṛhaspati," Bṛhaspati is indeed the Udgātṛ of the gods; it is him that he thereby yokes.
When he says, "Belonging to Prajāpati," for this Droṇakalaśa belongs to Prajāpati as its deity. When he says, "The head of Prajāpati," for it was produced from the head of Prajāpati.
When he says, "The vessel beyond life-span," for the Droṇakalaśa surpasses all other vessels; the Droṇakalaśa is the vessel of the gods.
He becomes a vessel for the gods who knows thus.
One should not scrutinize a Brāhmaṇa as a mere vessel; whoever considers someone to be a Brāhmaṇa attains the vessel of the gods and is not severed from the vessel of men.
Speech indeed departed from the gods; it entered into the waters. The gods begged it back. They...
They said, "If we were to give [it] back, what would happen to us? He replied, "Whatever you desire.
They said, "May we remain unmixed with whatever impurity men have introduced into us" (PB 6.5.11). For one who knows thus, the waters become pure and purified for him.

She went away from them; she entered the trees. The gods begged her back, but they did not give her back. They cursed them, saying, "May you cut yourselves with your own cubit-sized thunderbolt! Therefore, they cut the trees with their own cubit-sized thunderbolt, for they were cursed by the gods.

The trees distributed that speech into four parts: into the drum, the lute, the axle, and the flute. Therefore, this speech of the trees is the most eloquent and the most beautiful; for it was indeed the speech of the gods. They push the *droṇakalaśa* down below the axle for the sake of attaining that speech; they place the filter above the axle, and thus they encompass the speech on both sides.

(PB 6.5.15) If one should desire regarding someone, "May I make his sacrifice non-divine" or "May I obstruct his speech," then while pushing forward the *droṇakalaśa*, he should touch the axle with both arms; thus he makes his sacrifice non-divine and obstructs his speech.

But if someone should be dear to him, he should push it forward without touching the axle; for the *droṇakalaśa* is indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); verily, he thereby restores the vital breaths of that person.
(6.5.16) Now they say: "Since they choose other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) by means of speech, why do the *udgātṛ*s perform their priestly office (*ārtvijya*) once they have been chosen?
(6.5.17) Because they sit down at the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, the *udgātṛ*s are thereby chosen.
(6.5.18) The *udgātṛ*s belong to Prajāpati, and the *droṇakalaśa* belongs to Prajāpati; thus, through the *droṇakalaśa* itself, he chooses them for the priestly office.
They sit down facing east, thinking, "Let us perform the sacrifice at its head while facing east.
The eastern direction is indeed the unconquered quarter of the Udgātṛs; when they push the *droṇakalaśa* forward, it is for the conquest of the quarters.
Now, as for what they say: "The horse is yoked between the two side-reins (*prāseva*), and the ox is yoked between the two pins (*śamya*); what [is the yoking] of the Udgātṛs?"
"Yoga" is that which they approach the *droṇakalaśa* with; this is their "yoking. Therefore, one should approach it only when [the horses] are yoked, for what is unyoked does not draw [the load].

Having set down the pressing-stones (*grāvan*), they place the *droṇakalaśa* upon them. The pressing-stones are indeed the common people (*viś*), Soma is food, and the *droṇakalaśa* is the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*). In that they place the *droṇakalaśa* upon the pressing-stones, they thereby place the kingdom upon the common people.

(PB 6.6.2) If he should hate someone, having turned the pressing-stones away from him, he should set them aside with the words: "I cast this one, the son of such-and-such a man and such-and-such a woman, out from this clan and from this food. Thus he casts him out from the clan and from the food. (PB 6.6.3) If someone should be dear to him, having turned the pressing-stones toward him, he should set them down with the words: "I place this one, the son of such-and-such a man and such-and-such a woman, upon this clan and upon this food. Thus he places him upon the clan and upon the food.
Verily, he places him upon the people and upon food (PB 6.6.4).

Alternatively, disregarding both of those, he should place [the *upāṃśusavana* stone] with the formula, "Here I place myself upon splendor and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Verily, he thus places himself upon splendor and spiritual luster (PB 6.6.5).
He who should desire, "May I strike the kingdom with the people," should set down the *droṇakalaśa* below the pressing-stones after having arranged them, and then [set down] the *upāṃśusavana*.
He should place it down from above, saying, "With this people, I strike down that kingdom"; thus, by means of the people itself, he strikes down the kingdom.

He who knows the divine purifiers becomes pure and fit for sacrifice; the meters are indeed the divine purifiers; with them they purify the *droṇakalaśa*. "May the Vasus purify you with the Gāyatrī meter; may the Rudras purify you with the Triṣṭubh meter."
"May the Ādityas purify you with the Jagatī metre; may these divine purifiers purify you. He who knows this becomes pure and worthy of sacrifice.
Svarbhānu, the Asura, pierced the Sun with darkness; the gods did not recognize him, so they [approached] Atri.
Atri ran toward him; with his luster he drove away the darkness. What he first drove away became a black ewe;
what he secondly [drove away] became a silver one; what he thirdly [drove away] became a red one; that with which he overran the color was white.
Therefore, the filter is white, and Soma is bright; it is for the sake of brightness.

(6.6.10) For whomsoever one should hate, for him he should prepare these colors even on the *pavitra*; verily, he pierces him with evil, with darkness, for darkness is, as it were, black. For him who is dear to him, he should make it attached and white; gold is indeed light;
verily, he bestows light upon him.
(6.6.11) Therefore, they desire the descendant of Atri [as the Udgātṛ] by means of the moon, for Atri is his light.
(6.6.12) They pierce the filter and separate it; this is indeed a manual task of the sacrifice that is performed. This separation of the filter is the manual task of the Udgātṛs.
(6.6.13) He who knows thus does not fall away from his manual duties.
(6.6.14) Even if one does not dispute [with him], they cause him to perish from within by means of his vital breath.
(6.6.15) One should say to him while he is trembling, "You shall perish"; trembling, he indeed perishes.
(6.6.16) "May the divine inspired thought go forth from us, like a well-fashioned chariot, like a prize-winning steed"—with these words, the Udgātṛ consecrates the stream [of Soma].

"Flow for my life; flow for my splendor! [he says]. "May they who know [the way] from the earth and from the birthplace of heaven hear us; may the waters flowing below hear this. "Sing the *udgītha* for Soma," he says, "for my brilliance.

This indeed is the *udgītha* of Soma, namely that which flows. He sings the *sāman* as the very *udgītha* of Soma. They purify it uninterruptedly; thus they extend both the sacrifice and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). They purify it continuously for the continuity of the sacrifice.
Bṛhaspati indeed sang the Udgītha for the gods; the Rākṣasas sought to slay him. He approached those who are the lords of these worlds with their own share.

"May Sūrya protect me from the destructive powers of heaven, Vāyu from those of the intermediate space, and Agni from those of the earth—Svāhā! Thus he offers. These indeed are the lords of these worlds; it is to them that he has resorted with their own share.
(6.7.4) He who knows thus exerts his strength through speech and does not meet with misfortune in the assembly.

(6.7.5) Speech indeed departed from the gods; the gods called out after her. She said, "I am without a share; let there be a portion for me. They asked, "What portion shall we provide for you? She replied, "The Udgātṛs," and so it was the Udgātṛs [who provided it].

"They indeed make an offering-share for Speech" (PB 6.7.6). One should offer to her [with the mantra]: "Thou art Bekurā by name; thou art beloved by the gods. Homage to Speech! Homage to the Lord of Speech! O Goddess Speech, place me in that which is honeyed of thy speech—[this is] for Sarasvatī.
(PB 6.7.7). Sarasvatī is indeed Speech; thus he takes hold of her with her own offering-share.

(6.7.8) If he should hate someone, he should offer this oblation for him while meditating on speech with his mind; thus he deprives that person of speech. (6.7.9) They glide toward the *bahiṣpavamāna*; they glide toward the heavenly world itself. (6.7.10) They glide as if whistling, for the heavenly world is, as it were, hostile; they glide as if creeping, for sacrifice has the nature of a wild beast; it is for the pacification of the sacrifice and to prevent its being terrified.

(6.7.11) They restrain their speech; thereby they restrain the sacrifice itself. If they were to speak out of turn, they would utter the sacrifice [in vain]. Therefore, one must not speak out of turn. (6.7.12) Five officiating priests proceed, holding onto one another. The sacrifice consists of five parts; as great as the sacrifice is, that very thing they maintain in continuity. (6.7.13) If the Prastotṛ falters, the head of the sacrifice is severed. Having given a boon to the Brahman priest, he himself must proceed again; thus he restores what has been severed.

(PB 6.7.14) If the Udgātṛ is interrupted, the sacrificer is deprived of the sacrifice; that sacrificial rite is to be completed without a dakṣiṇā, and another [priest] is to be brought in; into him [the sacrificer] should give as much as he intended to give.

(PB 6.7.15) If the Pratihartṛ is interrupted, the sacrificer is deprived of cattle; for the Pratihartṛ is indeed cattle; [therefore] all one's possessions (sarvavedasa) should be given. If he does not give all his possessions, [he incurs] the loss of everything. (PB 6.7.16) The Adhvaryu carries away the prastara-bunch.
The sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) is indeed the sacrificer; he thus carries the sacrificer himself to the heavenly world.

The sacrifice, having become a horse, fled away from the gods. The gods bound it with the sacrificial grass-bundle; therefore, when a horse is being groomed with a grass-bundle, it submits [to it]. When the Adhvaryu carries the sacrificial grass-bundle, it is for the pacification of the sacrifice and to prevent its flight.
Prajāpati created cattle; once created, they departed from him, seeking food.

He offered the *prastara* (grass-bundle) to them as food, and they returned to him. Therefore, the *adhvaryu* should shake the *prastara* slightly; for cattle return to that which is shaken, like a blade of grass.
Cattle turn toward him who knows thus. Having sat upon the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), he should sing the *udgītha* so that the oblation does not spill.
However, he thereby holds back the sacrificer from the heavenly world.
(6.7.23) When he touches [the water] with his kneecap, one should sing; thereby his oblation becomes unspilled, and it does not hold back the sacrificer from the heavenly world.
(6.7.24) Having looked at the *cātvāla* pit, they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* hymn. For here indeed was that sun;
by means of the *bahiṣpavamāna*, the gods carried him to the heavenly world. Therefore, having looked at the *cātvāla*, they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna*.

"By that, they lead the sacrificer himself to the heavenly world" (PB 6.8.1). "But one should indeed sacrifice with the sacrifice," they say, "for him upon whose mouth of the sacrifice they place the *virāj*.
(PB 6.8.2) They praise with nine [verses]; the *hiṅkāra* is the tenth; the *virāj* has ten syllables; verily, he places the *virāj* at the mouth of his sacrifice.

(6.8.3) They praise with nine [verses]. The vital breaths are nine; verily, they cause him to prosper by means of the vital breaths. The *hiṅkāra* is the tenth; therefore, the navel is the tenth among the vital breaths, being unperforated.

(6.8.4) They praise with nine. Nine cups the Adhvaryu draws at the morning pressing; those he purifies then, and from them they release the vital breaths. (6.8.5) The *hiṅkāra* is Prajāpati. There are three *bahiṣpavamāna* verses. In that he begins the *prastāva* after uttering the *hiṅkāra*, he places a productive pair at the beginning of the sacrifice for the sake of procreation.

(PB 6.8.6) This indeed is the harnessing of the *stoma*, namely the *hiṅ* sound; when one begins the *prastāva* after uttering the *hiṅ*, one begins with the *stoma* already harnessed. (PB 6.8.7) This indeed is the essence of the *sāmans*, namely the *hiṅ* sound; when one begins the *prastāva* after uttering the *hiṅ*, one begins by rising up with that very essence.
(PB 6.8.8) They chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* for the wild animals; they chant with verses of a single form, therefore wild animals are uniform in appearance.
(6.8.9) They chant with verses directed forward; therefore offspring are born facing away, and they spread out facing away.
(6.8.10) They chant in an unenclosed space; therefore wild animals are not enclosed.
(6.8.11) They chant outside and recite the *anuśaṃsa* inside; therefore they enjoy themselves with things brought from the village.
(6.8.12) They chant with the *ājya* hymns for the sake of the village and the domestic animals; because they chant with various forms, therefore domestic animals are of various forms.
(6.8.13) They chant by returning again; therefore, having departed, men return again. (6.8.14) They chant within an enclosed space; therefore, domestic animals are kept enclosed.

(6.8.15) They chant this for that world above, namely the *bahiṣpavamāna*; they chant with single *hiṅ* utterances and with verses directed away (*parācībhiḥ*). For that world above is once-fertilized and turned away. (6.8.16) They chant this for this world here, namely with the *ājya* chants; they chant turning back again and again. Therefore, this world is born again and again.

(6.8.17) "The vital breaths of those who chant with the *bahiṣpavamāna* verses directed away depart," so they say. One should sing the final verse as one that turns back (*āvatīm*), for the support of the vital breaths.

"They fall indeed from this world," they say, "who chant the Bahiṣpavamāna with verses directed away. One should sing the last verse with the color of the *rathantara*; for the *rathantara* is this [earth], and thus one finds firm support on this very earth.
For one who desires a village, one should use "Sing forth to him, O men! as the introductory verse (*pratipad*).
(6.9.2) Man is indeed the host of the gods; verily, he provides a host for him. (6.9.3) Food is indeed near at hand; verily, he provides food for him.
(6.9.4) "Near to the one born, the swift one"—this should one make the introductory verse for one desiring offspring.
"Verily, he has brought forth that offspring which was born"—thus indeed he has caused it to be born. "Be auspicious for us, for our cattle"—with these words he should perform the *pratipad*.
In whichever year Mahādeva should slay the cattle, [he should recite] "be auspicious for us, for our cattle"; thus he provides a remedy for the four-footed.

"Peace to the people," [he says] for bipeds; "peace to the courser," for the single-hoofed. Indeed, during that year in which Mahādeva strikes down the cattle, the plants are smeared with poison. When he says, "O King, peace to the plants," he makes the plants palatable for him; thus both kinds of plants become palatable for him.
"Crops ripen both without being ploughed and those that ripen after being ploughed" (PB 6.9.10).
One should use "Flow on, the foremost of speech" as the introductory verse for one whom he desires: "May he be the most excellent among his peers" (PB 6.9.11).
By using "Flow on, the foremost of speech," he leads him to the very forefront.
(6.9.12) Prosperity is indeed the foremost part of speech; verily, he bestows prosperity upon him.
(6.9.13) He should employ "ete asṛgram indavaḥ" as the introductory verse for many [sacrificers].
(6.9.14) By saying "ete," he addresses them all for the sake of success and well-being.

(6.9.15) "Eta" (Come hither), with these words Prajāpati created the gods; "asṛgram" (They have been poured forth), with these he created human beings; "indavaḥ" (The drops), with these the fathers; "tiraḥ pavitram" (Across the filter), with these the cups; "āśavaḥ" (The swift ones), with these the stotra; "viśvāni" (All things), with these the śastra; "abhi saubhaga" (Toward prosperity), with these other creatures.
(6.9.16) Because [he said] "eta," therefore as many gods as there were at first, so many there are now.
(6.9.17) All attained prosperity; for this *vyāhṛti* stands as if established.
(6.9.18) Because [it says] "that which was poured forth," therefore human beings are produced day after day.
(6.9.19) Because [it says] "O drops (*indavas*)," for the ancestors are indeed like drops.
(PB 6.9.20) Like the mind (PB 6.9.21), the created subjects that went forth attained prosperity; those for whom one who knows thus makes this *pratipad* attain that same prosperity.
(PB 6.9.22) The meters indeed brought Soma; the Gandharva Viśvāvasu stole it away from them. With that [Soma], they [the meters] [reached] the waters.

The deities entered it; they sought him, and Viṣṇu beheld him within the waters. He longed for him, thinking, "Is this he? Is this not he? He struck him with his foot; from that, the drops were released separately. To the deities who stood on all sides, he said, "These drops have been released. Indeed, by means of the *bahiṣpavamāna*, the sacrifice is set in motion.
With the words, "As these drops have been poured forth," he performs the *prastāva*; thus he announces the sacrifice that has been created to the deities.

That which is the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*) is indeed unsuccessful and unfavorable to cattle, for it is without the *iḍā*. When he says, "The *iḍā* gathered for us," he makes the morning pressing possessed of the *iḍā* and possessed of cattle.
He should use "davidyūtatyā rucā" as the introductory verse (*pratipad*) for a troop (*vrāta*).
“*Davidyūtatyā receti* is the form of the *gāyatrī*; *pariṣṭobhantya* is that of the *triṣṭubh*; *kṛpa* is that of the *anuṣṭubh*;
and *somāḥ śukrā gavāśiraḥ* is that of the *jagatī*. Indeed, this [verse] is the form of all the meters; for this introductory verse is like the meters themselves.
Thus, he brings them into harmony by means of their own respective forms. (PB 6.9.25)

(6.9.26) These *vrātas* have indeed grown old in their sensory power (*indriya*) and vigor (*vīrya*). The meters are sensory power and vigor; thus, he causes them to prosper through sensory power and vigor itself.
(6.10.1) One should make "O Agni, you purify the lifespans" the opening verse (*pratipad*) for those consecrated ones (*dīkṣita*) who die.
(6.10.2) Those among the consecrated who die are, as it were, unpurified. If this *agnipāvamānī* hymn serves as the opening verse, Agni himself burns them thoroughly, and Pavamāna purifies them.

When he says, "Whatever lifespans," he bestows life upon those who are living. (PB 6.10.4) For one who has been ill for a long time, he should make "O Mitra and Varuṇa, come to us" the opening verse. Indeed, the out-breath and in-breath have departed from him whose illness is long-standing; Mitra and Varuṇa are the out-breath and in-breath; thus he bestows the out-breath and in-breath upon him. (PB 6.10.5)
(6.10.6) "Driving away the adversaries, Soma flows on, driving away the stingy ones"—this one should make the introductory verse for one who is falsely accused.
(6.10.7) For those who falsely accuse are indeed stingy; he thus drives them away from him.
(6.10.8) "Going to Indra’s appointed place"—he thus causes him, being purified and worthy of sacrifice, to go to Indra’s appointed place.
(6.10.9) "Flow on as a bull, O stream!"—with this he should make the introductory verse for a Rājanya; for the Rājanya is indeed a bull; verily, he makes him a bull.

(6.10.10) "And for the one accompanied by the Maruts, O exhilarating one!"—the Maruts are indeed the subjects (*viś*) of the gods; verily, he binds the subjects to him, and the subjects do not depart from him.
(6.10.11) "Bestowing all [powers] through might"—through might and heroism, he encompasses the subjects before him, and the subjects do not depart from him.
"One who desires, 'May I prosper among the people,' should use as the opening verse (*pratipad*) the hymn, 'Flow on, O Indu, as the pressed bull' (RV 9.101.1).

With the words, 'Make us glorious among the people,' he indeed prospers among the multitude of people. One should use the two verses beginning with 'For you two are the lords of heaven' (RV 8.58.1–2) as the opening verse; thus he makes these two share equally in the sacrifice and endows both with the glory of the sacrifice."
"One should employ *prāsya dhārā akṣaran* as the introductory verse (*pratipad*) for one who desires rain.
With *prāsya dhārā akṣaran*, he causes the rain from heaven to fall; with *vṛṣṇaḥ sutasyaujasaḥ*, [he causes it to fall] from the intermediate space;
with *devān anu prabhūṣataḥ*, he establishes it in this world."

(6.10.18) That which remains unoffered is indeed offered away by means of vital power (*ojas*) and manly vigor (*vīrya*). When he says, "Of the vigorous pressed [Soma], by its vital power," he bestows the rain of heaven upon him by means of that very vital power and manly vigor. (6.10.19) He who desires, "May the cattle belonging to the people bow down to me; may the people find cattle for me; may I obtain the kingdom," should employ as the introductory verse (*pratipad*): "Flow with that stream by which the cattle of the people have come here to our house. For this [verse] is such.
The *pratipad* becomes [his]; his kinsmen and cattle bow down to him; he obtains kinsmen and cattle from this kingdom.

(PB 7.1.1) These worlds indeed are the *gāyatra*; it should be sung with three repetitions, for these worlds are three. In that he sings with three repetitions, he measures him out by means of these very worlds.
(PB 7.1.2) He should nod twice and utter "fie! a third time.

When he bellows three times, he thereby causes the *gāyatra* to overflow. He who chants the *udgītha* with a *gāyatra* that has not been countered becomes unstable; for the *hiṅkāra* is indeed the counter-chant (*pratihāra*) of the *gāyatra*.
That [counter-chant] is to be meditated upon mentally; one chants the *udgītha* with a *gāyatra* that has been countered, and thus one becomes firmly established.
(7.1.6) Whoever sings the Gāyatra for these worlds is not cut off from these worlds; these worlds clothe him with strength.

(7.1.7) One should begin softly at first, then higher, then highest; thus he has sung for these worlds. (7.1.8) It should be sung unexpressed. That which is expressed is the harsh part of the Gāyatra; when one sings what is unexpressed, he avoids its harshness.
The *gāyatra* is breath; one should not interrupt it, for the non-interruption of breath. If one interrupts it, he becomes liable to die; if he does not interrupt it, he reaches a full lifespan.

(PB 7.1.10) If he should interrupt it, he should interrupt it in the middle of the *ṛc*; the *gāyatra* is indeed breath, and the *svara* is breath. Thus, he places breath in the very center of his self and reaches a full lifespan.

(PB 7.1.11) One desiring cattle should make the *iḍā* the finale (*nidhana*); one desiring heaven, the *svaḥ*; one desiring glory and Vedic splendor, the *yaśas*; one suffering from illness, the *āyus*; and one practicing sorcery, [he should use] "haṃsi."
(PB 7.1.12) These indeed are the milkings of the Gāyatra.
(PB 7.1.13) He who knows thus becomes possessed of spiritual luster and rich in cattle.

(PB 7.2.1) Prajāpati, having fashioned himself as the sacrifice, bestowed it upon the gods. They could not agree among themselves as to who should take precedence; he said to them, "Enter into a race for this," and they entered the race.
When they went to the race, that is why the *ājyās* have their name "race-goers" (*ājya*).

Indra perceived: "Agni, indeed, will win this first. He said: "Whichever of us two wins this first, let that be for both of us together. Agni won it first, then Mitra and Varuṇa, then Indra; and this one [verse] remained.
The Hotrā was not won; that Indra said to Agni, "That which we two have spoken together—let that be ours. Thus this [laud] belongs to Indra and Agni:
one and a half [verses] are for Agni, one and a half for Indra (PB 7.2.3). There are four [stotras], six deities in total.

The sacrifice is ordained as sixfold; he undertakes the sacrifice in its entirety. All the *ājya* chants have the same deity; that would be a repetition (*jāmi*), so they chant with different deities for the sake of avoiding repetition. They chant with the *ājya* chants for domestic animals; because they chant turning back again, therefore offspring are born facing backward, and therefore they are born facing forward. Therefore...
"They return again after departing" (PB 7.3.1); "By this much indeed he has pressed the midday pressing" (PB 7.3.2), with three meters and five *sāmans*.
(7.3.3) When they praise with the Mādhyandina Pavamāna, they purify that very Mādhyandina pressing.
(7.3.4) Indeed, there are only as many Sāmans in total as there are in the Mādhyandina Pavamāna.
(7.3.5) The Gāyatra has a *nidhana*, while the Aiḍa has no *nidhana*.
(PB 7.3.6) When they praise with the Mādhyandina Pavamāna, they praise with all the *sāmans*.

(PB 7.3.7) The Pavamāna is indeed the self of the sacrifice, the Gāyatrī is its mouth, and the Gāyatra is the breath. In that they praise with the Gāyatra upon the Gāyatrī, they place the vital breaths at the very beginning. (PB 7.3.8) These meters are indeed out-breath and in-breath: the Gāyatrī is the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the Bṛhatī is the diffused breath (*vyāna*), and the Triṣṭubh is the downward breath (*apāna*). In that they praise with these meters, it is for the sake of the non-interruption of the out-breath and in-breath.

(7.3.9) These worlds are indeed these meters: this [earth] is the *gāyatrī*, this middle [atmosphere] is the *bṛhatī*, and that [heaven] is the *triṣṭubh*. When they praise with these meters joined together, it is for the non-interruption of these worlds. (7.3.10) If another meter were to intervene between them, it would cause an interruption of these worlds.
Having praised with the *gāyatra*, they praise with the *nidhanavat* [chant]. This earth, indeed, is the *gāyatrī*; thus, its very abode is established.
(PB 7.3.12) If they were to praise first with that which lacks a *nidhana*, the sacrificer would be without an abode.
They praise with the *nidhanavat*; the *gāyatrī* is indeed vigor, and the *nidhana* is vigor; by means of vigor, he thus brings vigor to fulfillment. (PB 7.3.13)
(7.3.14) They take hold of the Bṛhatī by means of the Aiḍa [verse].
(7.3.15) Cattle indeed are the iḍā, and cattle are the Bṛhatī; thus he places cattle among cattle.
(7.3.16) Upon the Bṛhatī, the greatest number of Sāmans occur.
In that case as well, there is the *triṇidhana* (PB 7.3.18).
For this middle world is, as it were, weakest; therefore, its own abode is thus made.
It has the *triṇidhana*; there are three gaps in the *savana*s, and they are closed up by it.

It has three *nidhanas*; these worlds are three; verily, he finds firm support in these very worlds. It has three *nidhanas*; by this, indeed, the midday pressing is established. If it were not to have three *nidhanas*, the midday pressing would be unstable.

The *nidhana*s consist of two syllables; the sacrificer has two feet. [This] establishes the sacrificer himself upon the sacrifice and the cattle. (PB 7.3.23) It is without a *nidhana* at the end, so that there may be no falling away from the heavenly world. (PB 7.3.24) If it were to have a *nidhana*, it would strike the sacrificer down from the heavenly world.

It is performed with the *svāra* [melody] (PB 7.3.26). Indeed, by means of the *svara*, food is finally bestowed upon the gods; thus, by means of the *svara* itself, he bestows food upon the gods at the end. (PB 7.3.27) The *gāyatra* [chant] occurs at the beginning, and the *svāra* at the end.
The Gāyatra is indeed breath, and the Svara is breath; thus he places breath on both sides. Therefore, animals have breath on both sides.
In that the Gāyatra is at the beginning and the Svara is at the end, he goes forth by means of the out-breath and establishes himself in the in-breath.
This indeed is the heavenly part of the sacrifice: namely, the midday pressing and the Pavamāna-stotra of the midday pressing.

When the *bṛhatī* [verse] of the *pavamāna* [laud] is used, and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is given at the *bṛhatī* hymn, it is given in the very abode of the heavenly world (PB 7.4.2). The gods indeed said to the meters, "By means of you, let us go to the heavenly world. They employed the *gāyatrī*;
they did not reach [the goal] with it. They employed the *triṣṭubh*; they did not reach it with it. They employed the *jagatī*.

Not pervading [the world] with that, they employed the *anuṣṭubh*; not pervading even a small amount with that, they extracted the essences from these quarters and added four syllables; it became the *bṛhatī*. With it, they pervaded these worlds.
"By means of the *bṛhatī*, as a boundary, may we pervade these worlds"—that is the reason for the greatness (*bṛhattva*) of the *bṛhatī*.

(7.4.4) They placed cattle at her ends; for the *bṛhatī* is indeed cattle. When sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are given during the chant of the *bṛhatī*, they are given in their own proper abode. (7.4.5) Now, they say: "The other meters are larger; why then is this one called the *bṛhatī*? Because she pervades these worlds, and no other meter whatsoever does so—namely, those seven meters that increase by four syllables each.

They result in the *bṛhatī*; therefore it is called the *bṛhatī*. Now, they say: "The morning pressing is *gāyatra*, the midday pressing is *traiṣṭubha*, and the third pressing is *jāgata*; why then do they chant with the *bṛhatī* at the midday pressing?
By means of the *bahiṣpavamāna*, the gods carried the sun to the heavenly world; it did not remain steady. Him—

With the Bṛhatī they supported [the sun] at midday; therefore they praise with the Bṛhatī at midday, for this [meter] supports Āditya at midday. Whatever meters they employ for the midday pressing, they all resolve into the Triṣṭubh; therefore they lead from the midday libation with the Triṣṭubh.
Prajāpati desired, "May I become many; may I procreate. He stood there grieving and feeling insignificant.

He saw this Āmahīyava [Sāman]; with it, he created these creatures. Once created, they felt significant (*amahīyanta*). Because they felt significant, it is called the Āmahīyava. Once created, those creatures departed from him. Of them, [the seer] said, "Seated in heaven, take [them] to the earth," and thus he took away their vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

When his vital breaths had been taken away, they returned to him; he gave back the vital breaths with the words, "To them [be] fierce protection and great glory. They then strove to rise up against him; he struck down their fury with the words, "I shall praise them. Thereupon, indeed, they submitted to him for preeminence.
Those of equal status stand for preeminence for him who knows thus.
This Āmahīyava is indeed both the creation of living beings and the separation from evil;
he becomes separated from evil who knows thus.

The gods, desiring glory, performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*). Agni, Indra, Vāyu, and Makha were among them. They said, "Whatever glory comes to us, let that be common to us all. Glory came to Makha; having seized it, he departed. They sought to seize it from him by force. They surrounded him; he stood firm with his own bow as his support. The tip of his bow—
Falling upwards, it cut off the head; that became the *pravargya*. The *makha* is indeed the sacrifice; when they perform the *pravargya*, they restore the head of the sacrifice.
The gods then divided that glory (*yaśas*); from it, Agni extracted the *raurava* [sāman].
He indeed extracted that vigor of cattle; the *raurava* chant is indeed cattle.
He who knows thus becomes possessed of cattle.
Agni is indeed *ru*, and this *raurava* belongs to him.

The Asuras indeed surrounded the gods. Then Indra perceived these two *raura* chants, which spread in all directions; with them he scorched them. Being scorched, they cried out (*aravan*); because they cried out, it is called the *raurava*.
Then Indra drew forth the *yaudhājaya*; he drew forth that very thunderbolt, for the *yaudhājaya* is indeed the thunderbolt.
(7.5.13) He hurls the thunderbolt at his rival, he who knows thus.
(7.5.14) Indra is indeed the Conqueror by Battle; this [sāman] belongs to him, it is the Yaudhājaya.
(7.5.15) "O men, we have conquered by battle!"—therefore it is called the Yaudhājaya.
Then Vāyu extracted the Auśana [Sāman].
He indeed extracted that vital power of breath; for the Auśana is the vital breaths. He who knows thus attains a full lifespan.

Vāyu, indeed, is Uśanas; therefore this [sāman] belongs to Uśanas. Uśanas Kāvya was once the domestic priest of the Asuras. The gods invited him with their wish-fulfilling cows (*kāmadughā*). They gave these *auśana* [sāmans] to him. The *auśana* [sāmans] are indeed wish-fulfilling cows. Wish-fulfilling cows attend upon him who knows thus.

Prajāpati desired, "May I be many; may I procreate. He meditated silently with his mind. That which was in his mind became the Bṛhat-sāman. He thought, "This embryo has indeed entered within me; let me bring it forth by means of speech.
He emitted speech, and that speech followed after the Rathantara-sāman.
"The noble ones have crossed over the chariot by their speed"—that is the *rathantara*-ness of the *rathantara*.
"From that the *bṛhat* was born after; great, O men, he has long been within this"—that is the *bṛhat*-ness of the *bṛhat*.
Just as an eldest son is preeminent, so is the *bṛhat* among the offspring of Prajāpati.
This is indeed the eldest Brāhmaṇa;
he who knows thus attains pre-eminence.
Now, as they say: "The Bṛhat first arose in Prajāpati; why then did the Rathantara attain the first connection?"

The Bṛhat alone came into being first; however, he created the Rathantara first during the creation, and therefore it attained union first. Their *nidhana* was the same; they could not stand upon it. They entered into a contest (*ājī*). Of these two, the Bṛhat won out with "ha" as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), while the Rathantara coiled around it with "as" as the downward breath (*apāna*). Indeed, the Bṛhat and Rathantara are the vital breath and the downward breath. One should employ both for one who has been long ill; for the vital breath and the downward breath have departed from him who has been long ill. [Thus] one places the vital breath and the downward breath back into him.

(7.6.13) Now they say: "Since both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara have their *nidhana*s outside [the verse], why does the Bṛhat share *nidhana*s that are outside while the Rathantara shares those that are inside? (7.6.14–15) The Bṛhat is the out-breath (*prāṇa*); therefore it shares the *nidhana*s that are outside, for the out-breath is external. The Rathantara is the in-breath (*apāna*); therefore it shares the *nidhana*s that are inside, for the in-breath is internal.
Indeed, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara are two great trees joined together by the *nidhana*.
When two great trees collide, much of them lies shattered and broken there.
The *bṛhat* is indeed related to the cow (*ira*), while the *rathantara* is related to the sheep (*iḍā*). The *bṛhat* is mind, the *rathantara* is speech;
the *bṛhat* is the *sāman*, the *rathantara* is the *ṛc*; the *bṛhat* is the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the *rathantara* is the downward breath (*apāna*); the *bṛhat* is yonder world.

"Having mentally observed these [syllables] as the *rathantara*, he should chant the *udgītha*; thus he chants with these two [sāmans] already prepared. The *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* are indeed cattle; he introduces the first verse with an eight-syllable [foot]; thereby he wins eight-hoofed cattle."

(7.7.2) With a two-syllable [formula] he intones the *prastāva* of the two following verses; the sacrificer has two feet; verily he establishes the sacrificer himself upon the sacrifice and upon cattle.

(7.7.3) With a five-syllable [formula] he performs the *pratihāra* of the *rathantara*; that is fivefold (*pāṅkta*); thereby he wins cattle. (7.7.4) With a four-syllable [formula] he performs the *pratihāra* of the *bṛhat*; that is four-footed; thereby he wins cattle.
(7.7.5) Verily, neither the Bṛhat nor the Rathantara restrained a single metre; therefore they placed two Kakubhs above them.
Hence the Bṛhatī is first and the two Kakubhs are above it. Therefore they perform the Bṛhat and Rathantara with a single verse, for those two did not restrain a single metre.
(7.7.6) He ascends nine heights of the *bṛhatī*; there are nine vital breaths; verily, he wins the vital breaths.

(7.7.7) On the first [verse], he ascends three: the past, the present, and the future; verily, he wins those. On the middle [verse], he ascends three: himself, his offspring, and his cattle; verily, he wins those. On the last [verse], he ascends three: these are the three worlds.

He establishes himself in these very worlds and wins all desires, he who, knowing thus, ascends the ascending steps of the Bṛhat. With the thunderbolt, indeed, the Prastotṛ impels the Udgātṛ when he chants the Rathantara; he should chant while placing the ocean between [himself and the Prastotṛ], saying "Speech!"—for speech is indeed the ocean.
"He places the ocean within for the sake of non-injury" (PB 7.7.10).
"It should be sung powerfully; thus he takes up the thunderbolt as it is set forth" (PB 7.7.11). "By one performing with strength, it should be sung as if luring; he thus lures the thunderbolt."

It should be sung quickly for the attainment of the heavenly world. The *rathantara* is indeed the chariot of the gods; it should be sung so as to establish it with every syllable, for a chariot stands firm on each of its wheels.

He who stands upon the chariot of the gods without holding onto it falls away from it. This earth is indeed the chariot of the gods; one should sing the *udgītha* while holding onto this earth, and thus one does not fall away from it.

The *rathantara* is indeed the lord; it is the eye of the *udgātṛ*. When about to chant the *prastāva*, he should close his eyes; he should look at the "heaven-seer" (*svardṛś*). His sight does not desert him. The *rathantara* is procreation.

If he says, "of that which stands" (*yat tasthuṣaḥ*), the speech of the *udgātṛ* becomes unstable; he destroys even procreation. He should say, "of that which has stood" (*asthuṣaḥ*) or "of that which stands well" (*susthuṣaḥ*); thus the speech of the *udgātṛ* becomes stable.
"It does not destroy procreation either" (PB 7.7.17).
Indeed, the *pṛṣṭha* chants were created; by means of them, the gods went to the heavenly world. Of those, the *rathantara* was unable to fly up because of its greatness (*mahiman*).
Vasiṣṭha, having set aside that greatness and praised with it, went to the heavenly world. Having gathered those [parts] together, one should chant the *udgītha*.

(7.7.19) That greatness of yours which is in the cows, that which is in the waters, or that which is in your chariot, or that which is in your thunder, or that greatness of yours which is in the fire—with that, come together! O Rathantara, be rich in wealth for us!

(7.8.1) The waters indeed reached the seasonal [sacrifice]. Vāyu turned upon their surface; from that, desirable wealth came into being. Mitrāvaruṇa beheld it there. They both said, "O men, announce this desirable thing among the gods! Therefore, it is called the Vāmadevya.
As they were taking possession of it, they said, "We have found this; let us not exclude one another from this. Prajāpati said, "This has indeed been born from me; it is mine.
Agni said, "This food has indeed been born from me; it is mine. Indra said, "This is the station of the most excellent; it is mine. PB 7.8.2.

"I am the best among you, or rather, this belongs to me," said one; then all the gods said, "This which has arisen from the waters belongs to us as our deity; this is ours. Then Prajāpati said, "Let this be for all of us; let us all live upon this. They deposited it upon the *pṛṣṭha* chants; for the *Vāmadevya* belongs to all the deities.

In that [the verses] contain the word *kava*, by that it belongs to Prajāpati; for Prajāpati is indeed *kava*. In that they are unexpressed (*anirukta*), by that it belongs to Prajāpati; for Prajāpati is indeed unexpressed. In that they are in *gāyatrī* meters, by that it belongs to Agni; for Agni has the *gāyatrī* as his meter.
In that they placed them upon the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras], by that it belongs to Indra; for all the *pṛṣṭhas* are exclusively (*niṣkevalya*) Indra’s.
In that the Maitrāvaruṇa recites [the *anucara*], by that it belongs to Mitra and Varuṇa;
in that the final foot has many deities, by that it belongs to the Viśvedevas; thus he becomes established in all forms.
Prajāpati indeed saw this Gāyatrī womb; he meditated: "From this womb let me create the *pṛṣṭha* stotras."
He created the Rathantara; after it, the sound of a chariot was created.
He created the Bṛhat; after it, the sound of thunder was created. He created the Vairūpa; after it, the sound of that [wind] was created.
He created the Vairāja; after it, the sound of fire was created.
He created the Śakvarī verses; after that, the sound of the waters was created. He created the Revatī verses; after that, the sound of the cattle was created.
Indeed, these were created together with those sounds.
(7.8.15) All sounds, all holy words, speak for him who knows thus. (7.9.1) The Vāmadevya is indeed the father; the Pṛṣṭhas are the sons. (7.9.2) From this very womb, indeed, these were created.
Therefore, they perform the chant of the *pṛṣṭha* hymns with the Vāmadevya [Sāman] for the sake of peace (*śānti*).
For whatever the son does that is unpeaceful, the father pacifies it.
This middle world is indeed the Vāmadevya; from this [world], these two worlds, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, were emitted in all directions.
When they praise with the *rathaṃtara*, those animals which belong to the *rathaṃtara* resort to the intermediate space;
when they praise with the *bṛhat*, those animals which belong to the *bṛhat* resort to the intermediate space. These [animals] are secured by the *vāmadevya* chant.
Sitting firmly on the *dhruva* seat, one should chant the *udgītha* with the *vāmadevya* for the attainment of cattle.
(7.9.8) Cattle come to him who knows thus.

(7.9.9) The Vāmadevya is indeed the intermediate space; it should be sung as if shaking it, for the intermediate space is, as it were, shaken. The Vāmadevya is cattle; it should be sung as if not harming them, for the sake of the non-injury of cattle. (7.9.10) "How, indeed, should the Vāmadevya be sung? they ask.
Just as a finger-guard protects the fingers while gathering them together without crushing them, or as the wind blows gently upon the waters;
so should the *vāmadevya* be sung with its own inherent strength. Indeed, he who sings the *vāmadevya* with its own inherent strength becomes possessed of that very strength.
(7.9.14) One goes by another's path of departure; one does not go by another's path of departure.

(7.9.15) One should not sing in response to the *bṛhat* or the *rathantara*; it should be sung in its own proper place (*āyatana*). Thus, one becomes possessed of a proper place. (7.9.16) The gods indeed divided the cattle among themselves; they excluded Rudra. He overlooked them at the *vāmadevya* hymn.

It should be sung unexpressed (anirukta). (PB 7.9.18) If one expresses it [explicitly], he consigns the cattle to Rudra; Rudra becomes the master of the cattle for that year. (PB 7.9.19) One who desires cattle should chant with the Vāmadevya on the Revatī verses.
The *revatī* verses are indeed the waters, and the *vāmadevya* is cattle; verily, from the waters he produces cattle for him.
He becomes unassailable in respect of cattle, and his progeny becomes as if closed in upon itself.
For he goes from the *kavatī* verses to Prajāpati.
(PB 7.10.1) These two worlds were together; desiring to separate, they said, "Let us marry; let there be a union between us.
(PB 7.10.2) To them, this [world] gave the Śyaita for that [world], and that [world] gave the Naudhasa to this one.
(PB 10.3) Thereupon, their *nidhana*s became inverted; for the Śyaita and Naudhasa are indeed the marriage of the gods.
He who knows thus obtains a marriage that is more prosperous.

Indeed, from here these worlds go upward as they are being formed, and from there they come downward as they are being formed. When they chant with the *rathantara*, they thereby yoke this world; with the *vāmadevya* and the *naudhasa*, the intermediate space; and when they chant with the *bṛhat*, they thereby yoke that world.
"Verily, by means of the Vāmadevya and the Śyaita [sāmans], one worships these worlds as fashioned in the intermediate space—he who knows thus.
"The Bṛhat and Rathantara are indeed the Śyaita and Naudhasa; for they employ the Naudhasa in response to the Rathantara."
They offer that very Bṛhat to him, for the Naudhasa is the Bṛhat in a hidden sense;
and when they offer the Śyaita as a response to the Bṛhat, they offer the Rathantara to him, for the Śyaita is the Rathantara in a hidden sense.
(7.10.9) One who knows thus praises with both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara.

(7.10.10) The gods indeed divided the Brahman; Nodhas Kākṣīvata came to them, and they said, "A seer has come to us; let us give the Brahman to him. They bestowed this Sāman upon him; therefore it is called the Naudhasa.
"The Naudhasa is indeed Brahman" (PB 7.10.11). "One who desires spiritual luster should praise with this; he becomes possessed of spiritual luster" (PB 7.10.12).
Now follows this Śyaita [sāman].

Prajāpati created cattle; once they were created, they departed from him. He addressed them with this *sāman*, and they stood still for him; they became the *śyaita* [melody]. Because they became the *śyaita*, therefore it is called *śyaita*. Cattle, indeed, are the *śyaita*.
One who desires cattle should praise with this; he becomes possessed of cattle.
Prajāpati created offspring; once created, they grieved. He smelled them with the Śyaita [Sāman], saying "hum. Thereupon, indeed, they flourished.
The offspring flourish in that year in which one who knows thus chants the udgītha with the Śyaita.
The Udgātṛ is indeed Prajāpati for the sacrificer; in that he utters "hiṃ" with the Śyaita, having become Prajāpati himself, he smells the offspring.
(7.10.17) It has *vasu* as its finale; cattle indeed are wealth (*vasu*); verily, he finds firm support in cattle.

(8.1.1) One should perform the *brahmasāman* for one practicing sorcery with the *kāṇva* [sāman] which has *āṣ* as its finale or *vaṣaṭ* as its finale, and it should have *abhi* as its finale during the midday *pavamāna*.

(8.1.2) This *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed a divine arrow. Indra, saying "at him! (*abhi*), hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra; by saying "at him! (*abhi*), having hurled the thunderbolt at him, he pierces him among the gods with the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
One desiring cattle should perform the *traikakubha* as the *brahmasāman* upon these verses: "O Friend, you have indeed praised... (PB 8.1.4).
Indra delivered the *yatīs* to the *sālāvṛkas*; of them, three remained: Rāyovāja, Bṛhadgiri, and Pṛthuraśmi. They said, "Who will support our children? Indra replied, "I shall."
Having placed them upon the Trikakubh [verse], he went forth; he saw this *sāman*. Because he saw that which is the Trikakubh, it is therefore called the Traikakubha.
He ran back again toward himself [with the words]: "O most powerful god, you indeed have praised the mortal;
O Maghavan, there is no other than you who is a comforter, O Indra—I speak these words to you. With this *pragātha* and with this...

With the *sāman*, he created a thousand cattle and gave them to these [beings]; they became established. (PB 8.1.6) He who desires cattle, or he who desires stability, should chant with this *pragātha* using this *sāman*; he obtains a thousand cattle and becomes established. (PB 8.1.7) This *sāman* indeed possesses triple power; it has verses addressed to Indra and triple sensory power (*indriya*), and its finale (*nidhana*) is "Indra. Thus, he becomes established in sensory power and vigor.
(8.1.8) One should perform the *traiśoka* as the *brahmasāman* for one who has been long ill.
(8.1.9) These worlds were indeed together; they grieved. Indra removed their grief with this *sāman*. Because he removed the grief of those three who were grieving, it is called the *traiśoka*.

(8.1.10) That [grief] which he removed from this world entered a harlot; that which [he removed] from the intermediate space entered a eunuch; that which [he removed] from yonder world entered a sinner.
(8.1.11) Therefore, one should not seek to destroy them; for he who reaches their hope, it is to him alone that they distribute their sorrows.
(8.1.12) He whose illness is long-standing is indeed pierced by sorrow; when the *traiśoka* becomes the *brahmasāman*, it strikes away the sorrow from him.
(8.1.13) They conclude with the finale (*nidhana*) "divā" (by day); for "divā" is indeed the dawning of light (*vyuṣṭi*), and it causes the dawn to break for him.

One desiring a firm foundation should perform the *brahmasāman* known as the Kāṇva, which has the *āṣ* as its *nidhana*. Kaṇva indeed saw this *sāman* with the *nidhana* [ending] in *arte*; he did not find a firm foundation. He overheard a cat sneezing, "āṣ! He then saw that very [syllable] as the *nidhana*. From that, indeed, he found a firm foundation—namely, this *sāman*.
"It serves for stability" (PB 8.2.3).
One should perform the Vasiṣṭha-janitra as the Brahman-sāman for one who desires offspring.
Vasiṣṭha, having lost his son, saw this Sāman; he was procreated with offspring and cattle. In that this Sāman exists, it is for the sake of procreation.
(8.2.5) One should perform the *brahmasāman* as the *ātharvaṇa* for one who desires the world.
(8.2.6) For it was the *Atharvans*, desiring the world, who saw this *sāman*; by means of it, they beheld the immortal world. That this *sāman* exists is for the procreation of the heavenly world.
(8.2.7) One whose rival exists should perform the *abhīvarta* as the *brahmasāman*.
(8.2.8) By means of the *abhīvarta* [chant], the gods indeed overcame the Asuras; therefore, when the *abhīvarta* is the *brahmasāman*, it serves for the overcoming of the rival.
(8.2.9) One should perform the *śrāyantīya* as the *brahmasāman* for one who has fallen away from the sacrifice.

(8.2.10) Prajāpati lusted after his own daughter, Uṣas; his semen fell away and was discharged into her. He mixed it together, thinking, "Let this not be defiled for me," and thus he made it into something real (*sat*).
"Verily, cattle [are obtained]" (PB 8.2.11).
When the Śrāyantīya becomes the Brahman-sāman, it both provides him with prosperity and brings him into being (PB 8.3.1).
The gods and the asuras contended for these worlds; those gods then sought refuge with Prajāpati.
He gave this *sāman* to them, thinking, "With this I shall drive them away. With it they drove them away from these worlds;
because they drove them away (*akālayan*), it is called the *Kāleya*.
He who knows thus drives away his rival from these worlds.

(8.3.3) Among the gods there was a Stoma named Tara, and among the Asuras there was a sacrifice named Vidadvasu. With the words, "O gods, with the Taras [you seized] the Vidadvasu," the gods appropriated the sacrifice of the Asuras by means of the Stoma.
(8.3.4) He who knows thus appropriates the sacrifice of his rival by means of the Stoma.
(8.3.5) There were indeed gods named Sāhdyās; they, having cut off the third pressing, [retained it] by means of the midday pressing.
They went together to the heavenly world; that which the gods fashioned as the *loka* (world), that is the *kāleya*. It exists for the continuity of the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*).
The third pressing indeed belongs to Vidadvasu; when he intones, "With your hymns, [we praise] Vidadvasu," he thus speaks in reference to the third pressing itself.
All forms indeed are the *kāleya*: in that it has the *pada* as its *prastāva*, it is the *rāthantara*; in that it [has the *bṛhatī*...].

Because it rises up from what has risen, it is *bārhata*; because the *pratihāra* possesses *stobhas*, it is *bārhata*; because the *iḍā* is moving, it is *rāthaṃtara*. Thus, he finds firm footing in all forms. There were indeed gods named Sādhyas; they went to the heavenly world together with the entire sacrifice.
Those gods said to the meters, "Bring back the Soma. They sent forth the Jagatī;

it departed having left behind three syllables and returned as a single-syllabled meter. They sent forth the Triṣṭubh; it departed having left behind one syllable and returned as a three-syllabled meter.
They sent forth the Gāyatrī; at that time, the meters consisted of four syllables each, and she returned having taken those syllables with her.

She came, having become eight-syllabled; she sucked the three pressings with her two hands, and having bitten with her teeth at two pressings, she sucked the third pressing. Therefore, those two pressings are rich in *aṃśu* (stalks), while the third pressing is sucked (*dhīta*), for they suck it after having bitten it with their teeth. She carried it off; of that [Soma] being carried away, the stalks (*aṃśavaḥ*) which fell away became the *pūtīka* plants, as did the flowers.

Those *arjunā* shoots were scattered; because they were scattered (*prāprothat*), they are called *praprotha*. Therefore, at the third pressing, they pour in the *āśir* milk. It is the essence of that very Soma which the cows eat that they pour in, for the sake of its being accompanied by Soma.
(PB 8.4.2) Those two, the Triṣṭubh and the Jagatī, said to the Gāyatrī, "Come to you. She said, "What will I have from that?"
"Let it be as you desire," they said. She replied, "The morning pressing shall be mine entirely;
I shall lead forward the two later pressings. Therefore, the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī, and the Gāyatrī leads forward the two later pressings.
The Triṣṭubh approached them with three syllables; having become eleven-syllabled, she was propagated. The Jagatī approached her with one syllable; having become twelve-syllabled, she was propagated.

Therefore they say: "The *gāyatrī* indeed is all the meters, for it nourishes these nourishments. (PB 8.4.5) Indra went forth from the third pressing, loathing it; the gods made it sweet with the words "svādiṣṭhayā" ("most sweet"), they made it intoxicating with "madiṣṭhayā" ("most intoxicating"), and they caused it to flow with "pavasva soma dhārayā" ("flow, O Soma, in a stream"); he was pressed for Indra to drink.

Thus, it was from that very point that Indra turned back when [the priest] begins with the words "svādiṣṭhayā madiṣṭhayā" (with the sweetest, the most intoxicating), so that the third pressing may possess Indra. Indeed, among the gods the cattle were the sweetest (*svādiṣṭhā*), while among the Asuras they were the most intoxicating (*madiṣṭhā*). By means of the words "svādiṣṭhayā madiṣṭhayā," the gods appropriated the cattle of the Asuras.
He who knows this appropriates the cattle of his rival.
Regarding those [stotras], there is the *saṃhita*.

(PB 8.4.9) The Sādhyas were indeed gods by name; having cut off the third pressing, they went to the heavenly world together with the midday pressing. The gods restored that by means of the *saṃhita*;
because they restored it, it is called *saṃhita*.
The *kāleya* chant occurs at the beginning, and the *saṃhita* at the end; for by these two, the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) is made continuous.

Indeed, all forms are contained within the *saṃhita*: in that it has the *prastāva* on the words, it belongs to the *rathantara*; in that it ascends through the ascending notes of the *bṛhat*, it belongs to the *bṛhat*; and in that its *nidhana* is on the words, it belongs to the *rathantara*. Thus, one finds firm standing in all forms.
(8.5.1) These two [metres] are the Uṣṇih and the Kakubh.
(8.5.2) With the Uṣṇih and the Kakubh, Indra indeed struck Vṛtra with the thunderbolt; he struck him with the Kakubh as he was exerting his prowess, and with the Uṣṇih he struck him.
Therefore, the middle foot of the Kakubh has the most syllables, for that is the place of exertion.
He struck it down; therefore, the last foot of the *uṣṇih* has the most syllables, for the thunderbolt is like something heavy at the front.
He who knows thus hurls the thunderbolt at his rival.
