These two, the *uṣṇih* and the *kakubh*, are indeed the nostrils of the sacrifice; therefore, though they are the same metre, they carry the sacrifice in different ways. Therefore, from the same nose, though it is one, the two breaths are distinct.

The *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* meters are indeed the vital breaths; therefore, they do not utter the *vaṣaṭ* call with them, for if they were to utter the *vaṣaṭ*, they would cast the vital breaths into the fire.

In those [verses], there is the *sapha* and the *vipha*; the third pressing is indeed like a hoof-ring (*sapha*), and it is for the sake of providing the third pressing with a hoof-ring that this *auṣkala* chant is used.
By means of this, Prajāpati created abundant cattle; he bestowed form upon them when this *sāman* is performed.
He bestows form upon the cattle themselves.
(PB 8.5.7) "With your ancient conquest of the soma-juice"—these two Virājs consist of both pādas and syllables.
By means of the pāda-form, the gods went to the heavenly world; by means of the syllable-form, the seers attained understanding. Since these consist of both pādas and syllables...
"The two Virāj verses come into being for the perception of the heavenly world" (PB 8.5.8).
Among them is the Śyāvāśva [Sāman] (PB 8.5.9).

The Śyāvāśva, son of Arvānānas, while seated at a sacrificial session, was carried away by a desert; he beheld this Sāman and with it released rain. Thereupon he indeed established himself; thereupon he found a path.
"This *sāman* is indeed the finder of the way" (PB 8.5.10); he who praises with it finds the way and becomes firmly established (PB 8.5.11).

Indra departed from the third pressing, loathing it; the gods called after him with the *śyāvāśva* [chant], saying, "Come hither! Come hither! He returned. In that this *sāman* exists, it belongs to the third pressing.
(8.5.12) Now, this is the Āndhīgava. Andhīgu, desiring cattle, saw this *sāman*; by means of it, he created a thousand cattle.
That this *sāman* is performed is for the nourishment of cattle. There is an *aiḍa* finale in the middle.
By this, indeed, the third pressing is established. If there were no *aiḍa* finale in the middle, the third pressing would be unestablished.

(8.5.13) They approach the *nidhana* consisting of ten syllables in the middle; the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and thus he finds firm support in the *virāj*. (8.5.14) "He purifies himself toward what is dear" (*abhi priyāṇi pavate*): this is the *kāva* Sāman belonging to Prajāpati.
(8.5.15) Offspring are indeed what is dear, and cattle are what is dear; he finds firm support in offspring and in cattle as he seeks to find firm support.

(PB 8.5.16) These two, the *auśanaka* and the *kāva*, are indeed the reins of the sacrifice; this *devakośa* is the vessel that holds the sacrifice together when these two are at the end, for the sake of the sacrifice’s security.

(PB 8.6.1) The gods divided the *brahman*; the essence (*rasa*) that remained over became the *yajñāyajñīya*. (PB 8.6.2) This *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed the essence of the *brahman*; when they chant with the *yajñāyajñīya*, they establish the sacrifice in the very essence of the *brahman*.
The *yajñāyajñīya* is indeed the womb; from this womb Prajāpati created the sacrifice, therefore it is called the *yajñāyajñīya*.

For this reason, in former times, the Brāhmaṇas chanted the *bahiṣpavamāna* with this [sāman], thinking, "From the womb let us extend the sacrifice. Thereby they praise the sacrifice; thus he establishes the sacrifice in its womb.
Indeed, the entire sacrifice was among the Asuras; the gods perceived the *yajñāyajñīya*, and for them [there arose] the *yajñā-yajñā*.
With the verse "To you, O Agnis," they chose the Agnihotra; with "And with song after song for skill," the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
with "Ever forward we [serve] the immortal Jātavedas," the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; and with "I shall praise Mitra as dear," the Soma sacrifice (PB 8.6.6).
[The verses are: "Sacrifices to you, O Agni, and with song for skill"; "Ever forward we [serve] the immortal Jātavedas"; and "Mitra as dear."
"Indeed, at that time the meters did not exist [as such]; thus it was said. Those gods, having turned back the onset [of the Asuras], appropriated the sacrifice of the Asuras by means of the meters.
He who knows thus appropriates the sacrifice of his rival by means of the meters.
(8.6.8) Regarding this, Kūśāmba Svāyava, the Brahman Lātavya, used to say: "Which young porpoise, having been cast upon the path of the sacrifice today, will gulp it down?
(8.6.9) This *yajñāyajñīya* chant, when cast upon the path of the sacrifice, is indeed that young porpoise. When the Udgātṛ says "girā-girā," he thereby swallows his own self.
(8.6.10) Having made it *aira*, one should sing it; thus one establishes the sacrifice in *irā* (nourishment), and the Udgātṛ becomes free from premature death.

(8.6.11) In the Vaiśvānara [stotra], the Udgātṛ indeed places himself when he says, "pra-pra vayam" (forth and forth we). He should rather say, "praprīṃ vayam" (we have gladdened). Thus he circumambulates the Vaiśvānara itself.
(8.6.12) Whoever approaches the *chandas* while concealing [his performance] becomes worse after having sung.
This is what is meant by concealing the *chandas*: saying "I did not recite," when one should rather say "I recited," or "I recited well. One should not conceal [the performance].
“Desire comes to him who is more wealthy; he becomes one who has risen up” (PB 8.6.13). Indeed, the sacrifices of one whose speech is incomplete leak away through that deficiency of speech.

Those sacrifices whose conclusion is the *yajñāyajñīya* are indeed sacrifices with incomplete speech. That which is untruth is the deficiency of speech; whatever untruth an *agniṣṭoma*-sacrificer utters [is such a deficiency].
He said: "After that, his sacrifice flows away; [therefore] it must finally be established by means of the *akṣara*. By means of the *akṣara* alone, he heals even the breach of the sacrifice.
The *akṣara* is indeed the form of the *virāj*; thus, he finally finds firm support in the *virāj*. (PB 8.6.14)
(8.7.1) Indeed, from here in the morning the meters are yoked upwards; from there at the *yajñāyajñīya* chant they are yoked downwards.

"With song, for Agni, [I offer] you sacrifice" (*yajñā vo agnaye girā ca dakṣase*) has twelve syllables; "We [praise] the immortal Jātavedas" (*pra vayam amṛtaṃ jātavedasam*) has eleven syllables; "I have praised the dear friend" (*priyaṃ mitraṃ na śaṃsiṣam*) has eight syllables.
He brings the last [verse] to completion as an *anuṣṭubh*. The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed this [earth]; verily, he finds support on this very [earth].
The *anuṣṭubh* is speech; verily, he finds support in speech. The *anuṣṭubh* is preeminence; verily, he finds support in preeminence.
"How indeed should the *yajñāyajñīya* be sung? they ask. "Just like a draft-ox urinating, thinking 'thus indeed,' 'thus indeed.'"

(8.7.5) "The Udgātṛ approaches Vaiśvānara while following after him," they say, when he recites the verse of the *yajñāyajñīya*. He should sing as if stepping around; indeed, he thus steps around Vaiśvānara.

(8.7.6) "In Vaiśvānara, the Adhvaryu releases the members of the assembly (*sadasyas*)," they say, when he brings back the chant of the *yajñāyajñīya*. He should sing with his head covered, so that there may be no burning by Vaiśvānara.
(8.7.7) "For the ancestors do not perceive one who is covered; indeed, at the chanting of the *yajñāyajñīya*, the ancestors [perceive]..."
As they desire to know each thing according to its nature, covering with their ears, that which was covered they perceive as uncovered; the Fathers do not harm them, nor does Vaiśvānara.
Behind [the altar], the wives pour out water; thereby they appease Vaiśvānara, for water is indeed peace.
(8.7.9) Moreover, they pour out semen, for water is indeed semen.

(8.7.10) They sprinkle [him] upon his right thighs, for semen is poured out from the right side. (8.7.11) Having pushed back [the garment] as if it were something great, they thereby generate his mind.

(8.7.12) They cause the wives to be looked at by the Udgātṛ for the sake of the depositing of seed. (8.7.13) They cause them to be looked at in response to the *hiṅkāra*, for from the *hiṅkāra* seed is deposited. (8.7.14) They cause them to be looked at up to the third [look], for seed is threefold.

The gods, having conquered the Agniṣṭoma, were unable to conquer the Ukthas. They said to Agni, "By you as our mouth, let us win this. He said, "What shall be mine from that? They replied, "Whatever you desire. He said, "Let the Ukthas be led forward with hymns addressed to me as their deity."
Therefore they introduce the *uktha* hymns with verses addressed to Agni;
therefore, moreover, they are in *gāyatrī* verses, for Agni has the *gāyatrī* as his metre.
Having made Agni their mouth, they advanced together with the horse; because they advanced together with the horse, it is called the *Sākamaśva*.

(8.8.5) Therefore, they introduce the *uktha*s with the *sākamaśva* [chant], for by means of this they first conquered them. (8.8.6) Indra said, "Who and I shall we pursue this? "I," said Varuṇa. Varuṇa followed after it, and Indra brought it; therefore, the *aindrāvaruṇa* [stotra] is recited after it.
(8.8.7) He (Indra) said, "Who and I shall we pursue this? "I," said Bṛhaspati. He... him.

Bṛhaspati supported [the sacrifice] and Indra fetched [the oblation]; therefore, the offering to Indra and Bṛhaspati is recited. He said, "Who and I shall we two support this? "I," said Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu supported it and Indra fetched [the oblation];
therefore, the offering to Indra and Viṣṇu is recited.
(8.8.8) He brought cattle for them; indeed, the *ukthas* are cattle. One who desires cattle should praise with the *uktha*; he becomes possessed of cattle.
(8.8.9) With the *bṛhat* [sāman], Indra struck Vṛtra with his thunderbolt. Its brilliance flew away and became the *saubhara*.
(8.8.10) "A repetition (*jāmi*) is committed in the sacrifice," they say, "when the *rathantara* is the *pṛṣṭha* [laud] and the *rathantara* [is used again]."
"The junction is not within," they say, "for they praise with the Bṛhat. When they praise with the Saubhara, they thereby praise within the Bṛhat itself;
for the Saubhara is the splendor of the Bṛhat.
If the Atirātra should have the Bṛhat as its Sāman, the Saubhara should be performed as the Brahma-sāman of the Ukthas; thus he endows that very Bṛhat with splendor.
(8.8.12) If one should perform the *saubhara* with the *rathantara*-sāman for the sake of non-repetition (*ajāmitā*).

(8.8.13) When the gods were going to the heavenly world, the quarters collapsed; they propped them up with the *saubhara*, and then indeed they became firm, then they stood fast, and then they recognized the heavenly world. He who desires the heavenly world [should do so].
There may be one who, desiring a firm foundation, should chant with the *saubhara* [sāman]; he knows the heavenly world and becomes firmly established.
(PB 8.8.14) Prajāpati created offspring; once they were created, they hungered. For them, he bestowed food with the words "O *ūrj*! by means of the *saubhara*. Thereupon, indeed, they flourished.
(PB 8.8.15) The offspring flourish in that year in which one who knows thus chants the *udgītha* with the *saubhara*.
They said, "You have carried us well-nourished. Therefore it is called the *saubhara*.
He bestowed rain upon those who had been afflicted, as indeed food itself.
Whoever should desire rain, whoever should desire food, or whoever should desire heaven, he should praise with the *saubhara*.

One should employ "hīṣ" as the *nidhana* for one who desires rain; "ūrj" for one who desires food; and "ū" for one who desires heaven. Indeed, the *saubhara* contains all desires; thus, one becomes established in all desires.
Now, this is the *nārmedha*.
(Nṛmedha Āṅgirasa was seated at a sacrificial session when dogs barked at him;
he ran toward Agni, [saying], "O Agni, protect us with the one [verse]! Then Vaiśvānara rose up around him; from that he stood firm, and from that he found a way.
This Sāman is indeed a "way-finder"; he who praises with it finds a way and stands firm.
For this is neither the form of the day nor of the night, namely the *ukthas*.

First is the *kakubh*, then the *uṣṇih*, then the *purauṣṇih*, and the *anuṣṭubh*; therefore they lead [the verses] from the *acchāvāka-sāman* by means of the *anuṣṭubh*. The *hārivarṇa* [sāman] occurs.

(8.9.2) The Asuras were indeed in these worlds. The gods drove them away from this world with the words "hariśriyaṃ," from the intermediate space with "virājasī," and from yonder world with "divo-divaḥ.
(8.9.3) He who knows thus drives away his rival from these worlds and ascends these worlds.
(8.9.4) Harivarṇa, desiring cattle, saw this Sāman; by means of it, he created a thousand cattle. In that this Sāman exists, it serves for the nourishment of cattle.

When the Aṅgirasas were going to the heavenly world, the Rākṣasas followed them; they drove them away with this *harivarṇa* [chant]. That this Sāman exists is for the smiting away of the Rākṣasas. The Pṛṣṭha-stotras were indeed created; from them, that which was the superabundant brilliance and essence overflowed, and the gods gathered it together; that became the *udvaṃśīya*. This *udvaṃśīya* is the brilliance of all the Pṛṣṭhas; therefore, in ancient times, they used it against a kinsman to ward off misfortune.

(8.9.8) For he indeed praises with the *pṛṣṭha* chants who praises with the *udvaṃśīya*. (8.9.9) The *udvaṃśīya* contains all forms. (8.9.10) "They sing for thee, O Gāyatrins"—this is a form of the *rathantara*, for the *rathantara* comes [to him].
The *ādi* is for the *bṛhat*, for the *bṛhat* is, as it were, upright;
the *pariṣṭobha* is for the *vairūpa*, for the *vairūpa* is struck around; the *anutoda* is for the *vairāja*, for the *vairāja* is struck down.
The *ardheḍā* belongs to the *śakvarī* verses, and the *atisvāra* to the *revatī* verses.

By means of the *ardheḍā*, the gods struck down the Asuras; by means of the *atisvāra*, they ascended to the heavenly world. Therefore, he who knows thus strikes down his rival by means of the *ardheḍā* and ascends to the heavenly world by means of the *atisvāra*.
(8.9.17) By means of the *ardheḍā* they complete the sacrifice first; with the *atisvāra* they begin the latter part. (8.9.18) The subsequent sacrifice inclines toward him who knows thus.
(8.9.19) This *sāman* is fivefold, the sacrifice is fivefold, and cattle are fivefold; he finds firm support in the sacrifice and in cattle.
One should perform the *aṣṭādaṃṣṭra* for one who desires prosperity.

The eight-fanged Vairūpa was childless and without offspring; he grew old. He thought that he had cut himself off from these worlds. He saw these two *jarasāman*s. Because he did not employ them, he was afraid. He said, "May I prosper."
"He who praises with both Sāmans" (PB 8.9.22). This [pair] of Aṣṭādaṃṣṭra verses has indeed arisen from the mouth of the Seer; it serves for success.

For one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), they should introduce the *ukthas* upon *gāyatrī* verses; the *brahmasāman* is on a *gāyatrī*, and the *acchāvākasāman* is on an *anuṣṭubh*. Thus, this becomes a complete *gāyatrī*.
(8.10.2) Splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge belong to the *gāyatrī*; verily, he secures for himself splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge.

(8.10.3) For one who desires cattle, they should lead forth the *uktha* hymns in *gāyatrī* verses; the *brahmasāman* should be on an *uṣṇih*, and the *acchāvākasāman* on an *anuṣṭubh*. This very [verse] becomes an *uṣṇih*. (8.10.4) The *uṣṇih* is indeed cattle; verily, he secures cattle for himself.

For one who desires men, they should lead forward the *uktha* hymns on *gāyatrī* verses; the *brahmasāman* on a *kakubh* verse, and the *acchāvākasāman* on an *anuṣṭubh* verse. This [verse] becomes a *kakubh*. Man is indeed the *kakubh*; verily, he wins men.

For one who desires food, they should lead forward the *uktha* hymns on *virāj* verses; the *brahmasāman* on an *uṣṇih* verse, and the *acchāvākasāman* on an *anuṣṭubh* verse. This [verse] becomes a *virāj*.
Food is the *virāj*; verily, he secures food for himself.

For one who desires preeminence, they should perform the *uktha*s in *akṣarapaṅkti* verses; the *brahmasāman* is in the *uṣṇih* meter and the *acchāvākasāman* is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; thus it becomes an *anuṣṭubh*.
The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed preeminence; verily, he secures preeminence for himself.

The gods, having won the *ukthas*, were not able to win the night. They could not discern the Asuras who had entered the night and darkness. They saw this *pragātha* with the head of an *anuṣṭubh*; it was the *virāj*, the light.
Discerning them by means of the *virāj*, the light, they struck them out of the night with the *anuṣṭubh* as a thunderbolt.

(9.1.2) In that this *pragātha* has the *anuṣṭubh* as its head, it is as if one, beholding the *virāj* by means of light, strikes away the rival of the night with the *anuṣṭubh*-thunderbolt. (9.1.3) They pushed them away in a successive turn; because they pushed them away in a successive turn, that is the reason for the name "successive turns" (*paryāya*). (9.1.4) The first feet of the first successive turn are those which begin again.
For by means of the first verses, having taken up again from the first night, they drove it forward.
He begins with "pāntam ā vo andhasaḥ. The "pāntam andhaḥ" is indeed the day; thus, by means of the day, they take hold of the night.
(9.1.8) Among them is the Vaitahavya.

(9.1.9) Vītahavya Śrāyasa, having been long imprisoned, saw this Sāman; he understood it, and he was established. One who praises with this understands and becomes established. (9.1.10) Those who enter upon the night enter into him as it were. That there is a single Nidhana at the beginning of the night is for the sake of clear understanding.
When a man indeed comes to his own home, then he understands everything; for him, everything becomes manifest by day.
They resorted to the middle turn; by means of the *aurdhvasadmana* [chant], they appropriated the speech of their rivals.
He who knows thus appropriates the speech of his rival.
It has three *nidhanas*.

Just as the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) of the day has the three *nidhanas* as its foundation, so this middle round (*paryāya*) of the night has the three *nidhanas* as its foundation for the sake of attaining the same world (*salokatva*). The middle words are to be repeated; for by means of the middle words of the middle round, having taken them up again, they drove [the demons] away from the middle of the night.

They resorted to the final round (*paryāya*). By means of the *nidhana* "the dripping of ghee" (*ghṛtaścyut*), they appropriated the cattle for themselves; for cattle are indeed "the dripping of ghee.
He who knows thus appropriates the cattle of his rival.
The final verses are those that are repeated; for by means of the final verses of the final round, having taken them up again, they drove him away from the final night.
They fled toward them with the *sandhi* [stotra];
they caused them to go beyond reach with the *āśvina*. He who knows thus causes his rival to go beyond reach.
This night, indeed, is the measure of the Agniṣṭoma;
there are twelve stotras in the Agniṣṭoma and twelve stotras in the night. This night, indeed, is the measure of the Uktha.

(There are) three *ukthas* and the junction (*sandhi*) belongs to three deities. (PB 9.1.27) Just as there are *ukthas* for the day, so is this junction for the night; the *ukthas* of the day are of various forms, and these *ṛc*-verses of the night are likewise of various forms. (PB 9.1.28) One desiring a firm foundation should perform the junction with the *rathantara*.
The Rathantara is indeed this [earth]; he finds firm support on this very earth.
One should perform the *sandhi* for one who desires heaven; the Bṛhat is the heavenly world; verily, he finds firm support in the heavenly world itself.

Either the Vāravantīya, or the Vāmadevya, or the Śuddhyam—one of these he should make the *sandhi* for one who desires cattle. These *sāmans* are indeed cattle; verily, he finds firm standing in cattle.
The Hotṛ recites the Āśvina hymn.

Prajāpati indeed created this thousandfold [offering] and gave it to the gods. They could not agree upon it; they ran a race, making the sun the goalpost. Of them, the Aśvins ran first. They called out after them, "Let there be a share for us too! They asked, "What would come of that? [The others] said, "Whatever you two desire. They replied, "This [offering] shall have us as its deities."
"Let the hymn be recited"—therefore the *āśvina* [śastra] is recited.
Indeed, all the deities are praised.
The praise is to be performed quickly, for these [priests] run as if to a race until the rising of the sun; he should recite until the sun rises, for they made the sun their goal.

(9.2.1) "Pāntam ā vo andhasaḥ"—this is the Vaitahavya. Those who undertake the night-rite enter another's field; in that the Okonidhana occurs at the beginning of the night, it is for the sake of not being displaced from one's own dwelling.
(9.2.2) "Pra va indrāya mādanam"—this is the Gaurīvita.
(9.2.3) When the gods fashioned the *brahman*, that which remained over became the Gaurīvita.

The Gaurīvita is redundant; this *stotra* is redundant in that it is the night. By means of what is redundant, he places the redundant [into the sacrifice]. (PB 9.2.5) "And we, for that very purpose, [sing] unto thee"—this is the Kaṇva [sāman].
By this, indeed, Kaṇva attained harmony with Indra; by this, one attains harmony with Indra. (PB 9.2.6)
(9.2.7) "For Indra, who loves the intoxicating [juice], the pressed [Soma]"—this is the Śrautakakṣa, the Kṣatrasāman; by means of this, one truly becomes kṣatra-power.
(9.2.8) "This Soma is for thee, O Indra"—this is the Daivodāsa.
(9.2.9) By means of the Agniṣṭoma, the gods conquered this world; by the Uktha, the intermediate space; by the Atirātra, yonder world.
They desired this world again; they established themselves here in this world. That this *sāman* exists is for the sake of stability.
They chant it with its seat elevated even during the nights.
The Asuras were indeed in these worlds; the gods drove them out from these worlds by means of the *ūrdhvasadman* [chant].
He who knows thus, having driven his rival away from these worlds, dwells in his own abode performing the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
"Come to us, O Indra, with food," [is the hymn] ending with the *ākūpāra*.
Akūpāra was the son of Aṅgiras; his skin was just like the skin of a lizard.
Having purified it with this *triḥsāman*, Indra made him one whose skin is like the sun. Indeed, at that time she [the skin] desired what she desired;
whatever desire they praise with this *sāman* is fulfilled for them.
(9.2.15) "Towards you, O bull, [is] the pressed [juice]"—this is the *ārṣabha* chant, the *kṣatrasāman*; by means of this, one indeed becomes *kṣatra*.
(9.2.16) "This [pressed] soma-juice, O Vasu"—this is the *gāra*; by means of this, Gāra indeed gratified Indra; through this, Indra becomes gratified for him.
(9.2.17) "For this [has been pressed] with power"—this is the *mādhucchandasa* chant; this body of Prajāpati, which is never exhausted, is employed.
"Come hither, sit down upon these"—this is the *daivātitha* chant.

Devātithi, together with his sons, while wandering through the forest in search of food, found *urvāru* gourds. He approached them with this *sāman*, and they rose up for him, having become spotted cows.
That this *sāman* exists is for the nourishment of cattle.
(9.2.20) "In every endeavor, [O Indra], most powerful one"—this is the Saumedha *Rātriṣāman*, for the sake of the prosperity of the night.
(9.2.21) "O Indra, when the Soma juices are pressed"—this is the Kautsa.
(9.2.22) Both Kutsa and Luśa called upon Indra; that Indra turned toward Kutsa, but [Kutsa] with a hundred [sacrifices].
Luśa bound him with she-goats' sinews at his testicles; Kutsa spoke to him: "Release yourself and come here from Kutsa!
Why should one like you remain bound at your testicles? Having cut them off, he fled. Kutsa saw this *sāman*;
with it he called out after him, and he returned.
(9.2.23) That this *sāman* is performed is for the sake of [attaining] Indra’s companionship.

(9.3.1) If they should consecrate themselves for a sacrificial session (*sattra*), then he should depart from the session after distributing the *soma*. He should sacrifice with the *viśvajit* *atirātra*, giving away his entire property (*sarvavedasa*). He consecrates himself for everything;
(9.3.2) by whatever sacrificial gifts he gives, he employs them for that purpose.
(PB 9.3.3) If they should pass through [the night] without having chanted with the *paryāyas*, they should chant for the Hotṛ with fifteen [verses], and for the others with five each.

(PB 9.3.4) They should chant with the *sandhi* verse, "O Agni, radiant at dawn. The *trivṛt* is indeed the vital breaths among the *stomas*, and the *rathantara* is the foundation among the *sāmans*; thus they attain both the vital breaths and the foundation.
(PB 9.3.5) The Hotṛ recites three hundred and sixty [verses].

There are as many nights in a year; by means of those verses equal in measure to the year, he thereby obtains the Āśīvin. That which they chant before [the time] is unchanted; that which they chant at the right time is chanted; that which they chant beyond [the time] is well-chanted.
If they were to chant before [the time], they should chant with as many syllables as they do not chant, or rather with more syllables.
(PB 9.3.9) If they should chant excessively, or if they should not chant for as many [verses] as they have chanted, or with fewer syllables;
(PB 9.3.10) if they should chant too briefly, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman should be made with the *trīḍa* finale; by means of the one *iḍā* and those two [others], it is thereby made equal.

(PB 9.3.11) If they should chant excessively, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman should be made with the *svāra* [intonation]; for that which is deficient in the sāman is the *svarita*; by that very means, it is thereby made equal.
(PB 9.4.1) If two Soma sacrifices should be performed together, one should commence the Prātaranuvāka at the latter part of the night.
(PB 9.4.2) The one who acts first appropriates the speech, the meters, and the deities.
(PB 9.4.3) One should employ a *pratipad* containing the word "bull" (*vṛṣan*); for Indra is indeed the bull, and thus from the very morning pressing he appropriates Indra for them.
(9.4.4) Now, moreover, they say: "It should be offered at each opening of the *savana*; for by [offering] from each opening of the *savana*, one excludes Indra from them.
(9.4.5) It should be offered when the fire is well-kindled. Agni, indeed, is all the deities; he offers while beholding all the deities.
(9.4.6) "For the settling, for the sitting down, for the Gāyatrī metre, for the overpowering, svāhā! For the settling, for the sitting down..."

He offers with the formulas: "To the Triṣṭubh metre, for overcoming, svāhā! To the settling and the sitting down, to the Jagatī metre, for overcoming, svāhā! (PB 9.4.7). The metres are indeed the means of overcoming; by them he overcomes those [enemies]. Both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara [Sāmans] should be performed (PB 9.4.8). For where Indra's two bay horses are, there is Indra. The two bay horses of Indra are indeed the Bṛhat and the Rathantara. Since both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara are employed, they take hold of Indra's two bay horses from the very beginning.
(9.4.9) With these, one should perform the *kārya* for Aśrava.

(9.4.10) Indeed, the two Soma-pressings of Turaśravas and the Pārāvatās were held simultaneously; then Turaśravas beheld these two *sāmans*, and by means of them, Indra brought the oblation of the Śalmalins from the Yamunā for him. That which [was performed] with those...
"Their oblation indeed secures the waters for them" (PB 9.4.11).
"They should press first" (PB 9.4.12). Those who bathe first indeed win the ford first; they are the first to take hold of Indra.
The *vihavya* hymn is to be recited.

(PB 9.4.14) Once, the Soma sacrifices of Jamadagni and those of the *ṛṣis* were being performed together. Then Jamadagni saw this *vihavya* hymn; Indra turned toward it. When the Hotṛ recites the *vihavya*, he wins Indra for them.

(PB 9.4.15) If it should be an *agniṣṭoma*, an *ukthya* should be performed; if it is an *ukthya*, an *atirātra* [should be performed]. For whichever sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) is greater, that is dear to Indra. By means of a greater sacrificial rite, they thus reach Indra. (PB 9.4.16) Now, moreover, they say: "The further path is indeed difficult to traverse. One should not deviate from the very sacrificial rite which one has undertaken at the outset. (PB 9.4.17) The *sajanīya* hymn is to be recited; the *kayāśubhīya* of Agastya is to be recited.
(PB 9.4.18) By means of this [verse] and that [verse], "Today and tomorrow," he excludes them from the pair of day and night.
(PB 9.5.1) If they should carry off the Soma before it has been purchased, another must be purchased.
(PB 9.5.2) If it has already been purchased, whoever else is nearby should be brought; however, one should give something to the Soma-seller.
(PB 9.5.3) If they should not find *soma*, they should press *pūtīka* plants; if they do not find *pūtīkas*, [they should press] *arjunas*.
(PB 9.5.4) Gāyatrī brought *soma*; having let it go, the guardian of *soma* cut off a leaf from it.
The shoot that fell away became the *pūtīka*. In it the gods found protection (*ūti*); therefore this is called *ūtīka*, namely the *pūtīkas*.
"They press [the Soma] for him; they indeed find protection for him.
At dawn, there is fresh milk and *pūtīka* plants; at midday, boiled milk and *pūtīka* plants; in the afternoon, curds and *pūtīka* plants.
"The Soma-drink departs from him," they say, "for whom they carry away the Soma. It enters into the plants and the cattle; he recovers it from the plants and the cattle.
Indra slew Vṛtra; the Soma that flowed from his nose became those brown and white cotton-like fibers.
Those which came from the extracted omentum became the red cotton-like fibers. One should press those brown and white fibers;
for this is the form of the Brahman; thus he presses the Soma directly.

The Śrāyantīya should be made the Brahman-sāman; verily, he thus makes him to be Being. One should chant the Yajñāyajñīya on an Anuṣṭubh verse; verily, by means of speech, he causes him to prosper. The Vāravantīya should be made the Agniṣṭoma-sāman for the securing of power and vigor. Five sacrificial fees should be given.
The sacrifice is fivefold; as great as the sacrifice is, that very thing he undertakes.
Having emerged from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), he should undergo initiation (*dīkṣā*) again.
Therein, he should give whatever was intended to be given.

(PB 9.6.1) If the pitcher should break, one should perform the *brahmasāman* with the *vaṣaṭkāra* as its finale (*nidhana*). (PB 9.6.2) The Soma of that person whose pitcher breaks is poured away before the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered; when the *brahmasāman* has the *vaṣaṭkāra* as its finale, his Soma becomes one for which the *vaṣaṭ* has indeed been uttered. (PB 9.6.3) It should be performed upon these verses: "The waning moon, fleeing in the assembly of many... and so forth.
"For this [Soma] is split among many at the assembly, since it is the jar (*kalaśa*).

Regarding this, they say: "Indeed, misfortune does not follow upon misfortune; rather, he who performs [the rite] when the jar is split, in the *dadrāṇavatī* verses, follows after misfortune with misfortune.
Therefore, the *Śrāyantīya* alone should be performed.
Prajāpati created offspring; he felt himself emptied and depleted. He saw this Śrāyantīya [chant]; with it, he replenished himself with offspring, cattle, and vital power.
He who has a jar broken feels himself emptied and depleted, as if drained. If the Śrāyantīya becomes the *brahmasāman*, he replenishes himself once again with offspring, cattle, and vital power.
If the Śrāyantīya were to be the *brahmasāman*, one should perform the *vaṣaṭkāranidhana* upon *anuṣṭubh* verses dedicated to Viṣṇu.

(9.6.10) Whatever indeed flows away from the sacrifice, it flows back into speech; for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech and the sacrifice is Viṣṇu. By means of speech, he thus stops up the breach of the sacrifice.
(9.6.11) Whatever indeed flows away from the sacrifice, it flows away at the end; the *vāravantīya* should be made the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*, for it wards off the breach of the sacrifice.
(9.7.1) If the Soma should be left over from the morning pressing, they should chant on the *marutvatī* verses in the *gāyatrī* meter, [saying]: "This pressed Soma exists."
He who is left over from the morning pressing is left over while desiring the midday pressing;
therefore they chant on verses addressed to the Maruts, for the midday pressing belongs to the Maruts;
and therefore they chant on Gāyatrī verses, for the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī.
(PB 9.7.3) That *stoma* by which [the sacrifice] exceeds [the norm] is precisely the *stoma* that should be performed, for the sake of conformity (*salomatva*).
(PB 9.7.4) The Hotṛ recites the *anūśaṃsa* for Indra and Viṣṇu.
(PB 9.7.5) Indra is indeed vigor, and the sacrifice is Viṣṇu; thus he becomes firmly established in the sacrifice through vigor itself.

(PB 9.7.6) If [the sacrifice] should be left over from the midday pressing, they should chant with the *gaurīvita* [sāman] on verses addressed to Āditya, beginning with "O Bṛhan, thou art great, O Sūrya.
(PB 9.7.7) Indeed, he who is left over from the midday pressing is left over while desiring the third pressing;
therefore they chant on verses addressed to Āditya, for the third pressing belongs to Āditya; and therefore [they chant] on *bṛhatī* verses.
"For the midday pressing belongs to the Bṛhatī metre" (PB 9.7.8).

Whatever *stoma* might exceed [the prescribed number], that very *stoma* should be employed for the sake of maintaining the regularity of the *stomas*. The Hotṛ recites the *anuśaṃsa* for Indra and Viṣṇu; for Indra is vigor and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice—it is thus vigor in the sacrifice.
(PB 9.7.9) If it should exceed the third pressing, they should chant with the verses containing the word "Śipiviṣṭa" of Viṣṇu, using the Gaurīvita melody.

Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa is indeed the sacrifice; thus he establishes himself in the sacrifice, Viṣṇu. The Gaurīvita [sāman] is redundant; verily, by means of the redundant, he places the redundant [into the sacrifice]. They should perform this other [rite]: they should lead forward the *ukthas*. Indeed, he who exceeds the *agniṣṭoma* exceeds while desiring the *ukthas*. If it should exceed the *ukthya*s, an *atirātra* should be performed; for he exceeds while desiring the night.

"That which exceeds the *ukthya*s, that which exceeds [the sacrifice], if it should exceed the night—[then] they should chant with the *Bṛhat* [Sāman] upon verses containing the word *śipiviṣṭa* for Viṣṇu. Regarding this, however, they say: 'That which exceeds the night is indeed that which exceeds the world beyond. Verily, he who exceeds the night desires that world beyond; they chant with the *Bṛhat*, for the *Bṛhat* is worthy to attain that world beyond; he attains it. (PB 9.7.12)

(PB 9.8.1) If one among those who have been consecrated dies, they should cremate him, collect his bones, and having bound them [in a cloth], whichever person is nearest should be consecrated; then they should perform the sacrifice together.

(PB 9.8.2) They should do this other thing: having pressed the Soma, but without having drawn the cups (*graha*), they should either chant the praise on that southern corner of the altar, or on the *mārjālīya* mound.
(PB 9.8.3) Or rather, when one who has been consecrated dies during this sacrifice, they expiate for him by means of this rite.
They praise with the Yāma [Sāman]; they cause him to go to the world of Yama.
They praise with three [verses], for the ancestors are in the third world.
They praise with [verses] directed away, for that world is turned away from here.
They praise with the verses of the Queen of Serpents.
Arbuda the serpent struck off his dead skin with these; verily, with these they strike off their own dead skin.
Reciting those verses, they walk three times around the Mārjālīya fire, striking their left thighs.
He recites the *anuśaṃsana* after the hymn has been chanted; they thus establish him in that very world.
"Those who perform [the rites] for the dead go astray from the path," so they say; therefore, they draw the cups beginning with the one for Indra and Vāyu, and thus they return again to the path.
The verse "O Agni, you purify the lives" (*agna āyūṃṣi pavase*) should be used as the opening; he thereby bestows life upon those who are still living.

(9.8.13) They should cause the bones to sacrifice after a year; for the year is the pacification of everything. If they were to cause them to sacrifice before the year [is up], they would encounter harsh and cruel speech that has been made blood-red. (9.8.14) There should be *pavamāna* chants consisting of threefold verses (*trivṛt*), while everything else consists of seventeenfold verses (*saptadaśa*). (9.8.15) In that the *pavamāna* chants are threefold, and the threefold is indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), they thus attain the vital breaths. In that everything else consists of seventeenfold verses, and Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold, they attain procreation.

(9.8.16) "Those who perform [the rites] for one who is dead," they say, "are deprived of out-breath and in-breath. They draw the cups beginning with the Maitrāvaruṇa cup; Mitra and Varuṇa are out-breath and in-breath;
thus they are made complete through out-breath and in-breath.
(9.9.1) For him whose *kalaśa* vessel runs dry, the out-breath follows after his *kalaśa* as it runs dry; for Soma is indeed the out-breath.
Regarding this, they say: "One should pour milk [into it].
Now, however, they also say: "This milk is, as it were, concealed; one should rather pour gold into the water and raise up the gold.
Water is indeed the vital breaths, and gold is immortality; thus he bestows immortality upon his vital breaths, and he attains a full lifespan.

(PB 9.9.5) If the *nārāśaṃsa* cup spills, his vital breath (*prāṇa*) follows after that spilling *nārāśaṃsa*, for Soma is indeed the vital breath. (PB 9.9.6) The Adhvaryu should pour out that [Soma] from which he takes the final cup, so as to recover it. (PB 9.9.7) A cup is drawn for the sake of expiation; thus, by means of expiation itself, he effects an expiation for him.

(PB 9.9.8) If the Soma that has been drunk and the Soma that has not been drunk should come into contact, one should draw out embers from within the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and offer [the mixture] with the formula: "Of the offered and the unoffered, of the unoffered and the offered, of the Soma drunk and undrunk—O Indra and Agni, drink the pressed juice, svāhā! This indeed is the expiation for that.
(PB 9.9.9) One should offer [the portion] of what is not to be consumed with the formula, "To Prajāpati, svāhā!", at the northernmost and easternmost *uparava* pit.
(9.9.10) With the mantra, "The drop has entered the drop," he should consume what has been poured down.
(9.9.11) "Of thee, O Indra, who art drunk by Indra, who possessest power, who art accompanied by all the hosts—of thee, who art invited by all the hosts, I, being invited, partake.
(9.9.12) With the mantra, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning," he should offer an oblation of clarified butter for that which has been introduced [to the fire] by the Agnīdhra.
"Having gone forth, he was born as the sole lord of beings; he supported this earth and this heaven. To him, O Indu, let us do homage with an oblation, Svāhā!"—this indeed is the expiation for that.
If even the pressing-stone should break, the sacrificer is deprived of cattle; for the pressing-stones are indeed cattle. They should chant the *dyutāna* Sāman of the Maruts.
The pressing-stones indeed belong to the Maruts; thus he causes them to prosper by means of their own form.
If the Soma should burn [the sacrificer], the Adhvaryu should cause the cups to be watched over, the Udgātṛ the chants, and the Hotṛ the recitations;
then they should proceed with the sacrifice in its proper order. Five sacrificial gifts should be given; for the sacrifice is fivefold, as great as the sacrifice is.

He undertakes that [rite]; having emerged from the *avabhṛtha* bath, he is consecrated again. In that case, he should give whatever was intended to be given before the twelfth day; if he were to let the twelfth day pass by, he would be excluded.
(PB 9.10.1) If the *mahāvīra* vessel should break, he should touch it while broken with the verse: "He who, even without a bond, before the piercing of the collarbones..."

Maghavan, possessor of many riches, you are the uniter; you join together what has been torn asunder and restore what was shattered. Let us not fear like outcasts, O Indra; we have felt like strangers. Like trees cast away, O wielder of the stone, we have felt like those who are difficult to satisfy.
We have felt ourselves slow and without a helper, O slayer of Vṛtra.
"O hero, having once drunk with great wealth, let us rejoice in the hymn"—with these words, one should touch the broken *mahāvīra* vessel; that indeed is the expiation for it.

(PB 9.10.2) Verily, from him whose sacrificial post sprouts, the asura-like color departs, and his luster, sensory power, vigor, food, offspring, and cattle depart; he is liable to become worse off. (PB 9.10.3) He should sacrifice a multi-colored animal dedicated to Tvaṣṭṛ; for Tvaṣṭṛ is the fashioner of the forms of animals.
He indeed runs toward that very [deity]; he (the deity) makes him prosper again with splendor, sensory power, vigor, food, offspring, and cattle;
that itself is his expiation.
By means of Agni, the earth, and the plants, this world becomes threefold; by means of Vāyu, the intermediate space, and the birds...
By that, this world is threefold—namely, by means of the sun within it, by day, and by the stars; by that, yonder world is threefold.
This indeed is the abode of the threefold, and this is its kinship. He who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode and possessed of kinship.

(10.1.3) They say that it is "the foundation," for the Trivṛt is indeed established upon these worlds. (10.1.4) The half-month is the abode of the Pañcadaśa; this is its kinship. (10.1.5) He who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode and possessed of kinship.
(10.1.6) And they say of it: "It is vigor and strength," for month by month creatures and cattle nourish vigor and strength.

(10.1.7) The year indeed is the abode of the seventeenfold [Stoma]; there are twelve months and five seasons—this is the abode of the seventeenfold; this is its kinship. (10.1.8) He who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode and possessed of kinship.
(10.1.9) Regarding this, they say, "It is Prajāpati," for offspring and cattle are born after the year.

(10.1.10) The sun is the abode of the twenty-one-fold [stoma]; there are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first—this indeed is the abode of the twenty-one-fold; this is its kinship.
(10.1.11) He who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode and possessed of kinship.
(12) Regarding this, they say: "It is the couch of the gods. He who knows thus attains the couch of the gods.
(13) The *trivṛt* is indeed the abode of the *triṇava*; this is its kinship. (14) He who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode and possessed of kinship.
(10.1.15) Regarding this, they say it is "Nourishment," for this threefold [stoma] is indeed nourished.
(10.1.16) The deities are the abode of the thirty-threefold [stoma]; the thirty-three deities and Prajāpati as the thirty-fourth—this is the abode of the thirty-threefold; this is its kinship.
(10.1.17) He who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode and possessed of kinship.

(18) Regarding that, they call it "the firmament" (*nāka*), for Prajāpati is not a firmament for anyone. (19) The meters themselves are the abode of the Chandomas; this is their kinship. (20) He who knows thus becomes possessed of an abode and possessed of kinship.
(10.1.21) Regarding them, they say, "They are nourishment," for the Chandomas are indeed cattle. (10.2.1) Prajāpati created offspring; he became exhausted. For him, Vāja lifted up light.
He said, "Who has lifted this light up for me? "It was your own speech," he replied. He said to her, "I offer thee as Virāj."

"Having made the meters into lights, they end with sacrifice" (PB 10.2.2). Therefore, that which attains the *virāj* chant is called the *jyotiṣṭoma-agniṣṭoma*; for the *virāj* is the light among the meters (PB 10.2.3).
He who knows thus becomes a light among his peers.

The *anuṣṭubh* and the seventeenfold [stoma] came into being together. That *anuṣṭubh* created the meters increasing by four syllables each and the *stomas* increasing by six; these two [the *anuṣṭubh* and the seventeenfold] are in the middle of them. (PB 10.2.5) The ninefold and the twenty-sevenfold [stomas] belong to the *rathantara*; after them the goat and the horse were created. Therefore, those two shake the *rathantara* forward.
(PB 10.2.6) The fifteenfold and the twenty-onefold [stomas] belong to the *bṛhat*; after them the cow and the sheep were created. Therefore, those two shine forth the *bṛhat* forward.
(PB 10.2.7) Thus, they say of one who knows this: "He understands even the speech of domestic animals.
(PB 10.3.1) Prajāpati desired, "May I become many; may I procreate. He beheld within himself the *ṛtvyā* [the sacrificial office];

from that he created the *ṛtvij*s (priests). Because he created them from the *ṛtvyā*, that is the *ṛtvik-tva* (priesthood) of the *ṛtvij*s. With them, he approached this twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), and he prospered.
(ŚB 10.3.2) "Our father has prospered," said the months; they prospered through the consecration alone. During the *upasads*, they consecrated a thirteenth [month];
he became an *anuvya*. Therefore, one who is about to be consecrated during the *upasads* becomes an *anuvya*.
For they call him the thirteenth month, yet they do not [call him so].

(10.3.3) One person should undergo initiation, for Prajāpati alone attained success. Twelve should undergo initiation, for twelve months [attained success]. Twenty-four should undergo initiation, for twenty-four half-months [attained success].

(10.3.4) If fifteen should undergo initiation, they should designate them thus: "These five, these five, these five, these five, these five, and this one. Whomever they may desire to attain success for, success follows him alone; all the others attain success.
He who knows the householder of the gods attains the status of a householder; he truly reaches the position of a householder.
The year, indeed, is the householder of the gods; he is Prajāpati himself, and his months are those who undergo consecration together.
He who knows thus finds those who undergo consecration together, attains the status of a householder, and truly reaches the position of a householder.

(10.3.8) He who knows the self-ruler (*svarāj*) of the meters attains self-rule; he reaches and fully obtains self-rule. The *bṛhatī* is indeed the self-ruler of the meters; he who knows thus attains self-rule; he reaches and fully obtains self-rule.

(10.3.9) They sit apart for the sake of obtaining food by means of this very [rite], namely this twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), which consists of twelve initiations (*dīkṣā*), twelve preparatory days (*upasad*), and twelve pressings (*prasuta*). These nights amount to thirty-six.

The Bṛhatī consists of thirty-six syllables (PB 10.3.10). One is indeed born through the consecration (dīkṣā), one is purified by the Upasad rites, and one reaches the world of the gods through the Soma pressing (sutyā).
Indeed, this much is the power and vigor of the year: namely, these nights and the twelve full moons.

There are twelve *iṣṭakās* and twelve new-moon nights; as much as there is in a year—namely, sensory power and vigor—that he attains and secures by means of this twelve-day rite. This [verse] consists of thirty syllables; it is indeed the *virāj*. There are six seasons; verily, he finds firm support in the seasons by means of the *virāj*, and in the *virāj* by means of the seasons. This [verse] consists of thirty-two syllables; it is indeed the *anuṣṭubh*. Speech is the *anuṣṭubh*. Cattle are four-footed. By means of speech he supports cattle; therefore, they are established through speech, and when called with speech, they come. Therefore, it is called "speech" (*vāk*).

The past is the first Atirātra, the future is the second; the earth is the first Atirātra, the sky is the second; Agni is the first Atirātra, Āditya is the second; Prāṇa is the first Atirātra, Udāna is the second.
The two eyes are the two Atirātras, and the pupils are the two Agniṣṭomas. Because the two Agniṣṭomas are between the two Atirātras, therefore the two pupils, being in the middle, enjoy [the light].
(10.4.3) These two Atirātras are indeed the two fangs of the year; one must not sleep during them, lest one place oneself within the fangs of the year.
(10.4.4) Regarding this they say: "Who is capable of not sleeping? "That which the breath keeps awake—that alone is waking.

(10.4.5) They perform this Gāyatrī with light as its wings, namely this twelve-day rite: eight Ukthya sacrifices in the middle, and Agniṣṭomas on both sides. Having gone to the heavenly world, they reach the ageless state, beginning with Brahman.
"Shining, he eats food" (PB 10.4.6).
They perform the *rathantara* chant three times in front; for speech has a threefold turn, and having thus secured all speech, they extend the twelve-day sacrifice to obtain every kind of food.

"A repetition (*jāmi*) is indeed committed in the sacrifice," they say, "when they perform the *rathantara* three times in front. The *saubhara* becomes the *brahmasāman* of the *ukthas*; by that very means, it is made non-repetitive (*ajāmi*).
The opening verses (*pratipad*) of the introductory day (*prāyaṇīya*) consist of ancient hymns; therefore, that [day] is indeed free from repetition (*ajāmi*).

They perform the *rathantara* chant three times at the end; for speech is threefold, and having thus secured all speech, they rise from the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) possessing all food. Indeed, there are these three three-night periods within this twelve-day sacrifice: the first has the *gāyatra* at its beginning, the second has the *gāyatra* in the middle, and the third has the *gāyatra* at the end.

Because the first has the *gāyatra* as its head, therefore Agni shines upward; because the second has the *gāyatra* as its middle, therefore Vāyu blows crosswise. Indeed, they set forth with brilliance, they place brilliance in the middle, and they rise up with brilliance; indeed, they set forth with light, they place light in the middle, and they rise up with light; indeed, they set forth with sight, [they place sight in the middle, and they rise up with sight].

They place the eye in the middle as they rise; for by means of the breath these depart, and they place the breath in the middle as they rise. Those who depart by means of the *gāyatrī*, they place the *gāyatrī* in the middle as they rise.
This twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) is indeed stretched out as a web; of that [web], by these...
"Because the rays [of the sun] are the *gāyatrī* for the sake of non-distraction," said Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni, "regarding the Girikṣit and Uccāmanyu, 'How is the twelve-day rite?
'Just as the rim encircles the spokes, so does the *gāyatrī* encircle it, for the sake of non-slipping, just as the spokes are held fast in the hub.'"

"Thus the twelve-day rite is sustained in this [Anuṣṭubh]" (PB 10.5.8). "They sit apart from this Anuṣṭubh for the sake of food when they perform this twelve-day rite" (PB 10.5.9). By means of eight syllables, the Anuṣṭubh seizes the first day of the twelve-day rite; by eleven, the second; and by twelve, the third.
The syllable consisting of three letters remains; that indeed he performs as the subsequent three-night rite. Verily, the meters carry his third three-night rite.
They sit facing it, across it, and away from it for the sake of food; therefore, offspring and cattle subsist upon what is turned toward them, what is across them, and what is away from them.

(10.5.13) The meters, indeed, were intent upon one another’s world: the *gāyatrī* upon that of the *triṣṭubh*, the *triṣṭubh* upon that of the *jagatī*, and the *jagatī* upon that of the *gāyatrī*. They interchanged them according to their respective worlds; from that, whatever desire they wished for, they attained it.
(10.5.14) Whatever desire one has when sacrificing with the twelve-day rite in which the meters are interchanged, that desire of his is fulfilled.

The twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) is indeed the eye of the gods. Just as human beings have entered this world, so too have the deities entered the twelve-day rite. He who, knowing thus, performs the twelve-day rite, sacrifices with the deities themselves.
The twelve-day rite is the home of the gods; there is no fear for one who does not possess a home.

(ŚB 10.5.17) He who knows the twelve-day rite as being structured according to the Agniṣṭoma finds success for himself: by the morning pressing alone, the first three-night period is perfected; by the midday pressing, the second; by the third pressing, the third; and by the Agniṣṭoma-sāman alone, the tenth day is perfected.

It succeeds for him who knows thus. (PB 10.5.18) It goes forth, after departing, as something swift, possessing food, radiant, and brilliant; this is the form of the first day, of the *trivṛt* stoma, the *gāyatrī* metre, and the *rathantara* sāman.

(PB 10.6.2) It is bull-like, slaying Vṛtra, wealthy, and all-pervading, being well-established; this is the form of the second day, of the *pañcadaśa* stoma, the *triṣṭubh* metre, and the *bṛhat* sāman.

(10.6.3) That which has an ascent, that which has threefold [repetition], that which has the quarters, that which has cattle, and that which has the bull— this is the form of the third day, belonging to the seventeen-fold hymn-form (*stoma*), the Jagatī metre, and the Vairūpa Sāman. (10.6.4) That which has a king, that which has people, that which has the sun, that which has the Virāj, and that which has downward pressure— this is the form of the fourth day, belonging to the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, the Anuṣṭubh metre, and the Rājana Sāman.

The *pañkti* metre is variegated, the *śakvarī* has children, the [verse] has celestial syllables, it possesses cattle, it possesses a bull, and it is desired as the wielder of the thunderbolt; this is the form of the fifth day, of the twenty-sevenfold (*triṇava*) *stoma*, of the *pañkti* metre, and of the *śakvarī* chants.

(PB 10.6.6) That which revolves, that which corresponds, the seven-footed, the two-footed, that which lacks the *nārāśaṃsa* verses, that which possesses cattle, and that which possesses a bull—this is the form of the sixth day, of the thirty-threefold (*trayastriṃśa*) *stoma*, and the form of all metres.
"Of the Revatī verses, of the Sāman" (PB 10.6.7).
"Since this [six-day period], though being uniform, is a division of the six-day rite that possesses various forms, therefore the year is multiform (virūpa)" (PB 10.6.8).
"Multiform offspring is born after him who knows thus."

(10.7.1) "O Agni! is the form of the first day, from the case-ending of Agni; "Agni" is that of the second; "with Agni" is that of the third; "Agni" is that of the fourth. (10.7.2) The gods indeed sought prosperity; they did not find it on the first day, nor on the second, nor on the third;
they found it on the fourth day. He who knows this finds prosperity. "Of Agni" is the form of the fifth day.
"Therefore, they say, 'Fortune has arisen for him.
"His rival becomes one who cannot counter-argue against him, if he knows thus. With "O Agni," which belongs to the sixth [day], they rise up with the very same form with which they set out.
(PB 10.7.5) Because this division of Agni, while being uniform, is of various forms, therefore the sun shines according to the seasons.
(PB 10.8.1) "Indra" is the form of the first day; "Indra-vibhaktyā" (by the case-ending of Indra) is that of the second;
"indreṇa" (with Indra) is that of the third; "indra" is that of the fourth; "indrāt" (from Indra) is that of the fifth; and "indra" is that of the sixth—by whichever form [it occurs].
They go forth and they rise up again; because this *indravibhakti*, though being the same, is of various forms, therefore the plants ripen according to the seasons.

That which he introduces with a *ṛc* is the form of the first day; that which is the *svaravibhakti* with a *stobha* before it is that of the second; that which has a *stobha* on both sides is that of the third; and that which is without a *tunna*-insertion is that of the fourth.
That which has been undertaken belongs to the fifth day; that which is practiced here with the syllable *ihakāra* is the form of the sixth day.
Because this modulation of the tones (*svaravibhakti*), while being uniform, takes various forms among the tones, therefore the wind blows according to the seasons.
The *padanidhana* is the form of the first day; the *bahirnidhana*, due to the modulation of the *nidhana*, is the form of the second day.

The *niṃnidhana* belongs to the third [day], the *enidhana* to the fourth, and the *athakāranidhana* to the fifth; that which is repeated here with the syllable *ākāra* is the form of the sixth day among the *nidhanas*. Since this division of the *nidhanas*, though being the same, is of various forms, therefore these worlds, while being together, are indeed distinct.

(ŚB 10.11.1) That which contains *iḍ* in a liquid form is the characteristic form of the first day; that which has *iḍ* after the *iḍāvibhakti* is that of the second; that which has *iḍ* enclosed on all sides (*pariṣṭubdha*) is that of the third; that which has *iḍ* through the *aiḍā* verses is that of the fourth; that which has a half-measure *iḍ* (*adhyardheḍa*) is that of the fifth; and that which is repeated here with the vowel *ā* is the characteristic form of the sixth day. Since this *iḍāvibhakti*, though being the same, appears in various forms among the *iḍ*s, therefore [the days] are the same.
"Peaceful are the animals of various forms" (PB 10.12.1).

The descendants of Bharadvāja performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*). They were asked: "What did you accomplish with the first day? "We went forward," they replied. "What with the second? "We made for ourselves a dwelling place. "What with the third? "We swam all around."
"What with the fourth? "We would place the existent upon the existent. "What with the fifth? "We would go cutting through the vital breaths.
"What with the sixth? "We would come hither to this very world.
(PB 10.12.2) By means of which word he intones the *prastāva*, it was by that very word that the gods beheld the cattle.

That which has a *stobha* before and then a *svāra* tone—by that they sent them forth upward. That which has a *stobha* on both sides and then a *svāra* tone—by that the gods bestowed food upon these worlds and upon the cattle. That which is accompanied by low chanting (*anutunna*) and then a *svāra* tone—by that they instructed [them] closely. That which has a *nidhana* in the middle and then a *svāra* tone—by that they placed embryos within; through the *havat* call and the *svāra* tone, they brought them forth.
By means of the *padanidhana*, the gods conquered this very world; by means of the *bahirnidhana*, they conquered yonder world;

by means of the *diṅnidhana*, they conquered the intermediate space; by means of the *īnidhana*, they attained immortality; by means of the *athanidhana*, they acquired spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*);
and by means of the *ihanidhana*, they became firmly established in this very world.
(10.12.4) By means of the *dravadiḍ* the gods indeed conquered this world; by the *ūrdhveḍ*, yonder [world];
by the *pariṣṭubdheḍ*, the intermediate space; by the *iḍās*, they won over the *aiḍa*; by the *adhyardheḍ*, they gained a firm foundation;
and by the *iheḍ*, they established themselves in this very world.

Speech does not speak beyond the year; it is only *iḍā* that speaks beyond the year. Having returned in the year by means of the embryo, they are born; therefore, she speaks beyond [the year]. These four *iḍās* indeed pass beyond the six-day period: this one facing forward, this one facing upward, this one facing away, and this one facing backward—this is the firm foundation. Agni is the year, and speech is the year. When Agni is divided, they thereby divide speech itself.

(10.12.8) They divide two syllables each, for there are two months in a season; thus, the form of the months is thereby produced. (10.12.9) They divide six days, for there are six seasons; it is for the support of the seasons, for the stability of the seasons, and thus the form of the seasons is thereby produced. There are also six persons after whom Agni is divided.
(10.12.10) In that Agni is divided here in many ways, that is yonder sun facing all creatures; therefore these two deities have attained their division, and no other whatsoever.
The *stoma* is yoked for the sacrificial sessions (*sattriya*) days with verses that contain the word "ancient" (*pratnavatī*) and those containing the word "favorable" (*upavatī*).

(PB 11.1.2) Since the verses containing the word "ancient" are yoked before those containing the word "favorable," the spiritual power (*brahman*) is thus yoked before the ruling power (*kṣatra*); for the spiritual power is indeed prior to the ruling power.
(PB 11.1.3) Thus, the mind is yoked before speech; for whatever one reaches through the mind, that one speaks through speech.

That *bṛhat* is joined before the *rathantara*, for the *bṛhat* indeed precedes the *rathantara*; yet, through victory, the *rathantara* attained the prior connection. (PB 11.1.5) The *tṛcas* are to be combined (*sambhārya*), just as one would combine the most excellent and the best; even so do they combine these, for the sake of attainment. There are nine, for the purpose of yoking the nine-day period; by means of the *ṛc* he yokes the day, just as one would place the pins of a wagon in order; even so does he place the pins of the nine-day period, for the sake of attainment. (PB 11.1.6)
The *stoma* is indeed threefold for the sake of brilliance and spiritual luster.

The *bahiṣpavamāna* chants are joined by both forms: that which is the *sāman* occurs in the *ājya* [stotras], and the *ājya* chants contain the call "nirāha"; thus, he calls out with them as if they were already yoked.

(11.2.3) "O Agni, come for the feast; come to us, O Mitra and Varuṇa; for well-prepared is [the offering]; O Indra and Agni, come to the pressed [juice]"—this indeed reveals the Rathantara form as "stoma. (11.3.1) "The wise Soma juices flow forth"—this is a Gāyatrī verse for the purpose of departing; "the brown ones toward the wooden vats" is for the purpose of advancing;
"they have been prepared for Indra and Vāyu" is for the purpose of consecration; "O divine Soma, flow forth for the feast" is for the purpose of departing.
"Run forward!"— with this [verse] they go forth for the sake of departing;
it is a *gāyatra* [sāman], and its *brāhmaṇa* is the same as that of the *gāyatra*.
It belongs to the horse.

Having become a horse, Prajāpati indeed created offspring; he multiplied and became many. He who praises with the horse-stotra is born and becomes many. They employ a one-syllable *nidhana* for the sake of not overstepping the *rathantara*.
(11.3.7) An adversary does not overstep him who knows thus.
(11.3.8) It is the Soma-sāman. (11.3.9) Just as these other plants were, so was Soma; he performed austerity and saw this Soma-sāman.
"By that he attained kingship and sovereignty; glory comes to one who attains kingship and sovereignty," [saying this] while praising with the *soma*-sāman.
There is the *yaudhājaya* [sāman]; whatever is the *brāhmaṇa* of the *yaudhājaya*, that [is to be used].
The *auśana* [chant] belongs to Uśanas; its *stoma* is that of Uśanas.
"O Hero, come toward us now"—the word "toward" (*abhi*) is the form of the *rathantara*, for this day is indeed the *rathantara*.

"With what [splendor] has the Wondrous One appeared for us?"—these verses concern the seer Kavi; by means of them they belong to Prajāpati, for Prajāpati is Kavi. This is for the attainment of Prajāpati.

(11.4.3) "Him, your wondrous one, who overcomes the attackers, who rejoices in the exhilarating food of wealth—like cows lowing toward their calf in the stalls"—the word "toward" (*abhi*) is the form of the *rathantara* chant, for this is indeed the *rathantara*.

(11.4.4) "We invoke Indra with songs"—thus they truly invoke him. (11.4.5) "With your aids, [we call] the finder of wealth"—the aid (*taraḥ*) is indeed the *stoma*, and the finder of wealth (*vidadvasu*) is the sacrifice; for by means of the *stoma* the sacrifice is joined. When he says, "With your aids, the finder of wealth," he [joins] the sacrifice.
Thus he yokes it.

The *rathantara* [sāman] comes into being; the *rathantara* is indeed the Brahman, and the opening day (*prāyaṇīya*) is the Brahman. Having thus stepped upon the Brahman by means of the Brahman, they proceed.
This earth is indeed the *rathantara*; it is upon this very [earth] that they establish themselves and perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*).

The Vāmadevya [Sāman] is used; the Vāmadevya is indeed cattle, for the attainment of cattle. The Vāmadevya belongs to Prajāpati; having established themselves in Prajāpati, they perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
The Naudhasa [Sāman] is used; the Naudhasa is indeed the Brahman. The opening day (*prāyaṇīya*) is the Brahman; thus, by means of the Brahman, they ascend to the Brahman.

The Kāleya [Sāman] is used; the Kāleya and the Rathantara share the same world. The Rathantara is indeed this [earth], and the Kāleya is cattle; having established themselves both on this earth and in cattle, [they proceed].
(11.4.11) This [verse] contains the word *dravat* ("flowing"), for such is the form of this day; the *stoma* is [the same].

(11.5.1) "The Soma juices, distilling intoxication..."—this is a *gāyatrī* verse. The third pressing is indeed full of intoxication and essence; thus, he bestows that very intoxication and essence. "With this, low for the one seeking the gods"—this contains the form of the *rathantara*, for it belongs to the *rathantara*.

For on this day it purifies itself with [the words] "The day from which the tawny one [comes]," which is a form of the *bṛhat* [sāman]; thus he yokes the *bṛhat* on this very day, and they undertake what has been yoked on the following day. With [the words] "Pressing out the juice for the plant," there are verses containing the prefix *pra*;

for this day is, as it were, something to be led forward. With [the words] "It purifies itself toward our dear [desires], sent forth," there is the word *abhi*, which is a form of the *rathantara*; for this day belongs to the *rathantara*.
(11.5.2) "Sacrifice after sacrifice to your Agnis"—for the sacrifice belongs to Agni; thus he establishes the sacrifice within the sacrifice itself.

(11.5.3) It is in the Gāyatra [meter]; whatever is the Brāhmaṇa-explanation of the Gāyatra applies here. (11.5.4) It is the *saṃhita* [chant] with a *nidhana* consisting of three syllables; for the sake of stability, they sit for the sacrificial session (*sattra*) having attained stability.
It is *sapha*.

By means of the *sapha*, the gods reached these worlds; because they reached them, that is the *saphatva* of the *sapha*. Having thus reached these very worlds by means of this [rite], they perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
It is *ākṣāra*.
(11.5.8) There were eight milk-cows; one of them was shattered, and she became agriculture. He who knows this prospers in agriculture.

(11.5.9) Regarding those [cows], the gods and the Asuras contended. Those gods drove the Asuras away from the milk-cows by means of *ākṣāra*. One who praises with the *ākṣāra* drives away his rival from the milk-cows.

(11.5.10) From these worlds, indeed, the essence departed. Prajāpati caused it to flow away with the *ākṣāra*; because he caused it to flow away (*akṣārayat*), that is the *ākṣāra*-nature of the *ākṣāra*.

(11.5.11) Therefore, if one who was previously virtuous should later become worse, he should perform the *brahmasāman* as the *ākṣāra*; he causes the sensory power, the vigor, and the essence to flow away from himself.
(11.5.12) There are two verses for the *januṣ* [stotra] for the support of the day; whatever in this day is unsupported, that he supports by means of these two.
The Gaurīvita comes into being. Gaurīviti Śāktya, the Brāhmaṇa, saw this as something redundant; that became the Gaurīvita.
This is indeed redundant, and they praise with the redundant by means of the Gaurīvita. It is like a *chandoma* day for the *ahīna* sacrifices, and it is prepared even for progeny.
The *vājī-sāman* is indeed a bull, a stallion that bestows seed. They praise it today, and tomorrow it is procreated.

It is performed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; the *anuṣṭubh* is the womb of the meters. Thus, one places the seed in its own womb for the sake of procreation. He who knows this is procreated and becomes manifold.

There are two *udāsa* [stomas]; these two, indeed, are the *udāsa*s that behold the end of the heavenly world. By means of the former, they conclude the first day; by means of the latter, they speak beyond the subsequent day.

Just as those who, on the previous day, go toward a place where grass and water are clearly visible, even so do they, by means of these two, go toward the heavenly world. This is the *gautama* [sāman].
(11.5.22) It is joined with the heavenly world like one who possesses a lineage of seers; he who praises it does not fall from the heavenly worlds.
(11.5.23) And whatever is the Brāhmaṇa concerning the middle *nidhana* of the *anuṣṭubh*, that is also for this [sāman]. (11.5.24) It is the *kāva*.
The *lokabindu* Sāman finds the world for one who praises with it through the body.

With the *svāra* [Sāman], by means of the tone (*svara*), food is ultimately bestowed upon the gods; indeed, by means of the tone itself, he offers that food to the gods at the end. There is the *yajñāyajñīya* [Sāman].
The *yajñāyajñīya* is speech; the sacrifice is established in speech. Thus, they establish the sacrifice in speech at the very end. From that speech, they take hold of it again on the following day.
(PB 11.5.28–29) It is the *trivṛt* stoma, for the sake of splendor and spiritual luster.
(PB 11.6.1) It serves as the introductory verse (*pratipad*).
He undertakes [the *anurūpa*] for the sake of the non-laxity of the *dvirātra*.

"Flow on, O Indu, as the pressed bull"—this becomes the *anurūpa*. For this second day, belonging to Indra and in the *triṣṭubh* metre, is indeed "bull-like" (*vṛṣavat*); thus he speaks in accordance with that very [nature].
He repeats the former form by means of a subsequent form. That he repeats the former form by means of a subsequent form is the reason for the *anurūpa* being called an *anurūpa*.
A son is born to him who knows thus as a corresponding match.
There are two triplets, a *stotrīya* and an *anurūpa*, for the sake of securing the out-breath and the in-breath.
The triplets contain the word "vṛṣan" for the sake of securing sensory power and virility.
The final [hymn] consists of a triplet (ṛca).
By the very same vital breath (prāṇa) with which they set out, they rise up again.
It is indeed the fifteenfold (pañcadaśa) Stoma that occurs.
(11.6.11) Thus he finds firm footing in very vital power (*ojas*) and heroism (*vīrya*); the fifteenfold hymn-form (*pañcadaśa*) is vital power and heroism.
(11.7.1) The *bahiṣpavamāna* chants are joined with both forms: that which is the *sāman* is [present] in the *ājya* chants, and that which is the *stoma* is [present] in the *ājya* chants.
(11.7.2) The *ājya* chants are established as being devoid of [the *sāman*].

(11.7.3) “We choose Agni as the messenger; we invoke Mitra; we, the singers, [invoke] Indra greatly”—thus he illuminates that very form belonging to the Bṛhatī. (11.8.1) “Flow on, O bull, in your stream”—this is a Gāyatrī verse, for the support of the day. (11.8.2) The verses contain the word *vṛṣan* (bull) by way of the form of the Triṣṭubh, for this day belongs to the Triṣṭubh.
"Being purified, O Soma, flow in a stream"—this is for the sake of stability.

"The red bull, bellowing towards the cows"—these *triṣṭubh* verses are rich in the form of the "bull" (*vṛṣan*). Indeed, this second day belongs to Indra and is in the *triṣṭubh* meter; it is that very [day] which it thus praises.
(11.8.6) It is in the *gāyatra* metre; whatever is the *brāhmaṇa* of the *gāyatra*, that is its [explanation].
(11.8.7) There is the *yauktāśva* [sāman].
(11.8.8) Yuktāśva Āṅgirasa carried off two infants; therefore, the mantra departed from him.
He performed austerity; he saw this Yauktāśva [sāman]; the mantra returned to him. Indeed, at that time he desired: "May the Yauktāśva be a bestower of desires. Through it, one obtains desire itself.
There are two Āyāsya [sāmans].

Ayāsya Āṅgirasa ate the food of the consecrated Ādityas; grief seized him, and he performed austerity. He saw these two Āyāsya [Sāmans], and by means of them he drove away his grief. One who praises with the two Āyāsya [Sāmans] drives away grief. Rain departed from these worlds; Ayāsya caused it to descend by means of the two Āyāsya [Sāmans]. One who praises with the two Āyāsya [Sāmans] causes rain to descend.

Food indeed departed from these worlds; Ayāsya caused it to descend by means of the two Āyāsya [Sāmans]. One who praises with the two Āyāsya [Sāmans] causes food to descend. There is the Vāsiṣṭha [Stotra].

By means of this, Vaiḍava Vasiṣṭha, having praised, directly beheld the heavenly world. It is for the manifestation of the heavenly world; one who praises with it does not fall from the heavenly world. This is the Stoma.

(11.9.1) "For we invoke you indeed"—the word "you" (*tvam*) is the form of the *bṛhatī* [meter], for this day belongs to the *bṛhatī*. (11.9.2) "Toward you, the bounteous one..."—with the preceding day they indeed yoke [the sacrifice], for by means of this they set out.
(11.9.3) "The men indeed [invoke] you today and yesterday"—thus he undertakes both today and yesterday, so that there may be no loosening of the two-night rite.
It is the *bṛhat* [sāman]; for the *bṛhat* is indeed height, and the second day is height; thus they ascend from height to height.
It is the *śyeta*, the vehicle of the two *sāmans*, for the continuity of the sacrifice.
It is the *mādhucchandasa*; being possessed of the lineage of the seers (*ārṣeya*), it is yoked for the sake of heaven, and he who praises it does not fall from the heavenly worlds.
(11.9.7) This [laud] is upward-pointing, for such is the form of this day; the *stoma* is [the same].

(11.10.1) "That exhilaration of yours which is most excellent"—this is a *gāyatrī* verse. (11.10.2) For the third pressing is full of exhilaration and full of essence; thus he bestows exhilaration and essence upon it.
"Flow on, most rich in sweetness"—for with this day they flow as it were; "most rich in sweetness"—sweetness is indeed food; thus he bestows food upon the sacrificer.
"These pressed juices toward Indra"—this is for the attainment of power and vigor.
"This Pūṣan, wealth, Bhaga"—thus [he says].
(11.10.6) Though they are *anuṣṭubh*s, they are in the form of *triṣṭubh*s, for this day is indeed *traiṣṭubha*.
(11.10.7) "The far-seeing one purifies himself among the songs of the bull"—these are *jagatī*s, though they are in the form of *triṣṭubh*s, for this day is indeed *traiṣṭubha*.
(11.10.8) There is a *gāyatra* [sāman]; whatever is the *brāhmaṇa* regarding the *gāyatra*, that applies here as well.
(10) It belongs to the *haviṣmat* [day]. (11) Haviṣmān and Haviṣkṛt were two Aṅgirases. On the second day, Haviṣmān prospered; on the ninth day, Haviṣkṛt.

With the words "This one is Haviṣmān," he addresses the day as it is born and Soma as he is born for the sake of the gods. By means of the *sāman*, he invokes a blessing for him; for the *sāman* is a true blessing.
There is a *śaṅku* (stake) for the support of the day; indeed, whatever is not supported is held firm by the *śaṅku*.
Regarding this, they say it is the *sīdantīya* [Sāman]: "By means of this, Prajāpati sat upright upon these worlds. Because he sat (*asīdat*), that is the reason for the *sīdantīya*'s name.
One who praises with the *sīdantīya* sits upright upon these worlds.
(14) It becomes easy to understand.

(15) The form of the *rathantara* [sāman] possesses the celestial light (*svarvat*), while the form of the *bṛhat* [sāman] possesses wealth in heaven (*svarṇadhana*). (16) It possesses wealth in heaven, for such is the form of this day.
(17) These two indeed rain down; they are employed for the attainment of the heavenly world.
(18) There is the Gaurīvita; its Brāhmaṇa is the same as that of the Gaurīvita.
(19) There is the Krauñca.
Speech indeed is the *krauñca* chant; the twelve-day rite is speech. Thus, they praise with speech by means of speech for the prosperity of the sacrifice.
It becomes the *yāma* [chant].
By this, Yama indeed attained the invincible sovereignty over that world. One who has praised with the *yāma* attains the invincible sovereignty over that world.

By means of this, Yami indeed caused Yama to go to the heavenly world; it serves for the manifestation of the heavenly world, and he who praises with this *stoma* does not fall away from the heavenly worlds. (PB 11.11.1) "Come hither, I will speak to you"—these verses contain the word "come" (*ehi*) for the sake of an invitation on the third day, for the sake of continuity.
(PB 11.11.2) This section of the sacrifice consisting of the *ukthas* is, as it were, cut off; [the verses containing "come"] serve to ensure that it proceeds smoothly.
(11.11.3) "For thus you are one who seeks heroes"—thus they speak in common, saying, "May this be so.
(11.11.4) "All have magnified Indra"—for indeed, at this time they have magnified him; by means of this [verse], they magnify the sacrificer himself.
(11.11.5) It contains the word "together with horses" for the sake of winning the hymns and for advancing forward.

For by means of this, they indeed conquered the *ukthas* at the beginning; by means of this, they overcame [all things]. There is the *āmahīyava* chant; it constitutes both the arrangement and the food-eating. It is performed among the verses that speak in common: "May this be thus. This fifteenth day is indeed the *kṣatra*; that which is the *brahmasāman* upon the *gāyatrī* verses proclaims this very day.
It becomes both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*, and he unites them. He places the *brahman* before the *kṣatra*;
