he makes the *kṣatra* and the *viś* subordinate to the *brahman*. The first day is indeed the *brahman*, the second is the *kṣatra*. In that the *Brahmasāman* is performed on *gāyatrī* verses, he causes the *brahman* to prosper with glory; for the *gāyatrī* is the *brahman*.
(10) That is performed while they are singing the same [verses], for the sake of prosperity.
(11) There are two [Sāmans] called Āṣṭādaṃṣṭra.
(12) Indeed, with the cry "Ai-yā-hā," Indra slew Vṛtra; with the cry "Ai-yā-doho-vā," he seized him. These two Sāmans, dedicated to the slayer of Vṛtra, are full of vigor.
(11.11.13) By means of these two, he wins vigor and strength.
(11.11.14) The fifteenfold hymn-form (*stoma*) indeed occurs; thus he finds firm footing in vigor and strength, for the fifteenfold is vigor and strength.
(12.1.1) "Flashing forth, he shines" is the opening verse (*pratipad*) of the third day.

The Gāyatrī is indeed the shining one, the Triṣṭubh the resounding one, and the Jagatī the one desiring cattle; he undertakes these three forms for the sake of the non-laxity of the three-night rite. "These drops have been poured forth"—this is the *anurūpa* verse.
Indeed, Prajāpati created the gods with the word "these" (*ete*), humans with "they have been poured forth" (*asṛgram*), and the ancestors with "drops" (*indavaḥ*); thus he speaks of that very thing.

Moreover, he recites that which was previously the *repha* in another form; in that he recites the former form in another form, that is the "conformity" (*anurūpatva*) of the conforming verse (*anurūpa*).
A son who conforms to him is born for one who knows thus.
There are two triplets, the *stotrīya* and the *anurūpa*, for the sake of securing out-breath and in-breath.

(12.1.7) “The king is impelled by wisdoms, Pavamāna, upon the mind, in order to travel through the intermediate space,” (12.1.8) thus there is a triplet of verses addressed to the intermediate space as its deity; for this third day has the intermediate space as its deity, and so it speaks of that very thing.
(12.1.9) There are five verses; the *paṅkti* meter has five feet, and food is fivefold; it is for the attainment of food.
The final [verse] consists of a triplet; by means of that very vital breath with which they set forth, they return to it.
The Stoma is indeed the seventeenfold, for the sake of stability and procreation.
"By Agni, Agni is kindled"—thus there is an Āgneya (addressed to Agni) Ājya-stotra.
On those same two preceding days, having kindled them, he kindles the third day.
"I invoke Mitra, whose will is pure"—this is the *rāthaṃtara* chant addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa. Indeed, the form of the *rāthaṃtara* is "I invoke."
This Vairūpa [sāman] is the Rathantara in an indirect manner; it thus illuminates that very form which belongs to the Rathantara.

"For they have seen [him] together with Indra"—this is addressed to Indra. Indeed, these worlds appeared as if joined together; this third day has the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*) as its deity, and it is precisely that which it praises.
(TB 12.2.8) "I invoke those two by whom this [world was made]"—this is the *rāthaṃtara* [sāman] dedicated to Indra and Agni.

(TB 12.2.9) "I invoke"—this indeed is the form of the *rāthaṃtara*; that which is the *vairūpa* is the *rāthaṃtara* in its remote form; it thus manifests the form of the *rāthaṃtara* itself as the *stoma*.
(TB 12.3.1) "High is the birth of your juice"—this is a *gāyatrī* verse.
This third day is indeed ascending; he thus addresses that very [day].
It contains the word *andhas*; for the day is light (*andhas*), and it is the commencement of the day:
"The Soma-drops, seeking men... (RV 9.61.1).
(12.3.5) "Abhi" is a form of the *rathantara*; "bṛhat" is a form of the *bṛhat*. He approaches the form of both together, for this day contains both classes [of meters].
(12.3.6) "He sends forth the three voices, the carrier," says the *pravahni*—this is a form of the third day; by means of it they begin the third day.
(12.3.7) These are *triṣṭubhs* in the form of *jagatīs*, for this day belongs to the *jagatī* meter.
(12.3.8) There is a Gāyatra [Sāman]; its Brāhmaṇa is the same as that of the Gāyatra.
(12.3.9) There is a Vaiṣṭambha [Sāman]. (12.3.10) This day, indeed, was collapsing; the gods propped it up with supports (vaiṣṭambha). That is why the Vaiṣṭambha is called Vaiṣṭambha.
(11) They conclude with the *nidhana* "The Quarters," for the support of the quarters.

(12) There is the *paurūmadga*. (13) This day was indeed weakening; the *rakṣases* followed after it. Therefore, the gods struck away the *rakṣases* by means of the *paurūmadga*; one strikes away evil by means of the *paurūmadga*.

The gods and the asuras contended. Those gods submerged the asuras at Paurūmadga. Because they submerged them at Paurūmadga, therefore it is called Paurūmadga; by means of this [sāman], one indeed submerges evil and the rival.
It belongs to Gautama.
Whatever is the Brāhmaṇa of Gautama (PB 12.3.17),
there is a stotra on both sides, for such is the form of this day (PB 12.3.18);
it becomes the intermediate space.
This third day has the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*) as its deity; it is in the intermediate region itself that they praise with the intermediate region for the sake of stability.
The *kāṇva* chant has the *āṣkāra* as its finale (*nidhana*).
"As" is indeed the form of the *rathantara*, and "has" is the form of the *bṛhat*; thus they attain the very form of the third [day] for the sake of prosperity.

(12.3.22) There is the *saṃkrośa* of the Aṅgirases. (12.3.23) By means of this, the Aṅgirases, crying out together, attained the heavenly world; it is for the illumination of the heavenly world. One who praises with this *stoma* does not fall from the heavenly worlds. (12.4.1) If [the verses] begin with "O Indra, if a hundred [helps] of yours," they are those containing the word "hundred" (*śatavatyaḥ*).
The form of cattle is indeed characterized by hundreds; by means of these [verses] characterized by thousands, he obtains the very form of cattle.
“Having become birds, we, possessing the pressed juice,” are *satobṛhatī* verses; he ascends to a more extensive metre for the sake of non-degradation.
“The overcomer, with Purandhi as his companion, desires to win the prize.”

"Come to Indra, the much-invoked; do not [neglect] my song"—thus it says. The syllable is indeed raised up, as it were. For the third day is, as it were, elevated; in that there is this many-syllabled [verse], he thereby establishes the day.
The Vairūpa Pṛṣṭha-stotra has five *nidhanas*, for the support of the quarters. The *pañkti* meter has five feet; food is fivefold, for the attainment of food.
The Vairūpa is indeed the Sāman of the quarters, for with it one addresses the quarters. Now, as to why it has five *nidhanas*: it is for the sake of the seasons, for there are five seasons.

By means of both the seasons and the quarters, these worlds are encompassed; therein he establishes the sacrificer in both. As the sacrificer finds his firm footing, the Udgātṛ likewise finds his firm footing after him.
He who, knowing thus, chants the *udgītha* with the *vairūpa* [sāman],
becomes like the quarters for the removal of his rival.
They conclude with the *nidhana* "the quarter, the region," for the support of the quarters.

(12.4.12) Thus they conclude with the *nidhana* of the quarters above; therefore it belongs to the *bṛhat*. (12.4.13) This world is indeed *rāthaṃtara*, and that [world] is *bārhat*; thus he attains both by means of the form of the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*. (12.4.14) These two, the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*, are the draft-oxen of the path to the gods for the sacrificer; he yokes them for the attainment of the heavenly world.
It becomes like a horse for the sake of procreation.
Just as a frog makes the sound "āṭ," so do they approach the *nidhana* for the sake of non-exhaustion.
There are twelve *vairūpa* chants; the year has twelve months; verily, he finds firm support in the year.
The Virūpa is the year; it serves for the attainment of various kinds of food.
The Mahāvaiṣṭambha is the Brahman-sāman; it serves for the attainment of food.
For when a person eats food, he is supported from within.
They conclude with the *nidhana* "diśaḥ" for the support of the quarters. They chant on *sato bṛhatī* verses for the sake of counter-attacking during the two preceding days.
The *raurava* becomes the *acchāvāka*sāman.
Agni is indeed Ruru; Ruru is Agni.
Agni drives away the cattle of him whose cattle depart; Agni brings back the cattle of him whose cattle come back.
The cattle of one who, knowing this, praises with the *raurava* chant, come back to him again and again.
The *iḍā* is enclosed on all sides (*pariṣṭubdhā*), for such is the form of this day;
the *stoma* is "Three voices have arisen" (*tisro vāca udīrate*), which is the form of the third day; by means of that, they commence the third day.
This third day is indeed threefold and three-versed (*trivat*); it is precisely that which he expresses.
(12.5.3) “Come, sprinkle around!”—thus they become circumambient.
(12.5.4) The third day is indeed the end; these [verses] serve for its completion.
(12.5.5) “O friends, sit down!”—the third day is, as it were, elevated; when he says “sit down,” he thereby establishes the day.
(PB 12.5.6) "The pressed juices, most rich in sweetness"—these *anuṣṭubh* verses are in the form of *jagatī*s, for this day is indeed *jāgata*.

(PB 12.5.7) "Your filter is spread out, O Brahmaṇaspati"—(PB 12.5.8) this [verse] refers to that which is spread out, as it were; for this intermediate space is, as it were, spread out. This third day has the intermediate space as its deity; it is precisely that which it expresses.
There is a *gāyatra* [sāman]; its *brāhmaṇa* is the same as that of the *gāyatra*.
There is a *pāṣṭhauha*;

for it was by means of this that Paṣṭhavāṭ Aṅgirasa overheard the speech being uttered on the fourth day. He approached with "vāk" as the *nidhana*; that was revealed to him, and he stayed for that day.
It becomes the Sāman of Speech (vāk).
Speech, indeed, is the twelve-day rite; it is in speech that they chant with speech for the prosperity of the sacrifice.
The Niṣkirīyas performed a sacrificial session (sattra); they did not discern the third day. For them, this Sāman [was revealed].
Speech floated toward those who were singing; by that, they discerned the third day. They said, "This Speech indeed has revealed the third day for us. This is the vision of the third day;
it belongs to Śukta.

(16) By means of this, Śukti Aṅgiras directly beheld the heavenly world; it serves for the illumination of the heavenly world, and he who praises with it does not fall from the heavenly worlds. (17) There is the Gaurīvita [Sāman]; its Brāhmaṇa is the same as that of the Gaurīvita.
(18) There is the Tvaṣṭrīsāman.

The beings could not make Indra, who was afflicted with an eye-disease, sleep; however, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ made him sleep by means of this [Sāman]. At that time, those [beings] indeed desired it. The *Tvaṣṭrīya* Sāman is a wish-granting Sāman; by means of this, one obtains one's wish. Indra, fearing Vṛtra, entered a cow. The son of Tvaṣṭṛ said to him, "Let us procreate. They procreated him by means of these Sāmans. "We shall be born," they say, as they sit for the sacrificial session (*sattra*).
It becomes unharmed.

(PB 12.5.23) The gods and the asuras contended. That which they struck down among the gods did not come together; that which they struck down among the asuras came together. Those gods performed austerity; they saw this unharmed [hymn], and from that...

"That which was [the Soma] of the gods became whole; that which was of the Asuras did not become whole. Thinking, 'By this we shall be uninjured,' that is the reason for the 'uninjured' (ariṣṭa) nature of the uninjured [Soma]. By means of the uninjured [Soma], the uninjured state is finally established.
There are three [days], for the support of the three-night rite."
They approach the flowing *iḍā* as the final [verse] for the continuity of the fourth day; the *stoma* is "Sing to the most bountiful one" (*pramaṃhiṣṭhāya gāyata*).
In that it says "sing," the form of greatness itself is thereby produced.
(12.6.3) "That [Soma] of thine, O Aṅgiras, is intoxicating"—for the third pressing is indeed intoxicating and full of essence; thus he bestows upon it that very intoxication and essence.
(12.6.4) "Hear the call of Tiraścī"—by this very hearing, (12.6.5) the *pramaṃhiṣṭhīya* [sāman] comes into being.

(12.6.6) With the *pramaṃhiṣṭhīya* [sāman], Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra; he struck him down. One who has rivals should introduce the *ukthas* with the *pramaṃhiṣṭhīya*; he strikes down his rival and becomes more prosperous himself.
(12.6.7) There is the *hārivarṇa* [sāman].

Indra and the Asura Namuci made a compact: "Neither by night nor by day, neither with the wet nor with the dry shall we slay one another. When the dawn had broken but before the sun had risen, he cut off his head with the foam of the waters.
Indeed, that which is when the dawn has broken but before the sun has risen is neither night nor day; and that which is the foam of the waters is neither wet nor dry.

Phena followed after him as he spoke wicked words: "O slayer of heroes, do not harm, do not harm! But he was unable to strike him down with either a Ṛc or a Sāman; he struck him down only with the *nidhana* of the Hārivarṇa.
(10) By praising with the *nidhana* of the Hārivarṇa [sāman] after removing the impurity, one attains both prosperity and splendor.
(11) There is the Tairaścaya [sāman].
(12) When the Aṅgirases were going to the heavenly world, the *rakṣases* followed them; by means of this [sāman], the Aṅgirases [warded off] those [demons] from across.
It encompassed crosswise; it did not encompass crosswise. Therefore, that which belongs to the animals (tairaścya) is evil. Indeed, evil pursued them;
they struck it away with that which belongs to the animals. One who praises with that which belongs to the animals strikes away evil.
The *stoma* is indeed seventeenfold, for the sake of stability and procreation.
"O Pavamāna, let forth thy milk-cows that belong to the Aśvins"—this is the opening verse (*pratipad*) of the fourth day.

When the three-night period has been reached, they proceed with *gāyatrī* verses by way of its form; for the *gāyatrī* is indeed the form of the *pratipad*. The opening verse is a *jagatī*, for this third day belongs to the *jagatī*; thus, by means of the *jagatī*, they transition from the *jagatī* itself.
Whatever other path one might follow from this, whether it be adverse or favorable, [the response is:

"The Purifying One has generated. This is the *anurūpa* (corresponding verse). Indeed, this fourth day is characterized by generation; it generates food, it generates the *virāj* meter, and it generates the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*).
Moreover, he repeats that former form with a subsequent form; that is the "conformity" (*anurūpatva*) of the conforming verse (*anurūpa*).
A son who conforms to him is born for one who knows thus.
There are two triplets, the *stotrīya* and the *anurūpa*, for the sake of securing out-breath and in-breath.

There are two sets of six verses for the support of the seasons. The last [set] consists of three verses; by the very breath through which they proceed, they rise up again. The Stoma is indeed the twenty-onefold for the sake of stability; thus one becomes firmly established.
"Born as the watchful guardian of the people"—with these words, the *ājya* chant for Agni is performed.
This fourth day is indeed "possessing birth" (*janadvat*); it generates food, it generates the *virāj*, and it generates the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*).
"This one for you two, O Mitra and Varuṇa"—with this verse, the *maitrāvaruṇa* chant in the *bṛhatī* meter is performed.
This Vairāja [Sāman] is the Bṛhat in its hidden form; it thus illuminates the very nature of the Bṛhat.
(PB 12.8.5) "Indra with the bones of Dadhyañc"—thus there is a triplet belonging to Dadhyañc.
(PB 12.8.6) For Dadhyañc Āṅgirasa was the domestic priest of the gods; the domestic priesthood of a Brahmin is indeed food. It serves for the attainment of food.
(12.8.7) "This [is] the thought of you two who possess beauty," [this is] the hymn for Indra and Agni.

(12.8.8) "O Indra and Agni, the ancient praise has been born like rain from the cloud"—rain is indeed of the *anuṣṭubh* meter, and this fourth day is of the *anuṣṭubh* meter; he places two *virāj*s in agreement for the sake of food, [and] the *stoma*.
"Flow on, O you who accomplish skill," this *gāyatrī* verse serves for success.
In the words "flow on" (*pavasva*), there is the form of the *bṛhatī*, for this day belongs to the *bṛhatī*.
"O Soma, O Indu, I have delighted in your friendship day by day."

"Many [things], O tawny one, descend upon me; pass beyond the enclosures," so it is said (PB 12.9.4). For he has passed over them, as a bird flies; "he has flown over them," so it is said (PB 12.9.5).
Being purified, he has stepped forth toward them.
(12.9.6) Being Gāyatrīs, they possess the form of Triṣṭubhs; therefore, they are performed in the world of the Triṣṭubhs.
(12.9.7) There is a Gāyatra [sāman]; its Brāhmaṇa is the same as that of the Gāyatra.
(12.9.8) There is the Ātharvaṇa with four *nidhanas*, for the support of the four-night rite.
This fourth day is an Anuṣṭubh by means of a four-footed Anuṣṭubh verse. The Atharvan hymns are indeed medicine; he thus provides medicine.
It possesses a Nidhana according to one's desire.
(12.9.12) Or, by means of another expressed *nidhana*, one obtains desire; this is the *nidhana*-desire for the sake of securing all desires.
(12.9.13) There is the *āṣṭādaṃṣṭra* [sāman];
whatever is the Brāhmaṇa-explanation regarding the *āṣṭādaṃṣṭra*. (12.9.14) [End.]
The Ābhīśava [stotra] is performed for the support of the day;
indeed, whatever is not supported is held fast by means of a rein.
He sings it without pressing down, for that is the characteristic form of this day.
The Āṅgirasa chant, having four *nidhanas*, is employed for the stability of the four-night rite;
the *svaḥ* is the *pṛṣṭha* chant, for that is the characteristic form of this day;
it is the *sattrāsāhīya*.

Whatever was unbearable for the Asuras, that the gods overcame by means of the *Sattrāsāhīya*; they thought, "By means of the *sattra* we shall overcome them. That is why the *Sattrāsāhīya* is called *Sattrāsāhīya*. One who praises with the *Sattrāsāhīya* overcomes his rival through the *sattra*. They chant on *gāyatrī* verses for stability and for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); by the very breath with which they set out, they rise up again.
(12.9.24) There are *gāyatrī* verses containing the word "bull" (*vṛṣan*); they thus lead away from the form of the *triṣṭubh*.

(12.10.1) The *stoma* [is expressed by]: "Drink the soma, O Indra; let it exhilarate you! The stone has pressed it for you, O Lord of the bay horses (*haryaśva*), well-guided by the arms of the presser like a racing steed. For the fourth day is, as it were, unguided; this [verse] serves to guide it.

"May all the hosts overcome the enemies, O heroes"—this *ati-jagatī* verse ascends to a larger metre for the sake of non-degradation. Indeed, that which approaches a smaller metre from a larger metre is like a degradation; therefore, when this *ati-jagatī* is employed on the fourth day, it is for the sake of non-degradation.
"He who is the king of the people... [etc. (PB 12.10.4).
For at that time, the *vācas* went to the kingdom; verily, by means of this [verse], they cause the sacrificer to go to the kingdom.

By means of the meters, the gods carried the Āditya to the heavenly world; he did not stand firm. They made him firm with the *nidhana* of the Vairāja [sāman]. Therefore, the Āditya shines both away and hitherward;
the sound "ī" is both away and hitherward.
Having chanted the Prastāva, he supports the supports; thus he places food right at the beginning, for the Prastāva is the mouth of the Sāman.

He supports it ten times; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the food is of the nature of the Virāj, for the sake of securing food. He supports it thirty times, for the sake of securing even more abundant food.
The Vairāja Sāman is used; they chant upon the Virāj verses. The Virājs are the supports; he establishes the Virājs facing one another for the sake of obtaining food.
He sings the *anutunna* (the unpressed) for the sake of the emission of seed, for from the unpressed, seed is emitted.
They churn the fire on the right thigh of the Udgātṛ; for from the right, seed is poured forth.
When [the animal] has been brought near and the *ahiṅkāra* has been made, they churn [the fire]; once it is born, he makes the *ahiṅkāra* over it.
Therefore, when a son is born, the cattle low toward him. When he is born, they deliberate: "Shall we cast [the fire] into the Gārhapatya? Into the Āgnīdhra? Or into the Āhavanīya?"
They throw [the fire] into the Āhavanīya; for the sacrificer has his abode in the Āhavanīya. When he [does so], he makes his own abode radiant.
He who knows thus becomes radiant and endowed with spiritual luster.
He offers the oblation upon it for the sake of peace.
(19) He makes an oblation with clarified butter; clarified butter is indeed brilliance; thus he places brilliance within himself.
(20) With the verse, "O Agni, kindled, shine forth before us," he makes the oblation with a *virāj* meter; the *virāj* is food, for the sake of obtaining food.
(21) The *traiśoka* becomes the *brahmasāman*.
They chant on *atijagatī* verses for the sake of transcending the day; indeed, they transcend by means of this day.
They conclude with the *nidhana* "diva" for the sake of striking away evil; he who has praised with the *traiśoka* hymn strikes away evil.
The *pṛśni* of Bhāradvāja serves as the *achāvāka*sāman.
"The gods indeed call food 'pṛśni'"; this is for the attainment of food.
Through the *iḍā*-verses they attain the *aiḍa*; for such is the form of this day, its *stoma*.
"The sage of heaven, beloved on all sides"—these verses are *parivati* (enclosing); for the fourth day is the end, and these [verses] serve for its completion.
(12.11.2) "For you indeed, O divine one..."—the word "you" (*tvam*) is a form of the *bṛhat* [sāman], for this day belongs to the *bṛhat*.
(12.11.3) "Soma, purifying himself with his wave, flows through the filter;
at the head of speech, the purifying one bellows."
For they have now reached the summit of speech; by means of this [verse], they cause the sacrificer to reach the very summit.
With the two *virāj* verses, "Like conquerors with the soma-juice," for this day belongs to the *vairāja* melody.

At the morning pressing, with the words, "Soma flows, the progenitor of hymns," they procreate that *ṣoḍaśin* cup which was drawn at the morning pressing. It is at the third pressing that they bring it forth.
Being *triṣṭubh*s in reality, they have the form of *jagatī*s; therefore, they are performed in the world of the *jagatī*s.
There is a *gāyatra* [sāman]; its *brāhmaṇa* is the same as that of the *gāyatra*.
There is an *aurṇāyava* [sāman].

The Aṅgirases indeed performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*). For them, heaven was attained and won, but they did not know the path leading to the gods. While they were reflecting, the auspicious one of the Aṅgirases went forth.
He approached the Gandharva Ūrṇāyu, who was swinging amidst the Apsarases. Whichever woman he pointed out, saying, "Her! she desired him.

He addressed him, saying, "O auspicious one! Indeed, heaven has been won by you, but you do not know the path leading to the gods. This *sāman* leads to the heavenly world; go there, but do not say, 'I have seen it.
He went forth as one who was auspicious; he said, "Indeed, heaven has been attained by us, but [we do not know] the path..."
"But we know the path of the gods; this Sāman leads to heaven. Having praised with it, we shall go to the heavenly world.
"Who told you that? "I myself saw it. Having praised with it, they went to the heavenly world, but he was left behind, for he had spoken a falsehood. He is this leper (śvitra).
This *sāman* leads to heaven; he who praises with the *aurṇāyava* becomes one who dwells in the heavenly world, the world of merit.
There is the *bṛhaka*;
it is praised by its lineage of seers (*sāmārṣeya*). The word "tvam" is for the attainment of food, for food is indeed given with the word "hi"; and by this [verse], he also raises up the *ṣoḍaśin*.
The Ātīṣādīya chant is used;
the Ātīṣādīya is indeed life-force, for the non-obstruction of life-force.
They conclude with the *nidhana* at the very moment of exhaustion; thus they attain the entirety of life-force.
It becomes the *nānada*.
Having passed over the greater commencement, they commence the fifth day with the commencement of the sixth day; by that means they commence the sixth day for the sake of continuity.
He begins the chant with a sixteen-syllable [verse]; and by this he indeed raises up the *ṣoḍaśin* [stotra].
The Āndhīgava [sāman] occurs. By praising with the Āndhīgava, one secures food for both [parents].
The Vātsapra occurs.
In this [vātsapra], indeed, the Vairāja is established; he who praises with the vātsapra becomes firmly established.
Vatsaprī Bālandana found no faith; he performed austerity and saw this vātsapra. He found faith. "May we find faith," they say as they sit for the sacrificial session (*sattra*); they find faith.
It has the *īn* as its *nidhana*, for that is the form of this day; the *pavamāna* chants end with the *nidhana* for the stability of the day.
The *stotra* is "Agniṃ vo vṛdhantam" (The increasing Agni for you), for they have indeed increased at this time; thus they cause the sacrificer himself to increase.

(12.12.3) "We indeed [have come] to you, O matchless one"—for they have now approached that matchless body of Prajāpati; by means of this [verse], they cause the sacrificer to go to that which is matchless.

(12.12.4) "O Indra, drink this pressed [soma], the most excellent, immortal intoxication"—for they have now attained the preeminence of speech; by means of this [verse], they cause the sacrificer to attain preeminence. (12.12.5) It is the Saindhukṣita [sāman].
The Ṛṣi Sindhukṣit was indeed a royal seer who, wandering for a long time after having been exiled, saw this *saindhukṣita* [hymn]. He attained it; he found firm support.
One who praises with the *saindhukṣita* attains and finds firm support. There is the *saubhara*, which is the splendor of the *bṛhat*.
The fourth day is, as it were, fallen; by means of this *saubhara* chant, he supports it with the splendor of the *bṛhat*.
It becomes dear to Vasiṣṭha. By means of this, Vasiṣṭha indeed attained the favor of Indra; one who praises with the *vasiṣṭha-stotra* attains the favor of the deities. This is the *stoma*.
Indra and Bṛhat became united; that Bṛhat surpassed Indra by means of one body. He was afraid of it, thinking, "It will overcome me. He said, "Let this sacrificial rite of yours be the Ṣoḍaśin.
It became the Ṣoḍaśin; that is its origin.
(12.13.2) One is surpassed in glory by his rival who chants the *ṣoḍaśin* with the *bṛhat* on *gāyatrī* verses in the *dvipadā* meter.
(12.13.3) "With our bay steeds, come to the praise"—these indeed are the *gāyatrī* verses in the *dvipadā* meter; one should chant the *stotra* upon these.

(12.13.4) Indra sought refuge with Prajāpati, saying, "I shall slay Vṛtra. He gave him this *anuṣṭubh* verse as a weapon (*apaharasa*). With it he did not strike him down; because he was not struck down, he roared. That...
"The roar of Nānada is its nature" (PB 12.13.5).
He ran toward him again; having fashioned the vigor of the seven *hotṛ* priests, he gave it to him, and he overthrew him.
He who knows this overthrows whomever he wishes to overcome. (PB 12.13.6)

Therefore, they chant on verses containing the word *hari*; they recite verses containing the word *hari*; the cup is drawn on verses containing the word *hari*, for he bestowed the *hara* upon him after fashioning it.

This *ṣoḍaśin* has the twenty-one-fold as its foundation; for at the morning pressing the Hotṛ-priests utter the *vaṣaṭ*-call seven times, at the midday pressing seven times, and at the third pressing seven times.
There is the *gaurīvita* chant.
Gaurīviti Śāktya indeed perceived this surplus of the *brahman*; that became the Gaurīvita.
This is a surplus; they praise with the Gaurīvita as a surplus. By means of the *ṣoḍaśin*, he becomes possessed of the morrow;
he is also provided for his progeny.

"Viśāla addressed [him] with the *libjā* chant," said Upoditi Gopāleya; "he made the *nānada* cry in the *anuṣṭubh*, he praised the *ṣoḍaśin* with the *gaurīvita*, and he attained prosperity directly;
he did not fall away from prosperity.

(PB 12.13.12) He who, having performed the *nānada* in the *anuṣṭubh*, praises with the *ṣoḍaśin* using the *gaurīvita*, truly addresses Viśāla with the *libjā* chant for prosperity; he attains prosperity directly and does not fall away from prosperity.
One should chant the *ṣoḍaśin* on *śakvarī* verses if he should desire, "May I be a wielder of the thunderbolt.
The *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed a thunderbolt, and the *śakvarīs* are a thunderbolt; by means of the thunderbolt he secures the thunderbolt for him, and he becomes a wielder of the thunderbolt.
One should chant the *ṣoḍaśin* on *anuṣṭubh* verses if he should desire, "May speech not speak over me."
The *ṣoḍaśī* is indeed the thunderbolt (*vajra*), and the *anuṣṭubh* is speech. By means of the thunderbolt, he secures speech for him; speech does not speak over him.
One should chant the praise upon these verses beginning with "The Soma has been pressed for you, O Indra.

He who desires food should chant the *ṣoḍaśī* on *virāj* verses. The *ṣoḍaśī* is the thunderbolt, and food is of the *virāj* nature. By means of the thunderbolt, he secures food for him; he becomes an eater of food.
(12.13.19) One should praise with these verses beginning, "Bring forth [the song] for the great one, for increase.
(12.13.20) These *virāj* verses indeed consist of thirty-three syllables: twenty-one are the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), twelve are procreation (*prajāti*).
(12.13.21) He who knows this is established in the foundation and is procreated; he does not decay within the intermediate state.
(12.13.22) Or rather, these are one-footed, three-syllabled *bhurijas* and *śakvarīs*, the meters of Viṣṇu.
(12.13.23) By means of these, indeed, Indra slew Vṛtra; quickly by means of these one slays evil and quickly becomes more prosperous.

(12.13.24) When they are praised together, they consist of thirty-four syllables. There are thirty-three deities, and Prajāpati is the thirty-fourth among the deities; thus they go unto Prajāpati for safety.
Having bestowed gold as a gift, they chant with the *ṣoḍaśin* [stotra]; his *ṣoḍaśin* becomes luminous.

A black horse stands nearby for the sake of equality of gaze; he stands dispelling the very world of his rival. One syllable was indeed the lowest meter of the gods, seven syllables the highest, and nine syllables [was the middle].
The Asuras had the lowest *chandas*, consisting of fifteen syllables, while the highest belonged to the gods. The gods and the Asuras contended with one another;
Prajāpati, having become one who possesses the *ānuṣṭubh* meter, stood between them. The gods and the Asuras called out to him from both sides; he turned toward the gods.
Thereupon the gods prospered, and the Asuras were defeated.
He prospers in his own self, and his rival is defeated, for one who knows thus.
Those gods deprived the Asuras of the fifteen-syllable [meter] by means of the single-syllable [meter];
the fourteen-syllable by the two-syllable; the thirteen-syllable by the three-syllable; the twelve-syllable by the four-syllable; and the eleven-syllable by the five-syllable.

"With six syllables they took away ten syllables, with seven syllables nine syllables, and with eight [syllables] they took away eight" (PB 12.13.30). "In this very way, he who knows thus takes away prosperity from his rival" (PB 12.13.31). This *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice is indeed like one whose sacrifice has been obstructed; for at that time the gods were fewer and the Asuras were more numerous. From the fewer, [they take away] the more numerous rival...
"He who knows thus appropriates [the merit].

"From whom no other has been born, who has surpassed all beings, Prajāpati, in harmony with his offspring, he dwells with the three lights—he is the Ṣoḍaśin. With these words, the Udgātṛ looks at the cup.

(12.13.33) For him who knows thus, the *ṣoḍaśin* becomes luminous. (12.13.34) The *stoma* is indeed the twenty-onefold; he finds firm support for the sake of stability. (13.1.1) "Flow on, finding cattle, finding wealth, finding gold"—this is the opening verse (*pratipad*) of the fifth day.
(13.1.2) These Śakvarī verses are indeed finders of cattle, finders of wealth, and finders of gold.
(13.1.3) Cattle are the Śakvarīs; through cattle one finds everything.
(13.1.4) "O Soma, thou art a good hero, all-knowing"—this [verse] praises that very thing which belongs to him who has cattle, namely, that he is a good hero.
"May they pour for you honeyed ghee and milk"—for indeed, honeyed ghee and milk are what the cattle pour; thus he speaks of that very thing.
"Of the purifying one, the all-knowing"—this becomes the *anurūpa* (responding verse); he thereby speaks of him as the all-knowing, for by means of cattle one finds everything.

(13.1.8) "Your outpourings have been let loose"—for indeed, the days are now as if already created. (13.1.9) And he thus restates that former form by means of a subsequent form; in that he restates it by means of a former form, that is the "conformity" (*anurūpatva*) of the conforming verse (*anurūpa*).
A son who conforms to him is born for one who knows this. There are two *ṛc*-verses, a *stotrīyā* and an *anurūpa*, for the sake of securing the out-breath and the in-breath.
There are two hymns of seven verses each for the support of the meters; there is one of four verses for stability;
the last consists of a triplet, by which very breath they go forth, they rise up again toward it.

The Triṇava Stoma indeed occurs for the sake of stability and nourishment; for this [Stoma] is threefold and nourishing. "Thy splendors are like the lightning of the rain," thus is the Ājya-stotra for Agni.
Cattle are indeed prosperity (*śrī*), and the Śakvarī verses are prosperity; it is that very thing which it thus proclaims.
(13.2.3) "The brilliance of Agni is like the movement of the dawns," for nowadays the days are indeed as if they have already passed.
(13.2.4) "They strive apart for thee, like chariot-horses," for nowadays the days indeed strive apart.
(13.2.5) "For even from afar there is help for you both, O Varuṇa"—this is the Maitrāvaruṇa [śastra].
Whatever in the sacrifice is ill-performed, Varuṇa seizes that; he thereby expiates that very thing.
"Rising up with vigor"—this is addressed to Indra.
There are five seasons, which are the form of rising; by saying "with vigor," they rise indeed with vigor and with heroism.
(13.2.9) "O Indra and Agni, you two..."—this is the *rāthaṃtara* [sāman] dedicated to Indra and Agni.
(13.2.10) This *rāthaṃtara* is implicit in the *śakvarī* verses; it reveals that very form, the *stoma*. (13.3.1) "Flow on, O Soma, most resplendent!"—these are *gāyatrī* verses addressed to Viṣṇu.

The Gāyatrī is indeed Brahman, and Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; thus he establishes the sacrifice in Brahman itself. With the words, "Soma, pressed by the pressers," which is the form of the *simāns*, he thereby brings these [verses] into harmony with their own form.
With the words, "O Soma, that which is wondrous and worthy of praise," although they are Gāyatrīs, they are in the form of Triṣṭubhs; therefore, they are performed in the place of the Triṣṭubhs.

There is a *gāyatra* [sāman]; its *brāhmaṇa* is the same as that of the *gāyatra*. There is a *yaṇva* [sāman]; the *yaṇva* is indeed cattle; it is for the attainment of cattle. He sings it continuously, for the continuity of the sacrifice.
(13.3.8) It is [a hymn] with one and a half verses, for such is the form of this day.
(13.3.9) It is the Śākala.
(13.3.10) By means of this, indeed, Śakala established himself on the fifth day; he who praises with the Śākala establishes himself.
The Vārṣa [Sāman] comes into being.
Vṛśa Vaijāna was the domestic priest of Tryaruṇa Traidhātava, the Ikṣvāku king.
That Ikṣvāku king, while driving, cut off a Brahmin boy with his chariot. He said to his domestic priest: "It was by you that I..."
Thinking, "This [sacrifice] has come to such a state in its priesthood," he set it right with this *sāman*. Indeed, at that time, he desired this;
the *vārṣa* is a *sāman* that wins desires, and by means of it, one secures his desire.
It consists of one and a half *iḍās*, for such is the form of this day.
It is the Mānava [sāman].
(PB 13.3.15) By means of this, indeed, Manu attained abundance as Prajāpati; one who praises with the Mānava is procreated and becomes manifold.
(PB 13.3.16) It is the Ānūpa [sāman].
(13.3.17) By means of this, Vadhryaśva Ānūpa indeed attained abundance of cattle; he attained abundance of cattle by praising with the Ānūpa [hymn].

(13.3.18) It becomes the *vāmra* [verse]. (13.3.19) It is praised by its lineage of seers (*māma-ārṣeya*). Indeed, when they praise a cow, a horse, or a man, they praise him as "desirable" (*vāma*); by this [verse], they praise the day itself.
(13.3.20) It has one and a half *iḍās*, for such is the form of this day.
(13.3.21) The *āgneya* chant has three *nidhanas*; it serves for stability.

(13.3.22) When Agni was created, he did not blaze up; Prajāpati fanned him with this *sāman*, and he blazed up. This *sāman* is indeed brilliance and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); through it, one obtains both brilliance and spiritual luster.
He obtains spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa). It belongs to Śiśu;
for Śiśu Āṅgirasa was a composer of mantras among the composers of mantras. He addressed his ancestors as "O sons! (putrakāḥ).
The ancestors said to him, "You do not act according to dharma, you who address us, your own fathers, as 'little sons'.
He replied, "I am indeed your father, for I am the composer of the mantras.

They asked about him among the gods, and those gods said, "He is indeed the father who is the composer of the mantras. Thus he won that [victory]; he who praises with the *śaiśava* hymn likewise wins.

They chant on *gāyatrī* verses for stability and for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). By the very same breath with which they set out, they rise again. The *gāyatrīs* contain [the name] Viṣṇu; thus they do not depart from the form of the *triṣṭubh*.
As for the *stoma*: Indra went to Prajāpati, saying, "I will slay Vṛtra. For him, he [Prajāpati] extracted this power from the meters.

Having fashioned vigor, he gave it to her, saying, "With this you shall be able. That is the reason for the *śakvarī* verses being called *śakvarīs*. He split the boundary; that became the *simā*; he made it great (*mahnyam*); from that there was a great sound (*mahān ghoṣaḥ*), hence they are the *Mahānāmnīs*.
With five feet he supported the quarters; with six feet the seasons; with seven feet the meters; with two feet the person.
The *saṃstuta* chants are performed with two syllables each; therefore, animals have two hooves.
On both sides of the *iḍā* there is the syllable *atha*; therefore, the horns are sharper than the tuft [of hair on the forehead].
He sings the *upakṣudrā* verses; therefore, animals are small at their joints (*upakṣudra*).
(13.4.6) She sings with her shoulders touching; therefore animals are closely joined together.
(13.4.7) She sings in various forms; therefore animals are of various forms.

(13.4.8) The waters were indeed of the essence of milk; the gods were afraid of the worse state resulting from evil. In that they praise after placing water nearby, it is for the warding off of the worse state resulting from evil.
There is separation from evil and inferiority for one who knows thus.

There is the Gāyatra course for one desiring spiritual luster; with the *svar* finale, he is established in the world beyond through honey. There is the Triṣṭubh course for one desiring vigor; with the *athakāra* finale, he is established in the world beyond through clarified butter.

The *jāgata* *ayana* belongs to one who desires cattle; with the *iḍā* as the *nidhana*, he attains prosperity in yonder world. "Añjasārya Mālya released the *śakvarī* verses," so said Alamma Pārijānata Rajana Kauṇeya, "if he would be able to establish them. Indeed, this very [verse] makes them manifest; they are established.
Having quickly chanted with these [Śakvarī verses], he quickly sings the *udgītha* (PB 13.4.12).

Having praised with the Śakvarīs, they praise with the *purīṣa*. The Śakvarīs are indeed cattle, and the *purīṣa* is the cow-pen; thus they enclose the cow-pen for the sake of the cattle, and they cause them to turn back into it so that they may not stray.
(14) "Indra has grown strong for exhilaration"—for they have indeed grown strong at this time.
(15) Among those [verses], there is the Bārhadgira [sāman].
(16) "From the sweet, thus from the midpoint"—the fifth day is indeed the Viṣuvat; among those [verses], there is the Rāyovājīya.
Indra delivered the Yatis to the hyenas; of them, three remained: Pṛthuraśmi, Bṛhadgiri, and Rāyovāja. They said, "Who will nourish these sons of ours? Indra replied, "I shall.
Having placed them under his care and attended to them, he wandered about.
Increasing them, and having increased them, he said to those excellent youths, "Choose boons.

Pṛthuraśmi said, "Kṣatra for me. To him he gave the Kṣatra by means of this Pārthuraśma [Sāman]. One desiring kṣatra should praise with this; verily, the manifestation of kṣatra comes to him. Bṛhādgiri said, "Brahmavarcasa for me. To him he gave Brahmavarcasa by means of this Bārhadgira [Sāman]. One desiring Brahmavarcasa should praise with this; he becomes possessed of Brahmavarcasa.
"Give me cattle," he said; Rāyovāja granted him cattle by means of this Rāyovājīya [Sāman]. One who desires cattle should praise with this; he becomes possessed of cattle (PB 13.4.18).

One should perform the Pārthuraśma as the Brahmasāman for a Kṣatriya, the Bārhadgira for a Brāhmaṇa, and the Rāyovājīya for a Vaiśya; thus he endows them with their own respective forms (PB 13.5.1). "The stalk has been pressed for intoxication"—this is a Gāyatrī verse. For the third pressing is indeed full of intoxication and full of essence; thus he bestows that very intoxication and essence.

(13.5.2) "Toward lofty splendor and fame"—the word "toward" (*abhi*) is the form of the *rathantara*, and "lofty" (*bṛhat*) is the form of the *bṛhat*; thus he approaches the form of both together, for this day consists of both classes [of tones].
(13.5.3) "The breath, the child of the great ones"—this is the form of the *simā* chants, for the *simā*s are indeed great; he thus provides them with their own proper form.
(13.5.4) "Flow on for the winning of booty"—these are *anuṣṭubh* verses addressed to Viṣṇu.

Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; whatever is not performed here, that he performs by means of Viṣṇu, the sacrifice. With the verse, "The vigorous drop flows, the milk-stream," which is the form of the *simā* chants, he thus brings them into harmony with their own form. Although they are *triṣṭubh*s, they are in the form of *jagatīs*; therefore, they are performed in the place of the *jagatīs*.
There is a *gāyatra* [sāman]; its *brāhmaṇa* is the same as that of the *gāyatra*.

There is a *santani*; it is for the continuity of the fifth day. This twelve-day rite is indeed speech stretched out; of that, this fifth day is the equinox (*viṣuvān*). By means of this [sāman], he thus makes that [speech] continuous.
There is the *cyāvana* chant. Indeed, the *cyāvana* is procreation; he who praises with the *cyāvana* is procreated and becomes manifold through the *cyāvana*.

From these worlds, indeed, the rain departed. Prajāpati caused it to descend by means of the *cyāvana*. Because he caused it to descend (*acyāvayat*), that is the "causing-to-descend" nature of the *cyāvana*; [with it] he causes the rain to descend.
"Praising with the *cyāvana* [hymn], he becomes a *krośa*" (PB 13.5.14);
"He becomes a *krośa*" (PB 13.5.15).
By means of this, indeed, Indra, at the *indrakrośa*, Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni cried out, "These are the cows! for the sake of obtaining cattle; thus the *krośa* is performed.
The Gaurīvita chant is performed; its Brāhmaṇa explanation is the same as that previously stated.
The Ṛṣabha is in the Śākvara metre.
The Śākvaras are indeed cattle; thus he obtains this pair within cattle for the sake of procreation. Indeed, cattle do not propagate without a bull.
It becomes the *pārtha* [stotra] (PB 13.5.20).
By means of this, indeed, Pṛthu Vainya attained sovereignty over both kinds of cattle; he who praises with the *pārtha* attains sovereignty over both kinds of cattle (PB 13.5.21).
It is an eight-fold stoma with a pause at every foot.
Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra; Vṛtra enveloped it with sixteen coils. He [Indra] saw this *padastobha*; with it he unwound [the coils].
One should sing as if unwinding, for the sake of striking away evil.
Evil indeed seized him; he struck it away with the *padastobha*. One who praises with the *padastobha* strikes away evil.
He saw the highest [syllable] of the feet; that is why the *padastobha* is called *padastobha*. It has twelve finales for the sake of stability.
It belongs to the Lord of the Ten (*dāśaspatya*).
(13.5.27) That cow which they praise as "the lord of the ten" (dāśaspati), it is that very one they praise; by this [verse], they praise the day itself.
(13.5.28) The *pavamāna* chants end with the *nidhana* for the support of the day. (13.6.1) The *stoma* is: "O Agni, may we kindle thee."

This section of the sacrifice consisting of the *ukthas* is, as it were, severed; [the priest recites] "Sing the *sāman* for Indra" for the sake of continuity. The *kakubh* verses are full; therefore, one does not suffer from hunger.
The *kakubh* is indeed the person (*puruṣa*); thus, he gratifies the person itself in the middle.
(13.6.5) "The Soma has been pressed for you, O Indra"—this is the form of the *simāns*; by means of its own form, he thus brings them into harmony.
(13.6.6) There is the *sañjaya* [chant].
(13.6.7) The gods and the asuras contended; "Whichever of us wins, let our cattle belong to them."

"By means of the *sañjaya*, those gods completely conquered the Asuras; because they completely conquered (*samajayan*), therefore the *sañjaya* [chant] is performed for the sake of securing cattle. (PB 13.6.8). It is the *saumitra*.

(13.6.9) This Rākṣasa, the destroyer of sacrifice, who had long tongues, was prowling about licking the sacrificial animals. Indra did not wish to kill it by any means of magic. Now there was a handsome Sumitra Kutsa; Indra said to him, "Speak to her. He spoke to her, and she said to him, "I have neither seen nor heard this, but it seems dear to me."

"Of the heart," he commanded her; she purified it in the *saṃskṛta* [language]. Indeed, at that time those two desired it; this *saumitra* Sāman is a fulfiller of desires, and by means of it one secures desire.

"Being a good friend (*sumitra*), you have done a cruel deed," so Vāc addressed him. Grief (*śuc*) seized him; he practiced austerity (*tapas*), and he saw this *saumitra* [Sāman]. By means of it, he drove away the grief; he became free from grief.
When they were praised by Saumitra after the slaying [of Vṛtra],
it became the Mahāvaiśvāmitra. Having slain the evil, because they celebrated, that is the reason for the Mahāvaiśvāmitra’s name "Mahāvaiśvāmitra."
"Hāyā, ihayā, ohā, oheti"—with this they drove away the cattle. There is a *triḍa* [chant], for the support of the three-night rite.
They approach the final *iḍā* as it flows, for the continuity of the sixth day.
The *triṇava* chant itself becomes the stoma for the sake of stability and nourishment; for this *trivṛt* is indeed nourishment.
"The light of the sacrifice, the sweet and beloved, purifies itself"—this is the opening verse (*pratipad*) of the sixth day.
The *gāyatrī* is indeed the light among meters, the *revatī* is the light among *sāmans*, and the *trayastrimśa* is the light among stomas; thus he perfectly unites the lights, even for his son.

"The son becomes radiant" (PB 13.7.3). "Sweet and dear" (PB 13.7.4)—the *revatī* verses are indeed cattle; he thus speaks of that which is sweet and dear. "Most intoxicating, exhilarating, the essence of power" (PB 13.7.4)—power (*indriya*) is indeed vigor, and the essence is cattle; he thus speaks of that very thing.
"Amṛkṣata pravājina" is the *anurūpa* verse;
for at this time the days are as if already set in motion.
Moreover, he repeats that former form with a subsequent form; for what was a former form, he restates by means of a subsequent one.
He follows with the *anurūpa* verse; that is the conformity of the *anurūpa*. A son who conforms to him is born for one who knows thus.
There are two triplets as the *stotrīya* and the *anurūpa* for the sake of securing the out-breath and the in-breath.
They consist of ten verses each; the *virāj* has ten syllables, and food is of the nature of the *virāj*, for the sake of securing food.
The next [section] consists of ten verses with a common refrain (*sodarka*), for the sake of not losing the power, the vigor, and the essence.
Indeed, where the gods perceived power, vigor, and essence, they struck it down [into the earth].
It consists of four verses for the sake of stability.

Dhvasrā Puruṣantī was indeed unwilling to give thousands [of cattle] to Taranta and Purumīḍha. The two Aśvins reflected: "How might this which has been taken by us remain unaccepted? They returned to her, saying:
"We shall take back the thousands from Dhvasrā and Puruṣantī."
"Crossing over, he flows slowly, he runs"—thereby, indeed, that [portion] of theirs became taken but not formally accepted (*apratigṛhīta*).
He who knows thus, his [portion] becomes taken but not formally accepted.
It is without the *nārāśaṃsa* cup, for the sake of securing both kinds of food, that of men and that of the gods.
The final [stotra] consists of a triplet; by means of that very breath with which they set out, they rise up again.
The thirty-three-fold Stoma is used for the sake of stability; indeed, this [sacrifice] is established among the deities.
"This hymn for the worthy Jātavedas"—this is the Ājya-stotra for Agni, accompanied by the *udarka*.

So that the sensory power (*indriya*), the vigor (*vīrya*), and the essence (*rasa*) may not be lost—wherein indeed the gods perceived the sensory power, the vigor, and the essence, they struck it down accordingly (PB 13.8.2).
"Against you, O Sun, at your rising" (PB 13.8.3)—this [verse] for the Maitrāvaruṇa contains the word *sūra*.
The sun (*sūra*) is indeed the end; this sixth day of the days is the end. Thus, at the very end, they chant for the sake of a firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*).

(13.8.4) "Break all those who are hostile"—this verse addressed to Indra, accompanied by its concluding refrain (*sodarka*), is for the purpose of preventing the loss of sensory power, heroism, and vital essence. Indeed, wherever the gods perceived sensory power, heroism, and vital essence, they struck it down [into the earth]. (13.8.5) "For you two are the officiating priests of the sacrifice"—this verse addressed to Indra and Agni, accompanied by its concluding refrain, is for the purpose of preventing the loss of sensory power, heroism, and vital essence. Indeed, wherever the gods perceived sensory power, heroism, and vital essence...
Not seeing it, they pressed on with the *stoma*:
"O Indu, for Indra accompanied by the Maruts"— these *gāyatrī* verses addressed to the Maruts come into being,
for the midday pressing belongs to the Maruts.
(13.9.3) "Being cleansed by the skillful-handed one"—this is the form of the *simā* verses.
(13.9.4) Indeed, the form of the *simā* verses is common to the *revatī* verses, for from the *simā*s the *revatī*s are produced.
(13.9.5) "This very one, the ten fingers [have grasped]"—these are the *āditya* verses; these creatures are indeed the *ādityas*, and he establishes himself in their very midst.
Though they are *gāyatrīs*, they have the form of *triṣṭubhs*; therefore they are performed in the world of the *triṣṭubhs*.
There is a *gāyatra* [sāman]; its Brāhmaṇa is the same as that of the *gāyatra*.
There is the *iṣovṛdhīya* [sāman].

The *iṣovṛdhīya* is indeed cattle; it is for the acquisition of cattle. The fifth day is for nourishment (*iṣ*), and the sixth is for growth (*vṛdh*); for at this time they have grown, and by means of this [chant], they cause the sacrificer himself to grow.

(PB 13.9.10) There is the *krauñca* [chant]. The curlew (*kruñc*) found the day to be sought; indeed, the sixth day is like that which is sought, and by means of this [chant], they find it. (PB 13.9.11)

The *vājadāvaryas* are used; for *vāja* is indeed food, [and they serve] for the attainment of food. For when there is food, then there is the cow, then the horse, then the man as a possessor of vigor (*vājī*).
The *revatīs* are used for stability.
The *ṣaṇnidhana* [sāman] belongs to the six-night rite for the sake of stability.
The *revatī* verses are indeed the waters; if they were to make them the *pṛṣṭha*, the sacrificer would become devoid of cattle, for they would burn away his cattle.
Wherever the waters turn back, there plants are born; but where they stand still, they become barren.
In that regard, they exist; therefore, they perform [them] during the *pavamāna* [laud], for they praise with the *pavamāna* in a forward direction (PB 13.9.17).

The *iṣovṛdhīya* is a threshing-post, the *krauñca* a rope, the *vatsa* a calf, and the *vājadāvaryas* and *revatīs* are the mothers. When these *sāmans* are performed in this manner, it is as if one milks a cow that has already been let loose (PB 13.9.18).
They occur in the *aukṣṇorandhra* [laud].
(19) Ukṣṇorandhra Kāvya beheld the heavenly world directly by means of these two; it is for the illumination of the heavenly world that he who praises them does not fall from the heavenly worlds.

(20) He becomes a winner of prizes (*vājajit*) for the attainment of all and the conquest of all; for those who come to the sixth day win every prize (*vāja*). (21) Prizes are indeed food; [this is] for the securing of food.
The Varuṇa-sāman is performed.

By means of this, indeed, Varuṇa attained sovereignty and lordship; he became glorious. He who praises with the Varuṇa-sāman attains sovereignty and lordship and becomes glorious. The Aṅgirases’ cow-pen is performed.
The *revatī* verses are indeed cattle; thus they entrust the cow-pen to the cattle, and they cause them to set out toward that very place so that there may be no straying away.
The *vāmadevya* chant contains the word "here" (*iha*).
By means of this, Vāmadeva indeed attained the pre-eminence of food; for the pre-eminence of the Brahmin is food. It serves for the attainment of food.

They chant on *gāyatrī* verses for the sake of stability and for the attainment of spiritual power (*brahmavarcasa*). By means of the very same vital breath with which they set out, they rise up again.
The *gāyatrī* verses belong to the Maruts; thus they do not depart from the form of the *triṣṭubh*.
The other meters are exhausted, but the *gāyatrī* is inexhaustible; therefore, they chant on *gāyatrī* verses.
(13.10.2) "For aid, [we invoke] Surūpakṛtnu"—by beginning with this six-footed verse, which is the form of the sixth day, they undertake the sixth day for the sake of continuity.
(13.10.3) "When, O Indra, both worlds..."—this six-footed verse is the form of the sixth day; by means of it, they undertake the sixth day for the sake of continuity.
(13.10.4) The Vāravantīya is the Pṛṣṭha-stotra chanted upon the Revatī verses.

The essence of the waters is indeed the *revatī* verses; the essence of the *revatī* verses is the *vāravantīya*. Thus, when they praise with the *vāravantīya* as the *pṛṣṭha*, they employ the *revatī* verses together with their essence.
This *vāravantīya* is indeed wealthy and belongs to the *revatī* verses; from it, one who is wealthy is born through the *revatī* verses.
He who knows this becomes wealthy.
This *sāman* became manifest to Keśin Dālbhya; it spoke to him, saying, "The singers do not sing for me;
they have not sung with me as the *udgātṛ*. How, O venerable one, is your *āgā*? He replied, "I am indeed the *āgeya*;
one should sing as if singing the *āgā* for the sake of stability. [He saw] this man lying on his back, looking toward the west, singing this *āgā*, fully understanding it and having mastered it.
He did not know him; he said to him, "I place you in front. They said to him, "Who indeed is this? To what is he capable?
[He replied,] "He is indeed capable for me. That is the origin of Alamma's name as Alamma. One should sing "here and there" for the sake of stability.
The *ṛṣabha* chant belongs to Raivata.
Cattle indeed belong to Raivata; thus he secures that pairing within cattle for the sake of procreation, for cattle do not propagate without a bull.
It becomes the *śyena*.
The falcon indeed reaches birds that have already passed away; for the earlier days are like birds that have already passed away. To attain them, the falcon is employed.

The falcon is indeed capable of carrying this day across, for it is the swiftest among birds. To prevent its being driven back and to ensure the successful crossing, this [chant] is performed, for the sixth and seventh days constitute the end.
The exponents of Brahman say: "Since the *pṛṣṭha* chants have the *bṛhatī* as their abode, yet these two are *gāyatrīs* and two are *jagatīs*, where then do the *bṛhatīs* come to be?

Those two feet (*pada*) of the *jagatīs* which remain over are joined to the *gāyatrī*; thus all become *bṛhatīs*. He establishes the *pṛṣṭhas* in their proper abode; he becomes possessed of an abode.
They chant on verses of six feet for the support of the six-night rite.
He sacrifices with the *saptapadī* [verse] for the continuity of the seventh day; the *stoma* is [the same].
"The one who dwells on the mountains, surrounded by [the waters]"—these *gāyatrī* verses containing the word *pari* (around/surrounding) are used for the attainment of everything.
"To be pressed out together with the Vasus"—the Vasus are indeed cattle; [this is] for the acquisition of cattle.
(13.11.3) "O friends, for intoxication..."—thus [are] the Vālakhilyas.
(13.11.4) These two *ṛc*s of the Vālakhilyas [are used] on the sixth and the seventh day.
(13.11.5) In that these two *ṛc*s of the Vālakhilyas occur, it is for the interlocking of the two days, for non-disintegration, and for continuity.
(13.11.6) "The Soma drops, the Indus, flow clear"—these verses are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter with *nibhasada* (repeated syllables), for the sake of stability.
(13.11.7) "With this purification, flow forth these riches"—these are *triṣṭubh* verses that have the form of *jagatīs*; therefore they are performed in the world of the *jagatīs*.
(13.11.8) There is a *gāyatra* [sāman], which is the very essence (*brahmaṇam*) of the *gāyatra*.
The Vaidanvata hymns are used.
Vidanvān Bhārgava, indeed, struck Indra; grief seized him, and he performed austerity. He saw these Vaidanvata hymns; with them he drove away his grief.
One who praises with the Vaidanvatas drives away grief.
It belongs to Bharadvāja by virtue of its hair (loman).
Hair, indeed, is cattle; [it serves] for the attainment of cattle.
Regarding this, they say: "It is long"; for length is life; [it serves] for the attainment of life.
The *Kārṇaśravasa* comes into being; they indeed hear him as he praises.
Karṇaśravas Āṅgirasa, desiring cattle, saw this *sāman*; with it, he created a thousand cattle. That this *sāman* exists is for the nourishment of cattle.
The *Gaurīvita* comes into being; [it is] the cow.
The Brāhmaṇa on the *ivita* chant (PB 13.11.17): "The *madhuścyut* becomes the *nidhana* (PB 13.11.18);
it is for the attainment of the highest food, for this honey is indeed the highest food."

These two are indeed the breasts of Prajāpati: the *ghṛtaścyut* finale and the *madhuścyut* finale. Prajāpati is the sacrifice; by means of these two, he milks him for whatever desire he desires—he milks it.
There are two *krauñca* [verses].
It has the *śnauṣṭha* [melody] (PB 13.11.23).
By means of this *śnuṣṭi*, Aṅgiras directly beheld the heavenly world; it is for the illumination of the heavenly world that one who praises with it does not fall from the heavenly world.
This is the *Sāman* of Agni Vaiśvānara; they conclude with the *nidhana* "dīdihī," for Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed "shining" (*dīdā*).

The *pavamāna* chants end with the *nidhana* for the stability of the day. Regarding the *stoma*, the exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "Should the *dvipadā* verses be employed at the beginning (*prāyaṇataḥ*) or at the conclusion (*udayanataḥ*)? They should be employed at the conclusion; for the *dvipadā* verses are the person, [employed thus] for the sake of firm standing.
(13.12.3) By means of speech, indeed, they extend the entire sacrifice; therefore, a person speaks every kind of speech, for everything that has been praised finds its support in him.
(13.12.4) It becomes a *gūrda*.
(13.12.5) While the Gopāyanas were performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*), two Kirāta women, skilled in Asura-magic, [stood] within the enclosing sticks.
They scattered their vital breaths before him; they approached Agni with the verse, "Thou art our nearest [friend]," and by that they recovered their vital breaths.
At that time, they desired this very thing: "The *gūrda* is a *sāman* that wins desires; by means of this, one secures desire.
It belongs to Gotama and is auspicious.
(13.12.7) By this he indeed invokes a blessing for him, for the *sāman* is truly a blessing.

(13.12.8) By this, Gotama attained victory and greatness; therefore, both those who are descendants of Gotama in the line of descent and those who are his followers in the present day, all these sages call themselves "Gotamas.
(13.12.9) He becomes one whose sons are raised high.
That which is the *udvaṃśīya* [sāman] is the son of the *udvaṃśa*.
He chants over the half-portion of the *iḍā*.
Therefore, the streams flow upward; finally, he establishes himself in the cattle through the *iḍā*.

(13.12.13) The *ṛc* and the *sāman* are released when they have been prepared at the end; he chants the seventh day with a loud tone for the sake of continuity. (13.12.14) When the six-day period concludes, speech is as if exhausted; one should not speak much, nor ask another, nor give instruction to another.
(13.12.15) One should cause him to taste honey or ghee, just as one anoints a weary horse with oil.
The chant is indeed the thirty-threefold stoma for the sake of stability; he is established among the deities.
These stomas and meters are attained when the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*) is attained.
When the six-day rite has been attained, they proceed after having fashioned the meters into stomas.
(14.1.3) "Proclaiming poetic wisdom like Uśanas," with this [verse] they proceed in the form of the Gāyatrī.
(14.1.4) This earth is indeed the Gāyatrī; it is upon this very [earth] that they proceed, having established themselves.
(14.1.5) The *pratipad* is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
(14.1.6) Ojas is vigor; the Triṣṭubh is vigor. Having exerted themselves in vigor, they proceed.
(14.1.7) There is a triplet as the *stotrīya* for the sake of securing out-breath and in-breath.
(14.1.8) They consist of verses containing the word "bay" (*harivat*) for the sake of the freshness of the *Chandomas*.
There are two [hymns] consisting of twelve verses each.

There are twelve months in a year; thus he raises up the year for the sake of the preceding six-day period, so that it may be provided with a support. There are twenty-four [verses]; there are twenty-four half-months in a year; thus he raises up the year for the sake of the preceding six-day period, so that it may be provided with a support.
"Dṛta Aindota," said Abhipratārin Kākṣaseni, "what becomes of those who go to the top of a great tree? Do they fly away as winged birds, or do they fall down without wings?
"Those who are wise are the winged ones; those who are ignorant are the wingless. Having made the *trivṛt* and the *pañcadaśa* stoma-chants their two wings, they proceed to the heavenly world.
Indeed, the *caturviṃśa* stoma serves for splendor and for the luster of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*)."
(PB 14.2.1) "The head of heaven, the messenger of earth"—this is the *ājya* chant dedicated to Agni.
(PB 14.2.2) For this third three-night period is indeed the head of heaven.

(PB 14.2.3) "Agni Vaiśvānara, born from the cosmic order"—by saying "Vaiśvānara," he [the priest] thus indirectly instructs him with Agni’s own dear abode; for that is indeed Agni’s dear abode. With his very dear abode, he thus provides him with instruction.

(14.2.4) "Sing forth to Mitra—" with these words [he recites] the verse addressed to Heaven and Earth and to Mitra and Varuṇa. Heaven and Earth are indeed the beloved abode of Mitra and Varuṇa; by means of that very beloved abode, he thus indirectly honors them. (14.2.5) "O Indra of brilliant luster, come hither"—this is the Ārbhava hymn addressed to Indra. The Ṛbhus are indeed the beloved abode of Indra; by means of that very beloved abode, he thus indirectly honors him.

(14.2.6) "Praise him who with his flame..."—this is an undefined verse addressed to Indra and Agni; he recites it in the latter half [of the day] so that the deities may not be assailed and so that the deities may not perish. (14.3.1) The *stoma* is [established]. (14.3.2) "Flow on, O bull, in your stream"—this *gāyatrī* verse serves for the support of the day.
There are *triṣṭubh* verses containing the word "bull" (*vṛṣan*), for this day has the form of the *triṣṭubh*.
(14.3.3) "O Soma, being purified, flow in a stream"—this is for the sake of stability.
(14.3.4) "The drop has gone forth to the appointed place of Indra"—these verses have a downward motion, for this day is as if it were something to be led forward.
(14.3.5) Although they are Jagatīs, they take the form of Triṣṭubhs; therefore, they are performed in the world of the Triṣṭubhs.

It is a *santani* [chant] for the sake of continuity on the seventh day. Just as two people living in separate houses might run away from each other, even so do these two days—the sixth and the seventh—run away from one another. Just as one would bring them together and unite them, even so does he unite these two by means of this *sāman*.

(14.3.10) Sacrifice indeed departed from the gods; having assumed the form of a *suparṇa* bird, it wandered about. The gods seized it with these *sāmans*. These *chandomas* are indeed like sacrifice; they belong to the sacrifice itself. (14.3.11) The *rohitakūlīya* is performed for the sake of victory.
(14.3.12) By means of this, Viśvāmitra won the race at Rohitakūla with two red horses.
Viśvāmitra, whose mind was fixed on truth, went among the Bharatas. There, in a gathering, he was cast out as a portion by those called the Adantins with the words:

"Do not, do not! You shall conquer these stakes; you shall fulfill these for me, if these two red bulls carry this bank built of stones. He beheld these two *sāmans*; having harnessed them, he drove forward and won.
This twelve-day sacrifice is indeed a long-extended racecourse; these [chants] are for its victory.
The *kaṇvarathantara* is employed; for the *kaṇvarathantara* is the very brilliance of the *rathantara*.
When they chant on the seventh day with the *kaṇvarathantara*, they employ the *rathantara* in its full integrity.

(14.3.17) "There is a repetition (*jāmi*) in the twelve-day sacrifice," so said Ugradeva Rājani. "The sixth day is Bārhata, and the seventh is Bārhata; because the Kaṇvarathantara is performed, there is no repetition. (14.3.18) There is the Gauṅgava chant. (14.3.19) Agni desired, "May I be an eater of food. He practiced austerity and saw this Gauṅgava.
By means of that, he became an eater of food; because he ate the food after having found it and bellowed, that is the *gauṅgava* nature of the *gauṅgava*.
It is performed for the sake of securing food.

In that the *sāman* praises the deity, thereby the sacrificers become possessors of true blessings. "May we be possessors of true blessings," they say as they sit for the sacrificial session (*sattra*); indeed, they become possessors of true blessings.
The Āyāsya [sāman] occurs with a *tiraścīna* finale for the sake of stability.
Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, it is said, ate the food of the consecrated Ādityas;
he fell away from his state, and he saw these Āyāsya [sāmans]; with them he restored himself, for the seventh day is, as it were, fallen away.
That which is this *sāman* serves to beautify the day itself by means of it.
The *pravad-bharga* occurs;
[with the verse] "Having come, we, possessing the pressed juice," the *bṛhatī* meters ascend to a more extensive *chandas* for the sake of non-degeneration.

(14.4.2) "No one shall reach him with his ritual act"—these are *bṛhatī* verses; by means of their repetition, they become *jagatī*s. (14.4.3) Indeed, this is like a corruption when they proceed from a larger *stoma* to a smaller *stoma*. That these *jagatī*s occur through repetition is for the sake of supporting the day itself.
(14.4.4) There is the *kāṇva* *abhinidhana*.
(14.4.5) By means of the *abhinidhana*, Indra struck Vṛtra with the thunderbolt; he struck him down. One who praises with the *abhinidhana* strikes down his rival.

(14.4.7) The Vaikhānasa seers were dear to Indra. The demon Rahasyu, a plunderer of gods, killed them at the death of a sage. The gods said to him, "Where have those seers gone? He sought them out, but he did not find them. He purified these worlds with a single stream; [he found them] at the death of a sage.

He found them; with this *sāman* he set them in motion. At that time, he indeed desired: "The *Vaikhānasa* *sāman* is a wish-granting *sāman*; by means of it, one obtains one's wish. The *stoma* [is established].

"That exhilaration of yours which is most excellent"—this is a *gāyatrī* verse. For the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) is indeed full of exhilaration and full of essence; thus, he bestows exhilaration and essence upon it.
(14.5.2) "With this stream he has been pressed"—these are *kakubh* verses; they are indeed *triṣṭubh*s by their introductory character.
(14.5.3) This is like a falling away when they proceed from a larger *stoma* to a smaller *stoma*; that these *triṣṭubh*s occur as an introduction is for the sake of supporting the day.

(14.5.4) "O friends, sit down"—these are the *vālakhilya*s; these two triplets are the *vālakhilya*s on the sixth and the seventh days. That these two *vālakhilya* triplets occur is for the sake of the two days.
"For interconnection, for non-slipping, for continuity" (PB 14.5.5);
"With the conquest of your soma-juice" (RV 8.45.1)—this is the Virāj, and the Virāj is food; it is for the attainment of food.
"The prize-winning steed has flowed forth" (RV 8.93.20)—this is the Akṣarapaṅkti, the source of the Stomas.

(14.5.7) Moreover, this very *chandas* is indeed now free from weariness (*ayātayāman*), namely the *akṣarapaṅkti*; by means of that, the *chandomas* are performed as being free from weariness. (14.5.8) The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "Since the *stomas* and *chandases* are attained in the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), of what *chandas* are the *chandomas*? He should reply: "They are of that *chandas* which consists of these *akṣarapaṅktis*.
(14.5.9) With the verse, "Those Soma-draughts which are in the distance," the sacrifice has, as it were, gone to the far distance; they seek it back again by means of this [verse].
The *dakṣanidhana* chant is used.

Prajāpati created offspring; once created, they seemed weak and were unable to sustain themselves. With this *sāman*, [he sang] "for skill" (*dakṣāya*), and thereby bestowed vigor and strength upon them. In that this *sāman* is employed, one bestows vigor and strength upon oneself.
It consists of gravel.
Indra, whom all beings praised, approached the seer Śiśumāra who was at the gravel and said, "Praise me!
He, leaping into the waters, said, "I shall praise you for as much as this [distance]. Therefore, it is the impetus of the waters.
He was distressed and felt as if he were inferior. He saw this *sāman*; with it, he reached the waters.
Indeed, at that time, he desired: "May the *Sāman* of Śarkara be a granter of desires. Through it, one obtains one's desire.
There is a raft.

(14.5.17) "Those who undertake the twelve-day rite," they say, "plunge into the ocean. Just as one who enters the ocean without a boat does not emerge from it, so it would be were it not for the fact that there is a boat; [the twelve-day rite serves] for the complete attainment of the heavenly world. (14.5.18) "May we cross over all difficulties"—by this [rite], they cross over whatever in their performance has been ill-chanted or ill-recited.

It has a foundation of eleven syllables; the *triṣṭubh* consists of eleven syllables, and the *triṣṭubh* is vigor and strength; verily, he finds firm support in vigor and strength. There is the *gaurīvita*; that which is the *brahman*-formula of the *gaurīvita*.
There is the *kārtayaśa*.
They conclude with "hi" as the *nidhana* for the sake of striking away evil; one who praises with the *kārtayaśa* hymn strikes away evil;
it possesses the power of the *sāhaviṣa*.

(14.5.25) By means of this [sacrifice], the Aṅgirases, possessing good oblations, directly beheld the heavenly world; it is for the illumination of the heavenly world that one who has praised does not fall from the heavenly worlds. (14.5.26) Those who discourse on the Brahman say: "Since the *stomas* and the *chandas* are completed in the six-day period, of what *chandas* are the *Chandomas*?

One should reply: "The *chandas* is the person (*puruṣa*). For the person is fivefold (*pāṅkta*), and the person is the two-footed [verse-form] of the *Chandomas*; this is for the sake of their freedom from exhaustion.
The *jarābodhīya* hymn is used for the attainment of food.
Indeed, the *jarābodhīya* is food and the *gāyatrī* is the mouth; thus he places food in his very mouth and eats food. He who knows this becomes an eater of food.
They chant on *gāyatrī* verses for stability and for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). By means of the very breath with which they proceed, they rise up again.
The *pāvamāna* hymns end with the *iḍā*; the *iḍā* is cattle, and the *chandomas* are cattle; thus he places cattle within cattle. Regarding the hymn-form (*stoma*):
"May Vatsa direct your mind"—this part of the sacrifice, namely the *ukthas*, is as if severed; [he says this] so that there may be continuity.
(14.6.2) "Do thou, O Indra, bring to us..."—these are the full *kakubh* verses.
(14.6.3) This [practice] is like a corruption when they proceed from a larger *stoma* to a smaller *stoma*. In that these full *kakubh* verses occur, it is for the sake of non-corruption.
(14.6.6) Now, Vatsa and Medhātithi were both descendants of Kaṇva; Medhātithi reviled that Vatsa.
"You are no Brahmin, you are the son of a Śūdra," he said. "Let us two compete with the truth regarding Agni, whichever of us is more learned in the Veda (brahmīyān).

Vatsa competed with the Vātsa [Sāman], and Medhātithi with the Mādhātitha. Not even a single hair of his was harmed. Indeed, at that time he desired this; the Vātsa is a Sāman that wins desires; through it, one obtains one's desire.
It becomes one that brings renown (*sauśravasa*).
Upagu Sauśravasa was indeed the domestic priest of Kutsa Aorava; that Kutsa cursed him, saying, "He who shall sacrifice to Indra!
Indra approached Suśravas and said to him, "Sacrifice for me, as if you were hungry. To him—

Indra performed that sacrifice. That *puroḍāśa* approached Kutsa and said to him, "I have sacrificed; where has your curse fallen? "Who sacrificed for you? "Suśravas. Then Kutsa, the son of Urva, approached; while Sauśravasa was singing the *udgītha*, he cut off his head with an *audumbarī* branch. Sauśravas said to Indra, "Indeed, it was because of you that such a one came upon me."
Thus he set him in motion with this *sāman*. Indeed, at that time, it desired: "May I be a *sāman* that wins desires for the sake of renown.
By means of this, one secures one's very desire.
There is the *vīṅka*.
Cyavana Dādhīca was indeed dear to the Aśvins; he grew old, and they made him ageless by means of this *sāman*, causing him to shake off [his decrepitude] in the waters.
They restored him to youth. At that time, those two surely desired this; the *vīṅka* is a *sāman* that wins desires, and by means of it, one secures his desire.
The Stoma is indeed the twenty-fourfold for the sake of splendor and spiritual luster.
"They cleanse the newborn, the beloved infant"—this is the *pratipad* (opening verse) of the eighth day.
For he is born like an infant on the seventh day; him they cleanse on the eighth day.
The *stotrīya* consists of a triplet for the sake of securing out-breath and in-breath.
They are verses containing the word "bay" (*harivat*) for the sake of the freshness of the *chandomas*.
There are nine verses.

There are five verses; the *paṅkti* consists of five feet, and food is fivefold; it serves for the attainment of food. It contains the word "arrow" (*bāṇa*); the arrow is indeed the end, and this is the eighth day of the sacrifice; thus they praise with an end at the very end for the sake of stability. There are three triplets for the continuity of the out-breath and the in-breath.
(14.8.1) "Agni, the god, with the Agnis, in harmony"—with these words, the *ājya* chant for Agni takes place.
(14.8.2) By the phrase "with the Agnis," he kindles the eighth day together with those previous days that have already been kindled.
(14.8.3) "We invoke Mitra"—this is the *maitrāvaruṇa* chant in the *bṛhatī* meter.

(14.8.4) This Chandoma is, as it were, a place of deep bottomless water. Just as people, having bound themselves together, wade through a place of deep bottomless water, even so does he interlink these forms for the sake of the non-disturbance of the Chandomas.
(14.8.5) "We incite that Indra"—this is addressed to Indra.
(14.8.6) By means of the eighth day, the gods caused Indra to win; by the ninth, they slew evil. By this [day], they cause the day itself to win.
(14.8.7) "To Indra and Agni, a great homage"—this [verse] is in the Bṛhatī metre, dedicated to Indra and Agni.

(14.8.8) These Chandomas are, as it were, a deep ford; just as people wade through a deep ford by interlocking their hands, even so he interlocks these [verses], so that the Chandomas may not stumble.
(14.9.1) "O Adhvaryu, [the Soma] pressed with stones"—this is a Gāyatrī verse, for the support of the day.

(14.9.2) They are *gāyatrīs*, yet they have the form of *triṣṭubhs*, for this day belongs to the *triṣṭubh*. (14.9.3) "The Soma-drops, the active ones..."—the word "towards" (*abhi*) is the form of the *rathantara*; "the great one" (*bṛhat*) is the form of the *bṛhat*. He approaches the form of both together, for this day possesses both classes [of meters].
