(14.9.4) "The sustainer of heaven, the effective juice, flows clear"—for this three-day period is, as it were, unsupported; by saying "the sustainer," it is for the sake of support itself.
The *jagatī*s being real, they are performed in the world of the *triṣṭubh* by means of the form of the *triṣṭubh*; therefore, they are performed in the world of the *triṣṭubh*.
There is a *gāyatra* [sāman]; its *brāhmaṇa* is the same as that of the *gāyatra*.
There is a *vairūpa* [sāman].
The Vairūpa is indeed cattle; it serves for the acquisition of cattle. The year is multiform, and food is multiform; it serves for the acquisition of food.
The Āśu Bhārgava comes into being. Indeed, this day was weakened; the gods invigorated it with the Āśu, and that is the reason for the name Āśu.
The Mārgīyava [Sāman] is used.

Regarding this, they say, "He is indeed a hunter of gods. By means of this, he attained sovereignty over both kinds of cattle; through the Mārgīyava, one attains sovereignty over both kinds of cattle.
The Saumitra [Sāman] is used.

Whatever is the Brāhmaṇa concerning the *saumitra* [sāman], it is the *aiṭata*. Indeed, by means of this, Kāvya Iṭa directly beheld the heavenly world; it is for the manifestation of the heavenly world that one who praises with it does not fall from the heavenly worlds.
There is the Sākamaśva; its Brāhmaṇa is the same as that of the Sākamaśva.
They say that it is the *dhūr* sāman; the *dhūḥ* are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), [and it serves] for the attainment of the vital breaths.
There is the Vilambasauparṇa.

This [day] on the eighth day is indeed the self of the Sauparṇa hymns; these two which are on either side are the wings. Just as the inner self, as it were, extends between the two wings, so too the inner self extends between the wings;
therefore it is called the "Outstretched Sauparṇa."
The Sauparṇa is performed for the attainment of the heavenly world;
for these Chandomas are its second form.
The Vāmadevya is indeed cattle, and the Chandomas are cattle; thus he unites cattle with cattle.
It has the *gāyatrapārśva* as its side-piece.
This day, indeed, was shattered; the gods restored it by means of the *gāyatrapārśva*; therefore it is called *gāyatrapārśva*.
When the three-night rite was scattered, they treated it with these *sāmans*, and they approached it with the *gāyatrapārśva*.
They extended it with the *santanī* [verse] and they perfected it with the *saṃkṛti*; the two preceding three-night periods were firmly established, but this one was not firmly established.
When these very *sāmans* are performed, it is for the sake of its firm establishment.
There is the *pauruhanmana* [sāman].
Puruhanman Vaikhānasa saw the heavenly world directly by means of this [hymn]; it is for the manifestation of the heavenly world, and he who praises with it does not fall from the heavenly worlds.
It is an *abhyāghātya* [chant], for the *chandomas* have chants that are *abhyāghātya*.
It is a *dvaigata* [chant].

(14.9.32) By means of this, Bhārgava went twice to the heavenly world; having gone, he returned again. It is performed as a "twice-gone" (*dvaigata*) for the sake of securing two desires. (14.9.33) There is the *hārāyaṇa* [sāman]. (14.9.34) Indra, desiring splendor and desiring the power of Hari, performed austerities.
He saw this Hārāyaṇa; by it he enclosed the *tejas* and *haras*. One who praises with the Hārāyaṇa becomes possessed of *tejas* and *haras*.
It becomes flawless (*achidra*). Whatever flaw there was in this day, that the gods closed up with the flawless [hymn]; that is the flawlessness of the flawless.

The Bārhaduktha [Sāman] occurs. Indeed, by means of this, Vāmadeva Bṛhaduktha attained the pre-eminence of food; for food is indeed the pre-eminence of the Brahmin. It is for the attainment of the eating of food. The Udvaḍ Bhārgava occurs.
By a downward slope, indeed, the gods went to the heavenly world; by an upward slope, they returned.
The *pavamāna* chants end with the *nidhana* for the stability of the day.
The *stoma* is [accompanied by] *satobṛhatī* verses beginning with: "Who knows him when the soma is pressed? (RV 10.29.6).

(14.10.2) This [use of] *satobṛhatī* verses on the seventh day is indeed like a corruption (*apabhraṃśa*), for it does not occur on the eighth day; therefore, they should be employed on the eighth day to avoid corruption.

(14.10.3) Regarding this, they say: "This metre, the *satobṛhatī*, is as if loose. But that *bṛhatī* which has repeated feet (*punarpadā*) is firmly established. The verse, "O Indra, eastward, westward, northward... is an inquiry into the directions for the sake of firm establishment.

Among those [stotras], the *brahmasāman* is the *naipātitha*. It is joined for the sake of heaven like a *sāmārṣeya*; one who has praised it does not fall from the heavenly worlds. [It is accompanied by the verse: "And may he hear both."
(14.10.7) And for the sake of the continuity of both the *pṛṣṭha* chants and these days;
(14.10.8) among those [chants], there is the *vaiyaśva*.
(14.10.9) Vyaśva Aṅgiras indeed beheld the heavenly world directly by means of this; it is performed at the end of the *pṛṣṭhas* for the manifestation of the heavenly world, being the *stoma*.

(14.11.1) "Flow on, O god, for our life; let thy exhilaration go to Indra"—this is a *gāyatrī* verse. For the third pressing is indeed full of exhilaration and full of essence; thus he bestows exhilaration and essence upon it. (14.11.3) "The child of the great ones is breath"—these verses are possessed of breath; thus he bestows breath upon the sacrificer.
(14.11.4) "Toward us, most winning of booty"—the word "toward" (*abhi*) is the form of the *rathantara*; for this day belongs to the *rathantara*.

(PB 14.11.5) "Flow on, O Soma, great ocean"—this is the *akṣarapaṅkti* [meter], the source of the *stomas*; for this very meter, the *akṣarapaṅkti*, is now free from exhaustion (*ayātayāman*). By means of it, the *chandomas* are made free from exhaustion. The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "Since the *stomas* and meters are exhausted in the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), of what meter are the *chandomas*?"

Thus, according to the *Chandas*, one should say that these are "syllable-rows" (*akṣarapaṅkti*). The verses beginning with "They urge on the Sun, the ruddy ones" are actually *gāyatrīs* in form, yet they are performed in the place of the *jagatīs*;
therefore, there is a *gāyatra* [chant], for which the same explanatory passage (*brāhmaṇa*) as that of the *gāyatra* applies.
The *arka* chant consists of the *svāśiras* verses.
The *arka* is indeed food; it serves for the attainment of food. The *svāśiras* verses are the vital breaths; they serve for the non-obstruction of the vital breaths.
It is beautiful in form.
Cattle indeed are the "well-formed" (surūpa); it serves for the acquisition of cattle.
It becomes the "shining" (bhāsa); he who has praised shines forth. It has the "step" (pada) as its finale, for this day belongs to the Rathaṃtara.

Svarbhānu, the son of Asura, pierced the sun with darkness; he did not shine. Atri dispelled that darkness with his radiance (*bhās*), and he shone. Because that became *bhās*, that is the origin of the name *bhāsa*.
These days of the Chandomas are, as it were, darkness; by means of this *sāman*, one causes them to shine forth.
(16) There is the Kākṣīvata [Sāman].
(17) Indeed, by means of this, Kākṣīvān, the son of Uśij, attained progeny and abundance; he who praises with the Kākṣīvata is procreated and becomes many.
(18) There is the Āsita [Sāman].
By means of this, Asita Daivala beheld the vision of the three worlds; it is performed for the sake of securing the three desires.
There is an *aiṣira* [verse];
there is a *traita* [verse], for the sake of stability.

The *rāthantara* [sāman] has its finale on the word "pada," for this day belongs to the *rathantara*. The *nāthavindu* [sāman] wins what one seeks; these days, which are the *chandomas*, are indeed "winners of what is sought" (*nāthavindu*), and through them one finds what is sought.
The *gaurīvita* [sāman] is used; its *brāhmaṇa* is the same as that of the *gaurīvita*.
The Kautsa [sāman] occurs.

By means of this, Kutsa indeed perceived the drinking of the soma-juice; he used to maintain the fast-day with a skin full of liquor for the sake of securing both kinds of food. The Kautsa is performed.
The Śuddhāśuddhīya [sāman] occurs.
Indra gave the Yatis to the hyenas; a vulgar voice spoke out against him, and he thought himself impure. He saw this Śuddhāśuddhīya [sāman], and by it he became pure.
One who praises with the Śuddhāśuddhīya becomes pure.
There is the Krauñca [sāman]; that which is the Brāhmaṇa of the Krauñca is for the second day.
It becomes the *rayiṣṭha* (PB 14.11.32);
for cattle indeed are the *rayiṣṭha*, [and it serves] for the acquisition of cattle. It becomes the *audala* (PB 14.11.33).

By means of this [sāman], Audala Vaiśvāmitra attained progeny and abundance; he who praises with the Audala is procreated and becomes many. (PB 14.11.36) The exponents of Brahman say: "Since the *stomas* and *chandāṃsi* are obtained in the six-day period, of what *chandas* are the *Chandomas*?
One should reply: "Of the *puruṣa-chandas*. For man is fivefold (*pāṅkta*), and man is the two-footed [verse] among the *Chandomas*; thus they possess the quality of being unwearied.
The *viśoviśīya* [sāman] occurs. Agni desired: "May I be the guest of every people (*viś*); may I enjoy hospitality from every people.
He performed austerity; he saw this *viśoviśīya*; by means of it, he became the guest of every people. Every people...
"May the clans enjoy hospitality; he becomes a guest among every clan, and enjoys hospitality among every clan," [saying this] while praising with the *viśoviśīya* chant.
They praise in *gāyatrī* verses for stability and for spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); by the very breath through which they go forth, that same breath they rise up again.
The *pavamāna* chants end with the *iḍā*; the *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and the *chandomas* are cattle; thus he places cattle within cattle. This is the *stoma*.

(14.12.1) With the words, "Your most beloved guest," the form of the *ātithya* rite itself is thereby established. (14.12.2) With the words, "O Indra, come to us with what is dear," it is for the sake of attaining sensory power and vigor.
(14.12.3) "The breaker of forts, the youth, the sage, of immeasurable might, was born."

"Indra, the sustainer of every deed, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the much-praised"—this is for the sake of stability (PB 14.12.4). There is the Auśana [sāman] (PB 14.12.5). Uśanas Kāvya indeed desired: "May I win as much of the world as belongs to the other Kāvyas."

Thus he performed austerity; he saw this *auśana* [Sāman], and by it he won as much of the world as belonged to the other *kāvyas*. Indeed, that was what he desired at that time. The *auśana* is a Sāman that wins desires; by means of it, one secures his very desire. There follows the *sāṃvarta*.
The Rakṣases indeed sought to destroy the sacrifice of the gods; Indra scattered them with this *saṃvarta* hymn.

Because he scattered them with the *saṃvarta*, it is called the *sāṃvarta*. Evil indeed pursued them; he struck him down with the *sāṃvarta*, and thus one who praises with the *sāṃvarta* strikes away evil.
There is a hymn to the Maruts (PB 14.12.8).
The rays are indeed the months; the Maruts are the rays. The Maruts are the most numerous of the gods.

[They think,] "May we be the most numerous," and thus they perform the sacrificial session (*sattra*). They indeed become the most numerous. The earlier days possess the seasons, while the later days are seasonless.

In that this *chandoma* *sāman* occurs, by it these days become possessed of the seasons (*ṛtumant*). There is indeed the forty-four-fold hymn-form (*stoma*); thus he establishes himself in might and vigor, for the *triṣṭubh* is might and vigor. "The ocean has surged in the highest ordinance"—this is the introductory verse (*pratipad*) of the ninth day.

This day is indeed supreme; it is a day of distinct character (*vidharma*), for this ninth day is distinct from other days, being the eldest and the most excellent. "Do thou exhilarate Vāyu for the sake of sacrifice and bounty"—this verse addressed to Varuṇa occurs here. Whatever in the sacrifice is ill-performed, that Varuṇa seizes; he thereby expiates that very thing.
There is a *tṛca* as the *stotrīya* for the attainment of out-breath and in-breath.

It consists of ten verses; the *virāj* has ten syllables, and food is of the nature of the *virāj*; it serves for the attainment of food. They begin with the introductory verses so that there may be no transgression against sensory power, vigor, and essence. For when the gods perceived sensory power, vigor, and essence, they struck it down [into the sacrifice]. It consists of eight verses.
(15.1.8) "Animals have eight hooves; thus, by [the verses] according to their hooves, he obtains animals.

The Gāyatrī has eight syllables; the Gāyatrī is splendor and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Verily, he secures for himself splendor and spiritual luster. (15.1.9) "There are six *ṛc*s, for the support of the seasons."
(10) There are four [stotras] consisting of six verses each; there are twenty-four half-months in a year; verily, he finds firm support in the year itself.

(11) The last [stotra] consists of six verses for the sake of obtaining both the indirect and the direct. (12) The last [stotra] consists of three verses; by the very same breath with which they go forth, they rise up again.
The Stoma is indeed the forty-eightfold for the sake of stability and procreation. "We have approached with great reverence the youngest [Agni]"—this is the Ājya-stotra for Agni;
for those who go to the ninth day go as if they were departing.
(PB 15.2.3) “He who has shone forth, well-kindled in his own dwelling”—for he indeed shines forth who has praised with nine days;
“well-offered” (*svāhuta*)—for he is indeed well-offered who has been offered with nine days;
“facing in every direction”—for he indeed faces in every direction.
(15.2.4) “O Agni, you are Varuṇa and Mitra”—this verse addressed to Varuṇa is used. Whatever in the sacrifice is ill-performed, that Varuṇa seizes; it is precisely that which he thereby expiates.

(15.2.5) “I invoke Mitra of pure will”—this is the *rāthaṃtara* chant dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. (15.2.6) These *chandomas* are, as it were, a place with a formidable bottoming. Just as people, when at a place with a formidable bottoming, plunge in by interlocking their hands, even so does he interlock these two forms for the sake of the non-disturbance of the *chandomas*.

(15.2.7) "Great is Indra, who by his might"—this is a hymn to Indra belonging to the eighth day. By means of this [day], the gods caused Indra to conquer; by means of the lowest [day], they struck away evil. By this [hymn], they magnify the day itself.
(15.2.8) "I invoke those two of whom this [world]..."—this is the *rāthaṃtara* chant dedicated to Indra and Agni.

(15.2.9) These *chandomas* are indeed like a place with a formidable ford. Just as people, having interlocked their hands, wade across a place with a formidable ford, even so he interlocks these two forms for the sake of the *chandomas*'s lack of stumbling.

"Of the purifying, slaying, golden-hued [Soma], the bright drops have been poured forth"—thus there are *gāyatrī* verses containing the word "golden-hued" (*harivat*), for the sake of the non-exhaustion of the *chandomas*.

"Of the purifying, slaying"—this indeed is the form of the *bṛhatī*; "the golden-hued, bright drops have been poured forth"—this is the form of the *jagatī*. Thus he attains the combined form of both the *sāman* and the *chandas*.
"Pour out on every side the pressed [juice]"—these are verses containing the word "around" (*parivat*), for the ninth day is the end; these [verses] serve for its completion.
(15.3.4) "The Soma has been pressed, the ruddy, the bull, the tawny one"—these *jagatī* verses, though being true *triṣṭubhs* by their form, are therefore performed in the world of the *triṣṭubhs*.
(15.3.5) There is a *gāyatra* [sāman]; whatever is the *brāhmaṇa* regarding the *gāyatra*, that is its explanation.
(15.3.6) There is the *ādārasṛt* of Bharadvāja.
The various peoples surrounded Divodāsa, whose domestic priest was Bharadvāja. He approached [the people] and said, "O Seer, find a way out for me!
For him, he found a way out by means of this *sāman*. This *sāman* is indeed "way-finding" (*gātuvid*). [He sang], "May I not be split asunder. That is why it is called *adārasṛt*;
one who sings with the *adārasṛt* finds a way out and is not split asunder. One who praises with the *adārasṛt* does not rush toward being split asunder.
It becomes beautiful; this is the explanatory statement regarding that which is beautiful.
It has the *hariśrī* as its *nidhana*. Cattle indeed are the *hariśrī*; it is for the acquisition of cattle. By praising it, one attains both prosperity (*śrī*) and splendor (*hara*).

It is the Saindhukṣita; whatever is the Brāhmaṇa regarding the Saindhukṣita [is to be applied]. Or it is the Vābhrava with a *nidhana* at the end, for the sake of reaching [the goal]. By means of this, Vabhru Kaumbhya directly beheld the heavenly world; it is for the manifestation of the heavenly world, and one who praises with it does not fall from the heavenly world.
There is a mixing of the *iḍā* offerings.
The *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and the *Chandomas* are cattle; thus he places cattle within cattle.
The *Pāvamāna* hymn becomes the bull.
The Chandomas are indeed cattle; thus he brings that pair together among the cattle for the sake of procreation, for cattle do not procreate without a bull. There is the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra];
for this ninth day is indeed the *pṛṣṭha*. He praises with the *pṛṣṭha* upon the *pṛṣṭha* itself for the sake of stability.

(15.3.20) There is the *kaulmalabarhiṣa* [chant]. (15.3.21) For by means of this, Kaulmalabarhiṣ saw the heavenly world; he attained procreation and abundance. One who praises with the *kaulmalabarhiṣa* is procreated and becomes many.
(15.3.22) There is the *arkapuṣpa* [chant].

(15.3.23) "The gods indeed call food *arka*," they say; "its flower is *puṣpa*. By praising with the *arkapuṣpa*, one secures for oneself flavorful food. (15.3.24) It belongs to Dīrghaśravas. (15.3.25) For the royal seer Dīrghaśravas was long exiled and wandered about hungry; he [performed] this...

He saw the Dairghaśravasa [sāman]; by means of it, he won food from all the quarters; he who praises with the Dairghaśravasa wins food from all the quarters. There is the Vaiyaśva [sāman], for which the Brāhmaṇa is the same as that of the Vaiyaśva.

(15.3.27) When there is the *abhīśava* of the *ābhīśava*, (15.3.28) it becomes a station for the gods (*devasthāna*) for the sake of stability; it becomes a preparation (*saṃskṛti*) for the sake of refinement. (15.3.29) Verily, this day was distressed; the gods, standing at the station of the gods, refined it by means of the *saṃkṛti*.

That is the "made-ness" of the *saṃkṛti*; by means of the "station of the gods," the gods indeed established themselves in the heavenly world. "May we establish ourselves in the heavenly world"—this is what it means.

The deities did not submit to Varuṇa for the sake of sovereignty; he saw this "station of the gods," and then indeed they submitted to him for the sake of sovereignty. His peers submit to him for preeminence.

(15.3.31) His radiance becomes like that of the *kṣatra*; he who knows thus finds firm standing. (15.3.32) Praising with the *bharga* [verse], he becomes possessed of *bharga*; with the *yaśas* [verse], he becomes possessed of *yaśas*. (15.3.33) It belongs to Vasiṣṭha; it is the Brāhmaṇa-text concerning Vasiṣṭha.
The *arka* of Dīrghatamas is used; for the *arka* is food, [and it serves] for the attainment of food.

There is a *sāmarāja*; he attains sovereign rule and lordship by praising with the *sāmarāja*. Regarding this, they say: "It is a *saṃvat*"; for by means of the *saṃvat*, the gods went to the heavenly world, and by the *udvat*, they ascended.
The *pavamāna* chants end with the *nidhana* for the stability of the day.
The *stotra* consists of verses containing the word "sūrya," beginning with "They seem to be reaching toward the sun" (*āśrāyanta iva sūryam*).

For this day has Āditya as its deity; the sun is indeed the end, and this is the ninth day of the days. Thus, they praise at the very end by means of that which is the end, for the sake of firm establishment.
"O Indra, from whatever we fear, from that grant us security;

O Maghavan, be able to help us for our protection; slay our enemies and those who oppose us. Having struck down both the enemies (*dviṣ*) and the adversaries (*mṛdh*) by means of the ninth day, they rise up on the tenth day.
The *Śrāyantīya* chant is indeed prosperity (*śrī*), and the ninth day is prosperity; thus, he establishes prosperity within prosperity.
It is on all sides.
One who desires cattle should chant with that which is on all sides; one who desires the office of a domestic priest should chant with that which is on all sides.
The earth belongs to Agni, and the Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni; the sky belongs to Indra, and the Rājanya belongs to Indra; [one should chant] with the intermediate space.
He makes it complete with the intermediate space, as heaven and earth are complete; he who, knowing thus, praises with the *samanta* chant, finds cattle and attains the office of a domestic priest.

The *stoma* is: "O Soma, you are the sustainer" (*ātvaṃ somāsi dhārayuḥ*). It is a *gāyatrī* verse for the support of the day; the word "you" (*tvam*) is a form of the *bṛhatī*, for this day belongs to the *bṛhatī*.

(15.5.2) “For you indeed, O member, divine... — the word *tvam* (you) is a form of the Bṛhatī, for this day belongs to the Bṛhatī. (15.5.3) “Flow on, O god, for the feast... — this is a form of the Bṛhatī, for this day belongs to the Bṛhatī. (15.5.4) “The one who goes around, the desirable, the golden... — these verses are *parivatyaḥ* (encircling), for the ninth day is the end; they serve for the completion [of the cycle].

(ŚB 15.5.5) "Flow on, O Soma, for great skill"—this is the *akṣarapaṅkti* [meter], the source of the *stomas*; moreover, this very *akṣarapaṅkti* is the *chandas* that is now free from weariness (*ayātayāman*). By means of it, the *Chandomas* are performed as being free from weariness. The exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "Since the *stomas* and *chandases* are completed in the six-day rite, what *chandas* do the *Chandomas* possess?"
Thus, regarding the meter, one should say that these are "akṣarapaṅktis.
The verses beginning with "upoṣu jātam apturam," though being *gāyatrīs*, are in the form of *jagatīs*; therefore, they are performed in the world of the *jagatīs*.
There is a *gāyatra* [sāman], which is the very *brahman* of the *gāyatra*.
(15.5.8) There is the Āśvasūkta.

(15.5.9) With the preceding days, one indeed offers oblations to Agni; but this day belongs to the deity Aditya. [The verse] "The bright one has been offered" refers to yonder sun, for he is the bright one; it is him that one thereby offers with this.
(15.5.10) There is the Śāmmada hymn.
(15.5.11) By means of this, the Aṅgirasas Śamada directly beheld the heavenly world; it serves to illuminate the heavenly world, and he who praises with it does not fall from the heavenly world.
(15.5.13) By means of this, he invokes a blessing for him, for the Sāman is indeed a true blessing.
(15.5.14) Dāvasu Āṅgirasa, desiring cattle, beheld this Sāman; by it, he created a thousand cattle. That this Sāman exists is for the prosperity of cattle.
(15.5.15) This *iḍā*-invocation is turned toward the west.
(15.5.16) For by means of other *iḍā*-invocations that are directed forward, one bestows seed; but this *iḍā*-invocation turned toward the west is for the sake of procreation.
Therefore, embryos develop facing away [from the mother], yet they are born facing toward her. Therefore, indeed, from downward openings...

They do not fall, for by this very means they are supported (PB 15.5.17). It becomes "made manifest" (hāviṣkṛta) for the sake of stability; that is merely a restatement of what has already been established (PB 15.5.18).
It is the Suparṇa [sāman], which is the very Brāhmaṇa of the Suparṇa.

The Vaiśvamanasa [sāman] occurs. Once, while the seer Viśvamanas was wandering about his study, a Rakṣas seized him. Indra perceived this, thinking, "A Rakṣas has seized the seer. He addressed him, saying, "Seer, tell me, what kind of a stump is this? The Rakṣas replied.

He said to him, "It is a *sthāṇu* (a stump); strike it with this! As he was giving him a blade of grass as a thunderbolt, he said, "With that, split his boundary. Indra split his boundary with that very blade of grass. Evil indeed seized him; he drove away that evil by means of the *vaiśvamanasa* hymn.
One who praises with the *vaiśvamanasa* hymn strikes away evil.
The Gaurīvita [sāman] is used; its Brāhmaṇa explanation is the same as that of the Gaurīvita [in the preceding section].
There is a *nihava* (invocation), for the attainment of food.
Indeed, food is given with the sound "hī," and Agni eats food with the sound "ī."
The seers did not see Indra face to face. Vasiṣṭha desired, "How might I see Indra face to face? He saw this invocation (*nihava*). Thereupon, he indeed saw Indra face to face.
Indra said to him, "I shall tell you a *brāhmaṇa* [instruction], so that the Bharatas, having you as their domestic priest, shall multiply. Then...

"Do not speak these to venerable sages," he said; therefore, he taught him these *stomabhāga* verses. From that time on, the Bharatas with Vasiṣṭha as their domestic priest multiplied. This *sāman* is indeed possessed of Indra; it becomes this *sāman* for the sake of being possessed of Indra.
Furthermore, there is the *yad vāhiṣṭhīya*.

(15.5.26) These *sāmans* are indeed those that bring spiritual luster (*brahmayaśas*) through the *ṛc*; they belong to the ear, and one becomes possessed of spiritual luster when he praises with the *vāhiṣṭhīya*.
(15.5.27) It is the *āsita*; whatever is the *brāhmaṇa* regarding the *āsita*, [that applies here].
(15.5.28) It is the *sādhra*; it serves for success (*siddhi*).
(15.5.29) It is the Ākūpāra [Stoma].

(15.5.30) By means of this, Kaśyapa Akūpāra attained victory and greatness; he who praises with the Ākūpāra attains victory and greatness. (15.5.31) There is the Vidharma [Stoma], for the support of dharma.
(15.5.32) The exponents of Brahman say: "Since the *stomas* and meters are obtained in the six-day rite, of what meter are the *Chandomas*?
One should reply: "Of the *puruṣa*-meter. For man is fivefold (*pāṅkta*); man is the two-footed [meter]. This is for the sake of the non-exhaustion of the *Chandomas*.
(15.5.33) It becomes something to be heard.
The *śrudhya* is indeed cattle; it serves for the acquisition of cattle.

Prajāpati created cattle; once created, they departed from him. He called after them with this *sāman*, "O Śrudhiya! Come hither! They returned to him. In that this *sāman* exists, it is for the purpose of bringing cattle back.
Cattle turn toward him who knows thus.

They chant on *gāyatrī* verses for the sake of stability and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). By means of the very same vital breath with which they set out, they rise again. The *pavamāna* chants end with the *iḍā*; the *iḍā* is indeed cattle, and the *chandomas* are cattle; [thus] it is truly within cattle [that they find support].

"That bestows cattle; the Stoma [is established] upon the verses addressed to Agni. For the previous days they lead forward the *ukthas* with verses addressed to Agni, but for this day they lead them forward with a verse addressed to Indra. Thus he becomes firmly established in both forms. There is the *aidhmavāha* [verse].

(15.6.3) They chant the *aindrī* verses with *āgneyī* meters; thereby he unites the Brahman and the Kṣatra. He places the Brahman before the Kṣatra, and makes both the Kṣatra and the Vaiśya subordinate to the Brahman. (15.6.4) There is the *traikakubha* [sāman].
(15.6.5) Thus he finds firm support in very strength and valor; strength and valor are the Traikakubha.
(15.6.6) The Udvaṃśīya is performed; its Brāhmaṇa explanation is the same as that of the Udvaṃśīya. (15.6.7) The Stoma is indeed the forty-eightfold, for the sake of stability and procreation.

The seventh day is indeed Gāyatra, the eighth is Triṣṭubh, the ninth is Jāgata; then this tenth day is Ānuṣṭubha. Regarding that, they say: "If they were to approach the Stomyā verses directly with the Ānuṣṭubh metre, the sacrificer would go to the furthest distance and would not find firm support. Those twenty-four Gāyatrīs are indeed eighteen Ānuṣṭubhs; [thus it is] the Ānuṣṭubh.

Thus they approach the *stomyā* verses indirectly for the sake of firm standing; he stands firm. With this day, one serves Prajāpati. In that regard, there is something to be avoided: when one speaks while being served by a superior, that is an interruption of the food-eating; therefore, one should not speak. However, it is indeed to be spoken: just as one announces the path to a superior while an offering is being brought, so it is for the sake of reaching [the goal].
(15.7.5) Having prepared the speech to the extent that there is an *anuṣṭubh*, they should recite it; thus it is not excessive and is for the safety of their own sacrifice.

(15.7.6) "Those who chant with ten days," they say, "are indeed ascending toward the gods. They descend by means of the *anurūpa* verses of the five days; just as one would descend after having ascended, so it is. Thus there are nine verses.
Those very [bricks] which he bestows and those which he places down, these he now sets aside.

This [verse] belongs to Varuṇa; for whatever is badly performed in the sacrifice, that Varuṇa seizes—it is that very thing he thereby expiates. This [verse] belongs to Aditi; for Aditi is this earth—on her indeed [he establishes it].
The twenty-four-fold Stoma itself is employed for the sake of splendor and the Brahman’s luster.
(15.8.1) "Well-kindled, bring hither for us..."—these *āprī* verses consist of *ājya* offerings.

(15.8.2) Prajāpati created offspring; having been drained, he felt himself depleted. He saw these *āprī* *ājya* offerings and with them he gratified himself. Indeed, he who has praised with the ten days of the *daśarātra* is like one who has been drained and is depleted.
In that these *āprī* oblations of clarified butter exist, he gratifies his very self with them.
"O Sūrya, what today at the rising of the sun..."—thus the Maitrāvaruṇa [sings] the *sūravan*.
The sun is indeed the end; this tenth day is the end of the days. Thus, they praise with an end for the sake of stability at the very end.
(15.8.5) "May the Soma-draughts exhilarate you" (*ut tvā madantu somā*): this is an *udvat* [verse] addressed to Indra, the form of rising.
(15.8.6) "O Indra and Agni, come to the pressed juice" (*indrāgnī āgataṃ sutam*): with the very same form by which they proceed, they rise up again; such is the *stoma*.
(15.9.1) "High is the birth of your plant" (*uccā te jātam andhasa*): there are *udvat* verses in the *gāyatrī* meter, the form of rising.
(PB 15.9.2) With the words, "O Soma, being purified, flow forth," they indeed traverse the path.

(PB 15.9.3) With the words, "The wakeful sage [is] the truth of thoughts," if they were to perform the *pravatī* verses when [the sun] has reached [its zenith], they would overstep; therefore, *āvatī* verses are used so that there may be no overstepping.
(PB 15.9.4) It is in the *gāyatrī* meter; whatever is the *brāhmaṇa* explanation for the *gāyatrī*, that applies here.
There is the Āmahīyava [sāman]; it is both an arrangement and food; by means of this, they attain both arrangement and food.
There is the Ājiga [sāman] for the sake of winning the race.
Indeed, this twelve-day sacrifice is an extended race; it is for the sake of winning this.
The Ābhīka [Sāman] comes into being for the sake of advancing.

The Aṅgirases, performing austerities, suffered from heat; they saw this Sāman, and it rained upon them at the moment of encounter (*abhīke*). By means of it, they pacified their heat. Because it rained upon them at the moment of encounter, it is called the Ābhīka. Whatever [benefit] was attained by the former [seers],...
With days they grieve for their sorrow; having allayed that by means of this [sacrifice], they rise up.
There is an elevation (*utsedha*).
By means of elevation, indeed, the gods elevated the cattle; by means of the depression (*niṣedha*), they enclosed them around.
The *utsedha* and *niṣedha* [breaths] are the *yajñāyajñīya* chant (PB 15.9.12).
The *yajñāyajñīya* is cattle and food; by means of the *utsedha* and *niṣedha*, one thus encompasses both cattle and food (PB 15.9.14).
Indeed, at the midday *pavamāna*, the gods, having completed the sacrifice with the *yajñāyajñīya*, [attained] heaven...
Ascending to the world—he who knows this, having completed the sacrifice with the *yajñāyajñīya* chant during the midday *pavamāna*, ascends to the heavenly world.
Moreover, it becomes the *anuṣṭubh* in a hidden manner; for this day is indeed the *anuṣṭubh* manifest.
If they were to perform the Yajñāyajñīya at the third pressing, they would directly encounter the Anuṣṭubh;
therefore, they perform it at the midday pressing, and by that means they approach the Anuṣṭubh indirectly. The Gaurīvita chant occurs.

This Gaurīvita is indeed the "tomorrow" of the sacrifice; this is the dwelling-place of the sacrificer, since it belongs to the midday pressing. In that the Gaurīvita occurs at the midday pressing, the sacrificer thereby places the "tomorrow" within himself. As for the *stoma*: the verses beginning with "With what [splendor], O Wondrous One, has he come to us? are the *kavatya*s; by means of them they belong to Prajāpati, for Prajāpati is "Ka"; thus it is for the attainment of Prajāpati.
(15.10.2) "Do not praise anything else"—this is indeed the rising, for at this time it is a prayer for blessings.

(15.10.3) "Up rise these most honey-sweet ones"—on the day of the Udayanīya [offering], this is indeed a rising, for at this time it is a prayer for blessings. (15.10.4) "With hymns [tarobhiḥ] for you, the finder of wealth [vidadvasum]"—the hymn (*stoma*) is indeed *tara*, and the sacrifice (*yajña*) is the finder of wealth; by means of the hymn, the sacrifice is joined. When he says, "With hymns for you, the finder of wealth," he [joins] the sacrifice.
Thus he yokes it.
In the verses of the Vāmadevya, the Rathantara becomes the Pṛṣṭha-stotra.
The Gāyatrī is indeed the womb of the Rathantara; thus he establishes the Rathantara in its own womb.

The Gāyatrī is indeed brilliance among the meters; the Rathantara is brilliance among the Sāmans; the Caturviṃśa is brilliance among the Stomas. Thus, he truly joins brilliance together. Even the son of his son becomes brilliant.
He begins the first verse with an eight-syllable [phrase]; thereby he wins eight-hoofed cattle.
(10) With two syllables he intones the *prastāva* on the two following verses; the sacrificer has two feet; verily, he establishes the sacrificer himself upon the sacrifice and upon cattle.

(11) The *rathantara* is indeed of the *gāyatrī* nature, and its metre is the *gāyatrī*; in that the *rathantara* occurs upon *gāyatrī* verses, by that he prospers in his own community. These worlds are indeed the *gāyatrī*; in that the *rathantara* occurs upon *gāyatrī* verses, [he prospers] in these [worlds].
Having thus completed the worlds, they rise up.
The *maidhātitha* [sāman] is used;
for by means of this, Medhātithi Kāṇva released the cows that had been scattered by Vibhinduka, for the sake of obtaining cattle. The *maidhātitha* is performed.
The *abhīvarta* is the *brahmasāman*, having a single-syllable *nidhana*, for the sake of stability. Speech indeed consists of a single syllable; they rise up established in speech itself.
The *kāleya* is the *acchāvākasāman*.

The Kāleya and the Rathantara are indeed in the same world. This [earth] is the Rathantara, and cattle are the Kāleya; having established themselves both on this earth and among cattle, they rise up. The *stoma* is: "With the sweetest, with the most intoxicating... This is a *gāyatrī* verse; for the third pressing is full of exhilaration and full of essence, it thus bestows exhilaration and essence.
It is a *gāyatra* hymn; whatever is the *brāhmaṇa* of the *gāyatra*, that applies here.
It is *saṃhita* and has a *nidhana* consisting of two syllables; it is for the sake of stability, and they rise having attained stability.
It is *sapha*.
By means of the *sapha*, the gods reached these worlds; that is the reason for the *sapha*'s name as *sapha*. By this [chant], they rise having reached these very worlds.
(There is) the Rohitakūlīya; its Brāhmaṇa is the same as that of the Rohitakūlīya.
(There are) the Śyāvāśva and Andhīgava [Sāmans]; he places two convergent Virāj verses for the sake of obtaining food.
They chant on verses with a waist like an ant.

(15.11.9) Having slain Vṛtra, Indra, thinking "I have not overcome him," went to the furthest distance. He then expanded this *anuṣṭubh* [verse], and he crept into its middle. He who, knowing thus, praises with these [verses] sacrifices in a home that belongs to Indra, which is free from fear; he rises up in safety.
The *yajñāyajñīya* finale belongs to the *sauhaviṣa*; thus they do not depart from the *yajñāyajñīya* itself at the third pressing. It is the *vājajit* (winner of the prize);
it serves for the attainment of everything and the conquest of everything. Indeed, those who reach the tenth day win all that prize; for the prize is food, and it is for the securing of food.

They approach the ten-syllable *nidhana* for the support of the ten-night rite; the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and food is of the nature of the *virāj*, for the sake of securing food. They chant on verses containing the word "sun" (*sūryavatī*); the sun is indeed the end, and this is the end of the ten nights; thus they chant with the end at the very end for the sake of stability. There are verses containing the word "up" (*upavatī*) for the sake of stability; there are verses containing the word "around" (*parivatī*) for the sake of the complete attainment of everything.
The Stoma is indeed the twenty-fourfold for brilliance and spiritual luster.
The Vāmadevya, as the Agniṣṭoma-sāman, is performed upon the Virāj verses for peace and prosperity.

The Vāmadevya is indeed the essence (*sat*) of the Sāmans; the Virāj is the essence of the meters; the thirty-threefold is the essence of the Stomas. Joining these essences together, they rise up; even the very being (*sattva*) of a son is thereby secured.
The exponents of Brahman say: "From what did they arise? From that which stands? If they should say, "From what," he should tell them:
"They will be without support and without offspring. If they should say, "From that which stands," he should tell them:
"Their prosperity will be stable, but they will not become more wealthy. [It arose] from the full, indeed, the full.
"They should say, 'We have risen up,'" [it says in PB 15.12.4].
"Those who rise up after having praised with the Vāmadevya-sāman indeed rise up from fullness to fullness" [it says in PB 15.12.5].
"The Vāmadevya is indeed the intermediate space; by means of the intermediate space, this entire world is filled."
(15.12.6) This indeed is the perfect *stoma*, namely the thirty-threefold; they find firm support in perfection itself, for there are thirty-three syllables [in these verses].

(15.12.7) These [verses] are indeed the form of all meters: because they have three feet, they are *gāyatrīs*; because the feet consist of eleven syllables, they are *triṣṭubhs*; because there is a foot of twelve syllables, they are *jagatīs*; and because they consist of thirty-three syllables...

By that [the Virāj is attained], and by that very [means] the Anuṣṭubhs; for they do not fail by even a single syllable (PB 15.12.8). There is indeed the thirty-three-fold Stoma for the sake of stability; for this [Stoma] is established among the deities (PB 16.1.1).
Prajāpati was indeed this [universe] alone; there was neither day nor night. He was in this darkness...

He crept into the darkness; he desired it; he attained this [light]. Then indeed, light shone forth for him. This which is brought forward is indeed the dawning. That which became that light is the "lightness" (*jyotiṣṭva*) of the light.
This is truly the first of sacrifices. If one performs another sacrifice after not having performed this one, he falls into a pit or perishes.
(16.1.3) Just as from this fire, once it has been produced, other fires are drawn out, even so from this [Jyotiṣṭoma], other sacrifices are drawn out.

(16.1.4) For that which is the Trivṛt, when it enters another sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*), kindles it; that which is the Pañcadaśa, it [kindles] that; that which is the Saptadaśa, it [kindles] that; that which is the Ekaviṃśa, it [kindles] that.
(16.1.5) This is what they mean when they say, "The sacrifice is one," for all these are indeed Jyotiṣṭomas.
(16.1.6) This sacrifice is indeed continuous and without a break, for two by two the *stomas* carry the pressing.
The *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* carry the morning pressing; the *pañcadaśa* and *saptadaśa* carry the midday pressing; the *saptadaśa* and *ekaviṃśa* carry the third pressing.

(16.1.7) Even if there should be a sacrifice with limited sacrificial fees (*mitadakṣiṇa*), this very one must be performed. This [earth] is indeed light (*jyotis*); she is the restrainer of the unlimited. She alone is able to restrain it.

(PB 16.1.8) It has one hundred and ninety *stotrīya* verses. Of these, those which are one hundred and eighty are *virāj*s of thirty-six syllables each. There are six seasons; thus he finds firm support in the seasons by means of the *virāj*.

(PB 16.1.9) Now, as for the ten [remaining verses], this is indeed the *virāj* within the self (*ātman*), and upon this the person (*puruṣa*) is established. (PB 16.1.5) Cattle, horses, mules, donkeys, goats, sheep, rice, barley, sesame, and beans—all these find their support in this very *virāj*.

(PB 16.1.11) Its sacrificial fee consists of one hundred and twelve [cows]. (PB 16.1.12) He who presses the Soma is indeed a slayer of the heroes among the gods; by those [cows] which are a hundred, he pays a debt to the gods; and by those which are ten, he gratifies the ten vital breaths; and by that which is the eleventh, he [gratifies] the self.
"The twelfth [night] is indeed the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)," [it is said].

Now, the sacrificial fee is the phlegm of the sacrifice; for a chariot does not carry a load when it is without phlegm, yet with that which possesses phlegm, whatever desire one desires, that one surely attains. In the same way, by means of this [sacrifice] which possesses a sacrificial fee, whatever desire one desires, that one attains.
The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is indeed the prosperity of the sacrifice; when one sacrifices with that which possesses a sacrificial fee, he bestows prosperity upon himself. Now, this is the cow.
By means of the cow, the gods drove the Asuras away from these worlds; he who knows thus drives his rival away from these worlds.
When the gods indeed drove the Asuras away from these worlds, that became the "go" (cow) nature of the cow (*go*).
He who knows this drives away evil and the rival.
Its *bahiṣpavamāna* chant consists of fifteen verses; the fifteenfold [stoma] is indeed a thunderbolt. Thus he places the thunderbolt in front, and by means of it, he conquers.
This is indeed the Paśustoma; for thus is an animal composed: the head is the thickest, the neck is narrower, it is broader than the two flanks, and it is widest at the thighs.

In that the Bahiṣpavamāna consists of fifteen verses, the Ājya-stotras are Trivṛt, the midday pressing is Saptadaśa, and the third pressing is Ekaviṃśa—it is by this very form that he [the sacrifice] is [constituted]. One verse remains over from those chanted together; therefore, the hindquarters of the animal are redundant.
(16.2.1) Now, this is the Cow.
(16.2.2) By means of the cow, the gods drove the Asuras out from these worlds; he who knows thus drives his rival out from these worlds.
(16.2.3) When the gods indeed drove the Asuras out from these worlds by means of the cow, that is the "cow-nature" (*gotva*) of the cow.
He who knows this drives away evil and the rival.
Its *bahiṣpavamāna* chant consists of fifteen verses; the fifteenfold [stoma] is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*). He thus places the thunderbolt in front, and by means of it he conquers.
This sacrifice is indeed a "cattle-stoma"; for cattle are composed in this very way: the head is the thickest, the neck is narrower, they are broader at the two sides, and widest at the two thighs.

(16.2.7) That the *bahiṣpavamāna* consists of fifteen [verses], the *ājya* stotras consist of nine, the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*) consists of seventeen, and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) consists of twenty-one—by this very form he thus [establishes him]. (16.2.8) One [verse] remains over from those that have been chanted together; therefore, the excess of the animal is behind.
(16.3.1) Now, this is the *āyus* [stotra].
(16.3.2) By means of life-span indeed did the gods hold back the Asuras; he who knows thus holds back his rival.
(16.3.3) One who desires heaven should sacrifice.
(16.3.4) The Stomas proceed upwards so that there may be no falling away.

(PB 16.3.5) By means of this very [rite], one should sacrifice for one who is afflicted by disease; it should be performed as an Atirātra. (PB 16.3.6) It becomes the Gāyatrī; the Gāyatrī is breath, and this [Atirātra] is life-force. Thus, he bestows both life-force and breath upon him in a unified manner.
(PB 16.3.7) These Stomas are indeed conducive to heaven; in that there is the Jyotis [Stoma], he places light before him.

Now, this *gaura* [stoma] exceeds the *virāj* by one; that is merely the beginning. And this *āyuṣ* [stoma] is deficient by one from the *virāj*; that is merely the sitting down. Moreover, the deficient and the excessive *stomas* are a pair for the sake of procreation.
These indeed are the *trikadruka* *stomas*; by means of these, Indra attained all satisfaction.
(16.3.9) He who knows thus prospers with offspring and cattle.

(16.4.1) Prajāpati created offspring; they did not submit to his supremacy. He extracted the essence from these quarters and from the offspring, fashioned it into a garland, and fastened it on himself.
Thereupon, the offspring submitted to his supremacy.
(16.4.2) "His peers stand for his preeminence, he who knows thus.

(16.4.3) He desired, "May Indra be the most excellent among my offspring. He fastened that garland upon him; then indeed, the offspring stood for Indra’s preeminence. Seeing that artifice—that which they had seen in their father—[they did so].

Therefore, of those sons, he who receives the most excellent portion of the inheritance is thought of thus: "He alone will be this [world]. From that, indeed, Indra conquered all this; because he conquered all (*viśva*), it is called the *Viśvajit*.
He desired: "May I conquer that which has not yet been conquered by me. He saw this *Abhijit* sacrifice; with it, he conquered what had not been conquered.

(16.4.7) That there is the *abhijit* [sacrifice] is for the sake of conquering what has not yet been conquered. (16.4.8) These two, indeed, are the *indrastoma*s; they are powerful. (16.4.9) These two *stoma*s were indeed called "craft" (*śilpa*).
He who knows thus beholds craft in his own house.
(10) Indeed, there are no two chants named *yamau*; he who would sacrifice with the two *yamas* should sacrifice with these two for the sake of prosperity.
(11) The chants proceed by returning again and again, for by returning again and again, Indra conquered what was unconquered through these two.
(12) He leads forward three *trivṛt* chants, three *pañcadaśa*, three *saptadaśa*, and three *ekaviṃśa*; these amount to twelve. Twelve months are a year.
"Prajāpati attains Prajāpati himself" (PB 16.4.13).
He leads forward four Trivṛt Viśvajits; four Pañcadaśas; four Saptadaśas; these amount to twelve. Twelve months are a year; the year is Prajāpati; thus he attains Prajāpati himself.

(16.5.1) "Upa tvā jāmayo giraḥ"—this opening verse contains the word *upa* and is the form of the *stoma*. (16.5.2) "He who gives everything, who approaches all the *stomas* and all the *pṛṣṭhas*, is deprived of his vital breaths," so they say. In that there is a verse addressed to Vāyu, it is for the sake of the prosperity of the vital breaths. (16.5.3) The verses for Sarasvant and Sarasvatī follow.
(SB 16.5.4) This pair, indeed, is Sarasvant and Sarasvatī; he thus places a productive couple at the beginning of his sacrifice for the sake of procreation.
(SB 16.5.5) A verse to Savitṛ becomes the fourth.
(SB 16.5.6) He performs a difficult task who gives everything; in that there is a verse to Savitṛ, [it is so that] his rite may be impelled by Savitṛ—thus his rite indeed becomes impelled by Savitṛ.
The fifth [verse] belongs to Bṛhaspati;
for Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman, and thus he places the Brahman at the very beginning of his sacrifice.
The sixth [verse] belongs to Agni Pāvaka.

Agni himself heats him thoroughly; Pavamāna purifies him; once purified, he leads him toward the sacrificial *pṛṣṭha* chants. "Those who perform the *saṃbhāryā* rites," they say, "depart from the path.
Therefore, the final triplet is dedicated to Pavamāna; by means of it, they lead them back to the path.

"But one should indeed praise with the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]," they say, "for him who would yoke these [hymns] in the *bahiṣpavamāna*. The introductory verse (*pratipad*) contains the word "upa"; for the *rathantara* [sāman] contains the word "upa," and thus by means of it he yokes the *rathantara* for him.
Sarasvatī is the second [verse]; Sarasvat is the heavenly world, and the *bṛhat* [sāman] is the heavenly world; thus by means of it he yokes the *bṛhat* for him.

The third [verse] belongs to Sarasvatī; Sarasvatī is indeed speech, and the Vairūpa-sāman is speech; by means of that [verse], he yokes for him the Vairūpa-sāman. (PB 16.5.17) The fourth belongs to Savitṛ; Savitṛ is indeed Prajāpati, and the Vairāja-sāman is Prajāpati; by means of that [verse], he yokes for him the Vairāja-sāman. (PB 16.5.18) The fifth belongs to Bṛhaspati; Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman, and the Śakvarī verses are the Brahman; by means of that [verse], he yokes for him the Śakvarī verses.
The sixth [verse] is an *āgnipāvamānī*; the *revatī* verses are indeed *gāyatrī*, having the *gāyatrī* metre; Agni is rich (*revat*). By means of that [verse], he yokes the *revatī* verses for him.

(PB 16.5.20) Four do not suffice for six; insofar as they are undefined (*anirukta*), by that they suffice. All the *ājya* chants are [sung] with their own [specific] tones (*svāra*); that is a repetition (*jāmi*). They praise with verses dedicated to different deities to avoid repetition. (PB 16.5.21)
(16.5.22) "Well-kindled, bring hither for us..."—these *āprī* verses are the *ājya* offerings.
(16.5.23) Prajāpati created offspring; having been drained and emptied, he thought himself diminished. He saw these *āprī* *ājya* offerings; with them, he gratified his own self.
Indeed, he who gives everything is like one who is drained and emptied. In that there are *āprī* *ājya* offerings, he thereby gratifies his very self.
"But now," they say, "the *pṛṣṭha* stotras are properly arranged according to their respective places, since the *rathantara* is first, the *bṛhat* is last, and the others are in the middle.

"A repetition (*jāmi*) is indeed committed in the sacrifice," they say, "when all [the stotras] are performed together with the *nidhana*. "In that the *soma* libations proceed between [the stotras], the *ukthas* are recited between them, and the *vaṣaṭ*-calls are made between them, by that it is not a repetition."

(16.5.26) They say that the *iḍā* verses and the *nidhanas* are reversed; therefore, there is no repetition. (16.5.27) "The *revatī* verses fall away from their own abode," they say, "when they proceed from the thirty-three-fold hymn-form (*stoma*). In that the *gāyatrīs* occur, by that they do not fall away from their abode;
for whatever is a *gāyatrī*, that is a *revatī*.
(16.6.1) "He who gives everything is deprived of his axes," they say; he puts on a skin, and thus he prospers through cattle.
(16.6.2) The skin is that of a red cow; for red is the most abundant form among cattle; verily, he wins them directly.
(16.6.3) He dwells in the forest for three nights; by means of those [nights], he wins food from the wild.
The udumbara tree dwells in vigor; the udumbara is vigor; verily he wins vigor. He lives by means of a spade; he overcomes want of subsistence.
The spade has edges on both sides; from both sides, indeed, it bestows upon him food—both from this world and from yonder world.
(16.6.7) Among the Niṣādas he dwells for three nights; indeed, these [people] are limited in this [region], and thus he wins whatever food there is in this region.

(16.6.8) Among the people he dwells for three nights; by means of those [nights] he wins the food belonging to the people. (16.6.9) Among his own people he dwells for three nights; by means of those [nights] he wins the food belonging to his own people.

(10) These nights are twelve; the year consists of twelve months. Following the year, food is produced; having attained that very [year], he secures it for himself. (11) One should not beg for a year; for he who eats what is given on the same day eats as if eating raw [food]. The year, indeed, belongs to the gods. (12) One should not push back [a guest] who is departing; this is so that there may be no pushing back of food.
He wears a turban for the sake of craftsmanship.

He should not drink from anything made of clay; for the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa is indeed an oblation, and an oblation does not reach what is made of clay. Therefore, when he drinks from something other than clay, he offers the oblation in his own mouth.
The Agniṣṭoma is the twenty-fifth.
By means of the Sarvajit, the gods indeed conquered everything; for the attainment of all and the conquest of all, one attains everything and conquers everything by this [rite].
Its Pṛṣṭha-stotra is the Mahāvrata.
The *arkya* hymn is recited.
There are twenty-four half-months in a year; the year is the twenty-fifth, and the vow is food. By this [rite], one obtains food from the year. He who knows thus becomes an eater of food.
(16.7.7) By this indeed did Gaura Āṅgirasa overcome all evil; he who praises with this *stoma* overcomes all evil.
(16.8.1) Now, this is the *Jyotis*.
(16.8.2) The *Trirātra* is indeed turned away (*parāṅ*), while the *Agniṣṭoma* is turned hitherward (*arvāṅ*); for him who falters in the *Trirātra*, it does not [fail] in that [Agniṣṭoma].

Furthermore, there is also that which involves an expiation in the Agniṣṭoma; for he should sacrifice again with this [rite] having twenty-one sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). For whatever sacrificial rite one fails in, that itself is its expiation.

During the *upasad* ceremony, he recites a thousand-fold *prātaranuvāka*; that is the world above. There are a thousand sacrificial gifts; that is the intermediate space. There are these thousand syllables; that is this world. In these...

"He who knows thus stands firm in the worlds" (PB 16.8.4). "One thousand [verses] are based on the *ṛc*, while others are based on the syllable," they say. That which is given in the three-night sacrifice (*trirātra*) is based on the *ṛc*;
but that which is in the *agniṣṭoma* is based on the syllable.
(16.8.5) When the *brahmasāman* is performed on verses containing a thousand syllables, that is indeed the praise of the thousand.

(16.8.6) "As many as are a thousand cows, one above another," they say, "so great is the distance from this world to the heavenly world. Therefore they say: "The performer of a thousand-fold sacrifice attains these worlds. (16.8.7) "He is deprived of cattle," they say, "who gives away a thousand at once. The *brahmasāman* is performed on *paṅkti* verses; the sacrifice is fivefold (*pāṅkta*), and cattle are fivefold; [it is] the sacrifice.
Thus he finds firm support in cattle;
it attains the *trivṛt* Stoma and the *virāj* metre.

The *trivṛt* is indeed breath, and the *virāj* is food. Verily, breath does not carry one across without food, nor does food [carry one] without breath. Thus, he finds firm support in both the vital breaths and in the enjoyment of food.

(PB 16.9.1) Now, this is the All-Light; it is the attainment of all, the conquest of all; by means of this, one attains all and conquers all. (PB 16.9.2) This is indeed the supreme sacrifice; he who knows thus reaches the supreme thousand, the state of supremacy.
(PB 16.9.3) Its stotriya verses number two hundred; for two hundred is the end of speech, and a thousand is the end; thus, by means of the end, he establishes him in the end.

This sacrifice has its stoma completed; by means of it, one obtains everything and conquers everything, for one conquers everything through what is accomplished. It results in the Virāj; the Virāj is food, and thus one secures the eating of food.
There is an Ekaviṃśa Agniṣṭoma; the Ekaviṃśa is a firm foundation, and so one finds a firm foundation at the very end of the sacrifice.
Now this Viśvajyotis is an Ukthya sacrifice.

The Ukthas are indeed cattle, and cattle are all light; thus he establishes himself in all light, in cattle. By means of the days, one attains these worlds through the three-night rite; by means of the pressings, one attains the highest, the furthermost.
The day of the three-night rite is more extensive; each subsequent pressing is more extensive, and by that he attains the three-night rite.
Each subsequent one of these worlds is greater, and by that he attains these worlds.
This continuous sacrifice is indeed free from fracture, for two stomas at a time carry each pressing.
The *trivṛt* and *pañcadaśa* [stomas] constitute the morning pressing; the *saptadaśa* and *pañcaviṃśa* constitute the midday pressing; the *caturviṃśa* and *ekaviṃśa* constitute the third pressing.
Just as when something is placed upon a yoked [animal] that is continuous, it carries [the load], even so a thousand [verses] are placed upon this [sacrifice].
Both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara* [sāmans] are employed.
The *rathantara* is indeed this world, and the *bṛhat* is the sky; thus he sings from this world and from yonder world, and he finds firm support in both of these worlds.
The *ātharvaṇa* hymn is performed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter;
for the *Atharvans* are the healing medicine of the gods—it serves for medicine and for safety.

The *udvaṃśīya* occurs at the end of the *ukthas*; it is indeed the form of all the *pṛṣṭha* chants. He thus finds firm standing in all forms. (PB 16.10.12) There is an *uktha*; the *ukthas* are cattle, and a thousand is cattle; he thus bestows cattle upon cattle.
(PB 16.11.1) Whoever knows the three-night rite as woven into the *agniṣṭoma*, he should give a thousand [cattle] at the *agniṣṭoma*, for the thousand has the three-night rite as its foundation.

(16.11.2) "Sing forth to him, O men," "To him who has been born, the swift one," and "Flow on, the foremost of speech"—these are the introductory verses (*pratipad*). He has indeed made this [the *trirātra* sacrifice].
(16.11.3) He performs the *rathantara* on the *pavamāna* [laud]; the *vāmadevya* is at the end of the *pavamāna*, and the *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra].

(16.11.4) This earth is the *rathantara*, the intermediate space is the *vāmadevya*, and the sky is the *bṛhat*. These worlds are the *trirātra*. In that he makes these *sāmans* converge, he thereby [unites] these very worlds.
He joins it together; thereby he obtains the three nights.
He raises the Kakubh [verse] toward the east, for by means of this true [verse], he places the strength of cattle in front.
In that [chant], there is the mixing of the *iḍā*-verses. The *kakubh* is indeed man, and the mixing of the *iḍā*-verses is cattle; thus he establishes cattle within his own self.
"The ancient, primordial nectar which is the hymn"—with these *satobṛhatī* verses they proceed.
By means of the *satobṛhatī*, the gods pervaded these worlds; with these [verses], he likewise pervades these very worlds.

(16.11.10) These [verses] are indeed *gāyatrīs* because they have three feet; therefore they are *gāyatrīs*. They are indeed *jagatīs* because they have twelve syllables per foot; therefore they are *jagatīs*. They are indeed *bṛhatīs* because they have thirty-six syllables;
therefore they are *bṛhatīs*. These are the form of all the meters; he secures for himself all the forms of cattle.

This, indeed, is the manifest Mahāvrata. Of it, the Gāyatra is the head; the Bṛhat and Rathantara are the wings; the Vāmadevya is the body; the Yajñāyajñīya is the tail; and the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) are the *arkya*. Truly, he who sacrifices with this [rite] praises with the manifest Mahāvrata.

(12) Its *pṛṣṭha* is the *bṛhat*, and the *brahmasāman* is on *paṅkti* verses. Regarding this they say: "The metre is disturbed when the *pṛṣṭha* is the *bṛhat* while the *brahmasāman* is on *paṅkti* verses. (13) The *śrāyantīya* alone should be used; thus the metre is not disturbed.
(14) This is the counter-praise of the thousand.

"He overcomes another thousand," they say; "another thousand follows after him. He raises up a *kakubh* [verse] facing the east; now, since this two-footed [verse] is performed in the world of the *kakubh*, it serves as the means for standing upon that thousand.
It results in an *anuṣṭubh*; the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and the three-night rite (*trirātra*) is speech; thereby he attains the three-night rite.
The Ādityas and the Aṅgirases consecrated themselves; they contended for the heavenly world.

The Aṅgirases announced the Soma-pressing to the Ādityas for the following day. The Ādityas saw this [rite]; having purchased it immediately and chosen Ayāsya as their Udgātṛ, they praised with it and went to the heavenly world, while the Aṅgirases were left behind.
One who has rivals should sacrifice;
he prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated—he who knows thus.
For him, they brought that sun as a sacrificial gift, having made it a white horse. Having accepted it, they fell into ruin. He saw these *āyāsyā* [verses], and with them he restored himself.
(16.12.5) These [hymns] belong to Āyāsya; they serve for healing and for peace.
(16.12.6) One who desires heaven should sacrifice.
(16.12.7) It results in a Bṛhatī; by means of the Bṛhatī, the gods went to the heavenly world; through this [sacrifice], one attains the heavenly world.
One who desires cattle should sacrifice;
the *bṛhatī* is indeed cattle; verily, he finds firm support in cattle.
Having made the *ekaviṃśa* the *agniṣṭomasāman* of this very [sacrifice], one should cause one afflicted by illness to sacrifice.
The threefold is indeed breath; the sun is breath. He who is ill is deprived of his breaths; by means of the breaths, he thus endows him with abundance.
(PB 16.13.2) It results in the Virāj. Food indeed departs from him who is ill; the Virāj is food; verily, he places food and sustenance within him. (PB 16.13.3)

The Agniṣṭoma sacrifice consists of twenty-one [verses]. He who is afflicted by illness is indeed without a firm foundation; the twenty-one-fold [stoma] is a firm foundation, and thus he finds a firm foundation.

One who desires food or one who desires a firm foundation should sacrifice with this very [rite]. The Virāj is food, and the twenty-one-fold [stoma] is a firm foundation; he eats food and finds a firm foundation.
The sacrificial altar is a fertile field; for this is its most powerful aspect. By means of this power, he brings the sacrifice to fulfillment.
The threshing floor is the high altar; for here that essence comes together, and thus he makes the sacrifice possessed of essence.
A threshing-post becomes the sacrificial stake, for by means of it they draw forth that essence.
A three-year-old steer is the purchase-price for the Soma, for the sake of [securing] Indra's presence.
(10) Horse-chariots with Soma-proclaimers run in all directions.
(11) Verily, from all these directions he secures for himself food.
(12) With a chariot drawn by four horses, he says [the formula] in the eastern direction; for paths are measured out just like this. As for the paths—

They cause [the horses] to run at full speed: on a three-step distance with a side-horse carriage to the north; for two *gavyūtis* to the west; for one *krośa* with a single-seated carriage to the south.
This indeed is the form of the quarters; by that which is the form of the quarters, they bring the sacrifice to fulfillment.

The chariots have leather thongs moistened with milk; therefore, whatever fresh butter (*navanīta*) may arise from them, that should also be used as clarified butter (*ājya*) for the sake of immediate effect.

Now, this is the *anukrī* of the Aṅgirases. By means of this, indeed, the Aṅgirases attained the Ādityas. He who is excluded or as if inferior should sacrifice with this; he attains the precedence of his predecessors, for by means of this the Aṅgirases attained the Ādityas.
Its *pavamāna* stotras consist of the twenty-fourfold hymns.
The *gāyatrī* consists of twenty-four syllables. By means of the *gāyatrī*, the gods pervaded these worlds; by this [chant], he likewise pervades these very worlds.

The *gāyatrī* is splendor and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); verily, he secures for himself splendor and spiritual luster. The *gāyatrī* is breath; the *gāyatrī* is procreation; from breath, through the *gāyatrī*, one is born.
Both types of *stomas*—those with even and those with odd [syllables]—[are employed].
The *cāru* and the *yaśas*: that is a pair; from that pair offspring is born.
It attains the *virāj*; the *virāj* is food; verily he secures food.
There is an *agniṣṭoma* consisting of twenty-one [verses]; the twenty-one is a foundation; verily at the very end he finds firm support in the sacrifice.
Now this Viśvajit is a craft;
indeed, he who knows thus beholds the craft of the *stomas* in his own house as a craft. Its two *pavamāna* lauds consist of eighteen [verses] each.
This sacrifice is indeed like a chariot for the sake of desire; whatever desire one desires, one attains it by means of this. For wherever one desires with a chariot, there one attains it.
One who desires heaven should sacrifice.
The *pṛṣṭha* hymns are the heavenly world; by means of this, one attains the heavenly world itself.
(16.15.7) Radiance and spiritual luster are the *pṛṣṭha* chants. In that the *pṛṣṭha* chants are performed in a single way, he bestows radiance and spiritual luster upon him in a single way.
(16.15.8) Food and cattle are the *pṛṣṭha* chants. In that the *pṛṣṭha* chants are performed in a single way, he bestows food and cattle upon him in a single way.
(16.15.9) Regarding this they say: "The *pṛṣṭha* chants belong to different worlds; since they are encompassed within a single sacrificial rite, the sacrificer is liable to become unestablished."
The Hotṛ’s *pṛṣṭha* chant consists of the twenty-onefold [stoma]. The twenty-onefold is indeed a foundation; thus he finds firm support in the very center of the sacrifice.
The *agniṣṭoma* consists of the twenty-onefold; the twenty-onefold is indeed a foundation; thus he finds firm support at the very end of the sacrifice.
These two [twenty-onefold stomas] are both twenty-onefold; the sacrificer has two feet. He thereby establishes the sacrificer himself upon the sacrifice and upon cattle.
Now, this Ekatrika is the "breaker-out" of Prajāpati.
By means of it, Prajāpati indeed broke out these worlds.
This is a Kṛtastoma, for that which is broken out belongs to what has been made.

(16.16.4) When they praise with one [verse], Prajāpati is indeed one; verily, he attains Prajāpati. And when they praise with three, these worlds are three; verily, he finds firm support in these very worlds.

(16.16.5) These [verses] amount to four; cattle are four-footed; verily, he finds firm support in cattle. (16.16.6) It amounts to a Gāyatrī; the Gāyatrī is splendor and holy luster; verily, he wins splendor and holy luster.
The Gāyatrī is breath; through breath, one is procreated from the Gāyatrī. "With this golden luster, being purified"—this is the Ārbhava Pavamāna.
This is indeed the form of all meters; thus, he establishes the Ārbhava Pavamāna in all the meters.
In that [chant], the side of the *gāyatra* does not depart from the *gāyatra*, nor from the *sāman*, nor from the *nidhana*.
(PB 17.1.1) The gods indeed went to the heavenly world; of them, the divine ones were left behind as they wandered abroad as *vrātyas*.
They returned by the same path by which the gods had gone to the heavenly world, yet they did not find that *stoma* or that *chandas* by which [the gods had gone].
Desiring to reach them, those gods said to the Maruts, "Bestow upon these that *stoma* and that *chandas* by which you may reach us.
They bestowed upon them this sixteenfold *stoma* and the *anuṣṭubh* in an indirect manner; from that, they indeed reached them.

(PB 17.1.2) Those who travel as *vrātyas* are deprived and continue to be deprived, for they do not practice *brahmacarya*, nor do they engage in agriculture or trade. This sixteenfold *stoma* is capable of bringing [the journey] to completion.
This is indeed the Marut-stoma; those which are the minor meters belong to the Maruts.
He draws up the *kakubh* [verse] facing eastward; and since this *dvipadā* is performed in the place of the *kakubh*, he thereby brings them into harmony through their very form.
With the verse, "Then indeed, O Indra, lover of songs," he makes even the uneven meter [fit]; for a host is indeed uneven, and thus he makes all of these equal.
Among them, Dyutāna Māruta was their householder; they sacrificed with this *stoma* and all of them prospered. In that there is this *sāman*, it is for the sake of prosperity.

If they were to conclude with a defined (*nirukta*) finale (*nidhana*), only the householder would prosper while the others would not; but since they conclude with an undefined (*anirukta*) one, he establishes all of them in a state of prosperity.
(17.1.9) Verily, these are devourers of poison who eat the food of the people that belongs to the Brahman; they utter ill-spoken words and speak what is ill-spoken;

they go about striking with punishment those who deserve no punishment; being uninitiated, they utter the speech of the initiated. The *ṣoḍaśa* chant is indeed their hymn of praise, capable of striking away evil. Since these four [groups] consist of sixteen each, by that means they are released from evil.

(10) "The Agniṣṭoma-sāman should be performed with the verse, 'The god who bestows wealth upon you' (*devo vo draviṇodā*); thus he establishes them among the deities themselves. (11) Now they say: "It should be performed on the *satobṛhatī* verses with [the verse], 'The path-finder has been seen' (*adarśi gātuvittama*). For a host is, as it were, uneven; [by this] he makes them all truly *satobṛhatī*s. (12) Regarding this they say: "This metre, the *satobṛhatī*, is, as it were, loose and wavering; therefore it should be performed with [the verse], 'The god who bestows wealth upon you' (*devo vo draviṇodā*)."

(13) This *bṛhatī* is indeed established which has a repeated foot; because it begins the foot again, therefore the son goes after the mother. (14–15) A turban, a goad, a bowstring, a *jyāhṇoḍa*, a carriage with a single horse on each side (*vipatha*), a seat covered with wooden planks, a garment of black wool, two skins—one black and one white—and a silver necklace: these belong to the master of the house. For the others, there are fringed garments with woven loops; two ropes each, two pairs of sandals, and double-layered skins.
(16) This indeed is the wealth of the Vrātyas; those to whom they give this go away being purified.
(17) With thirty-three [verses] each, they come together toward the Gṛhapati, for the thirty-three gods prospered; it is for prosperity indeed.
(1.1) Now, this is the Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice: those who are cruel and censurable, yet have lived as Vrātyas, should sacrifice with this.
(17.2.2) Those who are cruel and censured, yet travel as *vrātyas*, are seized from the front by evil. In that there are sixteen-fold stotras, they thereby overcome evil.

(17.2.3) In that the *agniṣṭoma* is the twenty-one-fold, it is for the sake of support; the twenty-one-fold is in the middle of the sacrifice, and thus he finds firm support in the very center of the sacrifice.
(17.2.4) It is an *uktha*; the *ukthas* are indeed cattle, and cattle lead the cruel one to the forefront. Verily, by means of cattle, he leads them to the forefront.
(PB 17.3.1) Now, this [rite] consists of two sixteenfold [stomas]. Those who, being the youngest, have gone forth as *vrātyas*, they should sacrifice with this.

(PB 17.3.2) These who, being the youngest, go forth as *vrātyas* are indeed deficient and become further deficient. In that there are threefold *pavamāna* [stomas], and since the threefold is the mouth of the *stomas*, he leads them forward from the very mouth of the sacrifice.

(17.3.3) Indeed, because there are two [stotras] at the sixteenth *stotra*, by that they are released from evil. (17.3.4) The *agniṣṭoma* consists of twenty-one [verses]; the twenty-one is indeed a foundation; thus, at the very end, one finds firm support in the sacrifice.
(17.4.1) Now, this is the *stoma* of the *śamanīcāmeḍhra*s; those who, being the eldest, should wander as *vrātya*s, they should perform this sacrifice with it.
From the foremost they rise to the foremost; the *stomas* go upward so that there may be no falling away.
With this [rite], Śamanīca, Ameḍhra, and others performed sacrifice; Kuṣītaka Sāmaśravasa was their *gṛhapati*.
Luśākapi Khārgali addressed them, saying: "They have been scattered; you have resorted to two inferior *stomas*."

Therefore, among the Kauṣītakas, no one at all feels excessive shame, for they are consecrated by sacrifice. Indra, indeed, struck down Tvaṣṭṛ’s three-headed son; an obscene voice spoke out against him. He ran to Agni, and Agni saw this Agnistotra. Having applied it to himself, he caused Indra to perform sacrifice with it; thereby he drove away that obscene voice from him.
(17.5.2) He who knows this does not utter vulgar speech.

(17.5.3) He who feels as if he were impure should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭut; by means of Agni alone he strikes away his evil, and by means of the Trivṛt-stoma he bestows splendor and the luster of sacred knowledge.
(17.5.4) Regarding this they say: "In that it is the Trivṛt, he strikes away evil from a single limb—namely, from the mouth alone."
The Jyotiṣṭoma alone is to be performed.

In that it is threefold (*trivṛt*), he thereby removes whatever in him is unpurified from the mouth; in that it is fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*), he thereby removes whatever in him is unpurified from the chest and the arms; in that it is seventeenfold (*saptadaśa*), he thereby removes whatever in him is unpurified from the middle.
By that which is the twenty-first [stotra], he drives away whatever in him is impure from his feet and ankles; by that he drives it away.
"He who sacrifices with the Agniṣṭut enters Vaiśvānara," they say; therefore, the Vāravantīya should be made the Agniṣṭoma-sāman. Whatever in him is impure, Agni consumes that;
then he rises up pure and purified.
The Agniṣṭut is a Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma; for it, the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is performed on verses addressed to Vāyu. One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with this.
The Trivṛt is indeed splendor, and spiritual luster is what it is; in that the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is performed on verses addressed to Vāyu, he thereby kindles him [the sacrificer] from above.
Just as one would heat gold in a forge, so does the Agniṣṭut heat him.
Having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman upon the Revatī verses, one who desires cattle should sacrifice with this [rite].
He who is without cattle is like a withered thicket; just as cattle do not delight in a withered thicket, so [it is with him].

In this [fire], cattle do not delight; when the fire burns the withered grass, it rains upon it, and then plants are born therein—indeed, in that [fire] cattle do delight. Cattle delight in this [fire] for one who knows thus.
Whatever in it is unwholesome for cattle, that he burns away with the Agniṣṭut; whatever he burns away with the Agniṣṭut, that he pacifies with the Revatī verses.
One who has fallen away from a sacrifice should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma-Agniṣṭut, or at whichever sacrificial rite he might fall away.

Agni indeed consumes the oblation of him who falters at the sacrifice; he does not cause the deity to reach the oblation, but rather he alone appropriates the fire. When something is shattered, they fashion another [vessel] from it, and by that means it reaches [the deity]. Indeed, when they fashion that [new vessel], then it reaches [the deity]. One should perform the sacrifice with those very *stomas* and in that very sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*) in which one falters. In whichever [stomas]...
"He who falters in his hymns of praise finds firm support in those very [hymns] at which sacrifice he performs" (PB 17.9.1).
"One desiring food should sacrifice with the seventeen-fold Agniṣṭut" (PB 17.9.2).
The seventeen-fold [stoma] is indeed food; Agni is the giver of food. Agni himself bestows food upon him.
(17.9.3) He who knows thus becomes an eater of food.
(17.9.4) Everything is seventeenfold; Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold; verily, he attains Prajāpati.
(17.10.1) The Agniṣṭoma is threefold; its morning pressing is undefined.

Prajāpati created offspring; once they were created, they departed from him. He beheld this undefined morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*); with it he separated their midst, and they returned to him, entering into him on all sides.
One who desires a village should sacrifice; in that there is this undefined morning pressing, he separates their midst, and they return to him, entering into him on all sides.
(PB 17.10.4) This very [sacrifice] is prior to Prajāpati; he who knows thus becomes prior to no one.
(PB 17.11.1) The Agniṣṭoma is threefold.

(PB 17.11.2) At its morning pressing, when the Nārāśaṃsa cups have been set down, he assigns eleven sacrificial gifts; at the midday pressing, twelve including a horse; he distributes both these sets, and eleven at the third pressing.
He removes them from the barren cow (PB 17.11.3).

These sacrificial gifts amount to thirty-three; there are thirty-three deities; verily he attains the deities. The horse is the thirty-fourth among the gifts; Prajāpati is the thirty-fourth among the deities;
verily he attains Prajāpati.

This is the Bṛhaspatisava. Bṛhaspati desired, "May I attain the position of domestic priest among the gods. He sacrificed with this [rite], and he attained the position of domestic priest among the gods.
He who knows thus attains the position of domestic priest.
