This is the Sthapatisava; one for whom they should consecrate [the office] of a Sthapati should sacrifice with this.

He who knows this attains the status of a *sthapati*. He is consecrated upon a black antelope skin; for this is the manifest splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); verily, he is consecrated in the very splendor of sacred knowledge.
He is consecrated with clarified butter; clarified butter is brilliance; he bestows brilliance upon himself.

The Agniṣṭoma is threefold; that is the Sarvasvāra sacrifice for one who should desire, "May I go to that world free from disease. He should sacrifice with this. The threefold is indeed breath, and the *svara* (tonal chant) is breath; he thus places his breaths outside him, and he dies quickly. The threefold is indeed the swiftest of the Stomas; in that it is threefold, [it is so that] they may meet more abundantly. The *svara* is infinite, and that world is infinite; verily, he [attains] the infinite heavenly world.
It causes him to go to the world. The *abhivat* verses are ascending; from this very world they cause him to go to the heavenly world.
While the Ārbhavapavamāna is being chanted, he sits down on the southern side of the Udumbara post, covered [with a garment]; thus he unites with it.
(PB 17.12.6) This is the Śunaskarṇastoma. By means of this, Śunaskarṇa Bāṣkiha performed sacrifice; therefore it is called the Śunaskarṇastoma.

(PB 17.13.1) The Trivṛt Agniṣṭoma is the world of the Vaiśvadeva. (PB 17.13.2) The introductory verse belongs to Agni, the sacrificial animal is for the Viśvedevas, and the Anūbandhyā cow is dedicated to Bṛhaspati.
They do not erect a sacrificial post, nor do they prepare the high altar;
they bind the animal to a surrounding stick;
the sacrificial fee consists of fifty [cows].
(Wearing an unwashed garment, he emerges from the *avabhṛtha* bath; for four months he does not eat meat, nor does he approach a woman.
Then, after those four months, there is the *dvidiva* day in the section of the Varuṇapraghāsas.
The opening [offering] belongs to Varuṇa, and the animal sacrifice belongs to the Maruts.
The *kavatī* verses are the introductory hymn; the sacrificial animal is for Varuṇa.

The *anūbandhyā* cow is dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. They set up the sacrificial post and pour out the earth for the high altar (*uttaravedi*). They bind the animals to the post. A hundred cows are the sacrificial fees. Wearing a new garment, he emerges from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). For four months he does not eat meat, nor does he approach a woman.

Then, after four months, there is a three-night period for the Sākamedha sacrifices in the world. The *anīkavatī* verse is the introductory hymn (*pratipad*); there is an animal sacrifice for Agni, an introductory hymn for the Maruts, an animal sacrifice for Indra and Agni, an introductory hymn for Viśvakarman, and the eleven animal victims. They perform the *sauryānūbandhyā* sacrifice, erect the sacrificial post, and throw up the high altar (*uttaravedi*).
They bind the sacrificial animals to the sacrificial post; fifty or a hundred are the sacrificial fees.
Wearing an unwashed garment, he emerges from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*); for four months he does not eat meat and does not approach a woman.
Then, after those four months, there is the *Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma* sacrifice in the world of *Śunāsīrya*.

The opening day (*pratipad*) has the *upavat* [fasting] rule; there is an animal sacrifice for Vāyu, and an *anūbandhyā* cow for the Aśvins. They set up the sacrificial post, they throw up the *uttaravedi* altar, and they bind the animal to the post. There are one hundred and twelve [cows]. Agni is the *saṃvatsara*; Sūrya is the *parivatsara*; Candramas is the *idāvatsara*; Vāyu is the *anuvatsara*. One attains Agni, the *saṃvatsara*, by means of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice; Sūrya, the *parivatsara*, by means of the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifices; and Candramas [by means of the Sākamedha].
With the Sākamedha sacrifices he wins the current year, and with the Śunāsīrya sacrifice he wins the following year.

By means of the Haviryajñas the gods conquered this world, and by means of the animal and Soma sacrifices they conquered the intermediate region and yonder world. He who knows thus attains these very worlds and becomes firmly established in them.
When one performs the Agnihotra, one thereby attains the status of a householder for ten nights;
when one performs the Agnihotra for ten years, one thereby attains the status of one who sacrifices with the New and Full Moon sacrifices;
when one sacrifices with the New and Full Moon sacrifices for ten years, one thereby attains the status of one who sacrifices with the Agniṣṭoma.
When one sacrifices with ten *agniṣṭoma*s, one attains the status of a performer of a thousand [sacrifices];
when one sacrifices with ten thousands, one attains the status of a performer of ten thousand [sacrifices];
when one sacrifices with ten times ten thousand, one attains the status of a performer of a hundred thousand [sacrifices].
When one sacrifices with ten *prayuta*s, one attains the status of a performer of the *niyuta* sacrifice;
when one sacrifices with ten *niyuta*s, one attains the status of a performer of the *arbuda* sacrifice;
when one sacrifices with ten *arbuda*s, one attains the status of a performer of the *nyarbuda* sacrifice.
When one sacrifices with ten *nyarbudas*, one attains the sacrificer of a *nikharvaka*;
when one sacrifices with ten *nikharvakas*, one attains the sacrificer of a *badva*;
when one sacrifices with ten *badvas*, one attains the sacrificer of an *akṣiti*; when one sacrifices with ten *akṣitis*, one becomes a cow.
When he becomes a cow, then he becomes fire; when he becomes fire, then he attains the householder of the year.
When he becomes the householder of the year, then he attains the measure of the Vaiśvadeva. From this, indeed, all others become increasingly further and further away.
He who knows thus attains these worlds; he conquers these worlds.
(The *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice consists of seventeen [stomas].

The gods and the Asuras were both sons of Prajāpati; the Asuras were more numerous and more powerful, while the gods were fewer. Those gods approached Prajāpati, and he perceived this *upahavya* sacrifice.
He reflected: "If I bring the explicitly defined [text], the Asuras will destroy my sacrifice. He brought the undefined [text].
At the final Stotra, with the verse, "O gods, may the giver of wealth come to you," he turned toward the gods.
Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
(18.1.6) He prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated, who knows thus.
(18.1.7) Now, however, they say: "The verse 'yajñā-yajñā vo agnaye' must indeed be performed.
(18.1.8) Agni, indeed, is all the deities; therefore, he does not exclude any deity whatsoever.

(18.1.9) When Indra delivered the Yatis to the hyenas, a vulgar voice cried out at him. He ran to Prajāpati for refuge; he gave him this Upahavya sacrifice. All the gods called upon it, therefore it is called Upahavya.
(18.1.10) One should cause one who is being falsely accused to perform this sacrifice.
The deities indeed pursue him whom they accuse falsely; the deities themselves consume his food.
When he has been purified and made savory, men eat his food.
One who desires a village should sacrifice.
(14) It belongs to the Maruts. The Maruts are indeed the subjects (*viś*) of the gods; verily he unites the subjects with him, and the subjects do not depart from him.
(15) One who desires cattle should sacrifice. It belongs to Pūṣan. (16) Pūṣan is indeed cattle; verily he wins cattle.
It belongs to the Viśvedevas, for all the gods invited him;
it has the Bṛhat-sāman,
for Prajāpati gave him to Indra.
A dark-grey horse is the sacrificial fee;
for it is undefined;
it should be given to the Brahman priest.
(Brahman is indeed the unexpressed among the officiating priests; he thus endows him with his very own form.
For as long as there is no sin in a newborn boy, so long is there no sin in him who knows this.
The Agniṣṭoma is seventeenfold.
(PB 18.2.2) It has twelve initiation and upasad days.
(PB 18.2.3) One who desires heaven should sacrifice.
(PB 18.2.4) Twelve months are a year; the year is the heavenly world. By this [sacrifice], one attains the heavenly world itself.
He becomes one whose vow is clarified butter (ghṛtavrata).
Clarified butter is indeed the vow of the gods; by means of the vow of the gods, he approaches the deities.
He approaches by each successive section (kāṇḍa); for among these worlds, each higher one is greater than the one below, [and this serves] for the complete attainment of heaven.
The *Bṛhat* Sāman is used; by means of the *Bṛhat*, the gods went to the heavenly world; verily, by this he attains the heavenly world.
Having uttered the word "Truth" (*ṛta*), they proceed; by Truth itself they cause him to go to the heavenly world.
A soma-cup is the sacrificial fee; verily, by the deity itself, he approaches the deities.
It is made of Udumbara wood; the Udumbara is strength, and thus he wins strength for himself.
It is to be given to a Brahmin of the same lineage so that there may be no interruption of the Soma-drinking. Everything is seventeenfold.
There are twelve months and five seasons; that indeed is the year. The year is the heavenly world; by this [rite], one attains the heavenly world.
The Agniṣṭoma sacrifice consists of seventeen [stomas].
At its consecration offering (*dīkṣaṇīyā-iṣṭi*), he gives gold weighing twelve *mānas*, and twenty-four *mānas*.

At the Prāyaṇīyā [offering], there are two measures of twenty-four mānas; at the Ātithyā, four measures of twenty-four mānas; in the morning at the first Upasad, eight measures of twenty-four mānas; in the afternoon at the first Upasad, sixteen measures of twenty-four mānas;
in the morning at the middle Upasad, thirty-two measures of twenty-four mānas; and in the afternoon at the middle Upasad, [thirty-two measures of twenty-four mānas].

Sixty-four portions of twenty-four mānas each at the final morning *upasad*; one hundred and twenty-eight portions of twenty-four mānas each at the final afternoon *upasad*; two portions of two hundred and twenty-eight mānas each for the omentum of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma;

four portions of two hundred and twenty-eight mānas each for the omentum of the animal sacrifice in the morning; and eight portions of two hundred and twenty-eight mānas each during the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*).

When the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been set down at the midday pressing, there are sixteen pieces of gold weighing two hundred and eighty *mānas*, and a hundred oxen; the *hotṛ*’s gold ornament and the *udgātṛ*’s garland [are also given]. At the third pressing, when the *nārāśaṃsa* cups have been set down, there are sixty-four pieces of gold weighing two hundred and eighty *mānas*. At the *udayanīyā* offering, there are twenty-eight *mānas* [of gold].
There are one hundred and twenty-eight measures in the omentum of the barren cow (PB 18.3.3). He who knows thus attains the world of the ox (PB 18.3.4).
He who, knowing this, sacrifices with this [rite] indeed conquers the radiant, meritorious world.

The Agniṣṭoma sacrifice consists of seventeen [stomas]. At its morning pressing, one mixes the Soma-libations with curdled milk; at the midday pressing, with boiled milk; and at the third pressing, with curds.
One who desires cattle should perform this sacrifice.

(18.4.4) Since all the pressings possess the *āśis* (blessing), he thereby causes him to prosper with cattle at each pressing; yet his progeny becomes, as it were, closed up, for he mixes [the offering] with milk at the *śukriya* pressing. (18.4.5) One should cause a Vaiśya to sacrifice.
This indeed is the prosperity of a Vaiśya, namely cattle; verily, by means of cattle he causes him to prosper.
For this [sacrifice], the Kaṇvarathantara is the Pṛṣṭha-stotra;
the Sado-viśīya is the Brahman-sāman.
The Kaṇvarathantara is indeed cattle; the Sado-viśīya is cattle. He thus places cattle before him in succession.
The whole [stoma] is seventeenfold.
There are twelve months and five seasons; that is the year. Cattle are born in accordance with the year; having attained them, he secures them.
The Ukthya sacrifice consists of seventeen [stotras].
Indra slew Vṛtra; he was shattered in every direction by his own virility. The gods sought an expiation for him, but nothing at all restored him; only the *tīvrasoma* (intense Soma) restored him.
One should cause a person who has over-poured the Soma to perform this sacrifice.

(18.5.4) This one through whom Soma flows excessively is, as it were, perforated. When one sacrifices with the *tīvrasoma*, it is for the sake of covering [the opening] and for the sake of non-perforation.

(18.5.5–6) One should cause a king who has been deposed to sacrifice. The common people (*viś*) indeed flow away from him who is a deposed king. When he sacrifices with the *tīvrasoma*, it is for the sake of covering [the opening] and for the sake of non-perforation.
(18.5.7) One who desires a village should sacrifice.

(18.5.8) Verily, the village passes him by who, though being capable of obtaining a village, does not find a village; when he sacrifices with the *tīvrasoma*, it is for concealment and for the sake of flawlessness.

(18.5.9) One who desires offspring should sacrifice. Verily, offspring pass him by who, though being capable of obtaining offspring, does not find offspring; when he sacrifices with the *tīvrasoma*, it is for concealment and for the sake of flawlessness.

(10) One who desires cattle should sacrifice. Indeed, cattle pass him by who, though being fit for cattle, does not obtain cattle. In that he sacrifices with the *tīvrasoma*, it is for the sake of concealment and for the sake of non-deficiency.

(11) He should cause one who is afflicted by disease to sacrifice. Indeed, the vital breaths pass him by who is afflicted by disease. In that he sacrifices with the *tīvrasoma*, it is for the sake of concealment and for the sake of non-deficiency.
(12) They milk a hundred [vessels] of mixed soma; they indeed make it strong.
(13) Those very ones are the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās).
(14) They pour out the soma-libations one after another, thinking, "May it exhilarate him strongly. Both Adhvaryus and all the Camasādhvaryus respond for the Acchāvāka; they indeed make it strong.
The officiating priests did not consume that [Soma]; they merely smelled the cups. They thus intensify it; they consume it at the *acchāvāka*’s hymn, and thereby they indeed intensify it.

If they were to consume the Soma from each of the pressings separately, prosperity would depart from the sacrificer. Therefore, they consume it once from each pressing at the end, so as not to cause a separation between the pressings.
The *rathantara* chant is employed.
The *Rathantara* is indeed this [earth]. He who does not find firm standing finds no firm standing on this [earth]; verily, he establishes him upon this very [earth].
The *Śrāyantīya* is the *Brahmasāman*; it bestows glory (*śrī*) upon him.
The *Anuṣṭubh* is speech, and the *Yajñāyajñīya* is the essence of speech; verily, he places the essence of speech within him.

The *viśoviśīya* becomes the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*; verily, he thus establishes everything in this [sacrifice]. (PB 18.5.23) The *udvaṃśīya* occurs at the end of the *ukthas*; this is the form of all the *pṛṣṭhas*, and he finds firm standing in all forms.
(PB 18.5.24) It is an *ukthya* sacrifice; the *ukthas* are indeed cattle, and he finds firm standing in cattle.
The Ukthya sacrifice consists of seventeen [stotras], it includes the Ṣoḍaśin, and the seventeenth is the final one.
As great as Prajāpati is when standing upright, so great is he when lying horizontal; as great as these worlds are when upright, so great are they when horizontal.
(18.6.4) Indeed, the sacrificer of the Vājapeya attains Prajāpati.
(18.6.5) In that there are seventeen stotras, by that he attains the upward direction; in that the whole [sacrifice] consists of seventeens, by that [he attains] the horizontal direction.
(18.6.6) Its pressings possess diverse powers.
The morning pressing is undefined; the midday pressing is possessed of strength (*vāja*); the third pressing is variegated (*citra*).
In that the morning pressing is undefined, and Prajāpati is indeed undefined, he thereby attains Prajāpati.
In that the midday pressing is possessed of strength—and *vāja* is indeed food—it is for the securing of food. In that...
"The third pressing is variegated for the attainment of the heavenly world" (PB 18.6.9).
"The Vājapeya has no common womb," they say, "since it belongs to Prajāpati and possesses a defined Sāman. In that the morning pressing is undefined, by that it has a common womb;
the Rathantara Sāman is used for the sake of obtaining blessings.
This earth is indeed the *rathantara*; it is upon this very [earth] that he is consecrated.
Therefore, the sacrificer of the *vājapeya* does not descend from it;
for it is upon this [earth] that he is consecrated.
The *Abhīvarta* becomes the *brahmasāman*; this is indeed the bull of the *brahman*, and it causes him to attain the state of a bull.
The *yajñāyajñīya* occurs on an *anuṣṭubh* verse; the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and the *yajñāyajñīya* is the essence of speech; verily, he places the essence of his speech within speech.
The *vāravantīya* becomes the *agniṣṭomasāman* for the sake of securing power and vigor.
The *udvaṃśīya* occurs at the end of the *uktha*s; it is indeed the form of all the *pṛṣṭha* chants. Thus, he establishes himself in all forms.
The *gaurīvita* is the *ṣoḍaśin*-sāman. The *gaurīvita* is redundant, the *ṣoḍaśin* is redundant; thus, he places the redundant upon the redundant.

Regarding this they say: "In the sacrifice, a repetition (*jāmi*) is indeed committed when they chant with the *gaurīvita* after the *udvaṃśīya*, [thinking] 'from the *svāra* [tone] to the *svāra* [tone]'. (PB 18.6.21) There is no such repetition;
the pressing (*savana*) is brought to completion, the hymn (*uktha*) is recited, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call intervenes—therefore, there is no repetition. (PB 18.6.22)
"This section of the sacrifice is, as it were, severed by the *ṣoḍaśin*; therefore, there is no repetition (*ajāmi*).
"It concludes in the sacrificial forest," they say; "it passes beyond the *ukthas* and beyond the *ṣoḍaśin*, yet it does not reach the night.
The *Bṛhat* [Sāman] comes last, performed upon verses containing the word *śipiviṣṭa* of Viṣṇu.
This body of Prajāpati that dwells in cattle is indeed Śipiviṣṭa; the *bṛhat* is breath, and thus he establishes himself in breath among cattle.
They praise with the *bṛhat*; the *bṛhat* is worthy to attain that world beyond, and so he attains it.

Prajāpati desired, "May I obtain food (*vāja*), may I attain the heavenly world. He saw this Vājapeya sacrifice; the Vājapeya is indeed food, and by means of it he obtains food and the heavenly world.

At the morning pressing, they contain *śukra* and possess light; through them, he secures brilliance and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). At the midday pressing, they contain *vāja*; this is for the attainment of the heavenly world. At the third pressing, they contain food, they contain groups, and they contain cattle; through them, he secures abundance.
(18.7.5) Everything is seventeenfold; Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold; verily, one attains Prajāpati.
(18.7.6) The officiating priests wear golden garlands; thus the form of glory itself is created.
(18.7.7) "May this be my manifestation in yonder world," [he thinks].
Gold is indeed light; verily, he places light within him.
They run the race; they cause the sacrificer to win; verily, they cause him to win that world, the heavenly realm.
He ascends the firmament; verily, he ascends that world, the heavenly realm.
(11) It rises with the dust; verily he hides him from the world of men.
(12) He sings the Vājina-sāman over the two chariot wheels; the Vāja is indeed the heavenly world; verily he causes him to win that world, the heaven.
(13) Over the verses containing the word *śipiviṣṭa* of Viṣṇu, the Bṛhat is the final [Sāman]; having ascended to that very world, the heaven, he transcends the summit of the sun.

(18.8.1) He performs the Agniṣṭoma first; for the Agniṣṭoma is the mouth of the sacrifice. Having commenced at the very mouth of the sacrifice, he ascends to the consecration (sava). (18.8.2) Now follows this Abhiṣecanīya [Soma-sacrifice].

(18.8.3) Its Pavamāna stotras consist of thirty-two verses; the Anuṣṭubh consists of thirty-two syllables, and the Anuṣṭubh is speech. To the full extent of speech, by that very means he is consecrated.

(PB 18.8.4) "This [sacrifice] is like a fracture among the meters, in that the *stomas* are unequal and not in their proper order" (PB 18.8.5). Since the *pavamāna* chants are equal, it is therefore free from fracture; it is therefore in its proper order.

(PB 18.8.6) By means of the *ātman*, one prospers through the *agniṣṭoma*; by means of the *ātman*, one becomes meritorious. Now, as for the *ukthas*: the *ukthas* are indeed cattle, the *ukthas* are the people (*viś*); in that there are *ukthas*, it is for the sake of continuity.

(18.8.7) “O Vāyu, the bright one, unmeasured,” with these words the *pratipad* for Vāyu occurs. Vāyu is indeed speech; verily he yokes speech at the mouth of this sacrifice. By means of that [speech] he is consecrated; he is impelled by all speech; all speeches call him “King.

(18.8.8) The *saṃbhāryā* verses occur; by them he yokes the *pṛṣṭha* stotras. In that they have different deities, by that he yokes them. The *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed vigor; verily he is consecrated upon vigor itself.
(18.8.9) "Those who perform the *saṃbhāryas* depart from the mouth of the sacrifice," so they say.
(18.8.10) By [the words] "O you who purify the forefront of speech," they do not depart from the mouth of the sacrifice.
(18.8.11) "'With flashing radiance'—this is the form of the meters; he thus yokes the meters themselves at the mouth of his sacrifice, and by means of them he is consecrated."
(12) "This very one, the ten fingers..."—these are the Āditya verses; for these creatures are indeed the Ādityas, and he is born from their midst.
(13) "Flow on, O Indu, as the pressed bull"—they contain the word *vṛṣan* (bull); they are Triṣṭubh verses. The Triṣṭubh is indeed vigor; thus he is consecrated upon vigor itself.

(14) "Your powers rise up"—they are verses containing the word *udvat* (rising). The Anuṣṭubh has the form of rising, and the Rājanya is of the nature of the Anuṣṭubh; therefore, they are verses containing the word *udvat*.
(15) "O Pavamāna, what of yours?"—this is for the arrangement of the vital breaths.

(16) "And then, adorned by the nights"—this is an *anuṣṭubh*; the first [verse] is an *anuṣṭubh* or the last is an *anuṣṭubh*. The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed speech; by means of speech they set forth, and by means of speech they rise up.
(17) That which consists of single verses (*ekarcā*) is, as it were, severed. Since these two triplets (*tṛca*) are *anuṣṭubhs* on both sides, there are many who go before and many who follow behind.
The final [verse] is dedicated to Sūrya and is in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; it serves for the complete attainment of the heavenly world.

Indeed, when Varuṇa had performed the consecration (*soma-savana*), his splendor (*bhargas*) departed from him. It fell in three parts: one third became Bhṛgu, one third became the *Śrāyantīya* [sāman], and one third entered the waters. In that the *hotṛ* priest is a descendant of Bhṛgu (*bhārgava*), he thereby attains and secures for himself that very same power and vigor. As for...

The Śrāyantīya becomes the Brahman-sāman; by that very means he attains and secures that power and vigor. In that he puts on a lotus-garland, by that very means he attains and secures that power and vigor. (PB 18.9.3) It is the tenth [day].

There are ten cups and ten cup-attendants; they approach each cup by tens, tracing their lineage back through ten generations as they proceed. For this sacrifice is complete with ten; indeed, it was these very ones who sought after that sacrifice when he sacrificed with it.
Having taken hold of that very power and vigor, he bestows it upon him.
The whole [stoma] consists of seventeen parts. There are twelve months and five seasons; that indeed is the year. Having obtained power and vigor from the year itself, he secures them for himself.

Indra slew Vṛtra. His various forms entered this [earth]; those [forms] became the stars by means of the space of the constellations. The lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) is born; when he puts on the lotus-garland (*puṣkarasraj*), he puts on the form of Vṛtra himself—the sovereignty (*kṣatra*).
There are twelve lotuses; the year consists of twelve months. Within the year, he causes him to prosper through both what has been and what is to be.
(PB 18.9.8) A garland belongs to the Udgātṛ; it is solar. The Udgātṛ does not indeed shine forth for that [person], but rather he causes him to shine forth.
(PB 18.9.9) A golden plate belongs to the Hotṛ; it is Agni-related. The Hotṛ [is Agni]; moreover, he raises up yonder sun for him.
Two mirrors belong to the Adhvaryu; for the two Adhvaryus are as it were [his eyes], and thus he bestows the two eyes upon him.

The horse belongs to the Prastotṛ; the horse is of Prajāpati, and the Prastotṛ is of Prajāpati; moreover, the horse indeed neighs forth, and the Prastotṛ likewise chants forth. A milch-cow belongs to the Pratihartṛ; he thereby bestows milk upon him.
The cow is for the Maitrāvaruṇa, lest she lead him away from his will.
The bull is for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; the bull is indeed vigor, and thus he bestows vigor upon him.
The garment is for the Potṛ, for the sake of purification.
The *vara* is for the *neṣṭṛ*; for this office of the Hotṛ is like a hanging ornament.
The *sthūri* laden with barley is for the *acchāvāka*; for this office of the Hotṛ is like a one-horse cart, and furthermore, it serves to ward off Varuṇa.
Indeed, at that time, the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*) did not yet accrue to him; however, by means of this [barley], those very [gifts] become sought after and gratified for him.
An ox is for the Agnīdhra for the sake of yoking;
a goat is for the Subrahmaṇyā;
a heifer is for the Unnetṛ; a castrated three-year-old steer is for the Grāvastut, for the sake of pairing.

(TB 1.8.9.21) There are twelve pregnant heifers for the Brahman priest. Twelve months are a year; verily he finds firm support in the year. Now, as to why they are pregnant: the cow is indeed speech, and the mantra is the embryo;

verily he places the mantra in his speech, and he becomes one who is to be addressed with mantras. And as to why there are twelve heifers that are to become cows: those are the twelve milks; verily he bestows them upon him.
Therefore they say: "The king who possesses milk is meritorious" (PB 18.10.1).
Indeed, he who departs from the *sava*—the consecration—does not have the *sava* come to him; but he who departs for the *sāmans* becomes one who has been consecrated more excellently.
There are the *saṃbhāryā* verses; by means of them, he yokes the *pṛṣṭhas*.
(18.10.3) These *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed the *sāmans*.
(18.10.4) In that they are combined (*saṃbhāryā*), one does not depart from the *sāmans*.

(18.10.5) By means of those *sāmans* which belong to the kings of the gods, one prospers in yonder world; by means of those which belong to the kings of men, one prospers in this world; thus one prospers in both these worlds, in the world of the gods and in the world of men.

(18.10.6) He is consecrated over the *sāman* and the *triṣṭubh*. The *sāman* is indeed vigor, and the *triṣṭubh* is vigor; he is thus consecrated over vigor itself. (18.10.7) There are eleven *rājasāmans*; the *triṣṭubh* has eleven syllables. The *triṣṭubh* is force and vigor; he is thus consecrated over force and vigor itself. (18.10.8) If they were to perform the *trivṛt* stoma at the consecration ceremony, they would obstruct the *brahman* for the sake of the *kṣatra*; [therefore] if [they perform] the *trivṛt*...

They extract that Brahman from the Kṣatra; therefore, the Bharatas are subject to the counter-staff of the Brahman, for they do not perform the *trivṛt* at the consecration (*abhiṣecanīya*). The twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*) is the final [stoma] of the consecration, the seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*) is for the *daśapeya*, and the twenty-one-fold is for the hair-cutting sacrifice (*keśavapanīya*).

The twenty-onefold [stoma] is the Kṣatra, and the seventeenfold is the Viś; by means of the Kṣatra, he thus encompasses the Viś on both sides for him, so that the Viś does not depart from him. Indeed, when he is consecrated by the Rājasūya, he ascends to the heavenly world. As for this...
If this [sacrifice] were one with stomas directed hitherward for the shaving of the hair, one would either descend to the world below, go beyond the people, or become intoxicated;

therefore, it serves to prevent falling away from this world. Just as one would descend by grasping one branch after another, so does he descend to this world by means of this [rite] for the sake of firm support.

Indra slew Vṛtra; he fell apart from his vigor. He saw this Śrāyantīya [Sāman], and with it he restored himself. Indeed, he who is consecrated by the Rājasūya falls away from power and vigor, for he slays Vṛtra.
In that the Śrāyantīya becomes the Brahman-sāman, he restores himself once again.

The Yajñāyajñīya chant occurs in the Anuṣṭubh metre. He who is consecrated by the Rājasūya is indeed deprived of speech, for he slays Vṛtra; the Anuṣṭubh is speech, and the Yajñāyajñīya is the essence of speech.
Thus, he places the essence back into his speech.
The Vāravantīya becomes the Agniṣṭoma-sāman; he is indeed deprived of sensory power and vigor.
He who is consecrated by the Rājasūya slays Vṛtra; for when the Vāravantīya becomes the Agniṣṭoma-sāman, it is for the complete grasping of power and vigor.
By means of the Śrāyantīya they indeed caused [the gods] to resort [to him], and by the Vāravantīya they caused them to be warded off; this is the complete grasping of power and vigor.
(18.11.5) He who is consecrated by the Rājasūya is indeed without a firm foundation. When he sacrifices with this two-night rite, then indeed he finds a firm foundation.
(18.11.6) As many as are the days and nights of the year, so many are these stotriya verses; thus he finds a firm foundation in the year itself.
(18.11.7) The Agniṣṭoma is the first day, the Atirātra the latter; thus he finds a firm foundation separately in both the day and the night.

On the new moon day, the first day is the *udriṣṭa* (the day before the sacrifice), and the second is the following day; thus one establishes oneself separately in the two half-months. On the full moon day, the first day is the *vyaṣṭakā*, and the second is the following day; thus one establishes oneself separately in the two months. Regarding this, they say: "If there should be two auspicious days (*puṇyāha*) within the same fortnight..."

"For the success of the very work of those two," they say, "the two-night sacrifice is not conducive to cattle, for these two meters, the Gāyatrī and the Triṣṭubh, exclude the Jagatī. [To this they reply: "The Jagatī is not excluded by that which occurs at the third pressing;
for when this [Jagatī] shares in a day of the Ahīna or in a pressing of the Sāhna, then indeed the Jagatī is made present."

The *traiśoka* is the *brahmasāman* of the subsequent day, and the *vaikhānasa* is the *acchāvākasāman*; because these two are performed at the *śukriya* pressing, by that very means the *jagatī* metre is established, and by that means it is conducive to cattle.
This two-night rite is indeed a manifestation of dawn; it causes him to shine forth.
(PB 19.1.1) Now follows this *rāṭ* sacrifice.
(PB 19.1.2) He who, aspiring to kingship, does not obtain the kingdom, should sacrifice with this; it makes him a king indeed as a king. They would call him "Vairāja" whom a king might make a king;
it makes him a king indeed as a king.
(19.1.3) Other sacrifices are perfected as *chandas* meters; this [sacrifice] is the *stoma*. The *stoma* is indeed vigor; thus he is consecrated upon vigor itself.
(19.1.4) It becomes praised with eight twenty-one-fold hymns. For eight heroes support the kingdom:
the king’s brother, the prince, the domestic priest, the queen, the charioteer, the village headman, the steward, and the gatekeeper.
These heroes are indeed the gatherers; they uphold the kingdom, and it is upon them alone that he is consecrated.

The twenty-one-fold [stoma] is the ruling power (*kṣatra*), and its foundation is the ruling power. For one who knows this, there is the manifestation of the ruling power, and he becomes firmly established.
Now, this Virāj, desiring food, should sacrifice.
(19.2.2) Other sacrifices attain the *virāj* indirectly; this one has attained the *virāj* directly. (19.2.3) By means of this, he directly secures food; he becomes an eater of food who knows thus.
(19.2.4) Every [verse] consists of ten syllables; the *virāj* has ten syllables. Food belongs to the *virāj*; it is for the securing of food.
(19.2.5) These [stotras] become five by five; the sacrifice is fivefold, cattle are fivefold; he thus finds firm support in cattle within the sacrifice itself.
(19.2.6) One who desires a firm foundation should sacrifice with this very [rite]; for man is established here on earth by means of ten [fingers]; he thus finds firm support on this very [earth].
(19.3.1) Now follows this Aupaśada [sacrifice].

The Gandharva-Apsaras Stoma: one desiring offspring should sacrifice; for the Gandharvas and Apsarases indeed enter into a man’s offspring or his childlessness. They have their share of the Soma-drink here; he gratifies them with their own portion. Being satisfied and pleased, they bestow offspring upon him.
(19.3.3) Each *stotrīyā* verse is produced one by one; verily, he produces offspring for him.
(19.3.4) He raises the *kakubh* [verse] toward the east; the *kakubh* is indeed the person (*puruṣa*). That embryo is thus placed in the middle.
(19.3.5) Now, as to why this *dvipadā* [verse] is performed in the place of the *kakubh*: it is the embryo that thereby brings him forth.
There is a *cyāvana* [verse]; indeed, *cyāvana* is procreation.

He who knows thus is procreated and becomes numerous. There are the two *janitra* verses of Vasiṣṭha; Vasiṣṭha, whose sons had been slain, beheld these two *sāmans*. He was procreated with offspring and cattle. In that these two *sāmans* are performed, it is for the sake of procreation.

(PB 19.3.9) Of the verses that have been chanted together, two exceed the *virāj* metre; two are deficient in the woman for the sake of procreation. Thus, procreation itself is performed for the sake of generation.
(PB 19.4.1) Now follows this *punaḥstoma* sacrifice.
He who, having accepted much [gifts], might feel as if he has swallowed poison, should sacrifice with this.
That which is the eleventh [brick]—whatever one accepts as a gift in early life, whatever poison one swallows, and whatever unfit food one eats—that he removes for the sake of the morning pressing.
Then that which is the twelfth—whatever one accepts as a gift in later life, whatever poison one swallows, and whatever unfit food one eats—that he removes for the sake of the third pressing.
Man is indeed of the Vairāja nature; being impure in the middle, it is from the very middle that it releases him from evil.
(19.4.6) There are two [sāmans], the Śuddhā and the Aśuddhīya.

(19.4.7) When Indra delivered the Yatis to the jackals, a vulgar voice cried out after him; he considered himself impure. He saw these two, the Śuddhā and the Aśuddhīya; by means of them, he became pure.

(19.4.8) Whatever one accepts as a gift in excess, whatever one swallows as poison, whatever one eats that is not food, and whatever one considers himself impure—by these two [sāmans], one is purified from that.

(19.4.9) There are the Gauṣūkta and the Aśvasūkta. (19.4.10) Having accepted much [as a gift], Gauṣūkta and Aśvasūkta felt as if they had swallowed poison (*gara*). They saw these two *sāmans*; by means of them, they expelled the poison.
(19.4.11) Whatever much one accepts, whatever poison one swallows, and whatever unfit food one eats—that is expelled by these two.
There are fifteen stotras; the fifteenfold [stoma] is vigor and strength. Having freed him from evil, he endows him with vigor and strength. Now follows this Catuṣṭoma sacrifice;
one who desires cattle should perform it.

(19.5.3) In that the *bahiṣpavamāna* consists of four [verses], and cattle are four-footed, he wins cattle. (19.5.4) In that there are eight *ājya* [stotras], and cattle have eight hooves, he thereby obtains cattle hoof by hoof.
(19.5.5) In that the midday *pavamāna* consists of twelve [verses], and the year has twelve months, and cattle are born according to the year, he wins them.
(19.5.6) In that there are sixteen *pṛṣṭha* stotras, and cattle are sixteen parts (*kalā*), he thereby obtains cattle part by part.
(19.5.7) In that the *ārbhava-pavamāna* has twenty verses, he thereby obtains their fivefold nature (*pāṅktatva*).

(19.5.8) In that the *agniṣṭoma* has twenty-four [stotras], and the *gāyatrī* consists of twenty-four syllables—the *gāyatrī* being brilliance and spiritual luster—he thereby secures brilliance and spiritual luster.
The Gāyatrī is breath; procreation comes from breath. Therefore, from the Gāyatrī, offspring is produced. There is one *sāman* and many meters; therefore, one man nourishes many dependents.

The Agniṣṭoma is indeed the self, and the meters are cattle; thus he establishes cattle within his own self. It is neither an Uktha nor an Agniṣṭoma, for neither domestic nor wild cattle [are established] therein.
Now, he whose four stotras consist of four [verses] each, four of eight, four of twelve, and four of sixteen, does not overstep the cow;
for cattle consist of sixteen parts, and thus he obtains cattle part by part.

The Ukthya sacrifice includes the Ṣoḍaśin cup. The Ukthas are cattle, and the Ṣoḍaśin is the thunderbolt; by means of the thunderbolt, he thus secures cattle for him, and cattle do not depart from him. There is neither an Uktha nor an Atirātra, for there are neither domestic nor wild cattle [in that state].
The strength of the Asuras was indeed enveloped in darkness and covered with a stone lid; within it was the wealth consisting of cattle.

It was within; the gods were unable to break it open. They said to Bṛhaspati, "Release these for us. With the *udbhid* [sacrifice] he caused strength to flow forth, with the *balabhid* he split them open, with the *utsedha* he released them, and with the *niṣedha* he enclosed them.
One who desires cattle should sacrifice.
(19.7.3) If he sacrifices with the *udbhid*, he causes his very strength to surge forth; if [he sacrifices] with the *balabhid*, he indeed shatters his enemy's strength.

(19.7.4) The *brahmasāman*s are the *utsedha* and the *niṣedha*; by means of the *utsedha*, he causes the cattle to swell for him, and by means of the *niṣedha*, he encloses them. (19.7.5) "The sacrifice caused Indra to grow"—thus, the *ājya* chant of the Brahman priest is perfect in its form.
There are two [stomas], the sevenfold and the seventeenfold. In that they praise with seven, and there are seven domestic animals, he thereby wins cattle.
The *śakvarī* verse consists of seven feet; the *śakvarī* is cattle; he thereby wins cattle. Now, as for the seventeenfold:
Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold; he thereby attains Prajāpati.

It becomes the *gāyatrī*; the *gāyatrī* is brilliance and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Verily, he wins brilliance and spiritual luster. The *gāyatrī* is breath; the *gāyatrī* is procreation. From breath, indeed, through the *gāyatrī*—(PB 19.8.1). Now, this is the *apaciti* sacrifice; one who desires honor should sacrifice with it. Through honor itself, he finds honor for himself. (PB 19.8.2). Its *pavamāna* chants consist of twenty-four syllables; the *gāyatrī* has twenty-four syllables. The *gāyatrī* is brilliance and spiritual luster. Through brilliance and spiritual luster, he finds honor for himself.
(19.8.3) Both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara [Sāmans] are employed; by means of both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara, he obtains honor for himself.
(19.8.4) There are both *bhargas* and *yaśas*; by means of *bhargas*, he bestows *bhargas* upon him, and by means of *yaśas*, he bestows *yaśas*.
(19.8.5) There are both types of *stomas*, those with even numbers and those with odd numbers; by means of both types of *stomas*, he obtains honor for himself.
Regarding this they say: "The *stomas* are contrary; they are liable to scatter the sacrificer, for they pass beyond him.
(PB 19.8.7) There is an *agniṣṭoma* consisting of the twenty-onefold [stoma]. The twenty-onefold is indeed a foundation; thus he finds firm support at the very end of the sacrifice.
(PB 19.9.1) Now, this is the *sarvastoma*; one who desires honor should sacrifice with it. Verily, by means of all the *stomas*, he obtains honor for himself.
(19.9.2) He attains the Virāj; for he who eats food is indeed honored, and the Virāj is food. Thus, he bestows food-eating upon him.

(19.9.3) Both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara [Sāmans] are used; they become splendor and glory. There are both types of Stomas—the Chandomas and the Pṛṣṭhyas. By means of both these Stomas, he obtains honor for himself.

(19.9.4) His Chandomas are the Pṛṣṭhas; the Chandomas are indeed cattle, and the Pṛṣṭhas are food. Thus, he places food and cattle before him in succession. In that it possesses Chandomas, it belongs to one who performs the twelve-day sacrifice.

Regarding this they say: "The *stomas* and the *chandomas* have different worlds, as do the *pṛṣṭhas*; if they were all encompassed within a single sacrificial rite (*yajñakratu*), the sacrificer would be liable to lose his firm foundation.
(PB 19.9.6) There is an *ekaviṃśa* *agniṣṭoma*; the *ekaviṃśa* is indeed a firm foundation. Thus, they attain a firm foundation.
This *stoma* is indeed winged; it is deposited as something winged.
For one without wings does not reach a winged creature; and because this winged thing is deposited upon that which is unwinged, therefore winged creatures fly with their wings.
The winged one, full of light, traverses the auspicious worlds—he who knows thus.

There are two *trivṛt* [stomas] on both sides; *trivṛt* is splendor and holy luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Verily, he secures splendor and holy luster. Then there are two *pañcadaśa* [stomas]; the *pañcadaśa* is indeed vigor. Verily, he secures vigor.

(PB 19.10.7) Now, there are two [stotras] of seventeen; the seventeenfold is indeed cattle; verily, he wins cattle. (PB 19.10.8) Now, there are two of twenty-one; the twenty-onefold is indeed a foundation; verily, he finds support in the very center of the sacrifice. (PB 19.10.9) Now, there are two of twenty-three; these worlds are indeed the twenty-threefold; verily, he finds support in these very worlds.
(10) Now follows the thirty-third [stoma]. The thirty-third is indeed the summit. (11) He who knows thus becomes the summit among his own people.
(12) This, indeed, is the summit of the sun: that these two thirty-third [stomas] are joined together in the middle; by that he ascends to the summit of the sun.
Agni is indeed the most excellent in the middle; therefore, these *stomas* are performed as the most excellent in the middle.
By means of the *trivṛt*, one goes forth; by means of the *trivṛt*, one rises up. The *trivṛt* is indeed breath; verily, by means of breath one goes forth, and toward breath one rises up.
Now, this is the *jyotis*.
Its *bahiṣpavamāna* is the *trivṛt*; the *ājya* stotras are the *pañcadaśa*; the midday *pavamāna* is the *caturviṃśa*; and the *pṛṣṭha* stotras are the *saptadaśa*.
The *trivṛt* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the *pañcadaśa* is the self (*ātman*). The *gāyatrī* is the mouth, and the *saptadaśa* is food; thus, he places food in the very mouth.
(19.11.5) He who knows thus eats food and becomes an eater of food.

(19.11.6) By means of the midday *pavamāna*, the gods went to the heavenly world; in that this twenty-fourfold midday *pavamāna* exists, it is for the conquest of the heavenly world, for the *gāyatrī* consists of twenty-four syllables.
The Gāyatrī is splendor and holy luster; verily, he obtains splendor and holy luster. The Gāyatrī is breath, and procreation comes from breath;
verily, through the Gāyatrī he is procreated.
Both types of *stomas*—those with even numbers and those with odd numbers—constitute a pair; from that pair he is procreated.
(19.11.8) This metre is indeed winged; he who knows this becomes winged, luminous, and traverses the auspicious worlds.

(19.11.9) Fire is indeed the most excellent in the middle; therefore, these *stomas* are made most excellent in the middle. (19.11.10) One [verse] remains over from those that have been praised together as the *virāj*; thus he makes him alone the overseer of food.
(19.11.11) This Agniṣṭoma is indeed light; he who, knowing this, performs this sacrifice, wins a radiant and auspicious world.
(19.12.1) Now follows this "Bull" [sacrifice].
(19.12.2) He who knows this attains the state of being a bull among the Stomas.
One should cause a Rājanya to sacrifice. The bull is indeed the lord of cattle, and the Rājanya is the lord of men;
he who exists is the lord. He who knows thus becomes the lord of his equals.

(PB 19.12.6) For him, there is a *sadoviśīya* at the midday *pavamāna*. Verily, he encompasses the people for him by means of the two pressings; the people do not depart from him. (PB 19.12.7) It is performed all around; verily, he makes the people all-around for him; the people do not depart from him. (PB 19.12.8) Both the *bṛhat* and the *rathaṃtara* are used. The *rathaṃtara* is indeed this [earth], and the *bṛhat* is yonder [sky]. By means of the *gāyatrī*, he finds firm support in both these worlds.

The Bṛhat-sāman occurs in the Anuṣṭubh metre. The Anuṣṭubh is the end of the metres, the Bṛhat is the end of the Sāmans, and the Rājanya is the end of men. Thus he establishes the end upon the end; therefore, he who falls away from the rank of the Rājanyas does not reach the summit again.
That which is indeed the Vājapeya is the Rājasūya; that which is the Rājasūya is the Varuṇasava. Now, this Gosava is a sacrifice of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*).
He who knows thus attains self-sovereignty.
For Prajāpati is self-sovereignty, and Parameṣṭhin is self-sovereignty.
He who knows thus attains the state of the Supreme Lord (parameṣṭhitā).
Both the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are employed; for that is self-sovereignty (svārājya). He who knows thus attains self-sovereignty.
Ten thousand [cows] are the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā); for that is self-sovereignty. He who knows thus attains self-sovereignty.
(19.13.7) He is consecrated with the *pratiduh* [milk]; for that is self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). He who knows thus goes to self-sovereignty.
(19.13.8) He is consecrated at the *stotra* of the *Bṛhat*; for that is self-sovereignty. He who knows thus goes to self-sovereignty.
(19.13.9) He is consecrated on the south side of the *Āhavanīya* fire, on the unexcavated [ground], upon this very earth without any intervening space.

The whole [sacrifice] consists of thirty-six [verses]; therefore it is the Gosava. Now follows this Marut-stoma. By means of this, indeed, the Maruts attained unlimited prosperity; he who knows thus attains unlimited prosperity. Because the stomas are arranged in groups, it is the Marut-stoma, for the Maruts are indeed arranged in groups.
(19.14.3) With this very [rite] one should cause three [persons] to sacrifice.

(19.14.4) In that there are three *trivṛt* stotras, they become established separately in spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*). (19.14.5) In that there are three *pañcadaśa* [stotras], [they become established] separately in vigor (*vīrya*).
When there are three *saptadaśa* stomas at different animal sacrifices, and when there are three *ekaviṃśa* stomas, they find firm support;
he who knows thus finds firm support.

Now, this is the *kulāya* sacrifice for Indra and Agni; one who desires offspring or one who desires cattle should perform it. Offspring indeed are the *kulāya*, cattle are the *kulāya*, and houses are the *kulāya*; he truly becomes the *kulāya*.
One should cause two [persons] to sacrifice with this very rite. In that there are six *trivṛt* stotras, they both become firmly established in distinct spiritual splendor (*brahmavarcasa*).

In that two fifteen-fold [stomas] of different powers, and two seventeen-fold [stomas] of different cattle, and two twenty-one-fold [stomas], they find firm support; he who knows thus finds firm support. Now this is the fifteen-fold Indra-stoma Ukthya.
(19.16.2) By means of this, indeed, Indra surpassed all other deities; he who knows thus surpasses all other beings. (19.16.3) One should cause a Kṣatriya to sacrifice with this.
(19.16.4) Everything becomes fifteenfold; the fifteenfold [stoma] is force and vigor; verily, by means of force and vigor, he causes him to prosper.

They are performed with verses addressed to Indra; verily, he endows him with power and vigor. It is an Ukthya sacrifice; the Ukthas are cattle, and the Ukthas are the people; verily, he yokes the people and cattle to him, so that the people do not depart from him.
There are fifteen Stotras, each consisting of fifteen verses; the fifteenfold is vigor and strength; verily, he places vigor and strength in him in due order.
(PB 19.17.1) Now this is the *stoma* of Indra and Agni. By means of this, indeed, Indra and Agni surpassed all other deities; he who knows thus surpasses all other offspring.
(PB 19.17.2) It consists of the *trivṛt* and the *pañcadaśa*.
(PB 19.17.3) The *trivṛt* is indeed the *brahman*, and the *pañcadaśa* is the *kṣatra*. For him who knows thus, there is manifestation both as the *brahman* and as the *kṣatra*.

The king and the domestic priest should perform the sacrifice; thus the Gāyatrī and the Jagatī are brought together. Through the Gāyatrī, the Brāhmaṇa obtains splendor and Vedic luster; through the Jagatī, the king enters among the people.
(19.17.7) One who desires the office of domestic priest (*purodhā*) should sacrifice.

(19.17.8) Bṛhaspati desired, "May I attain the office of domestic priest among the gods. He sacrificed with this [rite], and he attained the office of domestic priest among the gods. Whoever knows thus attains the office of domestic priest.
(19.18.1) Now follows this *vighana* [sacrifice].
Indra desired, "May I strike away my wicked rival. He saw this *vighana* (striking-away) [stotra]; with it, he struck away his wicked rival.
He who knows thus strikes away his wicked rival. In that it is threefold (*trivṛt*), by that he wins the vital breaths; in that it is twelvefold, by that [he wins] the year.
In that it is the fifteenfold, it is by means of that vigor; in that it is the seventeenfold, it is by means of that food-eating; in that it is the twenty-onefold, it is by means of that foundation;

in that it is the nineteenfold, it is by means of that procreation; in that it is the twenty-fourfold, it is by means of that spiritual luster; and in that it is the twenty-sevenfold, he hurls the thunderbolt at his rival.

(19.18.4) One who desires cattle should sacrifice; it becomes a *bṛhatī*. The *bṛhatī* is indeed cattle; verily, he wins cattle. (19.18.5) These six *bṛhatīs* come to be; the year has six seasons. Cattle are born in accordance with the year; having reached them, he wins them. (19.19.1) The godless *māyās* assailed Indra. He ran to Prajāpati for help; he gave him this *vighana* (the shatterer). With it, he shattered all his adversaries. That which he shattered—[that became...]
(19.19.2) He who, knowing this, sacrifices with the Vighana [stotra], and he whom one, knowing this, causes to sacrifice with the Vighana—[he] overcomes all adversaries.
(19.19.3) One desiring cattle should sacrifice; the Bṛhatī is indeed cattle; verily, he finds firm support in cattle.
(20.1.1) The Bahiṣpavamāna is threefold; the Ājya-stotras are fifteenfold; the Mādhyandina-pavamāna is fifteenfold.

There are seventeen *pṛṣṭha* chants, seventeen *ārbhava* chants, a twenty-one-fold *agniṣṭoma*, an *ukthya* with fifteen-fold chants for the night, and a threefold *sandhi*. One desiring prosperity should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma-atirātra*; this is indeed the advance among the *stomas*, for by advancing one prospers through the sacrifice. This is the *agniṣṭoma*, this is the *ukthya*, this is the *atirātra*. By means of the *agniṣṭoma*, the gods conquered this world; by the *ukthyas*, the intermediate space; and by the night, they conquered that world; [thus] by day and night.

(20.1.4) Some dawns shine away [from us], others shine toward us; this one indeed shines toward us, she who shines with the Āśvina [laud]. He causes the dawns to shine toward him alone. (20.1.5) Two of the *saṃstuta* verses exceed the *virāj* meter. This is the "breast-bearing" *virāj*; whatever desire he may desire, he milks that from it.
(20.1.6) He goes forth by means of the *trivṛt*, he rises by means of the *trivṛt*. The *trivṛt* is indeed breath; verily by means of breath he goes forth, and he rises toward breath.
The *bahiṣpavamāna* is threefold; the *ājya* stotras are fifteenfold; the midday *pavamāna* is seventeenfold;
the *pṛṣṭha* stotras are twenty-onefold; the *ārbhava* is twenty-ninefold; the *agniṣṭoma* is thirty-threefold;

the *uktha* stotras descend in order, with the first being twenty-ninefold, followed by two twenty-onefold stotras accompanied by the *ṣoḍaśin*, and the night-stotra is fifteenfold; the *sandhi* is threefold.

(PB 20.2.2) One desiring prosperity should sacrifice with the *sarvastoma* *atirātra*; for the attainment of all, for the conquest of all—by this very rite he attains all and conquers all. (PB 20.2.3) In that the *bahiṣpavamāna* is threefold (*trivṛt*), he thereby attains the threefold *stoma* and the *gāyatrī* metre;
in that the *ājya* chants are fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*), he thereby attains the fifteenfold *stoma* and the *triṣṭubh* metre. In that...

The Mādhyandina Pavamāna is seventeenfold; thus he obtains the seventeenfold Stoma and the Jagatī metre. As for the Pṛṣṭhas being twenty-onefold, he thereby obtains the twenty-onefold Stoma and the Anuṣṭubh metre. As for the Ārbhava being twenty-sevenfold, he thereby obtains the twenty-sevenfold Stoma and the Paṅkti metre. As for the Agniṣṭoma being thirty-threefold, he thereby obtains the thirty-threefold [Stoma].
He obtains the *stoma* and the *virāj* metre; in that the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* are performed, he thereby obtains the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh*;

in that the *āśvina* [śastra] is recited, he obtains all this by means of it and conquers all (PB 20.2.4). The thirty-three-fold [stoma] indeed bends the sacrifice forward; the Adhvaryu [protects] it from the front with the set of eleven victims.

He raises up eleven cords; there are eleven animals and eleven sacrificial posts. Thus, upon the thirty-threefold [altar], he establishes the thirty-threefold. By means of that night thus raised up, whatever desire he desires, that he attains; whatever desire he desires, that he attains—he who knows thus.

The *bahiṣpavamāna* is threefold; the *ājya* stotras are fifteenfold; the midday *pavamāna* is seventeenfold; the *hotṛ*'s *pṛṣṭha* is twenty-onefold; the other [stotras] are the *chandomas*; the *ārbhava* is twenty-sevenfold; the *agniṣṭoma* is thirty-threefold;
the *uktha* stotras descend in order—the first is twenty-sevenfold, then twenty-onefold, then seventeenfold; [the final *agniṣṭoma*] is twenty-onefold.
The sixteenth [stoma] is the fifteenth night; the junction is the *trivṛt*; the first *atirikta-stotra* is the *trivṛt*, then the *pañcadaśa*, then the *saptadaśa*, and then the *ekaviṃśa*.
Prajāpati created cattle; once created, they departed from him; he did not obtain them by means of the *agniṣṭoma*.

He did not reach them with the *uktha* hymns; he did not reach them with the *ṣoḍaśin*; he did not reach them with the night; he did not reach them with the twilight; he did not reach them with the *āśvina* cup. He said to Agni, "Do you seek these for me. Agni did not reach them with the *trivṛt* stoma and the *jarābodhīya* sāman. He said to Indra, "Do you seek these for me. Indra [reached them] with the fifteenfold (*pañcadaśa*) stoma and the *sattrāsāhīya* [sāman].

He did not obtain them with the *sāman*. He said to the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*): "May you desire these for me. The All-gods did not obtain them with the seventeenfold hymn-form (*stoma*) and the *mārgīyava* *sāman*. He said to Viṣṇu: "May you desire these for me. Viṣṇu obtained them with the twenty-onefold hymn-form; he warded them off with the *vāravantīya*, and he strode across this [world] with [the verse]: "Viṣṇu strode across this."
(20.3.3) Because cattle might indeed fall away from him, he should sacrifice with this [rite].
(20.3.4) By means of this, indeed, the gods, having won all victories, attained whatever desire they desired; whatever desire one desires, that one attains by means of this.
(20.3.5) That is the reason for the Aptoryāman’s name as "Aptoryāman."

The *bahiṣpavamāna* is threefold; the *ājya* of the Hotṛ is fifteenfold; the stotras are ninefold and seventeenfold; the *agniṣṭoma* is twenty-onefold; it includes the *ukthas*; the night consists of fifteenfold [stotras]; the junction (*sandhi*) is threefold.

(PB 20.4.2) One desiring offspring should sacrifice with the *atirātra* consisting of ninefold and seventeenfold [stotras]. Nine indeed are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and Prajāpati is seventeenfold. From the vital breaths, therefore, and from Prajāpati, offspring are born. (PB 20.4.3) He raises the *kakubh* [verse] toward the east. The *kakubh* is indeed the person (*puruṣa*); this embryo is placed in the middle.
Upon that [day], the Sākamaśva [is performed].
Prajāpati created offspring; they did not multiply. He saw this Sāman; having become a horse, he sniffed at them, and they multiplied. This Sāman is indeed procreation.
He who knows thus is procreated and becomes many.

(20.4.7) He makes the Kakubhs among the two-footed verses in this world; he thus produces the embryo in the middle for its own benefit. (20.4.8) There is an Atirātra; indeed, offspring are produced following day and night; verily, following day and night, he is produced with offspring and cattle.
(20.5.1) The Bahiṣpavamāna is Trivṛt; the Ājya-stotras are Pañcadaśa; the Mādhyandina Pavamāna is Pañcadaśa.

There are seventeen *pṛṣṭha* stotras, seventeen *ārbhava* stotras, the *agniṣṭoma* is twenty-one-fold, the *uktha* stotras are seventeen-fold, the night-stotra is fifteen-fold, and the junction-stotra is three-fold.
With the *viṣuvat* *atirātra*, one should cause the eldest son of the eldest wife to sacrifice; for this *viṣuvat* is indeed the foremost among the *stomas*.
It indeed becomes the equinox when there is one twenty-one-fold [stoma]; for from here that sun is twenty-one-fold:
twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and that sun is the twenty-first; thus he causes him to reach the measure of the sun itself.
(20.5.4) This one indeed rises; no other light among lights rises against him. (20.5.5) No other rises against him among his own kinsmen, for one who knows thus.
(20.6.1) The *bahiṣpavamāna* is fifteenfold, the *ājya* stotras are threefold, and the midday pressing is seventeenfold.

The third pressing has twenty-one stomas; it is a *soktha* sacrifice with a fifteen-fold (*pañcadaśī*) night and a threefold (*trivṛt*) junction. One who has rivals should sacrifice with the *goṣṭoma-atirātra*. By means of the cow, the gods drove the Asuras away from these worlds; by means of the night, they conquered what was unconquerable.
Having driven his rival away from these worlds, he conquers what is unconquerable by means of the night.
The *bahiṣpavamāna* is threefold; the *ājya* stotras are fifteenfold; the midday pressing is seventeenfold;
the third pressing is twenty-onefold together with the *uktha* stotras; the night consists of fifteenfold stotras; the *sandhi* is threefold.
One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *āyuṣṭoma-atirātra*. The *stomas* proceed upwards for the sake of non-decline; that it is an *atirātra* is for the sake of day and night.
Thus one goes to the heavenly world. The *bahiṣpavamāna* is the *trivṛt*; the *ājya* of the Hotṛ is the *pañcadaśa*; that of the Maitrāvaruṇa is the *saptadaśa*;
that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin is the *pañcadaśa*; that of the Acchāvāka is the *saptadaśa*; and the midday *pavamāna* is the *ekaviṃśa*.

The *pṛṣṭha* chant of the Hotṛ is the seventeenfold; that of the Maitrāvaruṇa is the twenty-onefold; that of the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin is the twenty-sevenfold; and that of the Acchāvāka is the twenty-onefold.
The *ārbhava* is the twenty-sevenfold, and the *agniṣṭoma* is the thirty-threefold. The *uktha* chants descend in order:
the first is the twenty-sevenfold, followed by two twenty-onefolds including the *ṣoḍaśin*, and the night-chant is fifteenfold. The *sandhi* is ninefold; [this is] with the *abhijit* atirātra.
One who has rivals should sacrifice with the Abhijit. By means of the Abhijit, the gods conquered these worlds from the Asuras; they conquered that which could not be conquered by night.
Having conquered his rival through the Abhijit, he conquers these worlds, having won that which cannot be won back by night.
The Bahiṣpavamāna is threefold; the Hotṛ’s Ājya-stotra is fifteenfold; the Maitrāvaruṇa’s is seventeenfold; the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s is twenty-onefold.

The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s [stotra] is the fifteenfold; the Acchāvāka’s is the seventeenfold; the Mādhyandina Pavamāna is the twenty-onefold; the Hotṛ’s Pṛṣṭha is the twenty-sevenfold; the Maitrāvaruṇa’s is the seventeenfold;
the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s is the twenty-onefold; and the Acchāvāka’s Ārbhava is the twenty-sevenfold.

The Agniṣṭoma has thirty-three [stomas]; the Ukthas descend: the first is twenty-seven-fold, the next two are twenty-one-fold with the Ṣoḍaśin, and the night [laud] is fifteen-fold; the junction is threefold. One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Viśvajit Atirātra.
For the Nābhānediṣṭha is seed, and the Vālakhilyas are cattle; since the Nābhānediṣṭha comes first.
The Vālakhilyās are praised as superior; from that seed, cattle are produced. He transforms forms when [he uses] the Vārṣākapa;
he becomes established in the seasons when [he uses] the Evayāmarut.
One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should sacrifice with the *trivṛt* at the *atirātra*; the *trivṛt* is indeed splendor (*tejas*), and spiritual luster is splendor.

He wins splendor and sacred luster; he finds firm standing in splendor and sacred luster. One desiring vigor should sacrifice with the fifteen-fold Atirātra; the fifteen-fold is vigor and strength; verily he wins vigor and strength, and finds firm standing in vigor and strength.
One desiring food should sacrifice with the seventeen-fold Atirātra; the seventeen-fold is indeed food; verily he wins food. [One should sacrifice] with the twenty-one-fold Atirātra.
One who desires a firm foundation should sacrifice; for the twenty-one-fold [stoma] is indeed a firm foundation. In that there is an Atirātra, he finds a firm foundation in both day and night.

The first day is the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma, and the second day is an Atirātra consisting of all the stomas. Its Bahiṣpavamāna is the twenty-four-fold, the Ājya-stotras are fifteen-fold, and the Mādhyandina-pavamāna is seventeen-fold.
The Pavamāna stotras consist of the twenty-one-fold chants; the Pṛṣṭhas are the twenty-seven-fold; the Ārbhava is the thirty-three-fold; the Agniṣṭoma is the same;

the Ukthas descend in order, with the twenty-seven-fold first, then the twenty-one-fold, and then the seventeen-fold; the Ṣoḍaśī is twenty-one-fold; the Night-stotra is fifteen-fold; and the Sandhi is threefold.

The Aṅgirases went to the heavenly world. Of them, Haviṣmān and Haviṣkṛt, both belonging to the lineage of the Aṅgirases, were left behind. They arrived at the very place from which the Aṅgirases had gone to the heavenly world; there they performed austerities and perceived these two *sāmans*. With them, they performed a two-night sacrifice (*dvirātra*) and thereby went to the heavenly world.

(PB 20.11.4) He who is of the lineage of Puṇya, as if deficient, should sacrifice with this; he attains the preeminence of his ancestors, for those two Aṅgirasas attained it. (PB 20.11.5) One desiring offspring should sacrifice, for offspring is indeed the second.

(PB 20.11.6) One desiring heaven should sacrifice, for from the second world one must advance toward the world beyond. "The Dvirātra is difficult to accomplish," they say, in that the first day is an Agniṣṭoma and [the second] is an Ukthya.
"If the Ukthya does not follow the Agniṣṭoma" (PB 20.11.7);
"When the Jyotir Ukthya is the preceding day, they do not omit the Agniṣṭoma, nor do they omit the Ukthya-stotras" (PB 20.11.8).
Regarding this, they say: "This indeed is the measure of the sacrifice, namely the Agniṣṭoma; when the Agniṣṭoma is the preceding [day]..."
The day does not exceed the measure of the sacrifice; then they proceed from the *ukthas* of the following day to the night. Thus the *ukthas* are not omitted.
The *bahiṣpavamāna* of the following day consists of twenty-four verses; the *gāyatrī* has twenty-four syllables, and the *gāyatrī* is procreation—[this serves] for the sake of generation.
(20.11.10) Both types of *stomas*, those with an even number and those with an odd number, constitute a pair; from that pairing, offspring is produced.

(20.11.11) There is an *atirātra* sacrifice consisting of all *stomas*, for the attainment of everything and for the conquest of everything; by means of this, one attains everything and conquers everything.
(20.12.1) Now, for him whose first day is the *jyotis-ukthya* and whose subsequent day is the *āyus-atirātra*...
Three *virāj* verses remain over from the first day; the second day is deficient by two *virāj* verses. From this deficiency and surplus, offspring are born.
He who knows thus is propagated with offspring and cattle. One *virāj* verse remains over from those that have been chanted together; he makes him alone the overseer of food.

By means of this [rite], the Kāpeyas indeed caused Citraratha to sacrifice; they made him the sole overseer of food. Therefore, among the Caitrarathas, one is born as the lord of the kṣatriyas, while another is like a mere appendage. Now, for whomsoever the Trivṛt Pañcadaśa Agniṣṭoma is the first day and the Āyus Atirātra is the subsequent day—
By means of two paired *stomas*, they generate the subsequent day; that which has been generated, they undertake on the following day.
These two, the *trivṛt* and the *pañcadaśa* *stomas*, are indeed the two wheels that turn together. Whatever desire one desires, one attains it by means of this;
for wherever one desires with something that has wheels, there one attains it.
Now, as for the fact that the Atirātra is the Āyus: it is for the sake of firm foundation.
By means of this very sacrifice, Kapivana Bhauvāyana, having sacrificed, attained freedom from harshness.
He who, knowing thus, sacrifices with this [rite] becomes free from harshness.
The morning pressing is the *trivṛt*, the midday pressing is the *pañcadaśa*, and the third pressing is the *saptadaśa*.
The morning pressing is the *pañcadaśa*, the midday pressing is the *saptadaśa*, and the third pressing is the *ekaviṃśa*; that [third pressing] is with the *uktha* hymns.
The morning pressing is the *ekaviṃśa*, the midday pressing is the *triṇava*, and the *ārbhava* [pressing] is the *trayastriṃśa*.

The Agniṣṭoma has thirty-four stomas; the Ukthya-stotras have the twenty-one-fold stoma along with the Ṣoḍaśin; the first night-chant is the sixteen-fold stoma, the second night is the fifteen-fold stoma, and the junction is the nine-fold stoma.
(PB 20.14.2) Prajāpati was indeed this [universe] alone. Speech alone was his own property, speech as his second. He reflected upon her.

"Release speech, for this speech shall go forth pervading all this. He released speech; it went forth pervading all this. It rose upward like a continuous stream of water; thus its movement proceeded. He cut off a third part; that became the earth (*bhūmi*). "It has become (*abhūt*)," as it were—this is why the earth is called *bhūmi*. "Where (*kva*) is the third? he asked. That is the third.

He cut it; that became the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Because [he thought], "Truly, this is within," that is the *antarikṣatva* of the intermediate space. He threw the third part upward with the sound "Ho!"; that became the sky (*dyau*). Because it shone forth as it were, that is the *divatva* of the sky. This indeed is speech manifest: that which one speaks with the tip of the tongue, that is what one speaks of speech when [it says] "eti"; that which one speaks with the middle, that is what one speaks of speech when [it says] "keti. The essence of speech rises upward entirely.
"Upwards indeed [it goes], when it has been bound," [so it is said].
When these forms are manifested day by day, they release speech from the very beginning, and from the very beginning the sacrificial rite.
Prajāpati, indeed, having this speech consisting of a single syllable, divided it threefold; these are the worlds.

They became rough and uninhabitable. He considered: "How might these worlds take root? How might they become habitable? He saw this three-night rite; he performed it, and by means of it, he caused these worlds to take root. Therefore, these worlds took root, and therefore they became habitable. This abundance belongs to the three-night rite; it is the extraction of the three-night rite.

That which goes over these worlds—[he attains] the abundance of cattle, both bipeds and quadrupeds—he who knows thus. When Prajāpati emitted speech, it flowed forth; [thus] the first [verse] is established, the second.

The *ṛc* is the third; in whatever form Prajāpati emitted speech, in that very form the *ājya* chants are undertaken and the days are concluded. Regarding this, the exponents of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinaḥ*) say: "The three-night rite (*trirātra*) is indeed established upon the syllable (*akṣara-stha*). For speech consists of one syllable, while the syllable consists of three syllables; the person (*puruṣa*) consists of three syllables. "He indeed knows him," they say.
"He who knows this as measured by man" (PB 20.15.1).
By means of this, indeed, the gods prospered in these worlds; by means of this, they went to the heavenly world (PB 20.15.2).
Speech, indeed, is the three-night rite; in the form of speech, the *ājya* chants and the days are distributed. It is indeed monosyllabic...
Speech consists of three syllables; by means of the imperishable, they are divided into three forms of the imperishable. There are three Gandharvas; their distribution is as follows:
the earth belongs to Agni, the intermediate space to Vāyu, and the sky to yonder Āditya. There are three heats that attend the Dawn:
Agni attends the Dawn, Vāyu attends the Dawn, and yonder Āditya attends the Dawn.
(20.15.4) There are three pairs; this one [is] those. (20.15.5) Two become a pair; that which is born from the pair is the third.
(20.15.6) Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra; he said, "Do not strike me! This [which is here] exists."

"I shall give you that vigor within me," he said, and he gave it to him; Viṣṇu accepted it. He raised his arm a second time, and a third time. He (Prajāpati) spoke thus: "Do not strike me! Indeed, this vigor is in me; I shall give it to you.
He gave it to him, and Viṣṇu accepted it. This very thing is recited after that speech.

(20.15.7) "Both of you have conquered; you two are not defeated. Neither of these two has been defeated. O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you two contended, you bestowed a thousandfold [portion] in three ways.
(20.15.8) It was this very thing that he granted to them as that thousand.

(PB 20.15.9) His portion is this: it should be given on the first day to one who is an *ārṣeya* and learned; for as is this [earth], so is he—this [earth] being firmly established, he too is firmly established.

(PB 20.15.10) It should be given on the second day to one who is not an *ārṣeya* but is learned; for as is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), so is he. They know him as "the intermediate space," for they know the Veda as the intermediate space. (PB 20.15.11) It should be given on the third day to one who is an *ārṣeya* and learned; for as is the sky (*dyau*), so is he. They know him as "the sky," for they know his kinship.

(Hundreds are given every day; this indeed is the measure of the sacrifice, namely a hundred. That very [hundred] is given unbrokenly. Tens are given every day; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the sacrifice is of the nature of the Virāj. That very [Virāj] is given unbrokenly. Three hundred and thirty-three should be given on the first day, likewise on the second, and likewise on the third.
Now this [verse] addressed to two deities has three forms: two thirds belong to the Brahman and one third to the Agnīdh.

(PB 20.15.15) "Thou art desirable, thou art beloved, thou art worthy of oblation; I praise thee, O delighting Sarasvatī, great and far-famed! These are thy names, O inviolable one; announce us among the gods as doers of good deeds.

(PB 20.16.1) By the first day, he indeed differentiated that which is here upon this earth; by the second, that which is here, the root; by the third, that which moves from the breath and that which rains there above.
"When the constellations reached that world" (PB 20.16.2).

Regarding this, the exponents of sacred knowledge say: "This three-night rite is indeed the Mahāvrata. Of that [Mahāvrata], the Bahiṣpavamāna-stotra of these days is its very mouth; the two days on either side are its wings; and that which is in the middle is its body.

The day is the self, the *agniṣṭoma* chants are the tail. That which rises is the face; the two days on either side are the wings; that which is the middle day is the self, the fire is the tail. That which rises is the face; the two days on either side are the wings; that which is the middle day is the self; that which sets is the tail.

(20.16.5) This three-night rite is indeed as much as this: the Gāyatrī is breath, the Triṣṭubh is sight, and the Jagatī is hearing. He who knows thus attains a full lifespan. (20.16.6) Regarding this, the exponents of sacred knowledge say: "How great is the three-night rite? One should reply: "As much as this," for it is indeed as much as this; or one should reply: "As much as this," for it is indeed as much as this. They say: "Is it turned away or turned hither? One should reply: "It is turned away."

"For he speaks away, he sees away, he breathes away—'one, two, three,' so they say; one should say, 'one,' for this breath is the same, whether it be out-breathing, in-breathing, or diffused breathing. Just as a thread is woven through a gem, even so is the three-night rite woven through these worlds. The face of one who knows this shines."

Whatever in the three-night sacrifice is concordant (*saloma*), that is its discordant (*viloma*) aspect; whatever in it is discordant, that is its concordant aspect. When this later day is made earlier, it thereby secures cattle for the sacrificer for the sake of procreation, for cattle are not born in yonder world.
(20.16.8) These two indeed are the most powerful of the meters, namely the Gāyatrī and the Triṣṭubh.
Since these two are on both sides and the Jagatī is in the middle, he thereby encloses the cattle with those two powerful meters for the sake of procreation;
for cattle are not born in yonder world.

(20.16.9) This three-night rite is indeed like that [sun]: as it rises, so is the first day; as at midday, so is the second; as it sets, so is the third. He who knows this goes to union with that [sun], he goes to its very essence.
(21.1.1) Indra conquered a thousand Maruts after announcing it to King Soma; therefore, one should announce it to the king.

Having said, "The two of them conquer twenty," Yama heard that the Maruts had won a thousand. He went there and said, "Invite me to share in this thousand. They invited him. Then Yama saw a one-limbed cow, who, though among a thousand, was bearing the milk of a thousand. He said, "Let this one be mine; you two have the thousand."
"Let us divide [it]," they said. "Just as you see this, so do we two see it," they replied.
"With her indeed let us divide this thousand," they said; they caused her to enter into the water.
They said, "We will not bring our portions, for she will go first to whomever she chooses. Then they brought their portions.
"First [the milk] belonged to Soma, then to Indra, and then to Yama" (PB 21.1.3).

They said, "Rise up for King Soma with a third of yourself and a third of the thousandfold milk. She, a brown cow with reddish-brown eyes and one year old, rose up with a third of herself and a third of the thousandfold milk.
That which is the cow for purchasing the Soma is indeed that very milk;
by one-third of her body and by one-third of a thousand [cows] of milk, the Soma becomes purchased for him who, knowing thus, purchases the Soma, and for whomsoever he who knows thus [purchases it].
They said, "Go forth to Indra with one-third of yourself and with one-third of a thousand [cows] of milk."

Thus that brindled six-year-old cow arose with a third of her own self and a third of a thousand [cows] of milk; she was the one desired for power (*indriyaiṣyā*). She herself is that very same [cow].
A third of her own self and a third of a thousand [cows] of milk, as the one desired for power, is given to him who, knowing thus, gives the one desired for power to whomever [he intends].
[The gods] gave [her] to the learned man who desired the sense-organs. They said, "Bring her for Yama with a third of yourself and a third of the thousandfold milk.
She came as an old, spotted, hornless cow, or perhaps a smoky-colored Dityauhī; she was smaller by a third of herself.

And by the third [thousand], that very one becomes the cow for immolation (*anustaraṇī*). Thus, for him who, knowing this, performs the immolation, or for whom others perform the immolation while they know this, the immolation is performed with a third part of his own self and a third part of a thousand cows; he does not think, "They have not performed it."
Regarding this, the exponents of sacred knowledge say: "In that world, there is no space for one who does not sacrifice a thousand.

As far as a cow from this world is established within a thousand cows, so far is that world from this world. Indeed, the performer of the *sahasrayajña* pervades these worlds; furthermore, as far as a thousand *yojanas*, and furthermore, as far as a thousand horse-riders, and furthermore, as far as...
"A thousand days—he thereby ransoms [him] cow by cow. These are given for the purpose of stepping upon [the altar].
Since he created a thousand, the *tārpya* garment was its womb; that he leads [the victim] while casting it upon the *tārpya* is for the sake of providing a womb.
