"Prajāpati created offspring. Once created, they went away from him, thinking, 'He will not eat us.'"
Being afraid, they said to him, "Submit to us; we will eat you in such a way that, while being eaten, you will propagate even more.
They said to him, "Speak the Truth to us. To them he spoke the Truth with the *ṛtanidhana*;
he consumed them with the *īnidhana*, and he caused them to propagate with the *triṇidhana*. Indeed, by means of these Sāmans, Death both eats and propagates these creatures here.
(21.2.2) For one who knows thus, there is more even as he is being consumed.
(21.2.3) These are indeed the Jyeṣṭha-sāmans, the Śreṣṭha-sāmans, the Prajāpati-sāmans. (21.2.4) He who knows thus attains preeminence and excellence.

By means of these Sāmans, Prajāpati milked all these worlds and all desires. Because he milked them by means of the *āci*, that is the reason for the *āci-doha* of the milkings; hence the name *āci-doha*. He who, knowing this, praises with these Sāmans, milks all these worlds and all desires.
These worlds indeed are these Sāmans: this [earth] is the one with the *ṛtanidhana*, the intermediate space is the one with the *īnidhana*, and the sky is the one with the *triṇidhana*.

(21.2.8) Just as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) moves through the fields, so does he who knows this move through these worlds. (21.2.9) These are indeed the Sāmans of Agni Vaiśvānara; wherever they chant with these [Sāmans] while they are not yet appeased, there the deity becomes a slayer of offspring. They chant after having placed the fire nearby, for the sake of beholding their own deity in its likeness.
Having paid homage, he sings aloud; they praise with peaceful hymns.
Śabalī is indeed Speech; her calf is the three-night rite. He causes this [cow] to yield milk for the three-night rite. Thus, for one who knows this, she, being bestowed, yields milk.
(21.3.3) He who, being capable of eating food, nevertheless does not eat food—
(21.3.4) having put on a mat, drinking hot [milk], he should sleep on the ground for twelve nights.
(21.3.5) On the twelfth night, at the break of dawn, having offered the Śabalī-homa before the voices of men have begun to sound, [he should perform the rite].

Having gone to a forest where one cannot hear the cry of a domestic animal, and having touched a clump of darbha grass, he should call out three times, "Śabalī, Śabalī! If something other than a dog or a donkey responds, that is successful. If nothing responds, he should call again after a year.

(21.3.7) Śabalī! You are the ocean, all-pervading; you are the Brahman, the first-born of the gods; you are the food of the *ṛta*. You are the bright, you are the brilliance, you are the immortal. We know you as such, O Śabalī, shining forth. Of you, the earth is one foot, the intermediate space is one foot, the sky is one foot, and the ocean is one foot. Such are you, O Śabalī; we know you as such. May you grant us food and strength.
"Milk out the stream of wealth, O Śabalī; may I follow the most powerful vow of living beings, svāhā! (PB 21.4.1).
The Agniṣṭoma has four stomas, the Ukthya has twenty-one, and the Atirātra has all the stomas.

(PB 21.4.2). Indeed, the eye of Prajāpati fell away; it became a horse. That is the horse-nature of the horse. The gods restored it by means of the Aśvamedha. This [sacrifice] is indeed Prajāpati himself.

"He who performs the horse sacrifice accomplishes everything" (PB 21.4.3). "Verily, he who performs the horse sacrifice becomes possessed of a body for that world" (PB 21.4.4). The bees tore out the thigh of the horse; the gods restored it by means of the Catuṣṭoma; in that there is the Catuṣṭoma, it is for the sake of the completeness of the horse.
(21.4.5) Because he makes three *anuṣṭubh*s out of four *gāyatrī*s, therefore one stands firm with three [steps] even while fleeing from everything; he restores all [the lost].

(21.4.6) The horse is indeed the end of cattle, the *anuṣṭubh* the end of meters, Viṣṇu the end of deities, the *catuṣṭoma* the end of *stomas*, and the three-night rite (*trirātra*) the end of sacrifices. In that the *vaiplavya* verses serve as the introductory *anuṣṭubh*s...
The Catuṣṭoma is the stoma; the sacrifice is a three-night rite. Thus, he establishes that very end upon the end.

There is a twenty-one-fold day on which the horse is immolated. Indeed, from here, yonder sun is twenty-one-fold: twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first. He thus causes it to reach the measure of the sun itself.
For this [sacrifice], the Mahānāmnī verses constitute the *pṛṣṭha* stotra.

Indeed, these meters are each different from one another, and these animals are sacrificed one after another; it is by means of the Mahānāmnīs being the *pṛṣṭha* that they attain this [horse] for the sake of its completeness.
The *brahmasāman* is the Pārthuraśma.

This [sacrifice] is indeed liable to go astray and become uncontrolled, as if to the furthest distance; but since the *pārthuraśma* is the *brahmasāman*, the horse is held fast by its tethering-rope (*raśmi*). It serves for the control of the horse itself.
It is an *atirātra* with all the *stomas*, for the attainment of everything and the conquest of everything; by this, one attains everything and conquers everything.
For other sacrifices, there is either a single sacrificial post or a set of eleven; but for the *aśvamedha*, there is a set of twenty-one.

The sacrificial post for other sacrifices is made of khadira, bilva, or parṇa wood; but for the Aśvamedha, it is made of nicudāra wood and measures twenty-one aratnis in length, whereas for other animal sacrifices it is not so. They cut portions from the left side for other sacrifices, but they cut portions from the right side for the Aśvamedha. For other sacrifices, they cut portions upon branches of the Plakṣa tree.
They bind the domestic animals to the sacrificial posts of the horse sacrifice made of reed branches; they keep the wild animals on the cross-bars.
They seize the domestic animals and release the wild ones.
(PB 21.5.1) There are three *atirātra* sacrifices, each consisting of the *trivṛt* stoma, all of which include the *ṣoḍaśin*.

(21.5.2) He who should desire sovereignty should sacrifice with this [rite]. (21.5.3) This is indeed the king of the *stomas*; verily, it bestows sovereignty upon him. (21.5.4) In that they assign syllables to the first day, and since speech consists of single syllables, it is for the sake of not overstepping speech.

(21.5.5) Now, as for the fact that there is the *ājyadoha* chant with a two-syllable *nidhana*: this is for the sake of continuity between the latter two days; the *ājyadoha* chants occur on each successive day, and thus they cause him to prosper with cattle day by day.
(21.5.6) All [the days] possess the *ṣoḍaśin*; the *ṣoḍaśin* is power and vigor; verily, he causes them to prosper with power and vigor.
(21.6.1) The *pavamāna* stotras are twenty-four-fold, the *ājya* stotras are threefold, the *pṛṣṭha* stotras are fifteen-fold, and the *agniṣṭoma* is seventeen-fold.

The Agniṣṭoma has Pavamānas in the forty-four-fold stoma; the Ājya-stotras are fifteen-fold; the Pṛṣṭha-stotras are seventeen-fold; the Agniṣṭoma-stotra is twenty-one-fold, and it is accompanied by the Ukthas. The Pavamānas have the forty-eight-fold stoma; the Ājya-stotras are twenty-one-fold; the Pṛṣṭha-stotras are twenty-seven-fold;

the Agniṣṭoma-stotra is thirty-three-fold; the Uktha-stotras are twenty-one-fold along with the Ṣoḍaśin; the night-stotra is fifteen-fold; the Sandhi-stotra is nine-fold; and the Pavamāna is performed with the Chandomas.
"One desiring cattle should sacrifice.
The Chandomas are indeed cattle; in that the Pavamāna-stotras are Chandomas, he wins cattle themselves.
Both types of Stomas, those even and those odd, constitute a pair; from that pairing, offspring is produced.
The morning pressing is the *trivṛt*, the midday pressing is the *pañcadaśa*, and the third pressing is the *saptadaśa*.

The morning pressing is the *caturviṃśa*, the midday pressing is the *catuścatvāriṃśa*, and the third pressing is the *aṣṭācatvāriṃśa*; this is with the *uktha*. The morning pressing is the *ekaviṃśa*, the midday pressing is the *triṇava*, and the third pressing is the *trayastriṃśa*.
The Śoktha is the twenty-one-fold [stoma], the sixteen-fold, the fifteen-fold; the night has the nine-fold as its junction, with the Antarvasu [chant] within.
These worlds are the three-night sacrifice.
Indeed, this world exists, that world exists, and the intermediate space is, as it were, a void.
The first day of the three-night rite truly exists, and the last day truly exists; it is as if there were a gap in the middle.
The Chandomas are indeed cattle; that the Chandomas occur in the middle is for the sake of concealment and to prevent a gap.
The morning pressing is the Trivṛt, the midday pressing is the Pañcadaśa, and the third pressing is the Saptadaśa.
The morning pressing has twenty-one verses; the midday pressing has twenty-seven; the third pressing has thirty-three, including the *uktha*.

The morning pressing has twenty-four verses; the midday pressing has forty-four; the third pressing has forty-eight, including the *uktha*. The *ṣoḍaśī* chant has twenty-one verses; the night has fifteen; the *sandhi* has nine; it is the *parāka*.

(21.8.2) By means of the *parāka* [sacrifice], the gods indeed went to the heavenly world. One who desires heaven should sacrifice with it; by this very means, he ascends to the heavenly world in the *parāṅ* manner.
(21.8.3) Whatever was the lack (*aka*) of this [sacrifice], that was its *parāka*. That is the reason for the name *parāka*. (21.8.4) Indeed, there is no lack whatsoever for one who has gone there.
No harm comes to him who knows thus.

However, for his offspring it remains unestablished, for by this [rite] he indeed ascends to the heavenly world with his back turned away. In that the *ṣoḍaśin* is the twenty-first, the night is the fifteenfold, and the junction is the threefold, by that he becomes firmly established in this world.
The *pavamāna* lauds are twenty-four-fold; the *ājya* lauds are threefold; the *pṛṣṭha* lauds are fifteenfold;
the *agniṣṭoma* is seventeenfold; the *pavamāna* lauds are twenty-four-fold; the *ājya* lauds are fifteenfold; the *pṛṣṭha* lauds are seventeenfold;

the *agniṣṭoma* with its *ukthas* is twenty-one-fold; the *pavamāna* lauds are twenty-four-fold; the *ājya* lauds are seventeenfold; the *pṛṣṭha* lauds are twenty-one-fold; [the *ṣoḍaśin*] is twenty-nine-fold.
The Agniṣṭoma has the Ukthas; the Pavamāna-stotras are twenty-four-fold; the Ājya-stotras are twenty-one-fold; the Pṛṣṭha-stotras are twenty-seven-fold; the Agniṣṭoma is thirty-three-fold;
the Ukthas are twenty-one-fold together with the Ṣoḍaśin; the night-chant is fifteen-fold; the Sandhi-stotra is nine-fold.
(PB 21.9.2) Atri desired, "May four heroic sons be born to me. He saw this [sacrifice]; four heroic sons were born to him. Four heroic sons are born to him who knows thus.
(21.9.3) Having released one *stoma*, he undertakes another; for the *stoma* is indeed the procreator of heroes—it thus procreates a hero for him.
(21.9.4) The *pavamāna* chants consist of twenty-four [verses]; the *gāyatrī* has twenty-four syllables, and the *gāyatrī* is procreation—for the sake of procreation.
(21.9.5) There are both types of *stomas*, those with even numbers and those with odd numbers; that is a pair (*mithuna*). From that pair, he is procreated.

The Agniṣṭoma is the first day, the Ukthya the second, the Ṣoḍaśin the third, and the Atirātra the fourth; this is for the sake of providing diverse powers. He thus makes the days possess diverse powers. The first day is indeed in the Gāyatrī metre, the second in the Triṣṭubh, the third in the Jagatī, and the fourth in the Anuṣṭubh.

Regarding this they say: "If they were to take the *ṣoḍaśin* on the third day, they would reach the *anuṣṭubh* by means of the third day; the fourth day would then be without a metre, for the *ṣoḍaśin* is indeed of the *anuṣṭubh* nature. Therefore, the *ṣoḍaśin* should be taken on the fourth day; the *ṣoḍaśin* is taken in its own proper place. By means of the metres, he makes the days possessed of diverse powers.
The Naudhasa is the Brahmasāman of the first day, the Śyaita of the second, the Śrāyantīya of the third, and the Traiśoka of the fourth.
Regarding this, they say: "This is indeed like a corruption, that one approaches a smaller metre from a larger metre.
Therefore, when this Atijagatī is employed on the fourth day, it is for the sake of avoiding such corruption.

The *kāleya* is the *acchāvāka-sāman* for the first day; the *mādhucchandasa* for the second; the *raurava* for the third; and the *samanta* for the fourth. He thus makes the days possess diverse powers, for the sake of diverse powers.
"O bull, the pressed [juice] for thee" (*abhi tvā vṛṣabhā suta*) is the *rathantara* for the third day. "Who [is there], O Indra... (*kas tam indra*).
The Vāmadevya [Sāman] begins with "tvā vasavaḥ"; the Bṛhat [Sāman] for the fourth day begins with "yajñā yathā apūrva";
and the Vāmadevya [Sāman] begins with "ed u madhor madintaram. This is for the sake of providing various powers to the meters; he thus makes the days possess various powers (PB 21.10.1).
The first day is an Agniṣṭoma consisting of the Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa stomas.

(21.10.2) Now, for the following day: the *vahiṣpavamāna* is the twenty-four-fold; the three *ājya* stotras are fifteen-fold; the *acchāvāka’s* [stotra] is seventeen-fold; the midday *pavamāna* is twenty-one-fold; the two *pṛṣṭha* stotras are seventeen-fold; and the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) is twenty-one-fold, consisting of the *uktha*.

On the third day, the *bahiṣpavamāna* is the twenty-one-fold; three *ājya* stotras; the *acchāvāka*’s [stotra] is the fifteen-fold; the midday *pavamāna* is the twenty-four-fold; the *pṛṣṭha* stotras are twenty-one-fold; the third pressing is the twenty-seven-fold; there are two *uktha* stotras;
and the *acchāvāka*’s [stotra] is twenty-one-fold.

For the fourth day, the *pavamāna* chants are twenty-four-fold; the *ājya* chant of the Hotṛ is fifteen-fold; the three *pṛṣṭha* chants are seventeen-fold; the *agniṣṭoma* is thirty-three-fold; the *uktha* chants are twenty-one-fold including the *ṣoḍaśin*;
the night chant is fifteen-fold; and the *sandhi* is nine-fold.
Jamadagni, desiring prosperity, brought this [sacrifice]; he prospered in these forms of prosperity.
Regarding what they say here: "The two white-haired ones have agreed upon the two wide expanses," by means of this [sacrifice], he indeed prospers in all forms of prosperity.
It is perfected through the *jagatī* meters.

The *jagatī* is indeed the supreme nourishment among the meters; being nourished, these [performers] attain that very supreme nourishment. The *upasad* days consist of sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*). Sacrificial cakes are cattle; thus they find firm support in cattle.
O Agni, you who know the invocations, you who know the sacrifice, you have made Vaiśvānara our kinsman for our protection. Offer the oblation to Indra and to the gods; Svāhā!
O divine Aśvins, with honeyed stalks, sprinkle this sacrifice for the sacrificer. Offer the oblation to Indra and to the gods; Svāhā!
O divine Viṣṇu, stride out widely today upon this sacrifice for the sacrificer. Offer the oblation to Indra and to the gods; Svāhā!
(21.10.14) O divine Soma, bestower of seed, prosper today for the sacrificer at this sacrifice; offer the oblation to Indra and to the gods! Svāhā!
(21.10.15) O divine Savitṛ, grant us a good impulsion today at this sacrifice for the sacrificer; impel [the wealth] for Indra and to the gods! Offer the oblation! Svāhā!
(21.10.16) O divine Dhātṛ, a good ordainer, prosper today for the sacrificer at this sacrifice; offer the oblation to Indra and to the gods! Svāhā!
(21.10.17) O divine pressing-stones, speak today at this sacrifice a honeyed word for the sacrificer; offer the oblation to Indra and to the gods! Svāhā!
(21.10.18) O divine Anumati, favor today this sacrifice for the sacrificer; offer the oblation to Indra and to the gods! Svāhā!
(21.10.19) O divine Aditi, grant today at this sacrifice good light for the sacrificer; offer the oblation to Indra and to the gods! Svāhā!
O divine waters, bow down; today at this sacrifice, offer the oblation to Indra and to the gods for the sake of the sacrificer—*svāhā*!
Sitting in every seat, possessed of progeny, the skillful one, being pleased, offer the oblation to Indra and to the gods—*svāhā*!
O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, bestower of good seed, prosper today at this sacrifice for the sake of the sacrificer; offer the oblation to Indra and to the gods—*svāhā*!
(21.10.23) There is a cake on one potsherd for Agni; one on two potsherds for the Aśvins; one on three potsherds for Viṣṇu; one on four potsherds for Soma;
one on five potsherds for Savitṛ; one on six potsherds for Dhātṛ; one on seven potsherds for the Maruts; one on eight potsherds for Bṛhaspati;
one on nine potsherds for Mitra; one on ten potsherds for Varuṇa; one on eleven potsherds for Indra; and one on twelve potsherds for the Viśve Devas.
The morning pressing is threefold, the midday pressing is fifteenfold, and the third pressing is seventeenfold;
the morning pressing is fifteenfold, the midday pressing is seventeenfold, and the third pressing is twenty-onefold;
that [rite] with its hymns has a seventeenfold morning pressing, a twenty-onefold midday pressing, and a twenty-ninefold third pressing.

The morning pressing has the Ekaviṃśa stoma; the midday pressing has the Triṇava; the third pressing has the Trayastriṃśa. The Ukthas descend [in stoma]: the first is Triṇava, then two Ekaviṃśas with the Ṣoḍaśin, the night-chant is Pañcadaśa, and the junction is Trivṛt. Vasiṣṭha, having lost his son, felt as if he were deficient. He saw this [rite]; he reached the summit. Whoever feels as if he is deficient should sacrifice with this.

In that he passes from one hymn-form (*stoma*) to another, he ascends from the very beginning to the beginning; the two *janitras* of Vasiṣṭha are used for the sake of procreation. The *ukthas* of the final day are descending, for the sake of stability.
The *agniṣṭoma* is the threefold (*trivṛt*), the *uktha* is the fifteenfold, the *uktha* is the seventeenfold, and the *atirātra* is the twenty-one-fold; this is Viśvāmitra’s *sañjaya*.
The Jahnuvṛcīvantas were contending for sovereignty. Viśvāmitra Jāhnavi saw this [rite]; he became sovereign, while the others were without sovereignty.
One who has rivals should sacrifice with this;
he becomes [successful] himself and his rival is defeated—he who knows thus.
This is indeed light spread out;
he who knows this becomes light among living beings.
This is indeed the fourfold stoma; cattle have four feet; verily, he finds firm support in cattle.
The stomas do not exceed the twenty-onefold; the twenty-onefold is indeed a foundation, and thus he finds firm support at the very end of the sacrifice.
There are two threefold [stomas] at the pressings, one fifteenfold; there are two fifteenfold at the pressings, one seventeenfold;
there are two seventeenfold at the pressings, one twenty-onefold; there are two twenty-onefold at the pressings, one twenty-ninefold; and there are two twenty-ninefold.

In the third pressing there is one [stoma] of thirty-three; the *ukthas* descend: the first is twenty-sevenfold, two are twenty-onefold with the *ṣoḍaśin*, the night-chant is fifteenfold, and the junction is threefold.
(PB 21.13.2) The gods and the asuras contended; they did not achieve victory. They said, "By means of a union of speech..."

"Let us compete for victory, those of us who do not find a pair for our speech; they shall be defeated. The gods said, "One," and the Asuras found a pair for their speech, "One. The gods said, "Two," and the Asuras found a pair for their speech, "Two.
The gods said, "Three," and the Asuras found a pair for their speech, "Three."

"The gods said, 'We have found a pair in four,' while the Asuras said, 'In four [syllables]. The gods found a pair in speech consisting of five [syllables], whereas the Asuras did not find one. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated.
He who knows this prospers in himself, and his rival is defeated. (PB 21.13.3)
(21.13.4) They appropriated that strength and food for a year.
(21.13.5) He who knows thus appropriates the strength and food of his rival for a year.
(21.13.6) This is a five-night rite; man is fivefold, and cattle are fivefold; thereby he obtains both man and cattle.
This sacrifice is indeed a non-ox-cart, continuous, for it carries two *stomas* each day. Whatever desire one desires, that one attains by means of this.
For wherever one desires with a non-ox-cart, there one attains it.
The five-day rite consists of *abhyāsaṅgyas* for the sake of continuity.
The *ukthas* of the final day consist of descending [stomas] for the sake of stability.

The Agniṣṭoma is threefold; the *uktha* is fifteenfold; the *uktha* is seventeenfold; the *uktha* is fifteenfold; the Atirātra is seventeenfold; it is the five-autumnal sacrifice, the *stoma* of the Maruts.
He who should desire, "May I become much," let him sacrifice with this.
The Maruts are indeed the most numerous of the gods; he becomes truly abundant. The Saptadaśa stoma does not surpass [them]; Prajāpati is indeed the Saptadaśa; verily, he attains Prajāpati.
Agastya consecrated bulls for the Maruts and bound them for Indra. Indra, taking up his thunderbolt, rushed at them. He saw this *Kayāśubhīya* hymn; with it, he brought them to rest.
When the *Kayāśubhīya* is recited, it is for the sake of peace alone.

There are seventeen spotted bulls five years old, and seventeen spotted three-year-old heifers that have not yet calved; having been carried around the fire and sprinkled with water, they are sacrificed—the others are taken away, while the others are released.
Then, after a year, they bring reddish-brown ones spotted with fresh butter; these are the bulls, and they are carried around the fire.

They seize the *etarā* bulls from among those sprinkled with water and release the *pretarā* bulls; then, after a year, they bring in the *rājīvā* bulls and likewise those *ukṣan* bulls—having carried fire around them and sprinkled them—they seize the *etarā* bulls and release the *pretarā* bulls. Then, after another year, they bring in the *piśaṅgī* bulls and likewise those *ukṣan* bulls—having carried fire around them and sprinkled them—they seize the *etarā* bulls and release the *pretarā* bulls.
Then, after a year, they bring the spotted cows and those bulls; having performed the fire-circumambulation and sprinkled them, they sacrifice the females and release the males.
Then, after a year, the Soma sacrifices take place.
(21.14.10) Every day they sacrifice three [animals] each; on the final day, five.
(21.14.11) The goat is for Agni and Soma.
(21.14.12) The bulls are for Indra and the Maruts; the heifers are for the Maruts.
(PB 21.14.13) If Rudra should strike [the victim], one should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Raudravat and then immolate another animal.
(PB 21.14.14) If it should fall apart, one should offer a cake on a single potsherd to the Earth and then immolate another animal.

(PB 21.14.15) If it should sink down, one should offer a pap to Nirṛti and then immolate another animal. If it should die in the water, one should offer a pap to Apām Napāt and then immolate another animal. If it should be blind...
Having offered a *caru* oblation to Sūrya, he should then immolate another animal (PB 21.14.16).
If it should be lame or crippled, having offered a *caru* oblation to Bṛhaspati, he should then immolate another animal (PB 21.14.17).
If it should run away, having offered a *caru* oblation to Vāyu, he should then immolate another animal.
(PB 21.14.18) If they should conquer by force, one should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra Prasahvan; then one should immolate another victim.
(PB 21.14.19) If he should die by some other cause of death, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Prajāpati; then one should immolate another victim.
(PB 21.14.20) By means of this very sacrifice, Ekayāvan Gāndama, having sacrificed with the Vetasvatī, attained all prosperity.
(21.14.21) He who knows thus prospers with all prosperity.
(21.15.1) The Jyotiṣṭoma is an Agniṣṭoma; the Gaur is an Ukthya; the Mahāvrata is a Gaur Ukthya; the Āyus is an Atirātra.
(21.15.2) The vow is indeed the year; of it, spring is the head, summer and the rains are the two wings, autumn is the middle, and winter is the tail.
Therefore, the plants ripen in autumn, for autumn is the middle of the year. Those who undertake the vow before the year [is complete] perform what is unaccomplished.
This vow is indeed accomplished when it occurs in the five-night [rite], for there are five seasons.
(PB 21.15.6) When one has praised with the *āpta* vow, he who knows thus reaches a full lifespan.

(PB 22.1.1) The six-day period consists of the *pṛṣṭha* chants. (PB 22.1.2) The seasons did not find firm support; they found support through this [rite]. One who desires support should sacrifice; he indeed finds support.

There are six seasons; verily, by this [rite] he finds firm support in the seasons. There is a *ṣaḍaha* consisting of the *pṛṣṭha* chants for the sake of manifest success, for by this the seasons attained success manifestly; it is for the sake of success indeed.
The *agniṣṭoma* is the *trivṛt*, the *ukthya* is the *pañcadaśa*, the *ukthya* is the *saptadaśa*, and the *atirātra* consists of the *jyotis*, the *go*, and the *āyus*.
(22.2.2) He who should desire, "May I attain a full lifespan," let him sacrifice with this.
(22.2.3) In that there is a three-day period in front, [it is because] there are three vital breaths—out-breath, in-breath, and diffused breath—and these very ones are thereby joined together.
(22.2.4) Now, in that there are the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyus Atirātras, it is for the sake of firm establishment.

The five-day rite consists of the Abhyāsaṅgya and the Viśvajit Atirātra. Indeed, one sacrificial session (*sattra*) is for one purpose, while a sacrifice (*yajña*) is for another; he does not obtain through the *sattra* that which is obtained by the sacrifice, nor does he obtain through the sacrifice that which is obtained by the *sattra*.

This [five-day rite] is indeed like a *sattra* in that the *pṛṣṭha* stotras follow the natural order; in that the *pṛṣṭhas* are performed in a single way, he thereby bestows power and vigor upon him in a single way.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are food; verily, he bestows food upon him. The *pṛṣṭha* chants are cattle; verily, he finds firm support in cattle.
The five-day rite consists of *abhyāsaṅgya* chants for the sake of continuity.
(22.3.7) There is the Viśvajit Atirātra for the sake of conquering the universe.
(22.4.1) [The sacrifice consists of] the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra.
(22.4.2) The Seven Seers prospered by means of this; therefore it is prosperity. For that reason, they sacrifice with this for the sake of prosperity itself.
(22.4.3) There are seven vital breaths in the head; the vital breaths are the senses, and by this [rite] he obtains the senses.
(22.4.4) There are seven domestic animals; those he obtains by this.
(22.4.5) The *pṛṣṭha* chant of the seventh day is the *vrata*; for that [day] has food that is unobtained. The *vrata* is indeed food; by this he obtains the eating of food.
(22.4.6) There is a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period for the sake of manifest success;
for by means of this, the seven seers (*saptarṣi*) visibly attained prosperity, and it is for the sake of success itself.
(22.5.1) [The sacrifice consists of] a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period, a seventeen-fold day, the *mahāvrata*, and an *atirātra*.
Its head is the *trivṛt*, its two wings are the *pañcadaśa*, its body is the *saptadaśa*, and its tail is the *ekaviṃśa*.
By means of this, Prajāpati indeed created offspring.
He who knows thus is propagated with offspring and with cattle.
Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold; in that the vow consists of seventeen, one attains Prajāpati himself.
In that the head is threefold, there are nine vital breaths; thus one finds firm support in the vital breaths.
In that the two wings are fifteenfold, it is for the sake of providing strength.
The self consists of seventeen; Prajāpati indeed is seventeenfold; verily, he attains Prajāpati. The tail consists of twenty-one for the sake of stability.
There are the Pṛṣṭhya six-day period, the Chandoma-pavamāna, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra.
One who desires cattle should sacrifice. The meters (*chandāṃsi*) are indeed cattle.
In that there are Pavamāna-stotras in meters for the Mahāvrata, he wins cattle.

(PB 22.6.5) Both types of *stomas*, the even and the odd, constitute a pair; from that pair, procreation occurs. (PB 22.7.1) The five-day rite (*pañcāha*) is characterized by the *abhyāsaṅgya* [stoma]; then comes the day with the thirty-three-fold (*trayastriṃśa*) *stoma*. Its *agniṣṭoma* has the thirty-four-fold (*catustriṃśa*) *stoma*;

the *mahāvrata* has the seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*); it is an *atirātra*. Its *bahiṣpavamāna* has the twenty-four-fold (*caturviṃśa*) *stoma*; its "head" (*śiras*) has the nine-fold (*trivṛt*); the two [other *pavamānas*] have the fifteen-fold (*pañcadaśa*) *stoma*.
The two wings consist of seventeen [verses], the body twenty-one, and the tail [the same].
By this indeed Jamadagni nourished all forms of prosperity; by this one likewise nourishes all forms of prosperity.
In that there is a five-day period consisting of *abhyāsaṅgya* days at the beginning, it is for the sake of continuity.
Now, this is the thirty-third day; there are thirty-three deities, and thus he obtains the deities themselves.
Its Agniṣṭoma stotra consists of thirty-four verses; Prajāpati is the thirty-fourth among the deities, and thus he obtains Prajāpati himself.
The Bahiṣpavamāna chant consists of twenty-four verses; the Gāyatrī of the Mahāvrata has twenty-four syllables, and the Gāyatrī is procreation—for the sake of procreation.
(22.7.7) Both types of *stomas*—those with even numbers and those with odd numbers—constitute a pair; from that pairing, offspring is produced.

(22.7.8) In that the *trivṛt* becomes the head, there are nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*); thus he finds firm support in the vital breaths. In that the two wings are *pañcadaśa*, it is for the sake of providing strength. The trunk (*ātman*) is *saptadaśa*; Prajāpati indeed is the *saptadaśa*. [He attains] Prajāpati...
Thus he obtains the twenty-first; the tail is the twenty-first for the sake of stability.

(PB 22.8.1) There is the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma, the Gaur Ukthya, the Āyus Ukthya, the Abhijit Agniṣṭoma, the Viśvajit Agniṣṭoma, the Sarvajit Agniṣṭoma, and the Sarvastoma Atirātra. (PB 22.8.2) By means of this, indeed, Indra surpassed all other deities; he who knows thus surpasses all other creatures.

(22.8.3) That the *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus* [sāmans] constitute the three-day period at the beginning, he approaches these well-known *stomas*; verily, he finds firm support in these very worlds. (22.8.4) Now, there is the *abhijit* [day]. By means of the *abhijit*, the gods conquered these worlds; by means of the *viśvajit*, they conquered all; by means of the *sarvajit*, they conquered everything.
(22.8.5) It is an *atirātra* sacrifice containing all the *stomas*, for the attainment of all and the conquest of all; by this, one attains all and conquers all.
(22.9.1) There are four days consisting of threefold stomas, beginning with the Agniṣṭoma: the Viśvajit, the Mahāvrata, the Jyotiṣṭoma, and the Atirātra.
(22.9.2) By means of this, Prajāpati created the Puruṣa; he attained sovereignty over all kinds of food.
(22.9.3) He who knows thus attains sovereignty over all kinds of food.

(PB 22.9.4) Of one being born, the head indeed comes into being first; for the head is divided fourfold: breath, sight, hearing, and speech. The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed the self (*ātman*). In that he performs the *pṛṣṭhas*, he joins the self together with the head.
(PB 22.9.5) This indeed makes the person whole; therefore, he bestows food itself as his vow.
Now, as for the fact that the Jyotiṣṭoma is an Atirātra: it is for the sake of providing what has not been provided. There is the Pṛṣṭhya Stoma, the six-day period, and the Viśvajit Atirātra.
Indeed, one sacrifice is for one purpose and a sacrificial session (*sattra*) is for another; one does not obtain through a sacrificial session that which is intended for one [specific] purpose.
One does not obtain that through sacrifice by means of a sacrifice; for this is like a sacrificial session (*sattra*) in which each *pṛṣṭha* chant follows the other in regular order.
When the *pṛṣṭhas* are performed all at once, he bestows brilliance and vigor upon him in a single unit. The *pṛṣṭhas* are food;
verily, he bestows the eating of food upon him. The *pṛṣṭhas* are cattle; verily, he finds firm support in cattle.

(22.10.3) What is indeed manifest to humans is hidden from the gods, but what is hidden from humans is manifest to the gods. (22.10.4) This vow is indeed hidden—that which is the Viśvajit; by means of this, he directly obtains food.
(22.11.1) [The sacrifice consists of] the six-day period with the *pṛṣṭha* chants, the Mahāvrata, the Jyotiṣṭoma, and the Atirātra.
By this, indeed, the gods attained the state of divinity;
he who knows thus attains the state of divinity. This vow is indeed fulfilled when, in the eight-night rite, it results in an Agniṣṭoma.
Now, in that the Jyotiṣṭoma is an Atirātra, it is for the securing of what has not yet been secured.
By means of the eight-night rite, the gods attained everything;
he who knows thus attains everything.
The Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, Jyotis, Go, Āyus, and the Atirātra. The gods were indeed afraid of death; they approached Prajāpati, and for them he [bestowed] immortality by means of this nine-night rite.
This indeed is the immortality of a human being: that he reaches his full span of life and becomes more prosperous. He who knows thus reaches his full span of life and becomes more prosperous.
This is indeed a nine-night rite; there are nine vital breaths, and thus one finds firm support in the vital breaths.

There is a six-day period consisting of the *pṛṣṭha* chants for the sake of manifest prosperity. Now, as for the fact that there are the *jyotis*, *go*, and *āyus* *atirātras*, it is for the sake of stability. One who desires cattle should sacrifice with the five-day *abhyāsaṅgya*—the *agniṣṭoma* *jyotiṣṭoma*, the *ukthya* *go*, the *ukthya* *āyus*, the *viśvajit* *atirātra*.

(22.13.2) That the Jyotis, Gaur, and Āyus form the three-day period at the beginning, he approaches these well-known *stomas*; verily, he finds firm support in these very worlds. (22.13.3) Now, as for the fact that the Abhyāsaṅgya five-day period occurs in the middle: man is fivefold, and cattle are fivefold; by this means, he obtains both man and cattle.
(22.13.4) There is an Atirātra Viśvajit for the conquest of all.

The Agniṣṭoma is Trivṛt; the Ukthya is Pañcadaśa; the Agniṣṭoma is Trivṛt; the Ukthya is Saptadaśa; the Agniṣṭoma is Saptadaśa; the Ukthya is Ekaviṃśa; the Agniṣṭoma is Saptadaśa; the Agniṣṭoma is Triṇava; the Ukthya is Trayastriṃśa; the Agniṣṭoma is Triṇava; [and] the Viśvajit Atirātra.
Indra, having slain the Asuras, thought he had committed an improper act. The gods caused him to sacrifice with this *stoma*; he attained freedom from evil (*nairdaśya*).
Therefore, one who is struck by an arrow or struck by a staff reaches the tenth stage, which is freedom from evil.
This *virāj* consists of ten sets of ten; the *virāj* is food, and thus he bestows food upon him.

By means of the Agniṣṭoma, the gods, having subdued the Asuras, multiplied in the midst with the Ukthas through offspring and cattle. Having subdued his rival by means of the Agniṣṭoma itself, he multiplies in the midst with the Ukthas through offspring and cattle. This sacrifice is indeed three-peaked.
(22.14.7) It belongs to those who know thus, as well as to the *trikakubh* meters and to offspring.

(22.15.1) There are three *agniṣṭoma*s with the *trivṛt* stoma, three *ukthya*s with the *pañcadaśa* stoma, three *ukthya*s with the *saptadaśa* stoma, an *atirātra* with the *ekaviṃśa* stoma, and the ten-night sacrifice of Kusuruvinda.
(22.15.2) He who should desire, "May I become much," he should sacrifice with this.
When the Stoma is in groups, it becomes manifold:
there are Trivṛts together, Pañcadaśas together, and Saptadaśas together;
the Ekaviṃśa is the Atirātra for the sake of stability.
This [sacrifice] is indeed light spread out;
he who knows thus becomes light among living beings. This [sacrifice] is indeed the fourfold stoma; cattle are four-footed; he finds firm support in cattle.
The Stomas do not exceed the twenty-one-fold; the twenty-one-fold is indeed a foundation, and thus one finds firm support.
By means of this, Kusuruvinda Auḍālaki, having sacrificed, attained abundance. He who knows thus attains abundance.
The Abhyāsaṅgya five-day rite, four Chandomas, and the Viśvajit Atirātra—one desiring cattle should sacrifice with this.
In that the Abhyāsaṅgya five-day rite is at the beginning, and man is fivefold and cattle are fivefold, by that he obtains both man and cattle.
The Chandomas are in the middle; the Chandomas are indeed cattle, for the sake of securing cattle.
The Viśvajit is an Atirātra for the sake of conquering everything.
There is a Triṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma, a Jyotis Ukthya, a Triṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma, a Gaur Ukthya, an Abhijit Agniṣṭoma, a Gaur Ukthya, a Viśvajit Agniṣṭoma, an Āyus Ukthya, a Viśvajit,
and an Atirātra consisting of all the Stomas of the Agniṣṭoma.

The gods, being struck down by the Asuras, fled to Prajāpati; he gave this divine city to them, and they entered it. One should cause one who is being subjected to sorcery to sacrifice with this; he enters this very divine city for the sake of escaping death. It consists of a six-day period including the Abhyāsaṅgya, three Chandomas, a fourfold-stoma Agniṣṭoma, and a Viśvajit Atirātra.
This sacrifice is indeed self-sovereignty;
he who knows thus attains self-sovereignty,
for Prajāpati is self-sovereignty and Parameṣṭhin is self-sovereignty.
He who knows thus attains the state of the Supreme Lord (parameṣṭhitā).

Both the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are employed, for that is self-sovereignty (svārājya). The sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) amount to ten thousand, for that is self-sovereignty. The Stoma is the twenty-sixfold (ṣaḍviṃśastoma), for that is self-sovereignty. The Stoma is the fourfold (catuṣṭoma), for it is the end at the end.
"He goes with glory, he who knows thus" (PB 22.18.7).
By means of this, having secured his well-being and performed the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice on the northern bank of the Sudāman, [Sudās] attained all prosperity. He who knows thus attains all prosperity.
(23.1.1) An Atirātra, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, an Atirātra consisting of all the Stomas, four Chandomas, and an Atirātra. (23.1.2) This thirteen-night rite is indeed the completed twelve-day sacrifice.
(23.1.3) For it is the same as the opening and concluding Atirātras; whatever desire they may wish for, they attain it by means of these [days].

But the speech of the householder tends to fail; however, because there is an *atirātra* with all the *stomas* in the middle, by that means the speech of the householder does not fail. These indeed were the noble householders who had Āruṇi as their *hotṛ*; they entered upon the *subhaga* [sacrifices] and attained every prosperity. Those who enter upon these attain every prosperity. An *atirātra*, the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), the *mahāvrata*, and an *atirātra*.
This twelve-day sacrifice is indeed speech as it is extended; they would cut that speech asunder if they were to place an *atirātra* in the middle.
Since they undertake the vow at the end, they do not cut off speech; they attain the thirteenth month.
These thirteen nights are indeed firmly established; those who undertake them become firmly established.
(23.3.1) An Atirātra, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, and an Atirātra beginning with the Trayastriṃśa-stoma.
(23.3.2) These nights are indeed the fulfillers of desires.
(23.3.3) For the Virāj consists of ten; the eleventh is the self; the twelfth is progeny; the thirteenth is cattle; and the fourteenth is for the sake of desire.
(23.3.4) By means of these [Stomas], they obtain all desires indeed.
(23.3.5) These two Trayastrimśa [Stomas] joined in the middle are truly the summits of the sun; by that, they ascend to the summit of the sun.
(23.3.6) They perform the Pṛṣṭha [Stotras] twice; by means of these, they place food before them in due order.
(23.4.1) An Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyus—this is the Tryaha; then the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, the Āyus, the Gauḥ, the Jyotis, and an Atirātra.

(23.4.2) Those for whom they might deliberate whether [the marriage] is on a couch, in water, or at a wedding, they should perform these [sacrifices]. (23.4.3) Since they employ the well-known Stomas of the Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus Tryaha.
(23.4.4) It is these very worlds; they find firm support in these very worlds.

(23.4.5) Now, as for the fact that the *ṣaḍaha* of the *pṛṣṭha* stomas occurs in the middle: this is indeed the couch of the gods (*devatalpa*); it is upon that very couch of the gods that they mount, and thus they become those who possess a couch (*talpya*).
(23.4.6) They attain a more excellent couch.

(23.4.7) Now, as for the fact that they go by means of the *Āyus*, the *Go*, and the *Jyotis* *Atirātra*, they return again by that same means. (23.5.1) There are two days, the *Atirātra*, the *Go*, and the *Āyus*; [then] the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and finally the *Atirātra*.
(23.5.2) In that there are the two days, the *Go* and the *Āyus*, they employ the two *Stomas* as a pair for the sake of procreation.

(23.5.3) Now, as for those ten days of the twelve-day rite during which they employ speech without interruption for the sake of procreation—(23.5.4) these fourteen nights are indeed established; those who undertake them become established. (23.6.1) [The sequence is: an Atirātra, a Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, the Mahāvrata, a Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha, and an Atirātra beginning with the Trayastrimśa-stoma.

(23.6.2) By means of these [rites], indeed, the gods attained godhood; those who perform these attain godhood. (23.6.3) This is indeed the sacrificial session (*sattra*) of the gods; even today the gods continue to sit in that sacrificial session. (23.6.4) The full moon day is an *atirātra* sacrifice; then those six days constitute the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*; the eighth day of the waning moon is the *mahāvrata*; then those six days constitute the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*; and the new moon day is an *atirātra* sacrifice.

"Therefore, in that case, [the Soma] is not pressed for men; rather, it is pressed for the gods. Indeed, by means of these [days], they ascend visibly to the deities. However, there is danger of being repelled; therefore, they should undergo initiation without a companion in order to avoid being repelled.
[The sacrifice consists of: an Atirātra, a Trivṛt Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma, the three-day period of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus, the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, and the Āyus, Gauḥ, and Jyotis Atirātra."
(23.7.2) These nights indeed proclaim the *kṣatra*.
(23.7.3) Those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should perform them.
(23.7.4) In that there is the *Trivṛt Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma*, it bestows glory upon the *brahman*.
The Trivṛt is indeed Brahman.

Since they approach the well-known Stomas—the Jyotis, Gaus, and Āyus—of the Tryaha, they find firm support in these very worlds. Now, as for the fact that the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha occurs in the middle: the Pṛṣṭhas are indeed food.

Food itself is placed in the middle; therefore, being in the middle, food nourishes [the body]. Now, as for the *āyus*, the *go*, and the *jyotis* *atirātra*: by that same path by which they go from here, they return again.

The *trivṛt* *agniṣṭut* *agniṣṭoma*, the *jyotis*, the *go*, and the *āyus* constitute the three-day period (*tryaha*). There are the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), and the *atirātra*.

(23.8.2) For one purpose indeed is the *sattra*, and for another the *yajña*. That which one obtains through the *sattra* is not obtained by the *yajña*; that which one obtains by the *yajña* is not obtained by the *sattra*.
(23.8.3) Insofar as there are *atirātras* on either side, by that it is a *yajña*; and insofar as there are the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), by that it is a *sattra*.
(23.8.4) By means of these [days], they obtain both desires.
(23.9.1) An Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyus—this three-day period; ten days of the twelve-day rite; and an Atirātra: those desiring offspring should perform this.

(23.9.2) By means of these, Prajāpati indeed created offspring; they who perform these are propagated with offspring and with cattle. (23.9.3) In that they perform the three-day period of Jyotis, Gauḥ, and Āyus—the stomas of those already born—they find firm support in these very worlds.

Now, as for those twelve days of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice during which they employ speech without interruption for the sake of procreation—these fifteen nights are indeed established; those who perform these [sacrifices] become firmly established. These very [nights], together with the *mahāvrata*, are established.

By means of these [stotras], indeed, Indra conquered the supreme victory; by means of these, they likewise conquer the supreme victory. The thunderbolt is fifteenfold; one does not perform a heroic deed with a thunderbolt that has not been grasped. That which is the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup] is the very support; thus, with a thunderbolt that has been grasped, one performs a heroic deed.
It consists of an *atirātra*, the *jyotis*, the *go*, the *āyus*, the *go*, the *āyus*, the five-day period, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an *atirātra*.
By means of these, Prajāpati indeed conquered infinite prosperity; for these, which are the forms of the five-day rite, are indeed infinite.
Since it is a five-day rite, they are born from the infinite.
Now, as for those ten days of the twelve-day rite, they employ uninterrupted speech for the sake of procreation.

(23.11.5) These seventeen-night rites are indeed established; those who perform them become established. (23.12.1) An Atirātra, an Abhiplava six-day period, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra.
(23.12.2) The gods were afraid of death; they fled to Prajāpati, and he bestowed immortality upon them by means of this eighteen-night rite.
(23.12.3) This indeed is the immortality of a human being: that he reaches a full lifespan and becomes more prosperous.

(23.12.4) Those who perform these [rites] reach a full lifespan and become more prosperous. (23.12.5) These [days] are indeed twice nine; they are the vital breaths. By means of these, they place life-span within themselves in due order.
(23.13.1) These very [days] are accompanied by the Mahāvrata.
(23.13.2) By means of these, indeed, Vāyu attained sovereignty over the wild animals for those who perform them.
(23.13.3) This is indeed the Sacrifice of the Wild Animal (mṛgasatra).
(23.13.4) By means of these, wild animals are born already formed;
(23.13.5) for those who perform these [sacrifices], that which is unformed is born.
(23.14.1) There is an *atirātra*, an *abhiplava* six-day period, the *abhijit* and the *viśvajit*—these two days—the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an *atirātra*.
Those who desire manhood should approach with these; for by means of these Prajāpati created man.
He attained sovereignty over all kinds of food; those who approach with these attain sovereignty over all kinds of food. This is indeed the Man-Sacrifice (*puruṣasattra*).
Man is indeed twentyfold, for there are ten fingers on his hands and ten toes on his feet.
In that there are these twenty nights, they establish man in these very worlds by means of them.
These twenty nights are established; those who undertake them become firmly established.
(23.15.1) An Atirātra, an Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha, an Atirātra, an Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha, an Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha, an Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha, and an Atirātra—those desiring cattle should perform this.
(23.15.2) By means of these [days], the Ādityas released the seven domestic animals; by means of these, they release cattle.
(23.15.3) Three times indeed are there seven; the Ādityas are seven.
The cattle are the Ādityas;
the Ādityas have prospered in this world, the Ādityas in yonder world;
the cattle are in this [world], the seasons in yonder [world].

Those who undertake these [sacrifices] prosper in both of these worlds, in the world of the gods and in the world of men. An Atirātra, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, three Svarasāman days, a Divākīrtya day, three Svarasāman days, a Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, and an Atirātra beginning with the Trayastriṃśa— those desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should undertake this.
Svarbhānu, the son of Asura, pierced the sun with darkness. The gods sought an expiation for him; they found these [oblations], and by means of them they drove away the darkness from him.
Those who perform these [rites] drive away the darkness.
They should offer a sacrificial animal dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan.
Soma is indeed the Brahmin, and Pūṣan is cattle; thus they cause their own deity to swell with cattle. They have made it skin.
(PB 23.16.6) The *sāmidhenī* verses are those of Manu.
Whatever Manu spoke was indeed medicine; [the verses are used] for the sake of medicine. (PB 23.16.7)
They should enter upon the Naidāghīya [sacrifice], for then this [sun] shines most intensely against them; however,
there is danger from leprosy, for it strikes away from them excessively.
(23.16.11) Ugradeva Rājani indeed undertook these [sacrifices], and he became free from disease.
(23.16.12) He who, knowing thus, undertakes these becomes free from disease.

(23.17.1) An Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyus; a Tryaha Abhiplava consisting of six days; the ten days of the Dvādaśāha; the Mahāvrata and an Atirātra—those desiring food should undertake these.

(23.17.2) There are five seasons, twelve months, these three worlds, yonder sun as the twenty-first, and food as the twenty-second. Those who undertake these [sacrifices] obtain food from these worlds, from the year, from yonder sun. (23.18.1) An Atirātra, Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyus, Gauḥ, Āyus, the Pañcāha Abhiplava, the Ṣaḍaha, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra—those desiring a firm foundation should undertake this.
By means of these, Prajāpati indeed established himself in these worlds.
Since there are these twenty-three nights, and since these worlds are three, they establish themselves in these very worlds by means of them.
These twenty-three nights are indeed firmly established; those who undertake them become established.
The Atirātra, the Pṛṣṭhya Stoma, the six-day period, and the thirty-three-fold day are arranged in the framework of the Upahavya sacrifice.
Its Kaṇvarathantara is performed at the midday pressing. Then follows the manifest thirty-three-fold day; two twenty-nine-fold days;
two twenty-one-fold days; a twenty-nine-fold day; the manifest thirty-three-fold day; an unmanifest thirty-three-fold day; and the Pṛṣṭhya.
The Stoma is the six-day rite; the day is the Trivṛt, undefined, the Jyotiṣṭoma, the Agniṣṭoma, and the Atirātra.

(PB 23.19.2) By means of these, indeed, the gods settled in the heavenly world; "May we settle in the heavenly world," they said. (PB 23.19.3) These, indeed, are the rungs of the *bradhna* (the sun); for these thirty-three [verses] are joined together in the middle. Therefore, they ascend to the rung of the *bradhna*.
They perform the *pṛṣṭha* chants in the middle. The *pṛṣṭhas* are indeed food; thus, food itself is placed in the middle. Therefore, being in the middle, food nourishes.
These [days] consist of seven days;
from this, indeed, creatures are born.
(23.19.7) Those who undertake these [days] are propagated with offspring and with cattle.

(23.19.8) This sacrificial session (*sattra*) which lacks the *chandoma* days is indeed unfavorable for cattle; because it consists of seven-day periods, it possesses the *chandoma* days by means of them, and thus it is favorable for cattle.

(23.19.9) The thirty-threefold day follows upon the thirty-threefold day; from the threefold day they ascend to the threefold day, from the foremost to the foremost. In that the thirty-threefold day follows upon the thirty-threefold day, they find firm support in the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) through the vital breaths.
(23.19.10) That which is threefold, the threefold.
(23.19.11) These nights are indeed contrary; that the *jyotis* Agniṣṭoma becomes the concluding day is for the sake of the ordering of what was disordered.
(23.20.1) [The structure is: an Atirātra, two Abhiplava six-day periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra. Those desiring offspring or desiring cattle should undertake this.
(2) From a prepared womb indeed offspring and cattle are born; in that they perform two six-day periods in their prepared form, they are born with offspring and cattle from a prepared womb.

(3) Now, as for those ten days of the twelve-day rite during which they maintain uninterrupted speech, it is for the sake of procreation. (4) These twenty-four nights are indeed firmly established; those who perform these nights become firmly established.
(21.1) These very [days] are accompanied by the Mahāvrata.
(21.2) By means of these, Prajāpati indeed acquired all food.
(21.3) There are twenty-four half-months in a year; the year is the twenty-fifth, and the vow is food. Those who undertake these [days] obtain food from the year by means of them.
(23.22.1) An Atirātra, the Gauḥ and Āyus—these two days; two Abhiplava six-day periods; the ten days of the twelve-day rite; and an Atirātra.

(23.22.2) The seasons did not find firm standing; they found firm standing through these [days]. Those desiring firm standing should perform this sacrifice; they indeed find firm standing. (23.22.3) There are six seasons; it is in the seasons that they find firm standing through these [days].
(23.22.4) In that there are two days, the Gauh and the Ayuh, they approach two chanted hymns (*stoma*) in union for the sake of procreation.
(23.22.5) In that they approach two arranged six-day periods (*ṣaḍaha*), it is for the sake of proper arrangement.
(23.22.6) Now, as for those ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), they approach them with speech uninterrupted for the sake of generation.

(23.22.7) These twenty-six-night rites are indeed established; those who perform them become established. (23.23.1) An Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyus—this is the Tryaha; two Abhiplava Ṣaḍahas; the ten days of the twelve-day rite; and an Atirātra. Those desiring prosperity should perform these. (23.23.2) By means of these, the stars indeed attained all prosperity; those who perform these attain all prosperity.

(23.23.3) That there are these twenty-seven nights: there are twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*); these nights are commensurate with the lunar mansions; verily, they attain the prosperity of the lunar mansions. (23.24.1) Those desiring cattle should undertake these very [sacrifices] together with the *mahāvrata*. That there are these twenty-eight nights: cattle have eight hooves; by means of these [nights], they obtain cattle hoof by hoof. (23.25.1) An *atirātra*, the *jyotis*, the *go*, the *āyus*, the *go*, the *āyus*, a five-day period, two six-day periods consisting of *abhiplava* days, the ten days of the twelve-day period, and an *atirātra*.
By means of these, Prajāpati indeed conquered infinite prosperity.
These [days] are indeed infinite, in that they go from one to twenty-nine; for the infinite is the range of speech.
Since these are twenty-nine nights plus one, by means of them they conquer infinite prosperity.

An Atirātra, three Abhiplava six-day periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra—those desiring food should undertake this. Other sacrificial sessions (sattra) attain the Virāj indirectly; these, however, have attained the Virāj directly. Those who undertake these [sessions] directly obtain food through them.
These very [verses] are accompanied by the Mahāvrata; through them indeed Prajāpati successively acquired food.
The Virāj is food, and the Vrata is food.
Through these [verses], they successively acquire food.
(23.28.1) An Atirātra, the Gauḥ and Āyus—these two days, three Abhiplava six-day periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra: those desiring cattle should perform this.
(23.28.2) These nights are indeed the Anuṣṭubh; (23.28.3) the Anuṣṭubh consists of thirty-two syllables.
Speech is the *anuṣṭubh*;
cattle have four feet;
by means of speech he sustains the cattle.
By means of these nights;
therefore, they come having been accomplished through speech and summoned by speech. [The sequence is:
an Atirātra, three Pañcāhas, a Viśvajit, an Atirātra, one Pañcāha, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, and an Atirātra.
Prajāpati created offspring; they did not find firm support. By means of these [stotras], they found firm support.

These worlds did not find firm support; by means of these, they found firm support. Those who desire a firm foundation should approach [these rites]; they indeed find firm support. Indeed, by means of formlessness, these [worlds] are uniform; by means of formlessness, offspring are uniform; by means of formlessness, these worlds are uniform. In that the Bṛhat reaches the world of the Rathantara, and the Rathantara [reaches] the world of the Bṛhat, it is by means of formlessness alone that he [establishes them] for these.
They produce that which is of similar form.

Indeed, this sixth day is omitted when they perform the five-day rite; but since there are the *pṛṣṭha* days of the six-day rite, by that means the sixth day is not omitted, and by that means the seasons are established.
Now, as for those ten days of the twelve-day rite, by that means they do not depart from the five-day rites.
The intermediate space is indeed the udder, and the two [worlds] on either side are the two teats; by means of this [earth], he milks for the gods, and by means of that [heaven], for the creatures.
This intermediate space is indeed the expanse, and these two on either side are the two teats.
Regarding this, it has been declared: (PB 24.1.8) "That was spoken in accordance with."
(24.1.9) "The thirty gods who sit upon the sacrificial grass—may they grant us food twice a day.
(24.1.10) The middle *atirātra* is indeed the udder, and the two [surrounding] *rātris* are the two teats.
(24.1.11) If this were not an *atirātra*, one would lose the udder.
Therefore, the Atirātra should be performed so that there may be no obstruction to the udder.
By means of these [verses], the thirty-three deities prospered; therefore, this is prosperity. Consequently, they sacrifice with these [verses] for the sake of prosperity itself.
They proceed with different Brahman-sāmans day by day for the sake of distinct power; thus they acquire various powers.
An Atirātra, an Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha, an Atirātra, an Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha, an Atirātra, an Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, the Mahāvrata, and an Atirātra.

(PB 24.2.2) The Ādityas and the Aṅgirases performed this sacrificial session (*sattra*). There were twenty-one [days] for the Ādityas and twelve days for the Aṅgirases. The Ādityas prospered in this world; the Ādityas [prospered] in yonder world. The Aṅgirases [prospered] in this world; the Aṅgirases [prospered] in yonder world.
This sacrificial session (*sattra*) consists of two parts; as far as they succeed by means of these two parts, so great is the power (*ṛddhi*) of these [days].
There is an *atirātra*, three five-day periods (*pañcāha*), a *viśvajit*, an *atirātra*, three five-day periods, and an *atirātra*.

This sacrificial session is indeed unfavorable to cattle insofar as it lacks the *chandoma* days. Since they employ the *chandoma* days in the *viśvajit*, it possesses the *chandomas* and is therefore favorable to cattle.
(24.3.3) These nights are indeed like birds; whatever desire they desire, they attain it by means of these [nights], for wherever a bird desires to go, there it attains it.

(24.3.4) They proceed with the Trivṛt and they emerge from the Trivṛt; the Trivṛt is indeed the breath among the Stomas. Thus, they proceed by means of the breaths and they find firm support in the breaths.

(24.4.1) An Atirātra, Jyotis, Gauḥ, Āyus—this is the three-day period; three Abhiplava six-day periods; the ten days of the twelve-day rite; the Mahāvrata and an Atirātra. Those who desire prosperity should undertake this.
(24.4.2) By means of these, Prajāpati indeed attained all prosperity; they who undertake these attain all prosperity.

(24.4.3) In that there are these thirty-four nights—the thirty-three deities and Prajāpati as the thirty-fourth—they attain the prosperity of Prajāpati among the deities. (24.5.1) An Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, the Āyus, a five-day period, three Abhiplava six-day periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra—those desiring cattle should undertake this.
(24.5.2) In that there are these thirty-five nights, and cattle are fivefold, they win cattle by means of these.
(24.6.1) An *atirātra*, four *abhiplava* six-day periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an *atirātra*: those who desire cattle should undertake this.
(24.6.2) By means of these, indeed, the gods propped up the sun; they who undertake these win the world of the sun.

These nights are indeed Bṛhatīs; the Bṛhatī is the self-rule (*svārājya*) among the meters. He who attains abundance among cattle attains self-rule; those who undertake these [nights] attain self-rule.
These very [nights], together with the Mahāvrata [day], [are so].
(24.7.2) By means of these [rites], Prajāpati indeed obtained both desires: food and the vow; cattle are the Bṛhatī. By means of these, they obtain both desires.

(24.8.1) An Atirātra, the Gauḥ and Āyu days, two Ahan days, four Abhiplava Ṣaḍahas, the ten days of the twelve-day period, and an Atirātra—those desiring cattle should perform this. The meaning is clear.
(24.8.2) In that there are these thirty-eight nights, and cattle have eight hooves, they obtain cattle by their very hooves through these [nights].
(24.9.1) An Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, and the Āyus—a three-day period; four Abhiplava six-day periods; the ten days of the twelve-day rite; and an Atirātra.
(24.9.2) By means of these, Prajāpati indeed conquered infinite prosperity. These are indeed infinite, for there is no end to speech when it reaches forty-one.
(24.9.3) Since these forty-one nights are performed, they conquer infinite prosperity by means of them.
These very [days] include the Mahāvrata.

All these are indeed Virājs: the first is a ten-syllabled [Virāj], the second a twenty-syllabled one, and the third a thirty-syllabled one. This, namely the forty nights, is the supreme Virāj; for the Paṅkti is indeed the supreme [metre]. They thus find firm support in the supreme Virāj itself.

(24.11.1) An *atirātra*, three days consisting of the *trivṛt* stoma with the *agniṣṭoma* as the opening day, an *atirātra*; ten *ukthya* days with the *pañcadaśa* stoma; a tenth day with the *ṣoḍaśin*; an *atirātra*; twelve *ukthya* days with the *saptadaśa* stoma; an *atirātra*; a *pṛṣṭhya* six-day period; an *atirātra*; twelve *ukthya* days with the *ekaviṃśa* stoma; an *atirātra*.
Prajāpati created living beings; they were undifferentiated and did not agree with one another, and so they devoured each other.

Because of that, Prajāpati grieved. He saw these [verses], and from them this world became differentiated: cows became cows, horses became horses, men became men, and wild animals became wild animals.
Those who perform these [sacrifices] turn away from evil.
Because the Atirātras are placed in between for the sake of separation, therefore one does not deposit seed in the other.
Because the Pṛṣṭhya-stomas are joined together, therefore goats and sheep move about among the cattle; and for that reason, the donkey deposits seed in the mare.

This sacrificial session (*sattra*) that lacks the *chandomas* is indeed unfavorable to cattle. Because they employ the meters (*chandāṃsi*) in the *sandhi-sāmans*, it possesses the *chandomas* and is therefore favorable to cattle.

The *jarābodhīya* is in *gāyatrī*s; the *śrudhya* is in *uṣṇih*s; the *nānada* is in *anuṣṭubh*s; the *rathantara* is in *bṛhatī*s; the *rāyovājīya* is in *paṅkti*s; the *auśana* is in *triṣṭubh*s; and [the final *sāman*] is in *jagatī*s.
They employ the ascending meters for the sake of non-degradation.
The breath is indeed the *svara*. Since there are two *svaras* at the end, therefore there are two breaths at the end.

There are two *atirātras*, two *abhiplava* six-day periods, the *go* and *āyus* [days], two *atirātras*, two *abhiplava* six-day periods, the *abhijit* and *viśvajit*, two *atirātras*, one *abhiplava* six-day period, and the *sarvastoma*—that makes nine.

The seventeenth day is an Atirātra; there are ten days of the twelve-day rite, followed by the Mahāvrata and an Atirātra. These are the Yama-Atirātras of the Ādityas. Prosperity indeed attends him who performs these.
(24.12.4) By means of these [verses], indeed, the Ādityas attained prosperity in pairs: Mitra and Varuṇa, Dhātṛ and Aryaman, Aṃśa and Bhaga, Indra and Vivasvat.
Those who employ these [verses] attain the prosperity of these very deities.
(24.12.5) Regarding this, there is a verse:

(24.12.6) "Eight were the sons of Aditi who were born from her own body; with seven she approached the gods, but she cast Mārtāṇḍa away"—thus it is said. (24.12.7) The Ādityas prosper in this world, the Ādityas in yonder world; those who undertake these [rites] prosper in both of these worlds, in the world of the gods and in the world of men. (24.13.1) An Atirātra, four Abhiplava six-day periods, an Atirātra consisting of all the Stomas, two Abhiplava six-day periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra.
Prajāpati created offspring; he became rough, and they did not recognize him while he was rough. He anointed himself and rubbed himself with ointment.
Those who do not know themselves should approach these [ointments]. When they anoint themselves and rub themselves with ointment, they place beauty in themselves and recognize them.
[One should anoint] with *gauggulava* resin at the morning pressing, with *saugandhika* resin at the midday pressing, and with *paitudārava* resin at the third pressing.
Agni, indeed, when about to undertake the office of Hotṛ for the gods, shook his body.
That which was his flesh became guggulu; that which was his sinew became sugandhitejana; that which was his bone became potudāru.
These, indeed, are the fragrant things of the gods; with these very fragrant things of the gods he thus anoints him.
The Atirātra, the Caturviṃśa Prāyaṇīya day, three Abhiplava six-day periods,
the Abhijit, three Svarasāman days, the Divākīrtya day, three Svarasāman days, the Viśvajit, one Abhiplava six-day period,
the Āyus and the Go— these two days, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra constitute the year-long session.
"As great as is the prosperity of the year, so great is the prosperity of these [days]. Regarding this they say:

"If they were to make the twenty-fourth day the introductory day (*prayaṇīya*), they would begin the year but not complete it. Therefore, the *trivṛt* [stoma] alone should be performed; for the *trivṛt* is indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). [Thus they obtain] the vital breaths. Furthermore, they say: "The twenty-fourth day alone should be performed for the sake of success."

(PB 24.14.4) Now, these Svarasāmans are the head; the Divākīrtya is indeed the head, and the Svarasāmans are the vital breaths. In that the Svarasāmans are on both sides of the Divākīrtya, they place the vital breaths in the head itself.

(PB 24.14.5) Then, as many as there are two vital breaths, those are the Viśvajit and Abhijit. Then they approach these two paired Stomas, the Go and Āyus, for the sake of procreation. (PB 24.14.6) Then they approach these ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) with uninterrupted speech, for the sake of generation.
(24.14.7) Now, this vow is food; for food does not satisfy anywhere except in the mouth. Since they undertake the vow at the end, food for consumption is thereby placed in the mouth itself;
therefore, food situated in the mouth satisfies.
(24.14.8) Now, these two Atirātra sacrifices, the Prāyaṇīya and the Udayanīya—by the very same breath through which they set out, they rise again.

The Atirātra; nine Trivṛt days with the Agniṣṭoma as the opening; then a Ṣaḍaha; then those three days—the Agniṣṭomas on both sides and the Ukthya in the middle; nine Pañcadaśa days with the Agniṣṭoma as the opening; then a Ṣaḍaha; then those three days—the Agniṣṭomas on both sides and the Ukthya in the middle; nine Saptadaśa days.
The days consist of a six-day period beginning with the Agniṣṭoma; then those three days consisting of an Agniṣṭoma on either side and an Ukthya in the middle;

then nine days of twenty-one-fold stomas; then a six-day period beginning with the Agniṣṭoma; then those three days consisting of an Agniṣṭoma on either side and an Ukthya in the middle; then the ten days of the twelve-day rite (dvādaśāha), the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra.
(24.15.2) By means of these [verses], Savitṛ indeed attained the impulse of all.
(24.15.3) Those who employ these attain the impulse of all.

(24.15.4) In that the *stomas* are numerous in groups—threefold ones together, fifteen-fold ones together, seventeen-fold ones together, and twenty-one-fold ones together—these are the "peaks" (*kakubhaḥ*) of Savitṛ.
(24.15.5) They become leaders among their equals and among all creatures for those who undertake these [Sāmans].

(24.16.1) An Atirātra, four Abhiplava six-day periods, the Mahāvrata, two Abhiplava six-day periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, and an Atirātra. (24.16.2) The seasons did not find firm standing; they found firm standing by means of these [days]. Those desiring firm standing should undertake them.

They establish themselves right there; for there are six seasons, and it is in the seasons that they establish themselves by means of these [six-day periods]. When they undertake the arranged six-day periods, it is for the sake of arrangement. Now, this is the vow: food indeed is the vow. For food does not nourish anywhere other than in the middle. Since they undertake the vow in the middle, food is thereby placed in the middle; therefore, food in the middle nourishes.
When they perform the two *ṣaḍaha*s in accordance with the *kḷpti* (the established order), it is for the sake of successful accomplishment (*kḷpti*).

Then they perform these ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) with uninterrupted speech for the sake of procreation; then they perform these two *atirātra*s, the opening and the concluding ones, by which very breath they set out, that same they ascend again.

(24.17.1) An Atirātra, six Abhiplava ṣaḍahas, the ten days of the Dvādaśāha, the Mahāvrata, and an Atirātra—(24.17.2) by means of these, indeed, Indra and Agni surpassed all other deities; those who undertake these [sacrifices] surpass all other offspring. (24.17.3) Indra and Agni are indeed the most powerful among the gods; those who undertake these [sacrifices] become the most powerful.

In that they perform the arranged six-day periods, it is for the sake of arrangement; then they perform these ten days of the twelve-day rite with uninterrupted speech for the sake of procreation. Then comes this vow, and then these two *atirātra* rites, the introductory and the concluding. By the very same breath through which they set out, they rise again.
(24.18.1) An Atirātra; the twenty-four-fold Prāyaṇīya day; three six-day periods consisting of Abhiplavas; a Pṛṣṭhya six-day period;
the Abhijit; three Svarasāman days; the Divākīrtya day; three Svarasāman days; the Viśvajit; a Pṛṣṭhya six-day period beginning with the thirty-three-fold stoma;
one six-day period consisting of Abhiplavas; the Āyus and the Go—these two days; and the twelve-day rite.

Ten days of the Mahāvrata and an Atirātra—this constitutes the sixty-one-night sacrifice of the divine Vrātyas. The divine Vrātyas indeed performed a sacrificial session with Budha as their presiding priest. They wished to consecrate themselves for the place of divine sacrifice without having asked King Varuṇa for permission; then King Varuṇa addressed them, saying, "I pass between you."

"You shall not recognize the path leading to the gods from the sacrificial portion," [said the gods]; therefore, they do not take an oblation for them, nor a cup. Now, at that time, there was no milk in plants, no clarified butter in milk, no fat in meat, no hair on the skin, and no leaves on trees. Then the divine Vratyas performed this sixty-one-night sacrifice.
Then indeed those beings offered them up; by these heroic powers they were joined together, and they became truly radiant and full of milk.
Regarding this, this verse is recited:
"What did he do?"—thus he repeatedly asked the gods concerning his sons. Great was the consecration (*dīkṣā*) of Budha; he brought ghee into the milk.

(24.18.6) When Saumayani Budha undertook the great consecration (*dīkṣā*), everything rejoiced, thinking: "He has obtained my marrow; he has placed my fat within me. (24.18.7) The cattle were poor, emaciated, and disjointed; they were joined together by the fat during Saumayani’s consecration. (24.18.8) Therefore, those who undertake this sixty-one-night rite, having settled upon the sacrificial ground (*devayajana*), should offer an oblation on the *gārhapatya* fire with the words: "O God Varuṇa, grant us the sacrificial ground, svāhā!"
When those divine people were given [the sacrifice], they sacrificed (PB 24.18.9). They attained all prosperity; they attain all prosperity who undertake this (PB 24.19.1):
an Atirātra, the Jyotis, the Gauḥ, the Āyus, a three-day period, fourteen Abhiplava six-day periods, the ten days of the twelve-day rite, the Mahāvrata, and an Atirātra.

The gods were indeed afraid of death; they ran to Prajāpati, and he bestowed immortality upon them by means of this Śatarātra sacrifice. This, indeed, is the immortality of a human being: that he reaches his full span of life and becomes more prosperous.
Those who undertake this [sacrifice] reach their full span of life and become more prosperous.
They press [the Soma] while moving forward for the sake of advancement; they press together in one place for the sake of stability.
There is an Atirātra, the twenty-four-fold Prāyaṇīya day, four six-day periods consisting of Abhiplava days, and a Pṛṣṭhya six-day period;
that constitutes a month. That is the second, that the third, that the fourth, and that the fifth month. Then there are three Abhiplava [six-day] periods.

Six-day periods of *pṛṣṭhya* [stomas], the *abhijit*, three *svarasāman* days, the *divākīrtya* day, three *svarasāman* days, the *viśvajit*, a six-day period of *pṛṣṭhya* [stomas] beginning with the thirty-threefold [stoma], three *abhiplava* six-day periods, and a six-day period of *pṛṣṭhya* [stomas] beginning with the thirty-threefold [stoma]—that constitutes one month; that is the second; that is the third.

The third [is the Abhijit], and the fourth [is the Viśvajit]; there are three *abhilava* six-day periods; the *Āyus* and the *Go* are two days; the ten days of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*), the *Mahāvrata*, and the *Atirātra*—this is the Brāhmaṇa concerning the year; this is the Brāhmaṇa.

(25.1.1) An Atirātra; the twenty-four-fold Prāyaṇīya day; two six-day periods consisting of Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa stomas; a Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha; two six-day periods consisting of Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa stomas—that is one month. That is the second, that the third, that the fourth, and that the fifth. Three six-day periods consisting of Trivṛt and Pañcadaśa stomas; a Pṛṣṭhya ṣaḍaha; a Trivṛt Bṛhaspatistoma.
Three Svarasāman days; the Divākīrtya day; three Svarasāman days; the Pañcadaśa Indra-stoma Ukthya;
the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha beginning with the Trayastriṃśa; one Pañcadaśa; a Trivṛt Ṣaḍaha;
the ten days of the Dvādaśāha arranged in expanded form (vyūḍha) as Agniṣṭomas consisting of Trivṛt stomas; two days, the Udbhid and the Balabhid; and two [days] consisting of Pañcadaśa and Trivṛt.

Two six-day periods consisting of the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite; two six-day periods consisting of the fifteen-fold and the nine-fold stomas—this constitutes one month. This is the second, this the third, and this the fourth month. Then there is a six-day period consisting of the fifteen-fold and the nine-fold stomas, followed by the *pṛṣṭhya* six-day rite, another six-day period consisting of the fifteen-fold and the nine-fold stomas, the *go* and *āyus* days (two days), and the *chandoma* ten-day period. The first day has forty-eight verses, and then the next has forty-four verses.
The forty-day, thirty-six-day, thirty-two-day, and thirty-day [sattras], two twenty-eight-day [sattras], the twenty-five-day, the twenty-four-day, the Mahāvrata, and the Atirātra;
the Pṛṣṭhya [Saṃsthā] is in the midst of the Ādityas.
By means of the Pṛṣṭhya in the midst, the Ādityas ascended to the heavenly world; in that they employ the Pṛṣṭhas in the midst, it is for the sake of ascending to the heavenly world.
The *pṛṣṭha* chants are indeed food; thus food itself is placed in the middle. Therefore, being in the middle, food satisfies. The *pṛṣṭha* chants are cattle; they find firm support in cattle.

These two, the *trivṛt* and the *pañcadaśa*, are the wheels of the *sākaṃvṛti*. Whatever desire they may desire, they attain it by means of this. For wherever one desires with that which has wheels, there [one attains it].

"He attains that" (PB 25.1.7). Now, this Trivṛt Bṛhaspati-stoma: by means of this, indeed, Bṛhaspati attained the office of domestic priest among the gods. Those who desire the office of domestic priest should approach it; they attain the office of domestic priest, and he places them at the head. (PB 25.1.8) Now, these are the Svarasāmans. The Divākīrtya is indeed the head, and the Svarasāmans are the vital breaths. In that the Svarasāmans are on both sides of the Divākīrtya, the vital breaths are thus placed for the sake of well-being.

(PB 25.1.9) Now, this is the fifteen-fold *indrastoma* *ukthya*. By means of this, indeed, Indra surpassed all other deities; those who perform this surpass all other creatures. (PB 25.1.10) Now, these ten days of the twelve-day rite are arranged as *agniṣṭomas* with the threefold (*trivṛt*) stoma in the middle;
they are released from evil. This is truly the couch of the gods; they thus ascend the couch of the gods, they become worthy of the couch, and they attain a more excellent couch.

(25.1.11) Now, these two [sacrifices], Udbhid and Balabhid: by means of these two, Bṛhaspati indeed released cattle for the gods; verily, by means of these two, they release cattle. (25.1.12) Then they perform these two, Go and Āyus, which are a pair of *stomas*, for the sake of procreation.
